Title: European Commission HR hit by cyber attack
Context: ” ARTEX has been known to SOC operations since GitHub first released the tool in July, but widespread misuse of the tool prompted GitHub to make it unavailable on October 8
Full Text:
Barely a week after the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) warned companies of the cyber attacker interest in an open source penetration testing tool called ARTEX, the European Commission has confirmed that attackers armed with that tool broke into its HR systems.

The attack, which Commission officials detected on October 22, forced them to shut off much of the access to the systems for more than 10 days.

“As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several applications and most of them have since then been restored,” Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said Thursday. “We have not detected any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole.”

During a news media briefing, a transcript of which was provided to CSOonline, he said that the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) was informed of the attack, “so there was no hiding whatsoever.”

Regnier would not go into detail about the attacks, given that the matter is still being investigated, but he did say, “it is a campaign, so there was a series of incidents.”

In an email, Commission officials added, “we are also preventively checking other systems while staying in close contact with CERT-EU and the EDPS.”

ARTEX popular with attackers

The November 13 FBI statement about ARTEX, described as an autonomous penetration testing framework, said that the tool is becoming very popular with attackers.

“Since at least August 2026, a variety of malicious cyber actors have used ARTEX to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally across multiple sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal industries,” the FBI advisory said. “ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques, with some intrusions progressing from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. The framework enables threat actors with minimal technical expertise to conduct complex, multi-target operations simultaneously, fundamentally accelerating attack velocity and expanding operational scale.”

Although ARTEX can handle a wide range of pentesting functions, it appeared to be primarily used in the Commission attack to search for and locate credentials.

The FBI said that ARTEX can “automatically map effective permissions of Azure credentials–SAS tokens, Service Principals, Kudu credentials, Storage Account keys–using sub-second capability checks.”

ARTEX has been known to SOC operations since GitHub first released the tool in July, but widespread misuse of the tool prompted GitHub to make it unavailable on October 8. “Despite this action, ARTEX remains widely accessible through independent routes and mirrors on code-sharing platforms,” the FBI said.

Uses different tactics

Brian Levine, a partner with consulting firm Control Risks, added that ARTEX’s AI-fueled tactics are different from what many cybersecurity teams are used to.

“ARTEX doesn’t need to steal your keys. It finds the ones you left lying around, like a SAS token in a code repo, a storage key in a config file, or a Kudu credential nobody rotated. Then it tries each one against every door in under a second,” he said. “Picture a burglar walking the block at 3 a.m. and checking every car door handle. He isn’t breaking glass. He’s taking inventory of what you left unlocked and AI lets him work a thousand blocks at once.”

Companies need a secure fallback

Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, said he was unimpressed with the Commission’s attempts to tell EU citizens that all was well.

“The Commission says it has no evidence of a breach affecting its staff ‘as a whole,’ which is very different from saying that there is no evidence of a breach affecting any of the staff,” Kenney said. “The wording doesn’t give me much comfort.”

Kenney also said that the attackers’ decision to target HR was not an accident, and that the Commission’s decision to temporarily shut down some systems may have inadvertently helped the intruders.

“When payroll, leave, and medical reimbursement systems go down, people start using spreadsheets, email and manual approvals. Those workarounds often have weaker access controls and worse audit trails than the systems taken offline,” he said. “Enterprises need to define a secure fallback process before the attack, because improvising one often leads to greater exposure.”

HR systems a prize

Levine also said that the choice of an HR victim was understandable.

“HR systems are a prize. Names, home addresses, pay grades and health insurance records for EU civil servants make a ready-made targeting list for espionage and social engineering,” he said. “Whether or not data left the building, every Commission employee should prepare to receive a very convincing phishing email soon.”

His advice to CISOs: “Get secrets out of code and pipelines and rotate anything that has been exposed. Give every token and service principal only the access it needs, so a found key opens a closet, not the vault. Put cloud admin interfaces behind private access.”

Title: Flaws in VMware and KVM need attention, if you have time while fixing Java, PHP, and everything else
Context: If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by...
Full Text: If you’ve got a moment to spare in between sorting out emergency patches for PHP, Java, and PostgreSQL, VMware has just bid for any remaining space on your schedule by publishing two critical-rated security advisories. VMSA-2026-0009 addresses CVE-2026-123890, a 9.8-rated flaw that VMware says means a malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. vCenter is the tool admins use to manage fleets of virtual machines. The flaw is present in VMware’s flagship Cloud Foundation suite. VMSA-2026-0009 also details four more CVEs, some of them high-severity. VMware’s second advisory, VMSA-2026-0010, warns that Cloud Foundation, Aria Operations, and VCF Operations HCX products all use Apache – which has a 9.8-rated remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-119618). A KVM curiosity Admins who oversee virtual infrastructure also need to pay attention to Linux KVM, the subject of a curious incident over the last 24 hours. This mess started with the November 18 disclosure of CVE-2026-99312, a bug which allows an attacker to use a guest virtual machine to inflict Denial of Service (DoS) or memory corruption attacks on the host. It’s bad news whenever someone with access to a guest VM can attack the host, because it means gaining access to a single tenant can potentially harm all the other guest VMs or peer into the memory a guest uses. This flaw, however, isn’t a worst-case scenario guest-host escape, because it only impacts users of AMD processors who employ nested virtualization – the practice of running a hypervisor inside a virtual machine. Nested virtualization isn’t commonly used in the enterprise, but clouds employ it to do things like powering OS emulators. The bug’s CVSSv3 score is therefore a modest 5.5. Security researcher Oren Tomtov of Accomplish.ai says the flaw meant he could access 127 GB of host RAM on a Digital Ocean “Droplet” – the junior cloud’s name for its cloudy VMs. Yomtov says he told Digital Ocean and the Linux kernel security team about the flaw in October. Maintainers got busy and delivered a fix to the mainline kernel on November 2, full fixes landed on the 17th. The CVE then appeared on November 18. Yomtov and Terra Security quickly posted their analysis of the flaw – but then took the posts down within hours. The Register understands that Digital Ocean asked for the posts to come down because it needed more time to update its Linux implementations. The company has not responded to multiple requests for comment. Terra’s analysis of the flaw asserts that it was introduced to KVM in 2022, when developers wrote a fix for CVE-2022-3344. The company believes 3.2 percent of CVEs in the Linux kernel were introduced by the fix for another CVE. The good news about CVE-2026-99312 is it’s easy to defeat without an update, by disabling nested virtualization in KVM. ®

Title: VMware patches vCenter zero-day exploited in attacks since September
Context: Broadcom has released security updates to fix a critical VMware vCenter Server authentication bypass vulnerability that Chinese-linked hackers have exploited in zero-day attacks...
Full Text:
Broadcom has released security updates to fix a critical VMware vCenter Server authentication bypass vulnerability that Chinese-linked hackers have exploited in zero-day attacks since September 2026.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-123890, affects the VMware Directory Service in vCenter Server, a management platform organizations use to manage VMware virtualized environments.

According Broadcom, the flaw allows an unauthenticated attacker with network access to a vulnerable vCenter Server to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access.

Successful exploitation can allow attackers to obtain administrative access to vCenter, giving them control over the virtual machines managed by the server.

Broadcom patched the vulnerability on November 19 in VMSA-2026-0009, which also fixes four other vulnerabilities affecting VMware SDDC Manager and VMware Tools for Windows.

"You are affected if you are running any version of VMware vCenter, SDDC Manager, or VMware Tools for Windows prior to the versions listed as "fixed" in the VMSA," Broadcom's security advisory reads.

"This includes vCenter and SDDC Manager deployed standalone and as part of VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation, VMware Telco Cloud Platform, and VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure, as well as VMware Tools installed in Windows virtual machines."

The company considers the vCenter vulnerability as an emergency update, urging organizations to install the patches as soon as possible.

Broadcom says there are no official workarounds for the vulnerabilities, although network restrictions and firewall controls can help reduce exposure.

Furthermore, the vulnerability affects vCenter regardless of whether Enhanced Linked Mode is enabled.

While Broadcom has not confirmed that the flaw was exploited, researchers at Google's Mandiant have documented attacks exploiting CVE-2026-123890.

Chinese hackers exploited VMware zero-day

In a report published today, Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) revealed that a suspected Chinese state-sponsored hacking group tracked as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) exploited CVE-2026-123890 in early September 2026.

"Successful exploitation results in a remote authentication bypass which creates an authenticated session established as administrator@vsphere.local," explains Mandiant.

"Using the authenticated administrator session, the attacker can execute arbitrary commands and acquire files, including the data.mdb database, by leveraging the vCenter Server Directory Service (vmdird) RPC interface vmdirdbcp."

Armory Castle is a cyberespionage group known for exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities in enterprise network appliances, including Citrix NetScaler and Ivanti Connect Secure devices, to breach corporate networks and deploy custom malware.

The group was also recently linked to attacks exploiting a BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day, tracked as CVE-2026-102764, which has been exploited since late August.

Mandiant says the VMware exploitation was part of the same intrusion campaign, with the attackers first compromising BeyondTrust Remote Support appliances before moving laterally into internal Linux systems and targeting VMware infrastructure.

After gaining access to an internal Linux appliance, the hackers deployed the "SLIMSAVAGE" web shells to maintain persistent access, escalated privileges to root, and scanned the internal network for VMware systems.

The attackers then used a custom Golang exploitation tool named BONESAW to exploit CVE-2026-123890 and compromise a VMware vCenter Server.

Mandiant observed the tool successfully creating a vCenter Single Sign-On (SSO) administrator account and stealing the server's directory database, which can be used to extract further credentials.

BONESAW can also extract SAML signing keys, allowing attackers to forge authentication tokens and gain administrative access to VMware environments.

Following the exploitation, the hackers deployed another tool called SAWSNAKE, which enables so-called Golden SAML attacks to forge authentication tokens, bypass multifactor authentication, and impersonate legitimate users.

During the attack, the attackers also deployed additional web shells and backdoors, including CAGEMATCH, BEARBONES, and LAZYBONES, to execute commands, transfer files, steal credentials, and maintain access to compromised systems.

The attacks ultimately allowed Armory Castle to move deeper into the victims' virtualized environments, access ESXi hosts, and extract sensitive information from virtual machines, including Windows Active Directory database files.

Mandiant says the use of two zero-day vulnerabilities in the same campaign, along with multiple malware families tailored to the targeted platforms, demonstrates the threat actor's technical expertise.

The researchers urge admins to apply the VMware security updates as soon as possible and configure additional security controls to protect their virtualization infrastructure against future attacks.

Title: Germ Network infects Android, but in a good way
Context: "Our usage took a 20x jump yesterday from our Android launch," co-founder Tessa Brown, a communications scholar and former Stanford lecturer, told The Register in an interview
Full Text: The Germ Network encrypted messaging client, known as Germ DM, became available for Android on Wednesday, and made a bigger splash than its iOS touchdown back in 2023. "Our usage took a 20x jump yesterday from our Android launch," co-founder Tessa Brown, a communications scholar and former Stanford lecturer, told The Register in an interview. "Android has been really exciting for us because not only is it 70 percent of the global mobile market, but we rolled out on iOS first. People were so excited to use Germ for their end-to-end encrypted Bluesky DMs, but half of their friends couldn't talk to them." Building a new messaging platform isn't easy, much less one with credible end-to-end encryption. Co-founder Mark Xue hails from Apple, where he worked as a privacy engineer on systems like iMessage and FaceTime. "At the core level, the end-to-end encryption is built on a standardized encryption and Messaging Layer Security," Xue said. "The premise of Messaging Layer Security was to be as good as Signal and deployable by many, many different parties in different applications, which we're taking advantage of to extend the reach of that encryption." Xue said the app is built with its own transport protocol to minimize the amount of message metadata, adding that while the team hasn't gotten around to a formal security audit, it's a step they're considering. Germ Network's goal, said Brown, is to give people more confidence when they communicate. "We do that by giving you more tools to protect your identity, to control what you're sharing with whom," she explained. Instead of using a person's phone number as an identity key, Germ allows users to create cards which represent distinct identities on the network. "Instead of sharing your number, you share a card," Brown explained. "You can build multiple cards; they're not mutually discoverable. And our vision for the product that will continue shipping over the coming years is that these cards become a more intelligent way to manage your social life, even your work life." At some point, AI might play a role in that, but both Xue and Brown expressed reservations about the current state of play. Citing concerns Signal has raised about the integration of AI and messaging, Xue said, "The products today that I might characterize as technology demos, they're most powerful when they run on someone else's computer. So you end up with these systems where you upload all your messages or you give another entity the power to observe your computing, and that's extremely dangerous for what we protect as private content." Xue noted rapid progress toward addressing information exposure concerns and therefore plans to explore the kinds of smart tooling that users want while also meeting security and privacy requirements. "I think a lot of the AI conversation sometimes is a hammer in search of a nail," said Brown. "But people do want more tools to make sense of their busy lives and following our consumers, our users, and what they want, we do want to give them smart tooling that will help them organize threads, stay in touch, find the right people to talk to in groups, in a private way that's using a lot of the intelligence that's already on their device." If Germ DM were simply trying to win people away from widely adopted services like Instagram or respected encryption apps like Signal, it would be difficult to see a path to success. But Germ DM may be able to reach a point of sustainability by standing on the shoulders of Bluesky. Bluesky launched Direct Messages in 2024 but chose to focus its development resources elsewhere and left E2E DMs to Germ Network. Germ DM, which supports Bluesky's AT Protocol (ATproto), fills that gap and even has Bluesky promoting the app for that purpose. "On a business strategic level, it's been a really wonderful move for us," said Brown. "So we're natively a multi-identity messenger. And you can say that ATproto is the first external identity that we brought into the app, after we first shipped local identities that you just build in our app. "And so the way that we're marketing and growing right now is [by offering] end-to-end encrypted messages for Bluesky users. You log in with your handle into our app. We pull your friend graph so you can see your mutuals that already have Germ in the app." Bluesky assists further with marketing by allowing Germ DM users to add a Germ messaging button to their Bluesky profiles. So anyone interested in encrypted DMs in Bluesky may end up seeing that option. At some point, expect paid, premium features but at the moment, Germ Network is focused on spreading the encrypted word. ®

Title: Android developer verification will reach every install source, with a side door for power users
Context: Four countries went first The protections went live Sept
Full Text:
Google will extend Android developer verification to every country starting in January 2027, a check that already applies at participating app stores in four countries. Developers who have not verified their identity with Google and registered their apps will see those apps lose the normal install experience on certified Android devices.

The rollout opens with seven app distributors: Google Play, Galaxy Store, Honor, Oppo, Xiaomi, Transsion and Vivo. Over several months it widens to every installation source, which brings sideloaded apps and open-source registries under the same rule as the big stores. Developers who ship outside Google Play, and the people who install their apps, have the most to sort out.

Four countries went first

The protections went live Sept. 30 for participating stores in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand. Google and its partners had prepared for more than a year, working with distributors and Android communities, said Matthew Forsythe, Google’s director of product management for Android app safety. Verification opened to all developers in March. Millions of apps have been registered since then, and Google says they make up over 99% of Android installs worldwide.

The unregistered remainder accounts for under 1% of installs. That is a small number unless the app is yours.

The tools on offer

Google says registering an app takes less than ten minutes. Students and hobbyists can use limited distribution accounts, launched in August, which skip registration fees and government ID checks. Google raised their sharing cap from 20 to 50 authorized devices.

Teams with many apps can automate the work inside continuous integration pipelines, the systems that build and ship code automatically. Google offers two APIs for this: the Android Developer ID Status API and the Android Developer Console API. Play developers have one more item to check. Any app they also distribute outside Play needs to be registered too.

If you maintain an app on an open-source registry, Google has published a separate guide for registering existing and new apps there.

A side door for power users

“We built an advanced flow that allows experienced users to install unregistered apps when they choose to accept the risk, while keeping critical guardrails in place against social engineering scams for everyday users,” Forsythe said.

Title: Hackers steal data of 1.6 million SBC Medical Group customers
Context: The first compromise concerns the SBC databases, while the second involves unauthorized access to clinic administrator accounts on Tribeau, a third-party booking platform
Full Text:
SBC Medical Group has warned in a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) that two cybersecurity incidents exposed sensitive customer and employee information, including personal data belonging to 1.6 million people.

SBC Medical Group is a clinic management company whose main business is in Japan, but it also has a limited presence in the U.S., is traded on Nasdaq as SBC, and holds a minority stake in the medical spa chain OrangeTwist. Its clinics receive 7 million patient visits annually.

The first compromise concerns the SBC databases, while the second involves unauthorized access to clinic administrator accounts on Tribeau, a third-party booking platform.

The company discovered the database breach on November 16 and was notified of the Tribeau compromise the same day. Both incidents affected its Japan-based businesses.

"On November 16, 2026, unauthorized access occurred to certain databases within a website system managed and operated by SBC Medical Group, Ltd., the Company’s, Japanese subsidiary, in connection with its management services in Japan," reads a FORM 8-K filing with the SEC.

"The Company confirmed that an unauthorized third party accessed and extracted customer information. The method of intrusion and full scope remain under investigation."

The incident impacting SBC databases exposed basic personal information belonging to 1,624,000 people, including:

Full names

Contact details

Dates of birth

Patient card numbers

Member IDs

Passwords

Survey responses

Not all of the above data types were exposed for all 1.6 million people.

Additionally, the incident exposed 255,416 reservation requests, 217,769 inquiries submitted to SBC websites, and thousands of treatment description records, image filenames, and customer reviews.

The company said the attackers also stole approximately 20,000 employee account records, including names, IDs, and passwords. For a small subset of 459 employees, the affected data also included bank account and tax information.

The second incident involved administrator accounts on the Tribeau booking platform, a service used by 56 clinics.

The operator reported access to reservation information for 12,641 people, as well as access to treatment names, dates, and fees for 6,804 people who received treatment.

SBC noted that it has not confirmed unauthorized access to electronic medical records or information from its mySBC reservation site in the database breach.

As of November 18, when the Form 8-K was submitted, the company has not seen any evidence of misuse of the exposed data.

SBC said the investigation remains ongoing, and at this time, it could not estimate the financial impact of these cybersecurity incidents.

Title: Chaotic Eclipse Releases FastUnlock, a New Windows Zero-Day Vulnerability
Context: The researcher Chaotic Eclipse released FastUnlock, a new Windows zero-day vulnerability exploiting Narrator to bypass the lock screen
Full Text:
The researcher Chaotic Eclipse released FastUnlock, a new Windows zero-day vulnerability exploiting Narrator to bypass the lock screen.

Security researcher Chaotic Eclipse, also known as INFINITE NIGHTMARE, MSNightmare and Nightmare-Eclipse, released a new Windows zero-day vulnerability, dubbed FastUnlock, exploiting Narrator to bypass the lock screen.

According to the researcher, exploiting it can bypass BitLocker encryption and allow code execution under the lock screen’s WsiAccount. He claims he breached a fully encrypted Windows 11 26H2 system in just five minutes, even with the November security updates installed.

“It took a total of 5 minutes from finding this to breaching a fully encrypted bitlocker machine with Windows 11 26H2 November Patch installed, an issue caused by total negligence from Microsoft’s side… The vulnerability seems to be extremely consistent in every machine I tested it in, in other words, if you know how to control narrator in the background properly or just press the correct combination of buttons, you will get code execution in the target machine as well.” reads the advisory published by the researcher.

The attack requires physical access to the computer and at least one user account linked to an online account. The researcher says the flaw undermines BitLocker’s protection, which should prevent access to encrypted data even if an attacker has physical access to the device.

He explains that Microsoft introduced the issue while redesigning Narrator, failing to prevent its new interface from running in the lock screen account context. Unlike earlier lock screen bypass flaws, this one is reportedly easier to exploit. The attack can be triggered through the “I forgot my PIN” or password option.

The researcher explains that the attack starts from the Microsoft account recovery screen. Enabling Narrator causes it to focus on a hidden background window. By navigating its options with the keyboard, an attacker can open Narrator’s settings. From there, the researcher says several paths can lead to code execution under the WsiAccount user, including opening File Explorer through the Bluetooth and Devices and AutoPlay settings.

“Now I didn’t show the full code execution demo because I don’t really have a USB stick but I already did this enough times to know what happens next, your next step is to plugin a USB stick, as soon as you do, narrator will focus on explorer showing your mounted storage content and you can just navigate with the same button combination (CAPS LOCK + Arrow keys/Enter/Space), if you do everything properly the binary in your USB stick will be executed in the context of “WsiAccount”” concludes the report. “I have not checked other windows versions so I am not really sure if this might work on windows 10.”

Chaotic Eclipse is a researcher known for publicly releasing PoC exploits for zero-day vulnerabilities, often after criticizing vendors’ handling of vulnerability reports. His releases have mainly targeted Microsoft products, including Windows and Microsoft Defender, with some later exploited in the wild. Among the most notable are the Undefend and RedSun Defender zero-days.

His work has fueled debate over responsible disclosure and the risks of publishing working exploits.

Recently, Chaotic Eclipse revealed that he is Abdelhamid Naceri, a security researcher. Naceri previously worked with Microsoft in the UK and Germany. In a now-deleted X post, he described his departure from the company, claiming Microsoft terminated his employment without giving him a clear reason. He said Microsoft offered several financial settlements, but he rejected them because he wanted a formal explanation and help staying in Germany.

Naceri also said he challenged the dismissal in a German labor court. According to his account, Microsoft changed its arguments during the case, but the court ultimately upheld the termination. He said the long legal dispute left him with almost no compensation and caused serious financial and emotional problems, including treatment in a psychiatric hospital.

The researcher also admitted that an earlier claim that Microsoft had taken legal action against him was fabricated. The claim came during the controversy over Microsoft’s threats of legal action against security researchers who disclosed zero-day vulnerabilities.

In September, the researcher released a new zero-day exploit targeting Microsoft Defender. He named the exploit BigDiskBuster, it triggers a Denial of Service Vulnerability in Windows Defender Update.

In the same month, Chaotic Eclipse released multiple zero-day exploits targeting Nvidia (GreenSection) and Microsoft Defender (ShieldCrash).

He also released exploits targeting other anti-malware and defense solutions. Chaotic Eclipse released a zero-day exploit targeting Kaspersky Endpoint Security, which he named HardBreacher, that triggers a privilege escalation flaw. The researcher pointed out that the PoC is unstable and may require repeated attempts, but when successful, it creates a DLL in System32 with full user permissions. The researcher also claims that taking control of Kaspersky’s UI process can disrupt the antivirus and interfere with file-access controls, potentially leaving the system in an unstable state.

The researcher also released a zero-day exploit targeting GenDigital Avast Antivirus, named PrettyPrague. The exploit triggers a privilege escalation flaw.

Finally, Chaotic Eclipse released a new zero-day exploit targeting Crowdstrike Falcon cybersecurity platform. The researcher named the exploit FalconFlank, it triggers a privilege escalation flaw.

Title: ASUS warns of critical hard-coded key flaw in Control Center Express
Context: 29 to fix three critical vulnerabilities that could let remote attackers gain administrative control of the management console and the devices it manages
Full Text:
ASUS released Control Center Express v1.7.29 to fix three critical vulnerabilities that could let remote attackers gain administrative control of the management console and the devices it manages.

Of the three, one is a maximum-severity vulnerability (CVSS score: 10.0) tracked under CVE-2026-114202, arising from a hard-coded cryptographic key used in the product.

The flaw lets an unauthenticated remote attacker forge an authentication token and gain administrator privileges, without requiring any privileges or user interaction.

The second flaw is CVE-2026-114204, also a hard-coded key problem, which lets a remote attacker with low privileges forge a session token for a recently logged-in account.

The third is CVE-2026-114205, an authorization flaw that lets a low-privileged user create an administrator account.

ASUS Control Center Express is a central dashboard that IT administrators use to monitor and remotely manage fleets of PCs.

ASUS markets it to businesses and IT service providers and lists support for more than 200 of its business, workstation, and Corporate Stable Model motherboards.

While all three vulnerabilities are rated critical, CVE-2026-114204 has a recent-session prerequisite, and CVE-2026-114205 requires a low-privileged account, whereas CVE-2026-114202 enables remote administrative access with no prerequisites.

ASUS’s security bulletin says versions earlier than v1.7.29 are affected. However, the CVE records only list affected versions through v1.7.27, leaving the status of v1.7.28 unclear.

Impacted users are advised to install v1.7.29, then update the agents on managed devices through Select Function → Client Agent Updater, and verify their versions.

Also yesterday, ASUS released security updates for Control Center Enterprise, its centralized IT management platform, and Armoury Crate, a hardware configuration utility.

Specifically, ASUS patched CVE-2026-126574, a critical authorization flaw that lets a remote user with the low-privileged Viewer role change an administrator’s password and take over the account.

The flaw affects Control Center Datacenter 4.0.0.2 and earlier and Control Center Enterprise 3.1.0.8 and earlier.

The Armoury Crate update addressed CVE-2026-112115, a high-severity privilege escalation flaw.

The flaw affects all versions up to and including 6.7.2 and could allow a low-privileged local user to trick an elevated process into loading a malicious library.

Full Text: JPMorgan Chase, Visa, and Mastercard have all confirmed that they are investigating third-party breaches that may involve customer information after a data-theft-and-extortion gang claimed to have compromised the financial giants. “Visa is aware of these claims,” a spokesperson told The Register on Thursday. “They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific. At this time, the exposure has been contained and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed.” JPMorgan Chase did not respond to The Register’s request for comment, but confirmed it was investigating a cyberattack on social media. “We have learned that third parties who provide services to the firm were the target of a cyber attack,” America’s largest bank posted on X. “Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses.” According to Chase, the third-party breach didn’t disrupt any of its services, and it’s not connected to the outages earlier in the week attributed to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems. “There is no connection to service disruption some customers experienced earlier this week,” the bank said on Thursday. Title: Introducing the new AWS WAF security analytics dashboard
Context: You can also see which detections and labels matched and whether each action was enforced or only counted
Full Text:
When blocked requests spike or a customer reports being locked out, a security team has to work out what is happening, where it is happening, and if AWS WAF is making the right call. Currently, that usually means opening each protection pack (web ACL) in turn, across domains, AWS Regions, and Amazon CloudFront distributions, or querying AWS WAF logs. In 2024, we introduced the AWS WAF traffic overview dashboard, which gives you a near real-time view of each protection pack (web ACL). Today, we’re introducing the AWS WAF security analytics dashboard: a single global page that you can use to investigate traffic across all of your protection packs (web ACLs), Regional resources, Amazon CloudFront distributions and then act on what you find. The dashboard can help you investigate and contain threats faster and reduce false positives that block real customers. You don’t need to build or maintain your own log analytics pipeline to do it.

In this post, we introduce the new dashboard and walk you through two use cases: investigating a traffic spike, and tuning your rules to reduce false positives.

Introduction to the security analytics dashboard

To open the dashboard, go to the AWS WAF console and choose Security analytics in the navigation pane. The dashboard shows request data across all protection packs (web ACLs) in your account. You can narrow it to specific protection packs (web ACLs) and set the time range. As shown in the following figure, at the top of the page, you can see total requests split by action (Allow, Block, CAPTCHA, and Challenge). The Requests chart shows how the traffic changes over time. Below that, traffic breakdown widgets show the top values for each dimension. The dashboard is built on full-fidelity request data, not samples.

Figure 1: The security analytics dashboard across all protection packs

Dimensions

You can filter, group, and break down traffic by dimensions that include, but aren’t limited to, the following:

Who’s sending traffic – Client IP, country, Autonomous System Number (ASN), user-agent, and JA4 TLS fingerprints

What they’re requesting – Host, path (URI), protected resource (Amazon CloudFront distribution, AWS Application Load Balancers, and others), Region, or protection pack (web ACL)

How AWS WAF responded – Action, rule triggered, labels, or response code

We’ll continue to add dimensions to the security analytics dashboard over time. The rest of this post refers to the preceding dimensions by the names used here. Two dimensions deserve a closer look:

Host – Many customers think about their applications by domain rather than by protection pack (web ACL). Grouping or filtering by Host will show you which of your domains are under attack or if a spike is hitting www, the API, or a staging site, even when one protection pack (web ACL) protects several domains or one domain spans several protection packs (web ACLs).

Labels – Labels are metadata that AWS WAF rules add to the requests they inspect. AWS Managed Rules for AWS WAF add them (for example, Bot Control labels for bot category, verification status, and signals such as non_browser_user_agent), and you can create rules to add custom labels. Because labels are recorded even when a rule only counts, filtering by a label shows you what a rule detected across all of your protection packs (web ACLs), without changing how your traffic is handled.

Controls

The dashboard is built around a few controls:

Filter requests – Combine conditions on any dimension, using Equals or Does not equal. Filters apply to the whole dashboard: the action split, the Requests chart, every widget, and the request list update to match. Your dashboard view is saved in your browser.

Group by – Split the Requests chart by any dimension, such as Host, Rule triggered, Country, or JA4, to see how traffic changes over time.

Show only, Exclude, and Block – Select any value in any widget to focus on it, remove it from view, or block it. For example, you can block a high-risk or unexpected IP address, or block traffic from a country, directly from the dashboard.

Requests and detections – Review the individual requests behind the charts. For each request, see HTTP request fields such as host, path, headers, user agent, and JA4 fingerprint. You can also see which detections and labels matched and whether each action was enforced or only counted . Previously, this level of detail meant working from a limited sample of requests or setting up and querying your own AWS WAF logs. Now it’s available directly on the dashboard.

Together, these controls help you answer questions such as:

What share of traffic across all your protection packs (web ACLs) and domains is being blocked, challenged, or allowed, and how is it changing?

Which rules are doing the most work, and are any of them blocking legitimate users?

Which IP addresses, ASNs, JA4 fingerprints, or countries are behind a spike, and what are they targeting?

How much of your traffic comes from bots, and are the bots verified?

Use case 1: Investigate a traffic spike

Suppose you receive an alert that blocked requests have increased. To investigate:

Go to the Security analytics page in the AWS WAF console and select All protection packs.

Assess the scope: The action split shows the overall block rate. Group the Requests chart by Host to see which domains are affected and check the Protection pack widget to see whether one application or several are involved. A campaign hitting your storefront, API, and media domains at the same time calls for a different response than a problem on a single endpoint.

Identify the source: Group the Requests chart by Rule triggered to see which rules are mitigating the traffic and when they started firing. Then check the source and request dimensions. If one IP address sends a disproportionate share of requests, or many IP addresses share one JA4 fingerprint, the traffic likely originates from a single automated actor.

Figure 2: Requests grouped by Rule triggered, showing which rules fired and when

Confirm with request-level evidence: When you find an unexpected value, select it and choose Show only to filter the entire dashboard to it.

Then confirm what you’re seeing in Requests and detections. Expanding a request shows all its details, including the HTTP request fields. For example, a curl user agent with no Accept-Language header, coming from a cloud hosting ASN, is likely automated traffic.

Figure 3: Show only, exclude, or block it

After you confirm the source, choose a response that fits the traffic:

One clear source: Choose Block this IP address directly from the dashboard. Use a geographic block only if you don’t expect legitimate customers from that country.

Traffic spread across multiple IP addresses: Add a rate-based rule with a custom aggregation key such as JA4, or use AWS WAF Bot Control.

Known bad actors and application-layer floods: Add the Amazon IP reputation list and the Anti-DDoS managed rule group.

Faster detection time: Create Amazon CloudWatch alarms on AWS WAF metrics. For details, see Monitoring with Amazon CloudWatch.

When the change is in place, return to the dashboard to confirm that requests from that source now show the Block action.

Use case 2: Tune your rules and reduce false positives

Rules can fail in two ways: by blocking legitimate users, or by only counting traffic that they should stop. Filters and labels help you find both.

If you suspect that a rule is blocking a broad population, such as many distinct clients sending only a few requests each, enter Rule triggered = <rule name> in Filter requests. The dashboard shows only the requests that the rule acted on. Review the Country, Host, and Path (URI) breakdowns to understand who the blocked clients are and what they requested. If the blocked clients look like your typical customers, with common browsers, expected countries, and checkout or login paths, consider adding a scope-down statement to the rule or changing the action to Challenge.

Figure 4: The dashboard filtered to a single rule with Filter requests

Evaluate rules before you enforce them: When you evaluate a managed rule group in Count mode, filter by its labels to see exactly which requests each rule matched. For example, filter by a Bot Control label such as awswaf:managed:aws:bot-control:bot:unverified, then check Host, Path (URI), and User-Agent to see what those bots are after. Use Exclude on labels for known-good traffic, such as bot:verified search engine crawlers, to keep them out of your review.

On the Detections tab of Requests and detections, rows marked Counted, not enforced show what a rule would block. If the matches aren’t partners or monitoring tools, consider changing the rule action to Block.

Figure 5: Record details for a single request, including host, JA4 fingerprint, and protection pack

After you change a rule, compare the same time window on the dashboard to confirm that the rule now affects only the traffic you intended.

Conclusion

The traffic overview dashboard shows you what changed in each protection pack (web ACL). The security analytics dashboard helps you understand why it changed, and lets you act on it from the same page, across all of your protection packs (web ACLs), domains, Regions, and Amazon CloudFront distributions. Filters, grouping, and labels explain the traffic, and request-level evidence helps you act with more confidence. Together, they can help you investigate faster, reduce how often real users are blocked by mistake, and confirm that each rule changes affect the traffic you intend.

The security analytics dashboard is available at no extra cost in all AWS Regions where AWS WAF is offered, and shows up to 21 days of request data. To get started, open the AWS WAF console and choose Security analytics.

Title: Critical flaw in VMware vCenter allows authentication bypass
Context: Broadcom has released patches for bugs in multiple products, one of which, fixing a VMware vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability, is rated 9
Full Text:
Broadcom has released patches for bugs in multiple products, one of which, fixing a VMware vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability, is rated 9.8 out of 10 in severity.

The company’s advisory describes the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-123890, as “an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service,” that could let a threat actor with network access gain unauthorized access to the system, and says there are no workarounds. It advises immediate patching.

Broadcom has provided fixed vCenter versions 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 U3m; customers running v7.0 will only get a patch if they have an extended support contract. The patched version of VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x is 5.2.5.

Customers using the VMware Telco Cloud Platform and Infrastructure, also affected, should consult KB463116 for remediation instructions.

The remaining four issues are: SDDC Manager SQL-injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-123891), rated 8.1 (Important) in severity; SDDC Manager authenticated command-injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-123892), rated 7.2 (Important); SDDC Manager local privilege-escalation vulnerability (CVE-2026-123893), rated 6.7 (Moderate), and VMware Tools SAML Token Signature Bypass vulnerability (CVE-2026-123894), also rated 6.7. There are no workarounds for any of them.

Broadcom has released a supplementary FAQ providing addition information on all five bugs, in which it said, “You are affected if you are running any version of VMware vCenter, SDDC Manager, or VMware Tools for Windows prior to the versions listed as “fixed” in the [advisory]. This includes vCenter and SDDC Manager deployed standalone and as part of VMware Cloud Foundation, VMware vSphere Foundation, VMware Telco Cloud Platform, and VMware Telco Cloud Infrastructure, as well as VMware Tools installed in Windows virtual machines.”

Title: Newly Patched VMware vCenter Flaw Exploited as Zero-Day by Chinese APT
Context: A China-linked espionage group exploited a VMware vCenter zero-day vulnerability for more than two months before Broadcom released a patch on Thursday, according to Google
Full Text:
A China-linked espionage group exploited a VMware vCenter zero-day vulnerability for more than two months before Broadcom released a patch on Thursday, according to Google.

Tracked as CVE-2026-123890 (CVSS score of 9.8), the bug resides in the VMware Directory Service and could let remote, unauthenticated attackers obtain an authenticated session with administrator privileges.

Mandiant, which reported the bug to Broadcom, has linked its exploitation to Armory Castle, a suspected Chinese threat actor formerly tracked as UNC5221 and also known as Warp Panda.

According to Mandiant, the hackers gained initial access through CVE-2026-102764, a recently patched BeyondTrust Remote Support zero-day. They then pivoted to Linux appliances on the internal network and targeted vCenter in early September.

They used a custom tool called Bonesaw to exploit CVE-2026-123890, steal the Lightning Memory-Mapped Database (LMDB), extract SAML signing material, and create a single sign-on (SSO) administrator account.

Next, the attackers deployed a second tool to forge SAML tokens and installed backdoors. They also took the vCenter master encryption key and database credentials, then moved to an ESXi host and extracted additional information.

“Mandiant has evidence that Armory Castle had knowledge of CVE-2026-123890 prior to the disclosure of CVE-2026-59309 on July 29, 2026,” Google notes.

Bonesaw was used against a vCenter server already patched for CVE-2026-59309, a separate vCenter authentication bypass disclosed in July.

Charles Carmakal, CTO at Mandiant, said on LinkedIn that the company investigated multiple incidents involving Armory Castle’s exploitation of CVE-2026-123890.

Broadcom has released fixes in vCenter versions 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, and 8.0 U3m. According to Mandiant, Bonesaw works against vCenter 7.x and 8.x. However, there is no public patch for version 7.0, which reached end of general support in October 2025.

Broadcom’s advisory, which also resolves four SDDC Manager and VMware Tools flaws, does not mention in-the-wild exploitation.

“Organizations should both apply the patches and examine their systems for evidence of compromise,” Carmakal said.

Title: How AWS Security Incident Response triages your security findings
Context: If you send third-party detection findings to Security Hub CSPM from tools such as CrowdStrike, Trend Micro, or Lacework, their threat detection findings are also ingested
Full Text:
AWS Security Incident Response continuously triages the threat findings from Amazon GuardDuty and AWS Security Hub CSPM, but most of that work never shows up as a case. If cases are all you look at, it’s hard to tell whether the service is working at all, and that’s the question I hear most often when I help customers onboard. The Proactive response dashboard gives you a high-level view of this activity, and this post takes you behind the numbers to show what happens to an individual finding.

In this post, I walk you through what happens to a finding after it’s ingested by the service, what gets triaged, where each finding is sent, and how a triage decision becomes a case. I then show you how to confirm triage is working day-to-day, so your team can focus on the findings that require attention. The process flow is shown in Figure 1.

Figure 1: AWS Security Incident Response triage flow, from ingestion through to one of three outcomes

Ingestion

AWS Security Incident Response ingests threat findings from GuardDuty through Amazon EventBridge rules that are automatically deployed to your accounts during the onboarding process.

If you send third-party detection findings to Security Hub CSPM from tools such as CrowdStrike, Trend Micro, or Lacework, their threat detection findings are also ingested. Each of those findings must carry complete payload information such as resource ID, account ID, timestamp, and threat details. GuardDuty findings are ingested directly, so these findings aren’t re-ingested through Security Hub CSPM and there’s no duplication.

Triage

The service triages findings that indicate an active threat, such as compromised credentials, cryptomining, or data exfiltration. These represent activity that’s underway or has already occurred.

Posture and compliance findings aren’t triaged. A misconfiguration or a failed benchmark check reflects the state of your environment rather than an active threat, so those findings remain for your team to address through your existing remediation process.

Outcomes

For each threat finding, the service runs an automated triage process. It evaluates the finding payload, related AWS activity from AWS CloudTrail and Amazon VPC Flow Logs, AWS threat intelligence, and the context you provide about your environment. The service then maps the finding against a profile of known-good activity. What fits the profile is treated as expected, and what doesn’t is flagged for a closer look.

What happens next depends on that outcome. A finding is sent to one of three places:

Archived, no action needed – Automated triage or an AWS Security Incident Response engineer confirms the activity is benign or expected. The finding is archived in GuardDuty, with no case and no customer contact.

A proactive case is opened – Triage can’t confirm the activity is benign. This is either Unconfirmed Activity (the service needs you to confirm whether it’s expected) or Inappropriate/Unintended Activity (confirmed activity that needs your action). A proactive case is opened, your incident response team is engaged, and the finding stays Current until it’s resolved.

Retained for your review, no case – Posture-related findings, such as overly permissive policies, configuration, or missing encryption, aren’t threats. By design, they stay Current without archiving and no case is created.

When a proactive case is opened, you respond to it in the AWS Management Console for AWS Security Incident Response under Cases, where you can communicate directly with the team, share context, and resolve or reopen the case. Timely responses also help the service learn your environment, which helps reduce false positives over time. For the full workflow, see Responding to an AWS generated case.

The preceding outcomes use GuardDuty terms, because it’s the primary source. Third-party findings ingested through Security Hub CSPM follow the same triage logic, but their disposition shows as a workflow-status change rather than archiving. The finding moves from NEW to NOTIFIED when triage begins, which removes it from the default Security Hub CSPM view. If triage clears it as benign, it moves to SUPPRESSED. Otherwise it stays visible for your review.

Because only benign findings are archived, it’s normal to see many findings in Current, and that isn’t a sign the service missed them. Across customers, less than 1 percent of ingested findings result in a customer-facing escalation. Most are handled automatically, without a case.

Credential exfiltration finding example

Suppose GuardDuty generates an UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration.OutsideAWS finding: temporary credentials created on an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance were used from an IP address outside AWS. Triage cross-references the payload against what it knows about your environment.

Cleared – The external IP belongs to a corporate virtual private network (VPN) range that your workloads regularly call through, and the service has seen this pattern before. The finding is archived in GuardDuty.

Escalated – The IP is in a hosting-provider range with no prior association to your accounts, and the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role has never made calls from outside AWS. The service creates a proactive case, notifies your incident response team, and an engineer investigates whether the credentials were compromised.

Same finding type, two outcomes. The difference is context, and context is what triage builds by observing your environment over time.

How triage sharpens over time

The service builds a profile of what’s normal in your environment. It learns the IP ranges and domains you trust, and the IAM principals and behaviors your workloads rely on. When your team routinely connects from a known VPN range, or a specific IAM role runs nightly batch jobs, the service recognizes those patterns and measures new findings against them. Early on, engineers investigate more findings by hand as they learn your environment. Within a few weeks, automated triage handles most of those decisions on its own.

Triage is dynamic. A finding treated as expected today can be re-evaluated tomorrow if the context changes, so the service can still catch a real threat that reuses a pattern it formerly treated as safe. You can shape the profile by submitting known-good activity, such as trusted IP ranges or authorized scanning tools, through an AWS Support case. For details, see Submit known-good activity.

Archiving versus suppression

It’s possible to conflate the two mechanisms, so it’s worth separating them:

Archiving is the primary mechanism. When automated triage or an engineer determines a finding is benign, the service archives it in GuardDuty. The finding then stays there for 90 days.

Suppression rules are less common and work differently. A suppression rule acts on future findings. When the service identifies a recurring pattern of expected activity, it might create a GuardDuty suppression rule that automatically archives matching findings so they don’t generate new alerts. Suppressed findings aren’t sent to your configured export, such as an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket or SIEM. When the service creates a rule, your incident response team is notified, and you can view and manage it in the GuardDuty console under Suppression rules.

A healthy deployment typically shows many archived findings and few or no suppression rules. That’s expected, and it means the service is handling findings dynamically rather than relying on static filters.

How to see what triage is doing

Triage runs on its own, and the service gives you a few ways to confirm it’s working.

Proactive response dashboard

The Dashboard page in the AWS Security Incident Response console has a Proactive response section. It counts how many findings were ingested, triaged, investigated, and escalated over the timeframe you select, the last 7, 30, or 90 days.

The Overview leads with two figures. Noise reduction is the share of ingested findings that automated triage resolved without opening a case, so you can see for yourself how much volume never reached your team. Time saved estimates the analyst hours that automation returned to you, counted as one hour for each ingested finding.

Below that, Finding evaluations breaks those stages down:

Ingest – Threat findings collected from your detection sources

Triage – Findings evaluated automatically to decide whether the activity is expected

Investigation – Findings automated triage couldn’t confirm, passed to an AWS Security Incident Response engineer for a closer look

Escalation – Investigations raised as a case when a genuine risk was detected or the activity couldn’t be confirmed as expected

A flow diagram on the dashboard shows how those findings move from their sources through triage and investigation, with branches for the ones closed as false positives and the ones still in progress. For more, see Viewing proactive response metrics.

Monthly report

The monthly report is the periodic companion to the dashboard. AWS Security Incident Response emails it to your incident response team a week or two after each month closes. It opens with the accounts monitored, findings processed, and investigations, then lists each investigation and its status, the triage flows that show the checks run for each finding type, and the context the service has learned about your environment, such as the trusted networks it now recognizes as normal.

Archived findings in GuardDuty

For a quick confirmation outside either view, open Findings in the GuardDuty console and filter to see Archived. That list also includes findings archived by you or by suppression rules, so look for the threat findings AWS Security Incident Response archived after triage. Each one is a finding that the service cleared as benign so your team didn’t have to.

Conclusion

AWS Security Incident Response continuously evaluates your threat findings so your team can spend its time on confirmed threats rather than alert volume. Findings that are evaluated as benign are archived automatically, the ones that need a response become proactive cases, and posture issues stay in Current for your team to handle.

Cases show only a small part of that work. When I deliver AWS Security Incident Response to customers now, I walk them through the triage flow in Figure 1, the Proactive response dashboard, and their monthly report, so they can see how triage works end to end.

To get started, see the onboarding guide. Setup takes about 10 minutes. For more information, see the AWS Security Incident Response product page or the User Guide.

If you have questions about this post, contact AWS Support or start a new thread on AWS re:Post.

Anatoliy is a Technical Account Manager and AWS Security Incident Response SME. He works with AWS Enterprise customers, providing ongoing support and technical guidance to help them build secure, resilient solutions using AWS best practices.
