Title: Russian national accused of stalking San Francisco techie in plot against US defense-tech giant
Context: The first time, he was asked to leave the laptop for one hour while the handlers worked, and another time, he was told to drop it off in the middle of the night and only come...
Full Text: A Russian national is being held in custody after being arrested for allegedly spying on a US defense tech company in Palo Alto, shoulder-surfing employees, and dropping remote surveillance devices at their homes. Igor D'iu was indicted after FBI agents surveilled his activities between June and October 2026, which they say were issued as "tasks" from what is thought to be Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB), according to an affidavit [PDF] signed by an FBI special agent. After FBI agents secured a warrant to raid D'iu's temporary premises in October, they say that Telegram messages harvested from his seized devices confirmed investigators' findings and revealed that he was spying on an unnamed company. Court documents describe the company in question as a large technology and defense company with offices in Palo Alto, and media-reported links to the Russia-Ukraine war. While unconfirmed officially, the company has widely been reported as Palantir, which did not respond to our request for confirmation. D'iu allegedly received instructions from Telegram contacts, whom he only suspected were representatives of the Russian government, weeks after entering the US illegally in July. The indictment alleges he was ordered to surveil employees' homes, take photographs of their screens while working remotely at coffee shops, and permit his handlers to remotely access his laptop for the purpose of capturing data from nearby devices owned by the company’s employees. In some cases, the filing alleges, D’iu was asked to leave a laptop outside one employee's apartment complex, all while allowing his Telegram handlers to remotely operate the device. The first time, he was asked to leave the laptop for one hour while the handlers worked, and another time, he was told to drop it off in the middle of the night and only come back to collect it three hours later, the filing claims. D'iu is also allegedly to have followed two female employees in his rented car, driving dangerously and violating multiple road laws to do so. One of the two employees was followed briefly, but D'iu followed another for nearly 30 miles, according to the affidavit signed by FBI special agent Winston Wong. D'iu was said to have followed the woman as she performed U-turns, illegal left turns, ran red lights, navigated via back and side streets, and through grocery store parking lots. The car following her only peeled away after the woman drove to the San Francisco Mission police station on the advice of a 911 call handler. Questioned about the incident, which according to police reports caused the woman significant emotional distress, D'iu confirmed he was the driver but claimed he was following her to ask her out on a date. Inside recruitment The affidavit did not detail the suspect's background beyond his alleged offenses in the US earlier this year, although it mentioned Russian intelligence's history of recruiting "criminal proxies, organized crime groups, and other disposable agents" to carry out operations. According to the FBI's account, D'iu entered the US illegally – without relevant visas – in either June or July 2026. Travel records obtained on September 10 showed that his last recorded journey was from Istanbul to Mexico City. There was no record of him entering the US. Investigators would later come to know that he travelled on that Istanbul-Mexico City flight on June 7, allegedly using a ticket provided to him by one of the three contacts from whom he received orders via Telegram. A Facebook account, registered using a Mexican +528 number and D'iu's name, posted on June 30 asking for help getting "closer to New York," adding that "I'll pay as much as needed." The account replied to a response from someone who told him to contact a Mexico phone number on WhatsApp. The filing claims the first mobile phone signals associated with D'iu's devices did not ping US towers until a month later, on July 31, suggesting he did not arrive in the US - specifically McAllen, Texas - until around that date. Telegram messages would also go on to confirm that he was allegedly helped across the border by an "Uzbek contact" in Mexico. Records obtained from Google showed D'iu created a Google account in April. According to the affidavit, D'iu used it to search for the company's Wikipedia page on July 28, and on August 3, used Google's AI to devise a route around Texas that bypassed border checkpoints. The FBI believes D'iu's "spying" began in mid-August, after he bought a laptop, a Wi-Fi device, a puck device, and an additional phone. At this point, the agency claims, he had received his first order to visit a coffee shop near the Palo Alto company’s office and snap employees' laptop screens before sending copies back to his handlers. Three days later, D'iu was ordered to go back to a coffee shop and allow his Telegram contacts to remotely control the laptop and collect data from employee devices that were in range, claims the filing. D'iu was paid $15,000 on three occasions between August 12 and October 6, according to the court documents. To verify the transaction, he was told to send a picture of a dollar bill's serial number to the Telegram contacts, along with a description of what he was wearing. A courier would then arrive, confirming the serial number and handing D'iu the cash. The filing alleges he used this money to purchase the tech equipment, accommodation, and travel, including a rented silver 2026 Lexus RX 350 from a private owner in Los Angeles on August 22, which he is said to have driven back to San Francisco. The same Lexus was captured on security footage outside the unnamed company's office on September 1, and over the following two days was implicated in the two instances of female employees being followed. Contacted by Palo Alto police on September 4, D'iu confirmed he was the driver who dangerously followed the female staffer for nearly 30 minutes, but claimed he knew nothing about the nearby businesses. D'iu would then claim he followed the woman because he thought she was beautiful and wanted to ask her out on a date, and denied following anyone else. The affidavit goes on to allege that D'iu then traveled to Reno, Nevada, to lay low after his run-in with the police. He spent the time trying to reroute DHL deliveries from San Francisco to his hideout address, which US Customs would later intercept. These ended up containing fake IDs with the images the DoJ claims matched D'iu's, including Uzbek documents, a US passport whose number belonged to a New York woman, and a social security card registered to a "Hugo Landry Johns." He traveled back to the Bay Area in late September, swapping his silver Lexus for a white 2016 Dodge Challenger, and received additional instructions from his handlers, including the order to leave a remote-controlled laptop outside the apartment complex, says the filing. One Telegram contact named Ian Morales sent photos of at least four employees and their addresses, along with instructions for D'iu to dress as a food delivery worker and visit those locations, asking whoever answered to verify they lived there. FBI agents executed a search warrant on October 8, seizing a cache of evidence, including what they listed as being: The forged ID documents Two Russian passports $18,035 in cash Two laptops Two iPhones Two T-Mobile SIM cards Wi-Fi equipment A notebook with 10 handwritten addresses supplied by Telegram contacts, along with times the suspect was supposed to attend those locations, at least five of which were for company employees’ homes Profile packages for at least three employees, including: Names, personal information, education and employment histories, names of relatives, narrative histories, and assessments of leadership qualities, strengths, and weaknesses. Suspicions and charges Per the affidavit, D'iu was said to have only become suspicious of the tasks he was being ordered to complete in October, when his handlers ordered the laptop to be dropped near the apartment complex. "D'iu gradually began to understand he was doing something bad and that his actions were illegal," the affidavit stated. At this point, he allegedly asked the Telegram contacts who he was working for, to which they replied "the Motherland," and the company he was surveilling was involved in providing weapons to Ukraine, resulting in D’iu suspecting the Russian government. Wong said in the affidavit: "Based on my training, experience, and research, D'iu's communications with his Telegram contacts is consistent with the tactics of [Russian intelligence] and its criminal proxies for spotting, assessing, recruiting, and handling intelligence assets and sources. "D'iu's targeting of the company and its employees is also consistent with [Russian intelligence] objectives in Russia's war against Ukraine." The Russian national was indicted and charged with two counts related to spying offences, and one count related to the fake identity documents. He is next due in court on November 24 but remains in federal custody. ®

Title: PHP Patches Seven Critical RCE Vulnerabilities
Context: Residing in the session upload progress feature, it could be triggered to write attacker data using one session serialization format and then read it using another
Full Text:
PHP on Thursday rolled out a fresh set of security patches as part of its four-week update schedule, including fixes for seven critical-severity remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities.

First in line is CVE-2026-115560, which was publicly disclosed last month, two days after PHP2Shell patches landed. Residing in the session upload progress feature, it could be triggered to write attacker data using one session serialization format and then read it using another.

“A mismatched decoder can interpret part of a session key as serialized object data. An application with a suitable object gadget chain can then execute code with the privileges of the PHP worker,” PHP’s advisory reads.

Next in line is CVE-2026-129481, described as a use-after-free that occurs after a session shutdown has been interrupted, and which PHP describes as an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-109619, one of the two PHP2Shell flaws fixed in October and now widely exploited.

“An attacker who can cause an application’s session cleanup to fail in this way may corrupt memory or crash a reused PHP worker. The use-after-free could potentially lead to remote code execution, but code execution through this specific field has not been demonstrated,” PHP notes, adding that PHP 8.2 is not affected.

Another use-after-free, CVE-2026-129182, covers additional exploitation scenarios for CVE-2026-109619, an RCE via stale global state. According to PHP, however, RCE via these scenarios has not been demonstrated.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Impacting PHP 8.5 and later, CVE-2026-129474 is a use-after-free weakness that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to cause a fatal error and achieve RCE. “Exploitation depends on the application and requires control over enough request data to influence memory allocation, a reachable magic method call, and a fatal error at the relevant point,” PHP says.

Attackers able to influence session contents and interrupt the write of serialized data to a session file may trigger the deserialization of attacker-controlled content when the session is next opened. Tracked as CVE-2026-126714, the flaw could lead to RCE via a suitable object gadget chain in the application.

PHP also patched CVE-2026-129289, a PHP-FPM request smuggling issue caused by PHP reading a request-body stream lazily, treating a request body as handled during request shutdown and skipping the normal cleanup that discards unread input.

“PHP can fail to discard unread bytes from an HTTP request body before reusing a persistent PHP-FPM or LSAPI connection. In PHP-FPM, an unauthenticated attacker can make those bytes form a separate FastCGI request, bypass front-end routing and execute attacker-controlled PHP code with the privileges of the worker,” PHP explains.

The seventh critical-severity vulnerability patched today, CVE-2026-129496, resides in the timezone cache. PHP can retain a reference to it when writing a diagnostic to a PHP error log file during process startup, and a later diagnostic can access the freed cache before it is reset.

“On affected configurations, a remote attacker can trigger memory corruption, cause a worker to crash, and potentially execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the PHP worker,” PHP explains.

PHP 8.6.0 and PHP 8.5.13 were rolled out with fixes for all critical bugs and for 10 high and medium-severity flaws. Patches for most issues were also included in PHP 8.4.28, PHP 8.3.37, and PHP 8.2.36. More information is available on PHP’s news archive page.

Title: Typosquatted Domains Impersonate AI Platforms to Deliver ClickFix Attacks
Context: Researchers at Island discovered nearly 200 typosquatted domains impersonating dozens of AI brands, including Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Perplexity, Midjourney, ElevenLabs, and...
Full Text:
Researchers at Island discovered nearly 200 typosquatted domains impersonating dozens of AI brands, including Claude, ChatGPT, DeepSeek, Perplexity, Midjourney, ElevenLabs, and Cursor.

“One Claude typo, cloude[.]ai, ended at a ClickFix lure that runs a hidden PowerShell command fetched from a decimal-encoded IP address,” the researchers write. “The gate behind it serves 211 entry domains, including lookalikes of banks, insurers and enterprise software. Other AI typos led to fake ‘Security Check’ pages serving Net Guard, a Microsoft Store-signed app. The package matches the Store’s own hash, and inside it is browser-hijacking malware that changes the visitor’s existing browser and can run remotely supplied scripts through DevTools. A third route led to a search-hijacking browser extension, one of 30 built from the same kit. Thirteen have since been removed, and the 17 still listed show 972,000 declared users between them.”

Typosquatting isn’t a new technique, but attackers are taking advantage of current trends to mimic increasingly popular AI tools.

“ChatGPT draws the most lookalikes in our set, 25, from chatgpy[.]com to chtgpt[.]com,” Island says. “Claude follows with 18 and DeepSeek with 16, among them deepseel[.]com and deeepseek[.]com. Runway has 12, including runawayml[.]com, and Perplexity, Lovable, and Character.ai have 11 each, with names such as perplixity[.]ai, lovabe[.]dev and charactor[.]ai. The list reaches well past chat assistants: giemini[.]com, griok[.]com and mistrial[.]ai for Gemini, Grok and Mistral, notbooklm[.]com for NotebookLM and mauns[.]im for the agent platform Manus. Some lookalikes imitate the companies themselves, such as opnai[.]com and anthropiv[.]com, for people who type the company instead of the product.”

Title: CyberPower PowerPanel Exploited to Run Malicious Code on Domain Controller
Context: An attacker has abused CyberPower's PowerPanel Business (PBB) software to run malicious scripts on a domain controller, the server that controls logins across a Windows network,...
Full Text:
An attacker has abused CyberPower's PowerPanel Business (PBB) software to run malicious scripts on a domain controller, the server that controls logins across a Windows network, turning a power management feature into a remote command channel.

Symantec detailed the intrusion in research published November 18. PowerPanel Business manages uninterruptible power supply (UPS) battery backups. Because organizations rely on it to shut servers down safely in an outage, it often runs on important systems such as hypervisors and database and file servers.

How the UPS Software Was Abused

Administrators can configure PPB to launch a script when it detects a power problem, and its service executes that script with SYSTEM privileges, the highest level in Windows. Symantec said this meant the attacker could run code without a software bug and without setting up a service or scheduled task.

According to Symantec, the attacker uploaded scripts through the web console, then used them to stage an antivirus killer and copy the Active Directory database, which stores credentials for every account on the network. A persistent implant followed, loaded through DLL sideloading, in which a legitimate program is tricked into loading a malicious library.

The attacker leaned mostly on tools that ship with Windows, and the data collection scripts were rewritten several times during the intrusion. Symantec read that trial and error as a sign of a human operator working live.

Read more on management software attacks: Chinese State Actor Used AI to Compromise ConnectWise Tenants

What Defenders Should Check

Symantec did not say how the attacker got into the network or onto the PPB console. Possible routes to the console, it said, included stolen administrator credentials and previously disclosed weaknesses in the product, such as a default administrator password, hard-coded credentials and a file upload flaw.

Symantec said the feature "simply accepts a script, stores it, and runs it as SYSTEM." Since PPB often sits on the machines an attacker would prize most, it urged organizations to treat power-management software with the same suspicion as remote administration tools.

Its advice included limiting console access to specific administrator machines, keeping the console off the internet, replacing the default administrator password and staying patched. It also told organizations to check the folders PPB runs scripts from, assume any unfamiliar script is malicious, reset Active Directory credentials if indicators turned up and protect power-management hosts as high-value systems.

Symantec did not identify the victim or link the activity to any known group. With no data theft or ransomware seen, it said the attackers' motives remained unclear.

Title: PHP Releases Patches to Fix 18 Vulnerabilities
Context: The PHP Foundation has released security patches for a new set of 18 vulnerabilities, seven of which are marked critical
Full Text:
The PHP Foundation has released security patches for a new set of 18 vulnerabilities, seven of which are marked critical.

These vulnerabilities affect all supported PHP versions but require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups to be exploited.

This set of newly disclosed PHP vulnerabilities come a month after the disclosure of two critical flaws in PHP, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively known as ‘PHP2Shell.’

This was not merely a theoretical risk. In the weeks following the disclosure, security researchers began documenting real-world exploitation attempts and compromises involving internet-facing systems, demonstrating the potential consequences of leaving vulnerable PHP installations unpatched.

For example, Check Point reported campaigns exploiting PHP2Shell against its own security gateways, dating back to 30 October. The attacks involved the deployment of backdoors and even destructive tools targeting VMware ESXi virtualisation servers.

The exploitation activity also extended to Palo Alto Networks firewalls, with attackers targeting devices whose administrative interfaces were exposed to the internet.

Of the flaws published in the November update one is a remote code execution (RCE) vulnerability in session upload progress, tracked as CVE-2026-115560. It was disclosed by PHP on October 23, two days after PHP released emergency fixes for the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. It has been noted that exploitation of this vulnerability requires a highly specific and unlikely combination of conditions.

PHP Session Handling Flaws Enable Remote Code Execution

One of the new critical flaws, dubbed ‘PHPAfterShell’ and tracked as CVE-2026-126714, was discovered by security firm Depthfirst using AI frontier models tuned for cybersecurity tasks.

The vulnerability lives in PHP’s session handling with file-based storage, the default (session.save_handler = files).

By exploiting a flaw in this process, an attacker can manipulate a session while a file is being uploaded, potentially tricking the server into executing arbitrary code.

Successful exploitation could allow a remote attacker access to sensitive information, including login credentials and customer records, modify session data, spy on visitors or disrupt the affected service.

It affects the following versions:

PHP 8.5 < 8.5.13

PHP 8.4 < 8.4.28

PHP 8.3 < 8.3.37

PHP 8.2 < 8.2.36

PHP 8.1 and earlier are end-of-life

PHP Security Patches Address 16 Additional Vulnerabilities

The other vulnerabilities addressed in PHP’s 19 November 2026 security release include the following:

CVE-2026-129481 (CVSS 9.2): A use-after-free vulnerability triggered by an interrupted session shutdown, potentially allowing memory corruption and remote code execution

CVE-2026-129474 (CVSS 9.2): A use-after-free flaw in magic method backtraces that could allow attackers to execute arbitrary code

CVE-2026-129182 (CVSS 9.2): A use-after-free vulnerability involving the repopulation of the last fatal error backtrace after shutdown, potentially leading to remote code execution

CVE-2026-129496 (CVSS 9.2): A use-after-free vulnerability in the time zone cache that could potentially lead to remote code execution

CVE-2026-129501 (CVSS 6.3): A double-free vulnerability during DOM XML serialization that can cause memory corruption and denial of service

CVE-2026-129538 (CVSS 6.9): An out-of-bounds read and write vulnerability in PHP-CGI when correcting the PATH_INFO environment variable, potentially resulting in memory corruption

CVE-2026-129291 (CVSS 8.8): A use-after-free vulnerability in PHP-FPM's epoll event handling that could allow local privilege escalation

CVE-2026-129289 (CVSS 9.2): A request-smuggling vulnerability caused by unread HTTP request bodies, potentially allowing attackers to manipulate how requests are processed

CVE-2026-129292 (CVSS 5.3): A cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in the PHP-FPM status endpoint, caused by insufficient escaping of user and script fields

CVE-2026-128090 (CVSS 7.7): An OpenSSL signature verification bypass caused by an algorithm downgrade, potentially allowing malicious PHAR archives to pass signature checks

CVE-2026-15353 (CVSS 6.3): An information disclosure vulnerability involving malformed array dimensions during SOAP processing

CVE-2026-129506 (CVSS 6.3): A use-after-free vulnerability when processing DTD entity references, potentially resulting in memory corruption

CVE-2026-128064 (CVSS 8.2): A vulnerability involving mixed-case HTTPS and FTPS URLs that could cause sensitive information to be transmitted in plaintext rather than encrypted

CVE-2026-127960 (CVSS 8.7): A denial-of-service vulnerability involving folded HTTP response headers, potentially allowing attackers to disrupt service availability

CVE-2026-129438 (CVSS 6.3): An incorrect RFC 3986 URI serialization vulnerability affecting oversized input, potentially resulting in invalid URI output

CVE-2026-48841 (CVSS not published): a vulnerability in the bundled uriparser library (a PHP third-party dependency) addressed by upgrading the dependency to version 1.0.3

PHP Ecosystem Projects Prepare Security Updates

The patches, published on November 19, are part of PHP’s regular four-week release cycle and come alongside the release of several versions of PHP (8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13 and 8.6).

The PHP team warned users about the vulnerabilities and their forthcoming fixes on November 18.

Users are strongly encouraged to prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available. Technical details and fixed version numbers will be published alongside the releases.

Maintainers of open-source projects that rely on PHP have already been working to incorporate the security fixes into their software and distributions, helping ensure that patches reach downstream users as quickly as possible.

For instance, Kevin Dunglas, creator of FrankenPHP, a modern PHP application server built around the Caddy web server, said on X that the project is working with The PHP Foundation and Docker to provide updated builds as soon as the patched PHP version becomes available. These will include static binaries, RPM and DEB packages, Homebrew packages and Docker images based on Debian and Alpine Linux.

Meanwhile, Laravel, a popular open-source PHP framework used by developers to build websites, web applications and APIs, said on X it was already working on a remediation plan to protect applications running across its hosting and deployment services.

Title: PHP 8.6 is out, and here’s what changes for your code
Context: cookie_httponly turned on and session
Full Text:
PHP 8.6 has been released. The new version adds partial function application, a Time\Duration class, a polling API for event loops and a clamp() function.

PHP 8.6 also changes defaults that existing apps could trip over. Sessions now start with session.use_strict_mode and session.cookie_httponly turned on and session.cookie_samesite set to Lax. Custom session handlers that don’t implement both create_sid() and validateId() are deprecated. If your app relied on the old defaults, test your login flows before you upgrade.

Failed writes now report failure

fclose(), file_put_contents() and copy() return false when flushing or closing a file fails. Earlier versions ignored that failure, so a write that broke at the last step could still look like it succeeded. Many other functions now throw a ValueError on out-of-range values, invalid flags, or strings that contain NUL bytes. You can also set stream operations to throw a StreamException. The exception carries structured error objects that name the wrapper and the path or URL involved.

What you can write now

Partial function application lets you fill in some of a function’s arguments ahead of time. You get back a closure that waits for the rest, and a ? marks each argument still to come:

$slugify = str_replace(' ', '-', ?); echo $slugify('php 8.6 release'); // php-8.6-release

Time\Duration measures elapsed time the way a stopwatch does, with no clock time or timezone attached. It covers more than 250 years at nanosecond precision, which is more than any retry delay or timeout will need. Io\Poll watches many streams at once through epoll, kqueue, event ports or WSAPoll, without the limits of stream_select(). PHP’s developers built it as a base for event-loop libraries such as ReactPHP and AMPHP. And clamp(110, 0, 100) returns 100.

The release also adds a SortDirection enum, default values for readonly properties, and post-quantum key encapsulation in Sodium (X-Wing and ML-KEM-768). TLS streams gain support for TLS 1.3 early data.

What’s on the way out

The mbstring regex functions, including mb_ereg() and mb_split(), are deprecated because Oniguruma, the regex library behind them, is no longer maintained. PHP’s developers recommend PCRE with the u modifier instead. is_double(), is_long(), is_integer() and doubleval() are deprecated in favor of is_float(), is_int() and floatval(), and spl_object_hash() is deprecated in favor of spl_object_id(). Using return inside a finally block is deprecated too. One behavior change applies right away: trim(), ltrim() and rtrim() now strip form feeds (\f) by default.

Title: PHP Fixes 7 Critical Flaws, Including Bugs That Could Allow Remote Code Execution
Context: The PHP Foundation has released security updates to address multiple critical security flaws that could be exploited to achieve remote code execution on affected deployments,...
Full Text:
The PHP Foundation has released security updates to address multiple critical security flaws that could be exploited to achieve remote code execution on affected deployments, including CVE-2026-115560.

The list of vulnerabilities is as follows -

CVE-2026-115560 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An improper input validation vulnerability that could result in remote code execution, file modification, session corruption, or denial-of-service. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

CVE-2026-129182 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could result in memory corruption and possible full remote code execution, as in the case of CVE-2026-109619. (Fixed in PHP 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

CVE-2026-126714 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) vulnerability that could result in the execution of arbitrary code with the privileges of the PHP worker. Successful exploitation requires an attacker's influence over the session data, an interruption at a useful point in the write, and an application with a suitable deserialization gadget chain. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

CVE-2026-129289 (CVSS score: 9.2) - An inconsistent interpretation of HTTP requests vulnerability that could result in execution of attacker-controlled PHP code as the worker without another user's interaction or a non-default PHP configuration. Successful exploitation requires a front end that enables persistent backend connections and an application path that opens "php://input" without reading it fully, such as nginx with fastcgi_keep_conn on, Apache mod_proxy_fcgi with enablereuse=on, HAProxy FastCGI applications that retain backend connections, and LSAPI. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

CVE-2026-129474 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could result in remote code execution on PHP 8.5 and later. Successful exploitation depends on the application and requires control over enough request data to influence memory allocation, a reachable magic method call, and a fatal error at the relevant point. (Fixed in PHP 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

CVE-2026-129481 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could cause an application's session cleanup to fail and potentially corrupt memory, crash a reused PHP worker, or potentially allow remote code execution. (Fixed in PHP 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

CVE-2026-129496 (CVSS score: 9.2) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to crash PHP workers or execute arbitrary code with their privileges on an affected deployment. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

CVE-2026-129291 (CVSS score: 8.8) - A use-after-free vulnerability that could result in local privilege escalation. Successful exploitation requires local code execution in an FPM worker, an affected pool with catch_workers_output enabled, the epoll event backend, and the ability to manipulate worker lifetimes and retain inherited pipe descriptors. (Fixed in PHP 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, 8.5.13, 8.6.0)

Depthfirst, which has codenamed CVE-2026-126714 "phpAfterShell," has described it as a critical flaw that can enable a remote attacker to run arbitrary code on affected servers.

"If a pwrite()/ftruncate() update is interrupted, PHP may leave behind a malformed session file that is later loaded by session_start(), yielding an arbitrary deserialization primitive," Depthfirst said. "Chained with another of our PHP-native deserialization-to-RCE findings, this leads directly to remote code execution."

It affects any application that runs an affected PHP version with file-based sessions. If immediate patching is not possible, it's advised to turn off session upload progress.

Patches for the flaws are available in the following versions -

PHP 8.2.36

PHP 8.3.37

PHP 8.4.28

PHP 8.5.13

PHP 8.6.0

Users who are using existing 8.2.x, 8.3.x, 8.4.x, and 8.5.x versions of PHP are advised to update to the latest version for optimal protection.

Title: Critical VMware vCenter Flaw (CVSS 9.8) Lets Network Attackers Bypass Authentication
Context: A critical flaw in VMware vCenter lets an attacker with network access bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system, Broadcom, which owns VMware, said in an...
Full Text:
A critical flaw in VMware vCenter lets an attacker with network access bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system, Broadcom, which owns VMware, said in an advisory published today.

Fixed versions are out for all supported branches, and the company lists no workaround. vCenter is the central console for managing an organization's ESX hosts and virtual machines.

The vulnerability is tracked as CVE-2026-123890 and is rated 9.8 on the CVSS scoring system. "VMware vCenter contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service," the advisory says.

In an FAQ published with the advisory, the company says the issue "qualifies under ITIL methodologies as an emergency change," and urges organizations to consult their security staff immediately on timing.

The company has not reported any attacks exploiting the flaw, or any public exploit code. It also does not say what level of access an attacker gains after the bypass. Credit for reporting the bug goes to Google-owned Mandiant.

The bug is present in vCenter 8.0, 9.0, and 9.1, and in the vCenter builds that ship inside VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation, and the Telco Cloud Platform and Telco Cloud Infrastructure products. That includes the older Cloud Foundation 5.x line. It is there whether or not Enhanced Linked Mode is in use.

Older versions are not cleared. The company no longer evaluates versions past end of support, and says vSphere 6.5 and 6.7 should be presumed affected. The same goes for vSphere 7.0, which left general support in October 2025, and whose customers can request a patch under an extended support contract.

None of the five flaws in the advisory lets code run on an ESX host from inside a virtual machine, and ESX itself is not affected, the advisory FAQ says.

There is no fallback for systems that cannot be updated yet: asked whether a workaround exists, the FAQ answers "Not as listed by Broadcom," while noting that mitigations may still exist in an organization's own defenses.

The updates are cumulative and cannot be installed through vCenter Quick Patch. Virtual machines continue running while vCenter installs the update, though management access drops briefly, and some encryption operations against a Standard Key Provider become unavailable until vCenter is back online.

One warning applies to upgrades already in progress: installing vCenter 8.0 U3m or 9.0.2.0200 blocks a later upgrade to VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1.1, a conflict the FAQ calls a "Back-in-Time" issue. The options are to upgrade vCenter to 9.1.1 first and apply the security update there, or to wait briefly for VCF 9.1.2.

The bypass is the second critical authentication flaw in the VMware Directory Service this year. The earlier vCenter flaws, patched on July 29, included CVE-2026-59309, another 9.8-rated bypass in the same component per the July advisory, alongside a directory-traversal bug, CVE-2026-59310.

Attacks on that traversal flaw began five days after its disclosure, German incident response firm QUIRSO assessed in August, linking them with moderate confidence to a suspected China-nexus actor.

The August attacks compromised an estimated 361 IP addresses in 47 countries and deployed Babuk-derived ransomware on ESXi hosts. Broadcom has reported no attacks on the new bypass.

The advisory also fixes four lower-severity flaws, rated 6.7 to 8.1: a SQL injection (CVE-2026-123891) and a command injection (CVE-2026-123892) in SDDC Manager, a privilege escalation to root on the SDDC Manager appliance (CVE-2026-123893), and a SAML token signature bypass in VMware Tools for Windows (CVE-2026-123894), exploitable only where Guest Alias mapping is configured. Each needs an authenticated or already privileged actor, and the last one stays inside the guest virtual machine.

Title: European Commission Cyberattack: ARTEX AI Tool Suspected in Prolonged Disruption
Context: A cyberattack disrupted EU Commission services for over ten days
Full Text:
A cyberattack disrupted EU Commission services for over ten days. ARTEX is suspected, while investigators assess whether staff data was stolen.

A cyberattack has disrupted internal European Commission systems for more than ten days, hitting payroll, leave requests and medical reimbursements. Politico’s Brussels Playbook reports the Corporate Management Board, the Commission’s top internal crisis body, met urgently over the incident, and tech commissioner Henna Virkkunen briefed the full College of Commissioners on 18 November. An EU official told Politico the Commission believes it has contained most of the attack, while the full extent of any damage remains unclear.

Sysper, the HR platform for payslips, timesheets and leave, crashed briefly again on 18 November after access had been restored earlier in the week. MyPMO, the medical reimbursement system, came back online around the same time. JSIS, the staff health insurance portal, was still down on 19 November according to a Commission employee cited by Euronews, and translation services went offline on 17 November, prompting one official to admit to “swearing a lot.”

Pay still landed on time, according to staff Politico spoke to, even as some couldn’t submit timesheets or request leave. Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier confirmed the response to Politico: “Individual systems were targeted and, in line with our standard practice, we have informed those concerned.”

Some staff still complained the internal communication said little, and an IT reply about the Sysper problem cited a general technical issue without mentioning an attack.

CERT-EU, the cybersecurity team that protects EU institutions, detected the activity and identified ARTEX, an AI-powered penetration-testing tool, as a possible tool used in the attack. An EU official told Politico that some threat actors misuse tools like ARTEX and have targeted the Commission. In a technical note published on 5 November, CERT-EU described ARTEX as a system that uses AI agents. An operator gives it an objective in plain language, and the software breaks it down into smaller tasks that the agents carry out using real hacking tools.

ARTEX does not include its own AI model. Instead, it connects to an external AI model selected by the operator. Its original developer removed the project from its repository in October after reports of misuse. However, independent copies are still available, so removing the original project does not prevent others from using it. So far, there is no public information explaining how the attackers entered the Commission’s systems. The reference to ARTEX therefore points to a suspected tool, not a confirmed attack method or the identity of those responsible.

The biggest unanswered question is whether staff data was stolen. This could include names, salary details, home addresses or health information. Investigators have not yet confirmed whether anyone accessed this data, which explains why the Commission has shared little information with employees.

Taking systems offline or restoring them does not prove that no data was stolen. Getting a service back online only shows that it is working again. It does not mean attackers did not copy information before the system was shut down.

Under EU Regulation 2018/1725, a confirmed personal data breach must normally be reported to the European Data Protection Supervisor within 72 hours. If the breach creates a high risk for individuals, they must also be informed without delay. However, these deadlines only start once a personal data breach has been confirmed.

This is not the Commission’s first security incident this year, although no link between the cases has been established. On January 30, attackers left traces in the system used to manage staff mobile devices. Some names and phone numbers were exposed. The Commission said it contained and cleaned up the incident within nine hours.

A more serious incident happened in March. Attackers compromised a software update for Trivy, a security tool, and used it to enter an AWS cloud environment. They stole around 91.7 GB of compressed data, including personal information and email content. The breach may also have affected at least 29 other EU institutions and bodies.

The timeline shows that the Commission restored its systems before it fully understood what had happened. Services came back online in stages, but key questions remain unanswered: where did the attack start, which systems were affected, and was any data stolen, and who is behind the attack?

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, European Commission)

Title: Five warning signs of ransomware breach before encryption or data theft
Context: In data-extortion attacks it never happens at all: the operators steal data and threaten to leak it without encrypting anything
Full Text:
Ask many IT teams how they would recognize ransomware, and the answer is still “when files start changing extensions.” By then, the intrusion may already include credential theft, privilege escalation, defense evasion, recovery sabotage, lateral movement and data exfiltration.

Encryption is often a late-stage action, not the beginning of the attack. In data-extortion attacks it never happens at all: the operators steal data and threaten to leak it without encrypting anything.

Recent attacks against on-premises SharePoint servers illustrate that sequence. After exploiting internet-facing systems, operators used stolen credentials and legitimate administration tools to move through victim environments before deploying ransomware.

The practical lesson is simple: defenders need to detect the behaviors that precede encryption, not only the encryptor itself.

Five high-value signals deserve immediate attention:

Defense tampering: Attempts to stop security services, modify protection agents, load vulnerable drivers or clear event logs.

Privilege escalation and lateral movement: Unexpected privileged accounts, remote-execution tools spreading across hosts or unusual server-to-server remote access.

Data exfiltration: Unusual outbound transfers from systems that do not normally upload large volumes of data.

Recovery sabotage: Deletion of shadow copies, backup catalogs or recovery options with tools such as vssadmin.exe, wbadmin.exe or bcdedit.exe.

Pre-encryption file behavior: Rapid file enumeration, repeated read-write-rename activity and encryption-like changes across local or network locations.

How do ransomware gangs typically gain initial access to corporate networks?

Ransomware attacks rarely begin with the ransomware payload itself. Operators first need an initial foothold, and common entry paths include exploitation of vulnerable internet-facing systems, abuse of stolen credentials, and social engineering.

An unpatched externally accessible service can provide a route into the environment, while compromised credentials can allow an attacker to enter through legitimate remote-access or cloud services.

Social engineering adds another path by targeting users and the processes around identity and access.

Once attackers establish access, the initial compromise can become the starting point for credential theft, privilege escalation, defense evasion and lateral movement.

Organizations should reduce unnecessary internet exposure, prioritize patching of high-risk systems, strengthen identity and access controls, and protect email and collaboration channels.

Monitoring endpoints for suspicious post-compromise behavior provides another layer when preventive controls do not stop the initial intrusion.

Title: Critical NGINX ‘NGINX2Root’ bugs let attackers hijack servers
Context: Two critical NGINX vulnerabilities dubbed "nginx2root" allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely on vulnerable web servers, with researchers demonstrating how the...
Full Text:
Two critical NGINX vulnerabilities dubbed "nginx2root" allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code remotely on vulnerable web servers, with researchers demonstrating how the flaws can be chained with a Linux kernel bug to gain root access.

The two HTTP/2 vulnerabilities were discovered independently by researchers at Xint, Wiz, Ikotas Labs, Metnir, and Rapid7, while Xint also discovered three additional NGINX RCE flaws.

Censys later reproduced the underlying memory corruption conditions in four of the five flaws through lab testing, but did not achieve remote code execution.

The first of the two "nginx2root" flaws is CVE-2026-123007, a flow-control bug that can corrupt memory in an NGINX worker. It impacts all versions from 1.31.8 down to 1.9.5, released in 2015.

Wiz demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution on a server hosting ordinary static files over HTTP/2 with TLS, while Xint demoed root access by chaining it with a separate Linux kernel flaw.

Xint says the separate vulnerability affects the Linux kernel's SCTP subsystem and can be used to escape an NGINX Docker container and gain root privileges on the underlying host.

The second flaw is CVE-2026-123633, a use-after-free problem that affects NGINX when it accepts HTTP/2 connections and proxies requests to a backend. It impacts all versions from 1.19.7 through 1.31.8.

When the worker runs low on connection slots, it can close an active connection and free memory that a request still uses. Wiz also demonstrated remote code execution via CVE-2026-123633, but the firm is not publicly releasing its proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits at this time.

The other three flaws the researchers discovered and F5 fixed are CVE-2026-121810, CVE-2026-123634, and CVE-2026-113425, all use-after-free vulnerabilities affecting HTTP/3 reverse proxying, DNS resolution with subrequests, and mail proxy authentication, respectively.

The flaws were fixed in NGINX Open Source 1.30.7 stable and 1.31.9 mainline. NGINX Plus users should update to versions 37.0.8.1 or 37.3.0.1.

F5’s latest security update also addresses five more vulnerabilities not highlighted in the Wiz or Xint reports.

The most notable is CVE-2026-118899, a high-severity issue that allows an unauthenticated attacker to cause a worker to enter an infinite loop while reading a request body over TLS 1.3, resulting in denial of service.

For system administrators, it is recommended to upgrade immediately to the latest NGINX release, or temporarily disable HTTP/2 until an upgrade is possible. However, this mitigation only covers the two "nginx2root" flaws.

Evaluating the risk

Regarding the real exploitability risk of "nginx2root," security researcher Florian Roth says it's worse than Node2Shell and Java2Shell, but doesn’t appear to be an imminent threat for most NGINX deployments.

Commenting on X, Roth said the flaws are exploitable in non-default configurations, warning that claims of widespread exposure based solely on NGINX version numbers are misleading.

Xint previously reported that 98.9% of NGINX hosts disclosing recognizable versions were running software within the affected range, but this does not account for whether HTTP/2 is enabled or security fixes have been backported.

The two HTTP/2 flaws require an unpatched server with HTTP/2 enabled on a listener an attacker can reach, while CVE-2026-123633 also requires NGINX to proxy requests to a backend.

Roth scanned a sample of a few hundred NGINX HTTPS endpoints from Shodan and found that roughly 66% of them support HTTP/2, but confirming actual exposure requires checking the server’s configuration and whether a fix has been backported.

According to Censys' live exposure tracker, approximately 8.8 million NGINX services were potentially exposed to CVE-2026-123007 as of November 19, based on affected version numbers and HTTP/2 support.

The company reports that more than 511,000 previously exposed services have already been patched or mitigated, while another 104 million NGINX services do not disclose their versions, making it difficult to determine whether they are affected.

Title: European Commission Confirms AI-Driven Cyber-Attack Took Systems Offline
Context: He said the intrusion was detected on October 22, 2026, and confirmed as a cyber-attack on October 26, which triggered mitigation steps being carried out and an investigation...
Full Text:
The European Commission has confirmed it was hit by an AI-driven cyber-attack that resulted in services being taken offline.

Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier revealed the incident during a press briefing on November 19. He said the intrusion was detected on October 22, 2026, and confirmed as a cyber-attack on October 26, which triggered mitigation steps being carried out and an investigation launched.

“I can confirm that the Commission has recently taken necessary steps in response to a detected cyber campaign. As a protective and preventive measure, we temporarily took down several applications, and most of them have since then been restored,” Regnier said in response to a journalist question.

No information was given as to the potential perpetrators of the attack, or whether any data was accessed during the incident, with Regnier stating that the investigation was ongoing in response to questions on these points.

However, he said he was “not aware” of a ransomware demand being issued to the Commission and that the investigation has not detected “any evidence of a data breach affecting Commission staff.”

Regnier added that the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) has been notified about the attack.

In a statement emailed to Infosecurity after the press conference, a Commission spokesperson said the attack targeted “individual systems,” with impacted teams informed in line with standard practice.

“The Commission has been working to strengthen the security of its systems and continues to take appropriate measures. We are also preventively checking other systems while staying in close contact with CERT-EU and the EDPS. The investigation is still ongoing. We are taking any necessary steps based on the findings,” the spokesperson continued.

The comments follow a report published earlier in the day by Politico that the European Commission had been hit by a cyber-attack which may have breached the personal information of employees, and resulted in a number of systems being taken offline.

These included Sysper, an HR platform used by EU Commission staff members for payslips and time management and a system for medical reimbursements.

Commission Attack “AI Generated”

Regnier confirmed that the attack was “AI generated” involving the use of a “publicly available” tool.

“We have seen many global cyber-attacks recently and of course no one is immune to this, AI assisted tools can be used and especially misused to detect vulnerabilities. Indeed we can confirm that this was done with AI tools,” he said.

The Politico article claimed the attack had been launched using the Chinese AI penetration-testing tool ARTEX, which is believed to be widely used in campaigns over recent months.

Written in Go with an embedded Next.js web console, ARTEX offers an offensive command-and-control (C2) platform that communicates with several AI agents and can be plugged in to large language models (LLMs).

On November 5, CERT-EU, the EU’s cybersecurity emergency response team, warned that it had observed several threat actors around the world using ARTEX to automate their campaigns.

Similarly, an FBI Flash notice published on November 13 noted that a variety of malicious cyber actors have used ARTEX to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally since at least August 2026.

Commenting on the incident, Chris Dimitriadis, chief global strategy officer at ISACA, warned that AI is enabling attackers to hack “at the speed of intent”, which organizations from all sectors cannot keep pace with.

“Until organizations deploy AI defensively as fast as criminals deploy it aggressively, we will continue on this trajectory,” he said.

“In the short term, the Commission will investigate whether staff data has been compromised and what weakness hackers were able to use ARTEX to exploit. They should be bolstering their cybersecurity and building long-term resilience by investing in recruiting, training, and upskilling privacy professionals who can build defenses that are stronger than the AI tools now freely available to attackers.”

Title: Russian spies turn one cloud breach into a stepping stone for the next
Context: A Russian cyberespionage group is posing as employees of organizations it has already breached to phish new targets, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) found
Full Text:
A Russian cyberespionage group is posing as employees of organizations it has already breached to phish new targets, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) found.

Google tracks the group as COLD RELIC (also known as Star Blizzard, Callisto and Gossamer Bear), and the US Department of Justice has assessed that it operates within Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB).

COLD RELIC goes after government officials, defense contractors and NGOs in Europe and North America.

“The group is known for implementing sophisticated phishing and malware campaigns with the aim to gain access to information of strategic or political relevance to the Russian government, as well as to leverage compromised access to target compromised individuals’ broader social and professional networks,” researchers wrote.

The report’s authors say the group has drawn less public attention than other Russian groups while still breaking into high-value targets. “Once COLD RELIC compromises a target, it uses stolen emails and data to establish authentic pretexts and impersonate contacts when reaching out to subsequent targets,” they added.

A Super Admin account and a flood of MFA prompts

The first intrusion began with stolen credentials for a Super Admin account. The attackers logged in through a US residential proxy close to the victim’s location, so the sign-ins would not trigger alerts for impossible travel, and kept sending MFA push requests until the account holder approved one.

With admin rights in hand, they downloaded the contents of the organization’s entire cloud drive, exported employee lists and started a domain-wide data export through Google Workspace Customer Takeout. They searched the audit logs to see what defenders could see, and “viewed, modified, and deleted Alert Center notifications to remove forensic evidence of the initial intrusion.”

To keep their access, they enrolled passkeys, MFA backup codes and MFA devices of their own. They stayed inside for several months. During that time they synced inboxes to outside email clients, and their passkeys “persisted across password and session resets and bypassed device registration controls.”

Some employees had stored passwords in the company’s cloud storage, which made the damage worse. The attackers used those to get into other accounts, including employees’ personal accounts, “which are typically unmonitored by their employers.”

Even after the organization removed the intruders, GTIG observed COLD RELIC send phishing emails from accounts posing as its employees to their colleagues and to people in the same professional circles.

A familiar name on an encrypted messaging app

In 2026, someone posing as an employee of the first victim contacted a person at a second US organization over an encrypted messaging app. Partway through the conversation, the attacker shared phishing links.

“These phishing links, designed to steal credentials and authentication tokens for Entra ID, redirected the victim to document lures relevant to the ongoing conversation in order to avoid raising suspicion. Upon successful authentication using the stolen credentials, COLD RELIC registered and used a new MFA device in the SSO solution to retain access to the user account throughout the intrusion,” they explained.

“By impersonating someone known in the same professional circles as the new target, COLD RELIC increased their chance of phishing success.”

The group’s phishing links tied the two cases together. COLD RELIC usually sends targets through a compromised website that checks each visitor before passing them on to the phishing domain, and the attacker often adds a link parameter that names a previous victim or the lure. A redirector URL from the second intrusion was submitted to VirusTotal in June 2026, and its parameter referenced the first victim organization.

After the break-in, the attacker changed their profile name on the messaging app “to a completely new person.” GTIG believes the new persona was probably used to approach other organizations in the same circles.

Password resets weren’t enough

In at least one case, a victim spotted the intrusion and reset the passwords on affected accounts. COLD RELIC had hijacked sessions that were never revoked, so it kept its access, and Google warns that “password changes alone are insufficient.”

“COLD RELIC’s campaigns demonstrate the convergence of human-centric social engineering and cloud identity abuse. By obtaining access to strategic personnel rosters and operational documents, Russian intelligence services turn legitimate business communications into attack vectors against trusted partners. Their ability to navigate across multiple cloud ecosystems highlights that organizations must defend their entire identity estate holistically,” Google concluded.

Title: Drupal Patches Critical Installer Flaw That Could Give Unauthenticated Attackers Control of Sites
Context: Under specific conditions, a critical vulnerability in Drupal core can allow an attacker without login credentials to use the built-in installer to attempt to reinstall a site
Full Text:
Under specific conditions, a critical vulnerability in Drupal core can allow an attacker without login credentials to use the built-in installer to attempt to reinstall a site.

That can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution, and the project rates the vulnerable configurations as uncommon. Fixed releases for all supported branches shipped yesterday.

The Drupal Security Team disclosed the flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-132165, yesterday and rated it critical, 18 out of 25 on the project's risk scale.

The installer ships in every copy of Drupal core as the file /core/install.php and stays on the site after installation. Core's default .htaccess rules do not block requests to it, so blocking it is left to each site.

No attacks are reported in the security advisory, which rates exploitation as complex and records an existing proof-of-concept exploit. Some exploit paths are blocked where the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php.

The team had told site owners in an advance notice earlier this week to set aside time for the update, warning that exploits may be developed within hours or days.

Every release below 10.6.22 is affected, along with Drupal 11 releases from 11.0.0 before 11.3.22 and from 11.4.0 before 11.4.13.

What to Do Now

The fixed versions, detailed in the project's release notes, are:

Drupal 11.4.x: update to 11.4.13

Drupal 11.3.x: update to 11.3.22

Drupal 10.6.x: update to 10.6.22

The team recommends blocking the installer even after updating. Sites that cannot update yet should follow the project's installer guidance, updated yesterday, which describes three options: a deny rule in the web server configuration, an .htaccess rule, or removing the file and keeping it removed with Composer scripts.

Sites that use the Drupal Steward protection service are already protected from known attack vectors, according to the team, and should still update in case new vectors emerge.

Drupal 11.2.x and earlier, 10.5.x and earlier, and Drupal 8 and 9 are end-of-life and get no fix. The 11.3.x branch and Drupal 10 lose security coverage altogether in December under the project's support schedule.

In the week of November 8, 154,485 of the 528,430 sites reporting usage data to drupal.org, about 29 percent, were running end-of-life branches.

The flaw was found by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, an automated service the AI company launched on October 8 to look for vulnerabilities in open-source projects that opt in. Findings go to maintainers without human review, each with a reproducer and, where available, a candidate patch, according to its launch announcement.

Drupal's security team said on November 2 that a surge of security reports, which it attributes to AI tools, is more than it can sustain at its current funding, and that it is cutting security coverage for core minor versions from 12 months to 8 starting in 2027.

This is the second critical remote code execution flaw fixed in Drupal core in two months, after the Field UI flaw patched on October 14, which also had at least one exploit path that needed no login.

Title: Nvidia Responds to Gentlemen Ransomware Claim
Context: The group uses a double-extortion model in which attackers steal data and encrypt systems, threatening to publish the stolen information to pressure victims into paying
Full Text:
Nvidia says it has found no indication that its systems or networks were affected after the Gentlemen ransomware group named the company on its data leak website.

The group’s listing includes Nvidia’s logo and a general description of the chipmaker. It offers no explanation of the alleged attack, with the section about stolen information indicating that details will be provided later.

The company has acknowledged that it is investigating a possible security incident, but its statement points to a third party rather than Nvidia’s own infrastructure.

“Nvidia is investigating an incident that may have affected a third-party partner. We have found no indication that Nvidia systems or networks were affected. We continue to monitor the situation,” an Nvidia spokesperson told SecurityWeek.

The statement does not identify the partner or describe the nature of the incident. It also does not specify whether any Nvidia-related information may have been exposed.

The ransomware group’s listing does not establish that Nvidia was breached or that any of its data was stolen.

The Gentlemen ransomware operation emerged around mid-2025, initially operating as a closed group before launching an affiliate program later that year. Microsoft tracks its operators as Storm-2697.

The group uses a double-extortion model in which attackers steal data and encrypt systems, threatening to publish the stolen information to pressure victims into paying. Its affiliates have targeted organizations in numerous sectors, including manufacturing, healthcare, transportation, and financial services.

The Gentlemen has become increasingly active, with its leak website now listing more than 1,100 alleged victims.

According to Sophos, Gentlemen affiliates have used compromised credentials and legitimate administrative tools during intrusions. In one investigated incident, ransomware was deployed less than 24 hours after the earliest identified post-compromise activity.

Hackers Exploit Cisco Expressway Vulnerability Soon After PoC Release
Context: Hackers exploited a critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability to breach a Russian organization soon after proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit code was released publicly, according to...
Full Text:
Hackers exploited a critical Cisco Expressway vulnerability to breach a Russian organization soon after proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit code was released publicly, according to cybersecurity firm F6.

Expressway gateways allow remote employees, partners, and third-party users to securely connect to an organization’s collaboration services, including video calls, voice calls, and instant messaging.

Tracked as CVE-2026-76466 (CVSS score of 9.8), the flaw can be exploited without authentication by remote attackers with network access to a device, allowing them to execute commands as root. It affects virtual and appliance versions of Expressway Core and Expressway Edge, but only when the devices are clustered.

Cisco, which disclosed the issue on October 21, said it resides in the Expressway database service feature and stems from persistent cookies.

An attacker possessing the persistent cookies could reach the database service and issue certain remote procedure call (RPC) commands, gaining the ability to run root-level commands on the underlying operating system.

Expressway X15.5.20 resolves the vulnerability. There are no workarounds, and customers on X14 or earlier releases need to move to a fixed release, Cisco says.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

The advisory has not been revised since its initial release and still states that Cisco is unaware of public announcements or malicious use of the flaw. However, a PoC exploit has since been posted on GitHub, and F6 says the attack it investigated came shortly after.

According to F6, the attackers first breached two Expressway X15.5.3 devices exposed to the internet. They then pivoted from one of them to two other cluster nodes sitting on the organization’s internal network.

After securing root privileges, the attackers prepared tools for lateral movement. These included custom Python scripts designed to scan the network, locate SMB resources, interact with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories, aiming to exfiltrate credentials and other sensitive information.

F6 determined that the attackers modified the scripts on the fly, during the attack. “The source code contained characteristic comments and descriptions of fixes indicating the use of an AI assistant,” the company says.

F6 did not name the victim or attribute the attack to a known threat actor.

To detect exploitation, F6 points to the Erlang system log on Expressway devices. The security firm has also published IP addresses and file paths associated with the attack in a Russian-language press release.

Although Cisco lists no workarounds, F6 recommends that organizations unable to patch immediately block connections to TCP ports 4371–4372 at the firewall, except from the IP addresses of trusted cluster nodes.

SecurityWeek has reached out to Cisco for comment on F6’s findings and will update this article if the company responds.

Title: Drupal patches critical RCE flaw, warns exploits may surface quickly
Context: On Wednesday, Drupal also addressed a moderately critical gadget chain vulnerability (CVE-2026-132166) that attackers with admin privileges can exploit to gain remote code...
Full Text:
The Drupal Security Team has patched a critical remote code execution vulnerability that can let attackers take over vulnerable sites.

This content management system (CMS) is commonly used by large organizations that manage multi-site installations and massive data structures, including government entities, educational organizations, major research universities, and high-profile enterprise and media organizations.

The security flaw (tracked as CVE-2026-132165) was discovered by Anthropic's OSS Scanner, and anonymous users can exploit it to reinstall the Drupal CMS.

"Drupal core ships with an install.php file for installing Drupal core. Under specific conditions, an attacker can use the installer to attempt to reinstall Drupal. This can lead to a site takeover or remote code execution," the Drupal Security Team warned in a Wednesday advisory. "Some exploit paths are mitigated if the web server cannot write to or change permissions on settings.php."

Admins whose websites use the paid Drupal Steward Web Application Firewall (WAF) service are already protected from known attack vectors, but should still upgrade to Drupal 10.6.22, 11.3.22, or 11.4.13 in case other attack vectors are discovered.

Those who can't immediately upgrade should secure the Drupal installer by blocking access to /core/install.php in the web server configuration or the .htaccess file in the web root.

On Wednesday, Drupal also addressed a moderately critical gadget chain vulnerability (CVE-2026-132166) that attackers with admin privileges can exploit to gain remote code execution on a targeted site if the application deserializes untrusted data due to another security flaw.

"The Drupal Security Team urges you to reserve time for core updates at that time because exploits might be developed within hours or days," the security team said in a Monday advance warning. "The vulnerabilities are currently rated as critical and at least one can be exploited by anonymous users."

In May, Drupal also confirmed that attackers were actively exploiting an SQL injection vulnerability (CVE-2026-9082) in the database abstraction API that could let them escalate privileges, access sensitive information, or achieve remote code execution on unpatched servers.

More recently, Drupal warned that a critical access bypass vulnerability (CVE-2026-118539) in the Commerce Core module is being abused in attacks.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has flagged 5 Drupal vulnerabilities as exploited in the wild since November 2021, two of which have also been abused in ransomware attacks.

Title: Exploited Puppet flaw puts the server that configures your endpoint fleet at risk (CVE-2026-115731)
Context: Attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-115731, a critical remote code execution vulnerability in Perforce Puppet Enterprise, an enterprise solution used by IT teams to centralize and...
Full Text:
Attackers are exploiting CVE-2026-115731, a critical remote code execution vulnerability in Perforce Puppet Enterprise, an enterprise solution used by IT teams to centralize and automatize endpoint management.

Details about the in-the-wild attacks have yet to be made public, but the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Tuesday and ordered US federal civilian agencies to address it by December 1, 2026.

Perforce Puppet explained

Perforce Puppet works on a client-server model: a central Puppet Server holds the configuration code that describes how each managed machine should be set up, and a Puppet agent installed on every endpoint periodically checks in with the server, retrieves its configuration and applies it.

Agents and server authenticate each other with certificates issued by the Puppet Server’s own certificate authority (CA).

About CVE-2026-115731

CVE-2026-115731 is a deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability in Puppet’s report-processing code, i.e., the part of Puppet Server that ingests the reports agents send back after each configuration run.

A client holding any certificate signed by the Puppet CA can submit a report containing a crafted rich-data type via a PUT request and get the server to execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the Puppet Server service user, CISA explained.

It might seem that requiring a signed agent certificate is a meaningful barrier to exploitation, but if the CA signs certificate requests without strong verification (e.g., when autosigning is enabled) an unauthenticated attacker on the network could obtain a certificate and exploit the flaw.

“If exploited, this vulnerability could allow an attacker to run arbitrary code on the Puppet Server with the privileges of its service account. This could give the attacker access to sensitive data held on the server (Confidentiality), let them modify data and configuration on the server (Integrity), or disrupt the service (Availability),” Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium noted.

Patch and check for evidence of compromise

CVE-2026-115731 affects:

Puppet Enterprise 2023.8.0 before 2023.8.13, 2025.0.0 before 2025.12.1, and 2026.0.0 before 2026.0.1

Puppet Core 8.x before 8.22.2 and 9.0.0 before 9.1.3

OpenVox, a community-maintained open-source Puppet fork, is also affected: OpenVox Agent versions before 9.3.0 and 8.32.0 and OpenVox Server versions before 9.2.0 and 8.18.0 are vulnerable.

Perforce released security updates fixing CVE-2026-115731 and CVE-2026-115732, a certificate name authorization bypass flaw that was also reported by Alain Rödel of Neodyme AG, on November 3.

“Customers should upgrade to the latest applicable security release and then restart the server as soon as possible. Fixed versions are Puppet Enterprise/Advanced 2026.0.1, 2025.12.1, or 2023.8.13, and Puppet Core 9.1.3 or 8.22.2,” the company said and advised customers who are unable to upgrade immediately to review their autosign configuration and authorization rules as a temporary mitigation.

Patching should be a priority for any organization that relies on autosigning or whose Puppet Server is reachable from untrusted networks (it listens on port 8140 by default).

Admins should also check the list of signed certificates for nodes they don’t recognize and look for unexpected processes, files or outbound connections tied to the Puppet Server service user.

If the server shows signs of compromise, patching is not enough: the CA should be treated as compromised and rebuilt.

The OpenVox project’s GitHub advisory, published alongside the fixes, includes a proof-of-concept malicious report (in the form of a JSON event) that runs a shell command on the OpenVox / Puppet server.

“In configuration with autosign (which is common for enterprise deployment), this is an unauthenticated attack chain to compromise the OpenVox / Puppet server, as a valid cert can be requested via the OpenVox / Puppet client enrollment endpoint,” the maintainers noted.

“Code execution as puppet gives access to the CA signing key. This allows the attacker to sign certificates with EKU critical, serverAuth, clientAuth, which could enable direct command execution on other hosts if certain kinds of orchestration is configured.”

Title: Credential stealer slipped into Microsoft’s official Python agent framework
Context: “PyPI has quarantined both releases, but the attacker demonstrated continued publishing access by uploading 1
Full Text:
Two releases of Microsoft’s official agent-framework package on the Python Package Index (PyPI) carried code that steals cloud and CI/CD credentials from developers’ systems. Agent Framework is Microsoft’s open-source toolkit for building AI agents and running them in workflows.

Three supply chain security companies, StepSecurity, OX Security and Socket, caught the malicious versions and shared their analysis.

“On November 17, 2026, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 of the official Microsoft agent-framework package on PyPI were published carrying a credential-stealing payload. The payload is installed as a .pth startup hook, so it executes during Python startup in an affected environment when the interpreter processes the installed hook, with no import of the framework required,” wrote StepSecurity.

“PyPI has quarantined both releases, but the attacker demonstrated continued publishing access by uploading 1.26.2 after 1.26.1 was already quarantined,” they added.

With 192,534 monthly downloads, according to OX, the package has a wide reach. Agent-framework 1.26.0 is the last clean release. Both rigged versions kept their dependency on the genuine agent-framework-core 1.26.0, so the framework worked as usual while the credential stealer ran in the background.

In the second release, the attacker restored Microsoft’s original package initializer and moved the hook into a new file named af_runtime_diag.pth, which makes the change harder to spot.

Attack overview (Source: OX Security)

Stored secrets and new tokens

The stealer collects environment variables with names containing strings such as TOKEN, SECRET, AZURE, AWS and GITHUB. It reads the environments of up to 300 other processes and copies .env files along with credential files for Azure CLI, pip, npm, Git, Docker and Hugging Face.

It also asks cloud services for new tokens. “They actively request fresh Azure managed-identity and CI federation tokens,” Socket’s researchers noted. Version 1.26.2 added GitHub Actions OIDC tokens to the list. StepSecurity cautioned that the code only attempts these requests, and there is no confirmation that any tokens were issued.

The haul is compressed, encoded and sent to a webhook.site endpoint in a single request.

Build systems as credentials

Eric Paulsen, Field CTO, EMEA at Coder, says the token requests change how teams should respond.

“A build system that can ask a cloud provider for new access tokens is itself a credential, and this attack treated it as one. Replacing stored passwords and keys is therefore an incomplete response, as an attacker who can request new tokens does not need those passwords and keys,” he told Help Net Security.

“The attack worked because installing a package is an act of trust. Once a package is installed, Python runs certain files automatically every time it starts, so compromised code executes whether or not anyone uses the package. By the time anyone checks it, the code has already run.”

His advice is to limit what such code can reach. “Start by installing dependencies from an internal mirror of approved versions, not straight from the public index. Then make sure builds run in environments that are deleted after each job, and that any credentials they use expire within the hour. Finally, block outbound connections to anything that isn’t on an approved list. If you do those things, a compromised package has very little to steal and nowhere to send it.”

Anyone who installed either version should isolate the affected hosts and runners before running Python or pip again, rebuild from a clean base and pin agent-framework to 1.26.0, StepSecurity advises.

OX recommends treating “every secret reachable from that host as compromised.” StepSecurity warns that rotating stored secrets won’t cancel identity tokens that were already issued, so teams should also review OIDC permissions, federated credentials and managed-identity role assignments.

None of the reports explain how the attacker got publishing rights.
