On November 17, Google issued a security update to Chrome’s Stable channel for Windows, Mac, and Linux. The update is rolling out over the coming days and weeks.

Most users are on Chrome’s Stable channel. The desktop update brings Chrome to versions 158.0.8127.36/.37 for Windows and Mac, and 158.0.8127.36 for Linux. It includes 204 security fixes, six of which are rated critical—the highest severity level.

Google also released Chrome 158.0.8127.42 for Android on November 17, with the same security fixes. It’s rolling out through Google Play. On November 18, Google released Chrome 159.0.8154.18 for Android to a small percentage of users. It will become available to more users over the next few days.

Google credits Anthropic researcher Xinyang Ge, assisted by Claude, with finding the critical GPU and Media flaws. Ge is also credited with finding several high-severity flaws.

How to update Chrome

The easiest option is to allow Chrome to update automatically. But you can fall behind on updates if you never close your browser or if something goes wrong, such as an extension preventing the update.

If you don’t want to wait for the rollout to reach you, you can update manually.

Open About Google Chrome from Chrome’s Settings or Help menu. Chrome will check for updates and download any available update. If prompted, click Relaunch to apply it.

Chrome is up to date

You can find an explanation of the version numbering system and step-by-step instructions in our guide: How to update Chrome on every operating system.

Technical details

The update addresses six vulnerabilities Google rates critical, all involving memory-safety errors. These include out-of-bounds writes in GPU and ANGLE, a buffer overflow in Media, and use-after-free vulnerabilities in WebView, GarbageCollection, and WebAudio.

Graphics-related fixes also feature prominently among the high-severity entries, including additional ANGLE and GPU vulnerabilities.

I want to have a closer look at the vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-131031: a critical out-of-bounds write in GPU.

Google Chrome uses your GPU for graphics rendering, video playback, and web graphics Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) like WebGL and WebGPU.

An out-of-bounds write vulnerability allows a program to write outside the memory boundaries it is supposed to use. It can lead to memory corruption or allow an attacker to place malicious code in memory and trick the system into running it.

Title: Critical Apache Roller, Axis Vulnerabilities Exploited in Attacks
Context: Roughly twelve hours after the first exploit request, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 using an integration service account
Full Text:
Two critical vulnerabilities in Apache software are being exploited in attacks, and CISA added one of them to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on Wednesday.

Apache Axis vulnerability exploited in attacks

CVE-2026-90436, disclosed on November 6, is an unsafe reflection vulnerability in Apache Axis 1.x, an end-of-life Java-based SOAP implementation. The flaw has a CVSS score of 9.8 and can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable systems.

Rapid7 detected exploitation on November 13 in a customer environment running Atlassian Confluence Data Center. The attacker executed hundreds of commands, accessed Confluence’s database using the application’s credentials, and searched for sensitive information.

Within four hours of the initial exploitation, the attacker had obtained a service account credential and was querying a production cloud data warehouse. Roughly twelve hours after the first exploit request, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 using an integration service account.

Rapid7 also cited N-able’s report of attacks against N-central involving a vulnerability strongly correlated with CVE-2026-90436. Both Confluence and N-central require non-default configurations to be vulnerable.

Separately, Previdian reported detecting 50 exploitation attempts from 14 IP addresses between November 12 and 19. Its sensor data does not establish whether those attempts succeeded.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Apache does not plan to release a fixed Axis 1.x version and recommends migrating to another SOAP engine or applying its published patch.

Confluence Data Center users can upgrade to version 9.2.28 or an unaffected 10.x release. N-central 2026.4 HF3 disables the Legacy API functionality that exposes the vulnerable Axis component.

CISA has added CVE-2026-90436 to its KEV catalog, instructing federal agencies to address it by November 21.

Apache Roller vulnerability also exploited

Apache has also confirmed active exploitation of CVE-2026-129448, a CVSS 9.8 vulnerability affecting versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 of its Java-based blogging platform Roller. The flaw allows unauthenticated remote code execution.

“This issue is being actively exploited,” Apache said in its November 17 advisory, without providing further information about the attacks.

The vulnerability stems from unsafe deserialization in Roller’s XML-RPC interface, which processes malicious data before authentication. Disabling XML-RPC through the application’s administration interface does not prevent exploitation.

Apache initially disclosed the same underlying vulnerability in September as CVE-2026-82384.

“This is the same vulnerability as CVE-2026-82384, which listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected,” Apache explained.

The flaw was fixed in Roller 6.1.6. Apache recommends upgrading to that version or later. Version 6.1.7, released on November 11, addresses another 15 vulnerabilities.

Title: The Governance Gap in Open-Weight AI and What to Do About It
Context: Renting Capability Vs
Full Text:
Open-weight AI has gone mainstream. As of September 2026, some estimates suggest 42% of enterprises surveyed were running open-weight models in production, up from 31% just two months earlier. But downloading a model also means taking on responsibilities that a provider might otherwise handle, and many organizations have yet to put clear ownership and controls in place.

Renting Capability Vs. Running Your Own Copy

When you use an AI model through a provider’s app or service, you’re essentially renting its capabilities. The provider controls the model and handles the infrastructure, updates, and safety controls. You access it through an app or a software connection.

An open-weight AI model makes its learned parameters, the ‘weights’ that shape its behavior, available to download and run yourself. You can run the model on your own infrastructure and adapt it for a particular use case using your own data. The license may limit how you can use it, and running it still carries infrastructure and staffing costs.

Open-weight models are becoming more capable. One estimate puts the best open-weight models roughly four months behind leading models.

Open-weight does not necessarily mean open-source. Access to the weights does not guarantee access to the training code or details of the training data.

When Benefits Clash with Risks

Zoey is a bank analyst using a provider-hosted model to summarize a loan application. The model does a good job of delivering an actionable summary, but to do so, her request, loan file included, has to go to the provider’s servers. The customer’s data is no longer solely in the bank’s hands. A few quarters later, the provider raises its prices and changes its policies in ways that force workflow changes. Switching providers would take time and effort, so Zoey and her team have little choice but to go along, even though it hurts both their budget and their operations.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

Let’s look at the same scenario from the perspective of an open-weight model that is running on the bank’s server. If the model is configured to run entirely within the bank’s system, the loan file can stay there too. The bank can apply its own access controls to the model and the data.

In the above example, an open-weight model does seem like a good option, but there are risks that are easy to overlook:

Trojan horses: Some model files can execute malicious code when loaded. Others may contain hidden behavior that a particular input can trigger.

An origin story with missing chapters: A popular model on a public repository may not be the developer’s original. Someone may have modified and reuploaded it without explaining what changed. That version could contain a hidden backdoor or have weak safety rules.

The upgrade won’t knock on your door: A developer may release improved versions, but your copy is not updated automatically. Your team must track updates, test them, and decide when to switch.

Attack surface just got bigger: Running your own model creates new targets for attackers. You are essentially adding to your IT infrastructure. This includes the servers and GPUs that keep the model running and the systems that retrain it.

Controls to Address Risks

If an open-weight AI model makes sense for your organization, governance should walk in lockstep with deployment:

Set a regular review schedule for updates and security notices. Decide who approves a move to a new version.

Assign an owner for each model, with clear responsibility for approving its use, reviewing updates, and responding when something goes wrong.

Record each model’s source, version, license, and every fine-tune. Also record its file hash. It’s a unique fingerprint that changes if anyone alters the file.

Give teams an approved internal repository to fetch models. Before adding a model, verify its source and check its file fingerprint or digital signature against a trusted reference.

The rule of thumb should be: ‘trust after testing.’ Test the model as an attacker might. Try to bypass its safety rules and look for unexpected behavior, including whether it produces insecure code.

If you do choose to download a modified version, run the same tests on the developer’s original. This may help reveal weak safeguards or unexpected behavior.

Higher-risk models need more control. For example, a model that reads source code should also run in isolation, with no access to passwords or keys, and a person assigned to review its output.

Run the model on a separate server while giving it only the access it needs. Monitor all requests and outputs for unusual behavior, while protecting sensitive information in the logs. If you think a model is misbehaving, have a backup in the form of an earlier version you can switch back to quickly.

Open-weight models need to be scrutinized like any other software brought inhouse. Their benefits are clearly driving their popularity, but there are tradeoffs to be aware of. It’s wise to put ownership and controls in place before putting them into production.

Title: Everything Is a Web Application, Including Your Firewall
Context: On October 28, Palo Alto Networks confirmed that attackers were exploiting the two PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, against PAN-OS management interfaces...
Full Text:
One of the early targets of PHP2Shell exploitation was the firewall. On October 28, Palo Alto Networks confirmed that attackers were exploiting the two PHP vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, against PAN-OS management interfaces exposed to the internet. Both flaws let anyone execute code on the web server without authentication. The disclosure itself went a little wrong. Details leaked on October 20, ahead of the coordinated release, and the PHP project shipped an emergency patch the next day.

The vulnerabilities require no authentication, but they are not easy to exploit reliably. It takes skill and additional knowledge about the target system. Where it matters a lot is appliances, which run identical, often outdated software that an attacker can study in advance. That is the bigger picture. An awful lot of web applications control critical devices in your network. Almost anything is a web application to some extent. That often goes unrecognized, and as a result those applications aren't adequately protected.

Everything is a web application. That is the motto of the SANS course I teach, SEC522: Application Security: Securing Web Applications, APIs, and Microservices. Web application security has traditionally been treated as a developer issue, yet anyone protecting a network must understand how web applications work to properly defend them.

Why Appliances Are the Softer Target

On ordinary web servers, address space layout randomization (ASLR) is one of the features that makes exploitation harder. It shuffles where code and data sit in memory, so an exploit can't rely on fixed addresses. VulnCheck's early analysis found the bugs exploitable on ARM64 systems and on x86 systems without ASLR. Few public exploits bypassed ASLR on x86-64, and the one VulnCheck confirmed worked only against a single PHP build. VulnCheck's own exploit chained a memory leak to get code execution with ASLR enabled.

Appliances change that math, not because the protections are missing, but because every device on a given software version runs the same binaries, so an attacker can work out memory offsets in advance. The PAN-OS exploit still had to defeat ASLR, leaking the libphp.so base address through the Set-Cookie header, and SELinux confined the resulting shell. PAN-OS also ships end-of-life PHP versions (8.0.30 and 7.4.33). Israeli security firm Dream, working with Palo Alto Networks on the investigation, found the attacker had obtained PAN-OS firmware, decrypted it, extracted the PHP libraries, and built precise memory profiles for nine software versions. The actor then chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel flaw (Fragnesia, CVE-2026-46300) to gain root on 25 systems (24 firewalls and one management server) in the U.S., Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea.

Web application security tends to focus on large, cloud-based applications. It's often the little things, the mosquitoes on the internet, that do you in. Appliances run predictable, often outdated software, and they are everywhere.

HTTP Is More Complex Than Your Defenses Assume

HTTP is a very complex protocol with lots of options. To upload a file, a client doesn't have to send it in one piece. It can send the body in chunks without declaring its total length, and, if the server decompresses request bodies, compress it, which makes it difficult for a web server to calculate how much memory it needs to store it. Memory-safety bugs remain common as a result, in web applications and in the web servers running them. In PHP2Shell, a crafted multipart upload pushes PHP past its memory limit while it is still parsing the request, before any application code runs. The bugs are in what PHP leaves behind when it aborts the request: uninitialized request memory (CVE-2026-109618) and a pointer to freed memory (CVE-2026-109619). The request doesn't need to be large, either. Deeply nested, empty file fields make PHP allocate far more memory than the body contains, so a request well under the default 8 MB post_max_size can still exhaust the default 128 MB memory limit.

Defenders must understand the protocol to know what these vulnerabilities look like, for example to write signatures that detect the exploits. The same complexity limits the middle boxes we rely on. They can even interfere in ways nobody planned. Intruder found that nginx in front of PAN-OS buffered chunked request bodies, which broke public exploit chains. Web application firewalls are often not adequate, and file uploads are key functionality for a lot of web applications, so blocking them outright isn't an option.

That takes out many of the traditional defenses. What remains is knowing where your critical web applications are. Identify them, starting with the admin interfaces on your firewalls and other network equipment, and restrict access to them. Palo Alto's own guidance for PHP2Shell was to remove internet access to management interfaces and limit them to trusted internal IP addresses. If you rely on a web application firewall, configure it properly and understand how much protection it does and doesn't provide.

Risk Was the Hardest Call

The clearest lesson from PHP2Shell is how difficult it can be to accurately determine the risk from a vulnerability like this. Prioritization is always a big issue for defenders, particularly with today's flood of vulnerabilities, and this one was hard to read from every angle.

The scores told different stories. The PHP project rated both flaws 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, and Fortinet's PSIRT listed 9.8 under CVSS v3. Palo Alto initially scored the issue 8.7 for its own products and listed it at moderate urgency, raised it to 9.2 Critical with the highest urgency on October 27, and confirmed exploitation a week after its advisory went out. Many public proofs of concept didn't work, so a flood of attempts in your logs said little about whether a given server was at risk. And PHP core developer Gina Peter Banyard warned that one early workaround, turning off session upload progress, was not enough on its own.

We are adding these lessons to SEC522: how to assess risk, how protections like ASLR reduce it, and why appliances remain softer targets.

Defending What Runs on HTTP

I will be teaching SEC522: Application Security: Securing Web Applications, APIs, and Microservices at SANS Cyber Defense Initiative 2026, December 14-18 in Washington, D.C., and Live Online. The course starts with how HTTP works, including HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, and covers file upload handling, API security, and AI endpoints across 17 hands-on labs and a Defend the Flag capstone. It is built for the people who defend web applications, whether or not they wrote them.

Register for SEC522 at SANS Cyber Defense Initiative 2026.

Title: Microsoft tests new Edge Lockdown Mode that disables GPU APIs
Context: ​Microsoft is developing a new Edge security feature to reduce the attack surface by disabling the WebGL, WebGL2, and WebGPU APIs
Full Text:
​Microsoft is developing a new Edge security feature to reduce the attack surface by disabling the WebGL, WebGL2, and WebGPU APIs.

Inspired by Apple's Lockdown Mode, the new feature shares the same name and builds on Edge Enhanced Security Mode (also known internally as Super Duper Secure Mode), which disables Just-In-Time Compilation (JIT) from the V8 processing pipeline.

The new Edge Lockdown Mode offers optional, extreme protections for users facing highly targeted attacks who are willing to sacrifice website compatibility for stronger defenses.

"Lockdown Mode is designed for users who are at particular risk of being targeted in cybersecurity campaigns. This may include journalists, executives, security researchers, and administrators," said Partner Security Group Manager Gareth Evans.

"Individuals whose threat model justifies accepting reduced compatibility in exchange for stronger protection. It may also apply to devices operating within highly restricted environments."

Evans also warned that websites that use the disabled APIs (especially those with interactive graphics like games or maps) may not work as expected when this security feature is toggled on.

Edge users can test Lockdown Mode by switching to the Canary release channel, enabling the #edge-sdsm-plus flag, restarting the browser, then toggling on Strict mode for "Enhance your security on the web" and blocking WebGL graphics and WebGPU graphics.

After enabling it, users will see a new "Lockdown Enabled" indicator in the address bar when WebGL or WebGPU is blocked on a web page.

​While the current Edge Canary Lockdown Mode blocks websites from using WebGL, WebGL2, and WebGPU APIs to stop attacks that try to escalate privileges and escape the sandbox, Microsoft plans to extend the feature in upcoming releases.

"The initial set of Lockdown Mode mitigations focus is the GPU process, a more privileged component that handles complex graphics workloads across browser code, third-party libraries, and device drivers," Evans added.

"Results from this experiment will inform the finished Lockdown Mode experience, including clearer descriptions of restricted capabilities and site-level exceptions that restore trusted sites without weakening protection everywhere else."

According to the company's estimates, this new security feature would have blocked around 60% of privilege escalation attacks targeting Edge users in the wild.

Last year, Microsoft also introduced a new Edge scareware sensor to ensure Defender SmartScreen blocks scam pages faster, and restricted access to Edge's Internet Explorer mode after learning that hackers were leveraging zero-day exploits in the Chakra JavaScript engine to access target devices.

Title: Cyberattack on service provider exposes payee data at 40 Irish credit unions
Context: Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4
Full Text: An attack on software provider Wellington IT exposed saved payee details held by around 40 Irish credit unions, prompting a minister to criticize the company's delay in notifying them. Robert Troy, Ireland's minister of state with responsibility for credit unions, said the breach happened in October but many affected institutions only learned of it in recent days. Troy told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the breach occurred "sometime in October," and Wellington IT's delay in providing details to its credit union customers was "not acceptable." News of the issues affecting Irish credit unions broke on Tuesday, although the government said at the time it was only investigating a "possible cybersecurity incident" in the first instance, and did not name Wellington IT until Wednesday. Affected credit unions said attackers exploited a vulnerability in their provider's online banking platform between October 2 and 4. The flaw was closed on October 6. Troy said the affected credit unions were only informed for the first time in recent days. The exposed records concern payees saved in members' online banking accounts. Those records can also be linked to the members who created them. The information exposed varies between institutions and individual records, but disclosures list the following data types: Names on payee bank accounts and saved nicknames Business Identifier Codes (BICs) International Bank Account Numbers (IBANs) Sort codes Payment references Internal reference numbers that do not identify customers Payee addresses Credit unions including St. Canice's said online banking passwords, PINs, and login credentials were unaffected, and that the exposed payee details did not provide access to members' accounts or funds. St. Canice's warned members not to transfer money in response to anyone claiming it needed to be moved to safety because of the breach. The CEO of Belfast-based Wellington IT, Colin Mitchell, said in a statement that the company notified the affected organizations "as soon as we confirmed the potential risk to customer data." He said Wellington IT has engaged outside cybersecurity experts to help investigate the breach, and reported the matter to the relevant authorities. Mitchell added: "We are directly supporting our customers in their assessment of the potential impact on affected individuals and to help them meet any applicable regulatory obligations. "We recognize the importance of this matter to our customers and their members and are treating it with the utmost seriousness. We remain focused on completing a thorough investigation and communicating directly with our customers as the investigation progresses." Owned by Canadian company Vencora, Wellington IT has offices in Belfast and Dublin, and provides credit unions with software, mobile apps, private cloud infrastructure, and fully managed services. Around 40 credit unions in Ireland were affected, roughly a quarter of the national total, Troy said. Credit unions operate similarly to traditional banks, offering savings accounts and loans, but are owned by their members and are not-for-profit organizations. Troy told RTÉ that cybersecurity is a constant challenge for financial institutions, as technology and threats evolve over time. "What's most important is that financial institutions take all the right measures to mitigate against these threats and that is what is happening," he said. Separately, the UK's Financial Conduct Authority, Prudential Regulation Authority, and Bank of England opened a joint consultation on cyber resilience guidance on Thursday. The FCA said October brought its second-highest monthly tally of reported cyber incidents in five years, and the highest in 18 months. The proposed guidance clarifies how firms should meet existing requirements rather than introducing new rules. ®

Title: TfL Warns 265,000 Photocard Customers May Have Had Personal Data Exposed
Context: Commenting on the incident, Jamie Akhtar, CEO and co-founder at CyberSmart, warned that cybercriminals could use the compromised details to launch convincing phishing emails or...
Full Text:
Transport for London (TfL) has been impacted by a cyber incident, which may have exposed the personal data of around 265,000 photocard customers.

On November 16, unauthorized actors sent emails to Oyster Photocard customers from TfL’s system. TfL said these emails were “generated as a result of the compromise.”

The emails asked customers to create an account, despite them already having a photocard account.

In a statement shared with Infosecurity, Shashi Verma, TfL’s director of technology strategy & revenue, said the organization immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated.

"While we acted swiftly, we now believe that around 265,000 photocard customers may have had their account details compromised as part of this incident,” he warned.

Oyster photocards are personalized smartcards which can be used by eligible customers for free or discounted travel across public transport in London.

Customers whose account details were potentially compromised include children with Zip Oyster cards, whose ages range from 5-18. However, Verma said he does not believe the names or date of births of any children with a Zip Oyster card have been compromised.

Other customer accounts that may have been affected are those who have 18+ Student Oyster cards, 18-25 Care Leaver Oyster photocards, 60+ London Oyster photocards, Apprentice Oyster photocards and Veterans Oyster photocard.

TfL’s current assessment is that no passwords, bank or payment card details or customer journey information were accessed in the breach.

Verma added that TfL, which manages most of London’s public transport network, has now contained the incident.

“Due to the speed with which this incident was identified and addressed, we believe that the number of customers who could have been affected was significantly reduced,” he said.

“We are continuing to investigate what has happened but have already contacted affected customers to make them aware of this,” Verma continued.

The body has informed the UK’s data protection regulator, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO), of the incident.

TfL Customers Urged to Change Passwords

While there is currently no evidence that the affected data has been misused, TfL said it will be asking all photocard customers to change their password, security question and answer. It also advises customers to change their password on any other online service using the same information.

Commenting on the incident, Jamie Akhtar, CEO and co-founder at CyberSmart, warned that cybercriminals could use the compromised details to launch convincing phishing emails or text messages impersonating TfL.

“Account holders should be particularly cautious of unexpected communications, avoid clicking suspicious links and always verify messages through TfL's official website or customer service channels,” Akhtar said.

The TfL photocard website remains offline at the time of writing and displays the following message: “We are currently investigating an issue where photocard customers have received emails asking them to create an account, when they already have a Photocard account. We have temporarily taken the TfL Photocard portal down while this is being investigated and apologise for any inconvenience this may cause.”

Current Oyster photocard customers can continue to travel as normal, while any customer who need to renew their photocard or query any journey history can still do so by contacting TfL’s Customer Services.

Verma said TfL hopes to restore the affected website services “as quickly as possible.”

TfL was previously impacted by a cyber-attack in September 2024, resulting in customer data being breached. This included Oyster refund data, encompassing bank account numbers and sort codes for around 5000 customers.

Two individuals, Owen Flowers, 18, and Thalha Jubair, 20, were each sentenced to five years and six months in prison after being convicted of offenses relating to the attack in July 2026, which the judge said was motivated in part by “selfish bravado” rather than purely financial gain.

Title: TfL takes Oyster photocard website offline after attackers compromise customer accounts
Context: The capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them...
Full Text: Transport for London (TfL) has copped to another cybersecurity breach, this time involving the account details of around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers. The capital's transport operator told The Register it first became aware something was amiss on November 16, when Oyster photocard customers started receiving emails asking them to create accounts they already had. The emails came from TfL's own systems, the transport body confirmed, but were generated as a result of the compromise. "We immediately took the TfL photocard website down while this was being investigated," said Shashi Verma, TfL's director of technology strategy and revenue. "The protection of personal information is a priority for us, and I apologize to our customers affected by this incident." TfL reckons its speedy response spared a considerable number of customers from having their details compromised. The transport operator says it has since contained the incident and contacted those potentially affected, though it is rather more forthcoming about what the hackers didn't get their hands on than what they did. TfL says no passwords, bank or payment card details, or customer journey information were compromised. It also believes the names and dates of birth of children with Zip Oyster cards were unaffected. Among those whose accounts may have been compromised are holders of Zip Oyster cards – issued to children as young as five – as well as students, apprentices, care leavers, veterans, and Londoners aged 60 and over. Despite the assurances about passwords, TfL says it will ask all photocard customers to change theirs, along with their security questions and answers. Those in the habit of recycling passwords across multiple websites are being advised to change them elsewhere, too. TfL says it has yet to find any evidence that the compromised data has been used and has notified the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). The transport operator hasn't disclosed how the perpetrators got into its systems. Existing photocards will still let holders through the ticket barriers, though anyone needing to renew one or check their journey history will have to contact TfL's customer services team while the website is out of action. There's no word yet on when it'll be back. "We hope to restore the affected website services as quickly as possible," Verma said. TfL should be well versed in dealing with data breaches by now. In March, the transport operator told The Register it had notified more than 7 million customers following its September 2024 cyberattack. The hackers had accessed systems holding customers' names, email addresses, and home addresses, while around 5,000 customers were contacted as a priority because their bank account details may also have been compromised. Two teenagers were subsequently charged in connection with the attack, which authorities linked to the notorious Scattered Spider cybercrime crew. The ICO looked into that incident but opted not to take enforcement action against TfL, having deemed its response proportionate. There's nothing at present to suggest the two incidents are related. Londoners can at least rest assured that their Oyster photocards still work. Whether the information they handed over to obtain them is in someone else's hands is another matter. ®

Title: Microsoft confirms app installation, launch issues after hotpatch
Context: Microsoft first announced Windows Autopatch in April 2002, saying it would be available for free to customers with a Windows 10/11 Enterprise E3 license or greater starting in...
Full Text:
Microsoft has shared a workaround for installation and launch issues affecting Office and third-party applications after installing this month's Windows 11 hotpatch.

In a service alert seen by BleepingComputer, Microsoft told IT administrators that these problems may appear during installation, launch, or even during normal app use on systems running Windows 11 24H2 and later.

"Devices which installed the November 2026 hotpatch update (the Originating KBs listed above), might experience an error when installing, launching, or running some applications. Resulting from this issue, errors similar to "ERROR_ALLOTTED_SPACE_EXCEEDED (0xC0000099)" are displayed," Microsoft said.

"Current investigation suggests this issue occurs for applications which load the 32-bit Windows Installer DLL, found as msi.dll. This can happen more frequently with 32-bit applications, but can also occur for 64-bit applications under certain conditions."

Microsoft added that this known issue should not impact systems that have installed the standard November 2026 Patch Tuesday security updates, but only those that have installed the hotpatch updates pushed through the Windows Autopatch, the company's cloud-based enterprise service that automates Windows and Microsoft 365 software and security updates.

Until a fix is available, Microsoft has shared a workaround to help IT admins temporarily mitigate the bug on affected systems.

To do that, they have to edit the Windows Registry to increase the HotPatchTableSize using the following procedure:

Open the Windows Registry by opening the Start menu, typing "regedit", and selecting Registry Editor from the results.

Using the folders and address path, navigate to the HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management folder.

In the right-hand panel, locate the "HotPatchTableSize" registry key, open it, and set the Value to "2000". Click OK.

Close the registry editor and restart the device.

"Before you modify the registry, back it up and make sure that you know how to restore it if a problem occurs. For more information, see How to back up and restore the registry in Windows," Microsoft said.

Microsoft said in March that it would turn on hotpatch security updates by default for all eligible Windows devices managed through the Microsoft Graph API and Microsoft Intune, after the May 2026 Windows security updates are installed.

One month later, it fixed a Windows Autopatch bug that caused driver updates restricted by administrative policies to deploy on some Autopatch-managed Windows devices belonging to customers in the European Union.

Microsoft first announced Windows Autopatch in April 2002, saying it would be available for free to customers with a Windows 10/11 Enterprise E3 license or greater starting in July 2022. The feature reached public preview in early June and has been generally available since July 2022.

Title: A Fifth of UK Employees Share Passwords with AI
Context: It found that a fifth (19%) have shared a password, API key or login credential with an AI tool or agent, while nearly half (48%) have allowed AI to perform at least one...
Full Text:
Large numbers of UK employees are sharing sensitive information with unmanaged AI tools and allowing them to take actions on their accounts without considering the security risks, Dashlane has warned.

The credential security specialist polled 1000 UK workers and 250 IT execs as part of a wider survey group of 3800 across the UK, US and France to create its latest report, Misplaced Trust: Inside the Workplace’s New AI Security Blind Spot.

It found that a fifth (19%) have shared a password, API key or login credential with an AI tool or agent, while nearly half (48%) have allowed AI to perform at least one activity without seeking permission first, including accessing emails, company files and customer information.

Read more on AI risks: NCSC Publishes Guidance on Securing Agentic AI Use

Dashlane unearthed a high propensity among UK workers to use shadow AI without thinking about the repercussions for their employer.

It found that:

37% would be willing to lend their login credentials to a new AI tool after one week

15% have granted an AI tool access to a file, system or account they subsequently discovered it should not have accessed, with 45% claiming the access remains active

23% have copied sensitive information into AI that they would not normally share with a colleague, website or other work system

21% have failed to check where information would be stored or sent

Just a quarter (25%) say they always consider security risks when using an AI agent at work

“Our latest data shows an emerging ‘AI Colleague Effect’ where employees are overextending trust to AI systems, sharing credentials and granting access to AI agents, sometimes without fully understanding what those tools can do with the permissions they've been given,” explained Dashlane CPO, Christophe Frenet.

“That creates significant challenges for security teams trying to detect misuse or investigate incidents.”

Security Leaders Are Over-Confident

Sharing sensitive information with LLMs/agents or allowing agents access to internal corporate systems represent a significant compliance and security risk.

Information may end up on third-party servers which could be compromised, and it may be used to train models and regurgitated in responses to other users. Agents are a possible target for hijacking by threat actors.

In fact, 72% of IT and security executives Dashlane polled said their organization has experienced a security incident involving an AI agent’s credentials or access in the past 12 months.

Yet the vast majority (92%) also claimed they were confident that they know about every AI agent operating within their organization, the report found. That contradicts the claims from a quarter (25%) of employees who said they use AI tools their employer does not know about.

Business demands for adoption are weighing heavily on the minds of security leaders.

More than two-thirds (68%) of UK IT security executives claimed to feel caught between pressure to deploy AI quickly and the need to keep the organization secure.

"The challenge for security leaders is that the pace of change presented by AI and the potential consequences of misuse is unlike any other technology before it,” concluded Frenet.

“The principles that make up the foundation of a good security program for securing human identities – just-in-time provisioning, least privilege, good credential hygiene and authentication – have to be applied to our new AI colleagues as well."

Title: PHP Warns of Critical Flaws Ahead of November Security Release
Context: PHP will patch critical security flaws across supported versions, including a session handling bug that could allow remote code execution
Full Text:
PHP will patch critical security flaws across supported versions, including a session handling bug that could allow remote code execution.

The PHP development team announced a new security release scheduled for November 19, warning that the updates will address vulnerabilities across all supported versions of the widely used server-side programming language. The highest severity rating is CRITICAL, although the project says the affected issues require unusual configurations or non-default setups.

“The PHP security team announces upcoming security releases scheduled for Thursday, 19 November 2026, between 14:00 and 14:30 UTC.” reads the announcement. “The issues rated CRITICAL require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups. Users are strongly encouraged to prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available. Technical details and fixed version numbers will be published alongside the releases.”

The announcement places the release within PHP’s regular four-week update cycle.

PHP hasn’t disclosed the technical details, vulnerability identifiers, or fixed version numbers ahead of publication. The maintainers say they’ll release that information alongside the patches, giving administrators a short window to identify affected systems and prepare their upgrades.

One vulnerability expected to be addressed is CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution flaw involving PHP session handling.

In October, PHP warned of a new code execution vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-115560, just two days after releasing emergency patches for the critical PHP2Shell flaws.

The vulnerability affects only a specific PHP configuration that PHP says is unlikely to be used in practice. An application must meet several conditions: it must configure session.serialize_handler as php_binary or php_serialize, change it to php at runtime using ini_set(), and make this change before calling session_start(). Session upload progress must also remain enabled.

In an advisory published on October 23, the project recommended disabling session upload progress until a fix becomes available in a regular release. The vulnerability is separate from PHP2Shell and is not fixed by the October 21 updates for PHP versions 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12.

The November release also comes less than a month after PHP addressed two other critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively known as PHP2Shell. Those flaws let unauthenticated attackers execute code remotely through specially crafted HTTP requests, and they received emergency patches on October 21.

For organizations running PHP-based applications, the immediate priority is to identify the runtime versions in production, review custom session configurations and prepare to deploy the new packages as soon as they’re released. Teams should also check whether their Linux distributions or long-term support providers distribute PHP security fixes independently of the upstream release schedule.

PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive security updates directly from the PHP project, although some Linux distributions and commercial vendors continue to provide backported patches. Organizations still running these versions should verify their vendor’s coverage rather than assume that an upstream release automatically protects their installations.

“Users are strongly encouraged to prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available.” concludes the announcement. “Technical details and fixed version numbers will be published alongside the releases.”

Title: Sticky note on monitor provided keys to the company’s kingdom
Context: "Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained
Full Text: Welcome, once again, to PWNED, where we talk smack about organizations that have smacked themselves down by practicing poor security hygiene. This week's story involves everyone's favorite low-tech password manager: the sticky note. Our terrifying tale comes courtesy of Christian Espinosa, a certified penetration tester with over 30 years of experience and the CEO of Blue Goat Cyber, a security company. Espinosa shared an experience where critical credentials were right out in the open for any person in the office to see. During a walkthrough of a client's office, he noticed a password written on a sticky note that was taped to an employee's monitor. While writing down your password and placing it in a physically secure paper notebook might be ok, taping it to the computer is definitely not. "Before I get my fingers on any system, I first walk the physical area that the system is located in — attackers do that when they're looking at a target too," Espinosa explained. “Physical security vulnerabilities are neglected much more often than technical security vulnerabilities and firms invest in firewalls where a sticky note is placed 3 feet from the front door." Espinosa took a photo of the sticky note and immediately tried logging into that employee's account. Success. Then, he tried the very same password on the VPN, which apparently had been maintained by that employee. Once he connected to the VPN, Espinosa had full access to the company network and all of its shared drives. He opened a shared drive that this employee had access to and there was an HR folder with all kinds of personally identifiable information (PII) about employees, including home addresses, driver's licenses, and scanned W-4 forms. There were even spreadsheets that listed everyone's salaries. The employee account also had access to a document that contained a list of internal server names and the names of the people in charge of each server (great for phishing). Another document had instructions for how to log into the accounting server specifically. The accounting server was a particular treasure trove of client information. On that server, Espinosa found a folder with vendor banking information, invoices, and payment records. "At that point, a password I had read from a sticky note during a walk-through had taken me from one desk to information that could have been used for payroll fraud, identity theft, or vendor-payment fraud," Espinosa said. After getting access to all this information, the pen tester presented his findings to the client. They quickly disabled the rogue account and started reviewing VPN access logs to see who else might have gotten into the network. They then searched the office to see if anyone else was exposing a password on a sticky note. Finally, they tightened permissions on the HR and accounting shares so that only people who really needed access to that data could get in. The lessons here are pretty obvious. Don't expose your passwords and, perhaps even more importantly, limit who has access to file shares that contain mission-critical data such as employee or client information. "The part that really got the client's attention was how easily the attack could have continued after I left the building," Espinosa posited. "Someone could have photographed that sticky note, walked out, connected to the VPN later that night, and started going through employee and financial records from somewhere else." ®

A US court has sentenced a member of the Scattered Spider cybercrime group to six years in prison. Tyler Robert Buchanan, a 24-year-old British man, joins four other group members in jail for his part in crimes that netted $11.6 million in proceeds.

Texts, SIM swaps and $11.6 million

Buchanan and his co-conspirators hacked at least a dozen companies in a years-long campaign, according to the Department of Justice. They sent hundreds of SMS phishing messages, also known as smishing, to employees at their target companies. The messages pretended to come from the employer or one of its contractors, such as an IT support provider. They contained links to phishing websites impersonating company websites and designed to steal usernames and passwords. The criminal group used those stolen credentials to access company systems.

The group also used SIM swapping to steal from individuals. In a SIM swap, a criminal tricks a mobile phone carrier into transferring a victim’s phone number to a SIM card the criminal controls. The criminal can then receive calls and text messages intended for the victim, including SMS authentication codes.

SIM swapping allowed Buchanan and his co-conspirators to take over cryptocurrency accounts and wallets, stealing over $11.6 million from victims.

Buchanan was arrested in Spain in May 2024 and taken into US custody in April 2025. He pleaded guilty to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud and one count of aggravated identity theft. He faced a maximum possible sentence of 22 years.

The other four defendants in the US case have also been sentenced. The longest sentence, 10 years, went to 22-year-old Floridian Noah Michael Urban, who pleaded guilty to fraud-related charges.

Joel Martin Evans , aged 27, of North Carolina, is now serving a two-year federal prison sentence for conspiracy to commit wire fraud. Ahmed Hossam Eldin Elbadawy and Evans Onyeaka Osiebo, both from Texas, each received 45-month sentences for wire fraud and aggravated identity theft.

Does this end the reign of Scattered Spider?

Experts say it’s unlikely, partly because the group is fragmented. Cybersecurity company Group-IB has warned that it contains different subclusters connected by shared tools and techniques. Members sometimes share online chats, too, but the subclusters act separately and rarely include more than five people, the company said.

There is also a significant overlap between Scattered Spider and an online group known as The Com, Group-IB said. The Com has been linked to child sexual abuse material and attacks on companies, including Allianz Life.

Other Scattered Spider members were also sentenced in the UK in July this year. Eighteen-year-old Owen Flowers and 19-year-old Thalha Jubair each received five-and-a-half-year sentences for a cyberattack on Transport for London (TfL). The youths live-streamed that attack in August 2024, which stole the personal data of up to 10 million TfL customers.

We also reported last month on the arrest of another person linked to Scattered LAPSUS$ Hunters. The name brings together three groups—Scattered Spider, LAPSUS$, and ShinyHunters—that have reportedly worked together on and off since summer 2025.

How to protect your number from SIM swapping

Phishing texts and SIM swaps can put both work systems and personal accounts at risk. These steps can make it harder for someone to take over your number or use it to access your accounts:

Ask your mobile carrier whether it offers an account PIN, port-out lock, or number-transfer protection. These can make it harder for someone to move your number to another SIM.

Where possible, use an authenticator app, passkey, or security key instead of SMS codes. These options aren’t tied to your phone number in the same way.

Never approve a sign-in prompt you didn’t initiate. Attackers may flood you with requests in the hope that you’ll approve one.

Scammers know more about you than you think.

Title: Hackers Breach N-able Cloud Server, Disrupting Email Security Management Across 3 Regions
Context: N-able on Wednesday disclosed that unknown threat actors gained unauthorized access to one of the servers in the Mail Assure and Spam Experts Hosted Cloud, causing it to disable...
Full Text:
N-able on Wednesday disclosed that unknown threat actors gained unauthorized access to one of the servers in the Mail Assure and Spam Experts Hosted Cloud, causing it to disable management interfaces and APIs.

"We have taken steps to mitigate the threat and are continuing to harden our services to reduce the risk of recurrence," N-able said.

"The investigation is ongoing, but at this time we do not have evidence that customer data was compromised, including access to tenants' mailboxes."

The following services remain impacted -

Mail Assure (Americas)

Mail Assure (APAC)

Mail Assure (Europe)

SpamExperts (Americas)

SpamExperts (APAC)

SpamExperts (Europe)

The discovery comes after N-able began an investigation into a service disruption affecting Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud on November 16, 2026.

While it was initially traced to a combination of platform configuration and service dependencies within the Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud environment, it has since been determined that the disruption was actually caused by a security incident.

N-able said it's continuing to work on restoring Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud across all regions, while core mail flow and inbound and outbound mail filtering remain available.

"The management portal (UI), APIs, quarantine, and logging remain offline while our teams work to restore them securely. Access will be restored once validation is complete," it said.

The company also noted that it has directly reached out to Mail Assure and SpamExperts Hosted Cloud partners with "information relevant to their environment and whether action is required or not."

As of November 19, 2026, at 8 a.m. UTC, N-able said the restoration process is still underway, and that it's making steady progress on validating and hardening the management portal and its supporting services.

It's worth noting that the incident is unrelated to the discovery of multiple vulnerabilities impacting N-central referred to as Able2Shell, 4EverAble2Shell, and Agent2Shell.

Title: NVIDIA investigating Gentlemen ransomware breach claims
Context: On their leak site, the cybercrime gang threatens to release data and has added a countdown that ends in nine days, on November 28
Full Text:
NVIDIA is investigating claims of a security breach after the Gentlemen ransomware group has added the company to its dark web data leak site.

Although the ransomware operation now lists the American multinational tech giant, it has not yet shared any proof of the breach.

On their leak site, the cybercrime gang threatens to release data and has added a countdown that ends in nine days, on November 28.

While the company told BleepingComputer it hasn't found evidence that its systems were compromised, it said it's now looking into a separate incident that may have affected one of its service providers.

"NVIDIA is investigating an incident that may have affected a third-party partner," an NVIDIA spokesperson told BleepingComputer when asked to confirm the cybercrime gang's claims.

"We have found no indication that NVIDIA systems or networks were affected. We continue to monitor the situation."

​NVIDIA confirmed a data breach earlier this year, in May, when it told BleepingComputer that some Armenian users' information (including their names, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, and usernames) had been exposed after a regional GeForce NOW Alliance partner was hacked.

However, the company added that the May breach did not affect its network or NVIDIA-operated services.

The tech giant also disclosed another data breach in March 2022 (claimed by the Lapsus$ extortion gang) that affected more than 71,000 employees after attackers accessed its network a month earlier.

The Gentlemen surfaced last year as a closed ransomware group and then switched to a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) model, offering affiliates up to a 90% cut of ransom proceeds (compared to the typical 70%–80% other ransomware groups offer).

It operates as a double-extortion group, exfiltrating sensitive data from victims' networks before encrypting their systems and pressuring them with the threat of leaking the stolen information online.

Since it emerged, The Gentlemen has claimed more than 1,100 victims from various sectors, spanning manufacturing, healthcare, transportation, energy, education, financial services, and more.

Title: nginx2root:AI Discovers Five Critical nginx Flaws and a Path to Root
Context: What came next was different: Xint folded what it learned into a general feature, not tuned to nginx, and that version found the other four critical bugs with no human guidance
Full Text:
nginx2root exposes five critical nginx flaws and a Linux kernel bug that can lead to remote code execution and root access.

Xint Research has disclosed nginx2root, five distinct nginx vulnerabilities plus one Linux kernel bug, each with a proven exploit. The worst of the five, now tracked as CVE-2026-123007, lets an unauthenticated attacker run code remotely, and chaining it with the kernel bug reaches root on the host.

“This issue affects NGINX Plus or NGINX Open Source configurations that use HTTP/2. When NGINX processes undisclosed traffic, the flow control window can exceed the allowed threshold, potentially resulting in a heap buffer overflow typically followed by an NGINX worker segmentation fault. Additionally, attackers can execute code on systems with Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) disabled or when the attacker can bypass ASLR. (CVE-2026-123007)” reads the advisory. “An attacker could leverage this vulnerability to crash the NGINX worker process, corrupt its memory, or potentially execute code remotely. There is no control plane exposure; this is a data plane issue only.”

Affected nginx versions run from 1.9.5 to 1.31.8, and the fix landed in 1.31.9. According to Zakir Durumeric, Co-Founder and CEO Censys, nearly 10M Internet services are running versions of Nginx vulnerable to the NGINX2Root CVEs.

The bug sits in nginx’s HTTP/2 flow control, and it’s been there since nginx added HTTP/2 in 2015, eleven years ago. An attacker corrupts memory in an nginx worker, leaks memory addresses, and overwrites a pointer to a cleanup function that fires when a connection closes.

“Specifically, the most severe vulnerability is in nginx HTTP/2 flow control. An unauthenticated remote attacker can corrupt memory in an nginx worker, leak memory addresses, and overwrite the pointer to a cleanup function that runs when a connection closes.” reads the advisory. “This can be used to execute commands with worker privileges and receive the output over an existing connection.”

The figures show why this issue matters beyond nginx itself. In a Shodan scan on 10 November, 98.9% of nginx servers with a known version were running a vulnerable release. Xint also found that 88.6% of Fortune 500 companies use nginx. These figures show how widespread the vulnerable versions are, not how many servers can actually be attacked. Some servers may not have HTTP/2 enabled or may already include a fix provided by their software vendor. Still, administrators have a large number of systems to check.

To move from control of an nginx worker to full root access, an attacker needs to exploit a second flaw in the Linux kernel’s SCTP code. Xint tested this attack chain in environments running on AWS, GCP and Azure, including systems reachable through a public IP address. Luxembourg’s cybersecurity response team, CIRCL, also confirmed that exploiting the kernel flaw is necessary to gain root access. No active attacks have been reported so far, and CVE-2026-123007 was not on CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog at the time of writing.

The discovery story is worth pausing on. nginx has been fuzzed by the best researchers for two decades, and a pre-auth RCE in it is rare, the last known one dating to 2013.

“nginx runs roughly a third of the web and has been fuzzed and audited by the best researchers in the world for two decades. Pre-auth RCE in nginx almost never happens. The best known one is from 2013. This year every AI lab pointed models at it. Everyone figured the easy bugs were long gone.” continues the advisory. “While testing a new Xint capability ahead of ZeroDay Cloud, a Xint researcher pointed it at a slice of nginx, about 50,000 lines. He picked the target; Xint did the rest. Ninety minutes later it flagged high severity issues with reproduction steps specific enough to become a working exploit in under ten minutes.”

That first find was a human picking the target and an AI doing the digging. What came next was different: Xint folded what it learned into a general feature, not tuned to nginx, and that version found the other four critical bugs with no human guidance. One of those four was also found independently by other researchers around the same time, so Xint wasn’t working in a vacuum.

Four more flaws shipped fixes in the same release, each needing its own specific setup: a backend proxy running low on connections, a proxied server name built from variables combined with certain directives, HTTP/3 turned on, or nginx running as a mail proxy.

All five vulnerabilities have a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2 out of 10, making them critical. NGINX Plus is also affected across several release lines. The fixed versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 were released today, along with NGINX Plus versions 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1

Check exposure with a simple test: run openssl s_client with -alpn h2 against your server, and if it answers “ALPN protocol: h2,” HTTP/2 is on. If you’re behind a CDN, test the origin directly, since an origin serving only HTTP/1.1 can’t be hit through HTTP/2 even if your CDN speaks it to visitors. Update to the fixed version and restart nginx fully, because a reload alone leaves the old binary running.

If you can’t patch right away, turn off HTTP/2 on affected listeners as a stopgap. That blocks the worst flaw and one other, but not the remaining three, so it’s a bridge, not a destination. Distribution packages can carry a backported fix without changing the version string nginx -v reports, so check your vendor’s own advisory rather than trusting that number alone.

Xint says the main value of this discovery goes beyond finding these vulnerabilities. It’s about building a process that can quickly turn the next AI-driven attack, similar to ARTEX, into security detections before attackers can take advantage of it.

Title: Rakuten Securities Breach Could Impact 15 Million Customers
Context: The firm, which is part of Japanese tech conglomerate Rakuten Group, issued an apology to customers on November 17, stating that it first discovered unauthorized access to its...
Full Text:
One of Japan’s leading online brokerages has revealed a major breach of customer account data which could impact nearly 16 million people.

Tokyo-headquartered Rakuten Securities allows retail investors to trade stocks, bonds, foreign exchange and other financial instruments.

The firm, which is part of Japanese tech conglomerate Rakuten Group, issued an apology to customers on November 17, stating that it first discovered unauthorized access to its systems the day before.

“As a result of our investigation, we confirmed that on Wednesday, November 11 some information managed within our test environment system may have been leaked to an external party,” it said. “We are continuing our investigation into the cause and detailed circumstances of the unauthorized access.”

Read more on Japanese breaches: Japan’s GMO Internet Urges Customers to Disconnect PCs

The securities giant said that branch/customer code, login ID, name, date of birth, address, phone number, email address, employer, withdrawal account details, annual income, asset information, and last login date for around 4.47 million accounts had been compromised.

An even larger group of 11.25 million accounts had just their Rakuten Securities branch/customer code and login IDs taken, it added.

The firm confirmed passwords, PINs and other information have not been taken and there’s no sign of unauthorized access to customer accounts.

Security experts questioned why production data was allowed to be used in a test environment.

“This isn’t some advanced security concept or something that requires sophisticated technology to address. It’s one of the most fundamental rules of protecting sensitive information, and yet we continue to see organizations make these mistakes,” argued Black Hills Information Security owner John Strand.ㅤ

“The proper way to do this is to have separate development, testing, and staging environments, each with clearly defined security controls.”

Rakuten Urges Passkey Adoption

Rakuten Securities warned customers of follow-on phishing attempts, presumably trying to trick individuals into handing over their logins.

It said over 90% of customers currently log in using phishing-resistant passkeys, and urged the remainder to switch to mitigate the risk of account takeover.

Last year, regulator the Financial Services Agency (FSA) warned of a sharp increase in account hijacking at Japanese securities companies, with hackers making illegal trades of over 304 billion yen ($2bn).

It claimed the hackers were attempting to manipulate the market by boosting the value of small-cap stocks that they own, in order to sell them at a bigger profit.

Rakuten Securities’ woes come at the end of a bad year for Japanese companies, which have been hit by a string of data breaches and extortion attacks.

They include Burger King (11 million customers), car rental company Times Car (6.6 million), karaoke giant Daiichi Kosho (8 million), and restaurant chain Yakiniku King (11 million).

In October, GMO, a virtual desktop company popular with foreign-exchange traders told customers to disconnect their machines from the internet after being breached by ransomware actors.

Title: Java4Shell Exploitation Attempts Begin as Vendors Rush Out Advisories
Context: Exploitation requires an x86-64 processor supporting AVX-512 VBMI, a feature found in newer Intel and AMD CPUs
Full Text:
Threat actors have started targeting the recently disclosed Java4Shell vulnerability, as more vendors publish advisories detailing the flaw’s impact on their products.

Tracked as CVE-2026-114938, Java4Shell is a memory corruption bug in the way OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer handle Base64 data. Exploitation requires an x86-64 processor supporting AVX-512 VBMI, a feature found in newer Intel and AMD CPUs. ARM-based systems are not affected.

Calif disclosed the bug on November 17, the same day Oracle and the OpenJDK project released patches.

Calif said it achieved unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) against the default configurations of Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak and other enterprise applications. However, it noted that no single exploit works against all of them, and that each needs a tailored attack chain.

Attackers are probing for vulnerable systems

As of early November 19, threat intelligence firm GreyNoise had recorded over 150 requests matching the shape of a Java4Shell attack, coming from five IP addresses. The company has not seen any successful intrusions on its sensors.

WatchTowr has also seen activity. “We are already seeing attackers spray the internet and hit our global honeypot network with requests decorated in ‘java4shell-recon’ User-Agents, alongside blind exploitation attempts using correctly shaped requests,” said Jake Knott, head of threat intelligence at WatchTowr.

Advertisement. Scroll to continue reading.

“While what we’re seeing so far isn’t particularly functional or scary yet, it shows the clear signal that attackers want to leverage this vulnerability. Over the coming days, we expect attackers to iterate product-by-product to refine and build more reliable target-specific exploits, and that is where we start to see real exploitation happen,” Knott added.

Cloudflare’s Cloudforce One team has noticed that those scanning for the flaw are starting to conceal the tools they use. In one case, an IP address probed a target using a user agent that clearly referenced Java4Shell, then returned roughly 17 hours later with the exploit trigger while impersonating the Chrome browser.

On November 18, Cloudforce One also saw an IP address being used for both Artex and Java4Shell activity for the first time. Artex is an open source AI penetration testing framework that threat actors have been abusing to automate intrusions.

Threat intelligence firm Previdian says its sensors logged nine exploitation attempts from six IPs on November 18 and 19. However, it cautioned that its sensor data cannot confirm whether any targets were compromised.

Cisco’s product security team says it is aware of proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit code but has no knowledge of malicious use.

The PoC released by Calif only triggers the memory corruption. Meanwhile, VulnCheck has made a full RCE exploit available to its customers, and Immersive’s Kevin Breen has reported developing a working exploit.

Vendors confirm impact, but fixes are still rolling out

So far, Cisco has confirmed that more than a dozen of its products are affected, including Catalyst Center, Secure Network Analytics, Secure Workload, Smart Software Manager On-Prem, Splunk AppDynamics On-Premises Virtual Appliance, and Intersight Virtual Appliance.

The networking giant has yet to release fixes and says there are no workarounds. It is still investigating whether IOS XE and UCS Central are impacted.

Siemens says three of its Industrial Edge Management products are affected. The company is working on patches and, in the meantime, recommends taking these instances offline.

According to Elastic, every Elasticsearch release from 7.17.3 onward is affected. Attackers need valid credentials with read permissions or higher to achieve RCE, but they can trigger a denial-of-service (DoS) condition without authentication.

Logstash 8.6.2 and later are also affected, although exploitation requires a specific configuration and can only cause a crash. Elastic plans to address the issue in upcoming releases.

The company has already deployed a hotfix for Elastic Cloud Serverless and a configuration change for Elastic Cloud Hosted. It says only a small share of Elastic Cloud Hosted deployments run on vulnerable CPUs.

Red Hat has rated the issue Critical, saying that RHEL 8, 9 and 10 are affected, along with its own builds of OpenJDK 17, 21 and 25.

“No special configuration or non-default features are required. The accelerated code path is selected automatically whenever the JVM runs on a CPU reporting AVX-512 VBMI support, so affected systems are vulnerable out of the box,” Red Hat said, noting that patches are being fast-tracked.

The Keycloak team warned that its 26.8.2-1 and 26.8.2-2 container images bundled a vulnerable OpenJDK 21 build. On November 19, it announced updated images containing a patched Java runtime, including the 26.8.2-3 release.

Atlassian says it is working to address the issue in its cloud products, and that cloud customers do not need to take any action. For its Data Center products, until patches become available, Atlassian recommends disabling AVX-512 support as a workaround for the latest versions of Bamboo, Bitbucket, Confluence, Crowd, Jira and Jira Service Management Data Center in standard installations.

The Jenkins project says controllers are only at risk if they run a vulnerable Java 17, 21 or 25 release on a CPU that supports AVX-512 VBMI. It advises users to update to the November Java releases and restart Jenkins. Workarounds are also available.

Among Java distributors, Amazon, Microsoft, and Azul have released patched builds of their OpenJDK distributions.
