Title: Vulnerability management: The cybersecurity industry is still solving the wrong problem
Context: That has driven the development of risk-based vulnerability management, exploitability intelligence, asset criticality models and sophisticated exposure prioritization platforms
Full Text:
We have never been short of vulnerabilities. We have always struggled with remedial work.

For decades, the cybersecurity industry has approached vulnerability management from the wrong end. The emphasis has consistently been on finding vulnerabilities, cataloguing them, scoring them and, more recently, prioritising them through increasingly sophisticated risk models.

An entire industry has developed around vulnerability scanning, exposure management, threat intelligence and remediation prioritization. Artificial intelligence is now promising to take those capabilities to another level.

But there is something fundamentally wrong with that approach.

The real challenge in vulnerability management has never been identifying what needs fixing. It has always been getting the remedial work done.

Most large organizations already know they have significant numbers of vulnerabilities across their technology estates. They have known for years. They have dashboards, reports, inventories, risk ratings and remediation backlogs.

What they frequently lack is the organizational machinery to translate that knowledge into effective, sustained remedial action.

And that is not primarily a technology problem.

The uncomfortable reality behind remediation backlogs

Consider what happens when a large enterprise identifies a critical vulnerability.

The security team assesses its severity and potential impact. It raises a ticket, assigns a priority, identifies an owner and requests remediation.

On paper, the process looks straightforward.

In practice, that is often where the real problems begin.

The infrastructure team may be managing ageing systems with complex dependencies. The development team may have committed to a demanding release schedule. Production operations may be unwilling to accept additional downtime. Business stakeholders may resist disruption to revenue-generating services.

Some systems may have very limited maintenance windows. Others may require extensive regression testing before deploying patches. Legacy applications may depend on components that cannot easily be upgraded.

And ownership itself may be disputed.

Security teams frequently have the responsibility to identify and report vulnerabilities but lack the authority to enforce remediation. Technology teams control the systems but may have competing priorities and insufficient resources.

The result is familiar: escalating tickets, repeated exceptions, missed deadlines, unresolved disputes and growing remediation backlogs.

None of these problems can be solved simply by producing a better vulnerability score.

Prioritization is necessary, but it is not the answer

The industry has increasingly recognized that organizations cannot remediate everything.

That has driven the development of risk-based vulnerability management, exploitability intelligence, asset criticality models and sophisticated exposure prioritization platforms.

These capabilities have genuine value: There is an obvious difference between a vulnerability that is actively exploited on an internet-facing critical system and one that exists on an isolated, low-value asset.

But prioritization is only the beginning of a management process. It is not its outcome: A perfectly prioritized remediation backlog remains a backlog.

In many organizations, the difficulty is not deciding which vulnerabilities matter most. It is securing agreement on who will fix them, when the work will take place and who has the authority to resolve conflicts or accept the risk.

These are matters of governance, accountability and business priorities.

The cybersecurity industry remains disproportionately focused on the what, when the real challenge lies in the how and the who.

AI is about to make the problem considerably worse

Artificial intelligence is fundamentally changing the economics of vulnerability discovery.

AI-assisted tools can analyse code, identify weaknesses and accelerate vulnerability research on a scale and at a speed that would previously have required substantial human effort.

According to Google Threat Intelligence Group, monthly vulnerability disclosures more than doubled between January and August 2026, while observed exploitation also increased significantly. AI is contributing to that acceleration, although changes in disclosure practices also influence the figures.

The consequences for large organizations could be significant.

We are moving towards a world where the identification of vulnerabilities becomes increasingly automated, increasingly inexpensive and potentially continuous.

But what happens when the volume of identified vulnerabilities increases dramatically while the organization’s capacity to remediate them remains essentially unchanged?

The answer is predictable: Larger backlogs. More pressure on technology teams. More exceptions. More disputes over priorities. And potentially greater exposure, despite unprecedented visibility into technical weaknesses.

The Cloud Security Alliance has already highlighted this growing disconnect between accelerated vulnerability discovery and the capacity of organizations to absorb and remediate findings.

AI is industrialising vulnerability discovery while remediation remains trapped in organizational structures designed for another era.

That is the real emerging challenge.

AI cannot negotiate a production maintenance window

Of course, AI can also contribute to remediation.

It can establish proofs of concept, generate and test fixes, propose configuration changes, analyse dependencies and automate certain deployment activities.

These are important developments, and organizations should embrace them where appropriate.

But their practical impact must not be overstated.

AI cannot independently decide that a critical production system should be taken offline during a peak business period. It cannot assume accountability for disrupting customer services or resolve competing priorities between a business unit, an infrastructure team and the security function.

It cannot simply override legacy dependencies, contractual obligations or regulatory constraints.

Even where AI can technically generate a suitable fix, somebody still needs to validate it, approve its deployment, ensure that the fix has not broken something else and verify that remediation has been successful.

Some of those steps can be automated. Others require judgement, authority and organizational coordination.

The more powerful AI becomes, the more visible those remaining management bottlenecks will be.

And this is where the traditional cybersecurity approach is increasingly inadequate.

Vulnerability management needs an operating model, not another dashboard

What large organizations need is not simply better vulnerability management technology.

They need a remediation operating model that establishes clear accountability across security, development, infrastructure, operations and business management.

That model should address several fundamental questions.

Who owns the remediation of vulnerabilities affecting shared platforms or complex applications? Who allocates the necessary resources? Who can authorize emergency changes? Who resolves disagreements when remediation conflicts with business priorities?

How are maintenance windows negotiated and secured? How are persistent exceptions challenged? Who accepts the residual business risk when remediation cannot be completed within the expected timeframe?

And, crucially, who is responsible for ensuring that agreed actions happen?

These responsibilities cannot be left to informal relationships between technical teams or to the persistence of individual security managers.

They need to be embedded in management processes, supported by executive authority and reinforced through meaningful performance measures.

Security should provide risk intelligence, challenge and assurance. Technology teams should own the delivery of remediation within their environments. Business management should participate in decisions where operational disruption or investment trade-offs are unavoidable.

The CISO’s role is to help establish and oversee that machinery, not to become the organization’s chief ticket chaser.

Measuring remediation effectiveness, not just reporting activity

There is also a fundamental problem with how vulnerability management performance is measured.

Too many organizations remain focused on the number of vulnerabilities identified, severity distributions, compliance with remediation deadlines and the volume of outstanding findings.

Those indicators have their place, but they can encourage an administrative approach to vulnerability management: Closing tickets becomes a proxy for reducing risk.

What matters is whether material exposures are being eliminated within acceptable timeframes and whether the organization can demonstrate that remediation has worked.

Management should pay particular attention to recurring remediation failures, ageing high-risk exposures, operational bottlenecks, the effectiveness of exception handling and the time required to implement verified fixes.

The distinction between a vulnerability being reported as resolved and genuinely being remediated is essential.

AI can help generate more accurate and timely evidence. But it cannot substitute for accountability over the results.

Auditability and regulatory obligations add another critical dimension to this challenge.

Regulators increasingly expect organizations not only to identify and assess vulnerabilities, but also to demonstrate that appropriate remedial actions have been taken within reasonable timeframes.

This requires clear ownership, documented decisions, traceable exceptions periodically reviewed and reliable evidence that remediation has been completed.

As AI accelerates vulnerability discovery and potentially automates parts of the remediation process, maintaining an auditable chain of accountability becomes even more important.

Ultimately, compliance cannot rest on the ability to identify problems: It needs to rest on the ability to demonstrate that they have been effectively addressed.

The real opportunity for AI is to transform execution

This is where I believe the cybersecurity industry should concentrate its attention.

Rather than simply applying AI to discover more vulnerabilities and refine their prioritization or their treatment, vendors and practitioners should focus on how AI can accelerate the entire remediation lifecycle.

That means understanding dependencies, identifying suitable deployment opportunities, preparing changes, automating testing, coordinating workflows, validating results and providing management with reliable evidence of progress across the whole cycle.

In highly automated environments, AI agents may eventually execute substantial portions of that process under clearly defined controls.

But the objective should not be automation for its own sake: It should be to reduce the friction between identifying a problem and resolving it.

And that requires technology to be designed around a functioning governance model, rather than expecting governance to emerge from the technology.

The technology will change. The management problem will not.

I have argued for years that cybersecurity is fundamentally a leadership and management challenge supported by technology.

Vulnerability management provides perhaps one of the clearest demonstrations of that principle.

The same structural problems that prevented organizations from patching critical systems fifteen years ago remain visible today: fragmented responsibilities, competing priorities, operational constraints, weak governance and insufficient management follow-through.

AI will not make those problems disappear.

On the contrary, by accelerating vulnerability discovery and shortening the time available to respond, it is exposing them more brutally than ever.

The organizations that succeed will not necessarily be those with the most sophisticated vulnerability discovery capabilities.

They will be those that have built the governance, accountability and operational discipline required to translate technical intelligence into effective remedial action.

The future of vulnerability management will not be determined by how quickly we can find what is wrong. It will be determined by how effectively organizations can get things fixed.

And that has always been a management problem.

Title: Ruby Releases Fixes for 7 Regex and String Flaws, Warns 5 Have Proof-of-Concept RCE
Context: The maintainers say one has proof-of-concept code that corrupts memory under an attacker's control but has not been shown to run code, and the other can only read memory it...
Full Text:
Ruby contains seven memory-safety flaws in its regular expression engine and its string case-conversion code. For five of them, its maintainers say, proof-of-concept exploits, or PoCs, have shown that crafted input can run code on the machine.

"We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution," the maintainers said.

The project released fixed versions yesterday: Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14. Whether an application is at risk depends on whether an attacker can get crafted patterns or strings into the affected code, and the advisories report no attacks so far.

The other two flaws are weaker. The maintainers say one has proof-of-concept code that corrupts memory under an attacker's control but has not been shown to run code, and the other can only read memory it should not or crash the program.

The project set the seven out in a security announcement and a separate advisory for each. The advisories rate three flaws critical, three high, and one moderate, and say which carry the remote-code-execution PoCs. In order of severity:

Critical. GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5, a one-byte heap overflow when Ruby changes the case of a string in certain single-byte encodings, such as ISO-8859-1 or Windows-1252. It has a remote-code-execution PoC. (GitHub advisory)

Critical. GHSA-7x2q-68qv-6p8x, a double free when Ruby compiles a crafted regular expression that uses a character-class intersection (&&). It has a remote-code-execution PoC. (GitHub advisory)

Critical. GHSA-3p8q-wmhx-vm2w, a heap overflow when the size of a compiled regular expression overflows during compilation. It has a remote-code-execution PoC. (GitHub advisory)

High. GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px, a heap overflow when a case change produces a result larger than 4 GiB. It has a remote-code-execution PoC, though the size needed puts it out of reach for most requests. (GitHub advisory)

High. GHSA-7whj-cfh7-xgm4, a heap overflow when Ruby turns a crafted compiled regular expression back into text with Regexp#to_s. It has a remote-code-execution PoC. (GitHub advisory)

High. GHSA-wpqw-5qxg-m68r, an out-of-bounds read during case-insensitive matching. Its PoC shows attacker-controlled memory corruption, and the maintainers say remote code execution is possible but not shown. (GitHub advisory)

Moderate. GHSA-pvgc-g7gj-pv6h, an out-of-bounds read when Ruby matches a case-insensitive backreference against a crafted subject string. The advisory says it "may disclose memory contents or crash the process." (GitHub advisory)

The project credits Stephan Lipp of Ada Logics and Anthropic with four of the findings, and baba__yaga, aphantom, Hiroya Fujinami and Hiroshi SHIBATA with the other three.

Which Applications Are Exposed

The flaws are in Ruby's own code, so every application on an affected version carries them. Whether an attacker can reach one depends on how the application handles external input.

The regex flaws need an application that builds a regular expression from input an attacker controls and then compiles or runs it. Matching untrusted text against a pattern the developers wrote themselves does not pose the same risk, except in one case below.

The two case-conversion flaws do not involve regular expressions at all. They fire when the application changes the case of a crafted string, so code that runs case conversion over imported or outside text is worth checking.

The one case is the moderate read flaw, which fires when the application matches a crafted subject string against a fixed pattern that uses a case-insensitive backreference. The announcement and advisories do not include the proof-of-concept code.

The fixes are in Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14. The affected ranges are:

Ruby 4.0.0 through 4.0.9, fixed in 4.0.10.

Ruby 3.4.0 through 3.4.12, fixed in 3.4.13.

Ruby 3.3.13 and earlier, fixed in 3.3.14.

Ruby 3.2 and earlier, end of life and not fixed.

Those older versions will not get a fix, and the project recommends moving to a supported line. With 3.3.14, the maintainers renamed the Ruby 3.3 phase from security maintenance to legacy maintenance, and support still ends at the end of March 2027.

Because the fixes ship inside Ruby, updating an application's gems or framework does not replace a vulnerable interpreter. The version that matters is the Ruby running on application servers, background workers, and container images, which must be updated and then restarted or rebuilt.

The seven do not have CVE numbers yet. The project says it has requested them, and until they are assigned, the GitHub advisory IDs are the only way to track flaws in scanners and software inventories.

It is the second time in a month that the project has patched its regular expression engine. In the October fixes, released on October 23, it shipped Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12, and 3.3.13 to patch compilation bugs GitLab found, which sat behind four critical GitLab flaws.

One of those GitLab flaws drew an attempted attack on Alpine Linux's own GitLab server. CISA later added it to the KEV catalog, its list of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, as actively exploited.

Those are different bugs from this week's seven, and the new advisories do not say that GitLab or any other named product can be attacked through them. What the October case showed is that a regular expression built from user input can become a real way onto a server, not just a theoretical one.

Title: Researcher Demonstrates Database RCE Exploits Affecting PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle
Context: The exploits, published yesterday, are the researcher's proofs of concept against PostgreSQL, MySQL and ClickHouse, plus a separate Oracle chain that needs no login
Full Text:
Low-privilege database accounts that cannot read a single application table can still be used to run code on the database server itself, a researcher has shown, by reaching memory-corruption bugs in the engine code behind ordinary SQL.

The exploits, published yesterday, are the researcher's proofs of concept against PostgreSQL, MySQL and ClickHouse, plus a separate Oracle chain that needs no login. None has been seen in a real attack.

The work is by Zheng Yu, a researcher at Depthfirst. A database account's SQL permissions control which tables and schemas it can access, the researcher argues, not the memory-unsafe C and C++ code the engine runs to read, plan, and execute a query.

Common grants give an account enough room to reach that code. PostgreSQL's default TEMPORARY privilege, or the right to create temporary tables in MySQL and ClickHouse, allows an account to create objects or send input that triggers a memory bug.

Four of the flaws now have vendor CVEs and fixes, but the full attack chains were not reproduced independently, and the research reports no sign that any of them has been used in an attack.

In PostgreSQL, the flaw CVE-2026-116331 allows an account that can create database objects to run code as the operating system user that runs the database.

It was fixed last week in a security advisory, and the CVE record credits the researcher for the report. The researcher's technical analysis shows a plain login role building the objects it needs in its own temporary schema, without touching application data, then turning a type-confusion bug into control of the server.

MySQL has a similar flaw in its query optimizer, CVE-2026-101786, in Server and Cluster versions 26.7.0 to 26.7.1. Oracle's MySQL October advisory rates it as needing high privileges.

The researcher reached code execution on the 26.7.0 image with an account that could only create temporary tables and could not read existing ones, a narrower kind of access than that rating suggests.

Oracle Database is the one case where an attacker needs no account at all, the researcher says. A bug in Oracle Text and a flaw in the GraphQL interface of Oracle REST Data Services, chained against an exposed web endpoint, reach the engine code and run commands before any login.

Oracle patched the Oracle Text bug, CVE-2026-114819, rated 9.9, earlier this week in its November update, and the GraphQL flaw, CVE-2026-91609, in the October update. On their own, the company rates neither as exploitable without a login.

ClickHouse is the fourth target. The researcher reports an integer-overflow write in how it reads a binary row format, reached by a user who sets a single option, format_binary_max_string_size, to zero, and reproduced a shell on version 26.7.5.10.

This one has no CVE and no confirmed fixed version, so operators should check with the vendor for the fix.

Title: CISA Warns of 4 Exploited Flaws Linked to Ransomware, Cryptomining, and LLMjacking Attacks
Context: About 12 hours after the first exploit request, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 as an integration service account using legacy authentication from "192
Full Text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Wednesday added four vulnerabilities impacting Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM), BerriAI LiteLLM, Apache Axis, and Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation.

The vulnerabilities are listed below -

CVE-2026-90436 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An unsafe reflection vulnerability in Apache Axis that could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code.

CVE-2026-90817 (CVSS score: 9.8) - A code injection vulnerability in REDCap that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on the server.

CVE-2026-40217 (CVSS score: 8.8) - An unprotected alternate channel vulnerability in LiteLLM that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via bytecode rewriting at the /guardrails/test_custom_code URI.

CVE-2024-10441 (CVSS score: 9.8) - An improper encoding or escaping of output vulnerability in Synology DSM that could allow a remote attacker to execute arbitrary code via unspecified vectors.

"An attacker could exploit this via crafted HTTP requests that access an unintended controller route from a public survey context and supply a crafted file-path or stream parameter during data import processing," CISA said about CVE-2026-90817. "Exploitation requires knowledge of a valid public survey hash."

The addition of CVE-2026-90436 to the KEV catalog follows reports that the flaw is exploited in conjunction with the 4EverAble2Shell vulnerabilities affecting N-able N-central to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers.

Rapid7, in its own analysis of the flaw, said it detected exploitation of CVE-2026-90436 against Atlassian Confluence Data Center in a customer environment by taking advantage of the fact that the corporate workspace platform uses the Axis library as part of its XML-RPC and SOAP APIs.

"To be vulnerable, the Confluence instance must have the 'Remote API (XML-RPC & SOAP)' enabled," Atlassian said. "Please note that this setting was turned off by default for new installations starting in Confluence 3.0. This feature was fully removed in Confluence 10.0."

In the activity documented by Rapid7, threat actors are said to have weaponized the flaw to run shell commands and scripts fetched from temporary Pinggy and Cloudflare Tunnel domains, followed by enumerating the compromised environment. The incident was flagged on November 13, 2026.

"Just over three minutes after the first observed execution, the attackers were authenticating to MySQL with Confluence's own database credentials, querying page bodies, application links, and attachments with names associated with credentials, tokens, VPN configurations, and private keys," Rapid7 said.

"The attacker's scripts, likely AI-generated, then targeted files in Confluence's default location for uploaded page attachments (/var/atlassian/application-data/confluence/attachments/v4/), parsed Office documents, searched for credentials, and hunted for payment card numbers, using Luhn checks to filter out false positives."

In addition, the attackers have been found to map various internal services, use a Confluence application credential to query the internal Atlassian Crowd API for users and group memberships, and attempt to carry out a Kerberos-based credential harvesting technique called AS-REP Roasting.

Although these efforts were unsuccessful, the threat actor managed to acquire a service account credential and queried a production cloud data warehouse. About 12 hours after the first exploit request, the attacker signed in to Microsoft 365 as an integration service account using legacy authentication from "192.238.253[.]176."

CVE-2026-90436, which affects Axis 1.x versions, remains unpatched as Axis 1 has reached end-of-life (EoL) status. It's recommended to migrate to a different SOAP engine, such as Apache Axis 2/Java. Alternatively, users can use a build of Axis with the patch from a July 12, 2026, commit applied.

As for CVE-2026-90817, Safe Security said in a report published late last month that it observed an unknown threat abusing the flaw to "stage a transient web shell, followed by an in-memory loader that retrieved XMRig disguised as image files, masqueraded the miner as syslog-ng, and established persistence through cron and an added SSH key."

The exploitation of CVE-2026-40217 stems from a Google Threat Intelligence Group report this week in which threat actors have leveraged the vulnerability to elevate limited-access inference keys into full administrative credentials and establish persistence as part of LLMjacking attacks aimed at financial services, retail, transportation, and technology organizations in North America, South America, and the Asia Pacific region.

Rounding off the list is CVE-2024-10441, which Synology disclosed earlier this month as being exploited in ransomware attacks targeting Network Attached Storage (NAS) devices. The attacks have been found to result in the deployment of C3RB3R ransomware.

In light of active exploitation, federal agencies have been recommended to apply fixes or necessary mitigations for DSM, REDCap, and Axis flaws by November 21, 2026, and for the LiteLLM flaw by December 2, 2026.

Title: PHP Warns of Critical Security Flaws Affecting All Supported Versions, Fixes Coming November 19
Context: The shortcomings have since come under limited active exploitation, targeting publicly-accessible Palo Alto Networks management interfaces and Check Point Security Gateways to...
Full Text:
The maintainers of the PHP programming language on Wednesday issued an advisory announcing an upcoming security release that addresses critical flaws.

The release is scheduled for November 19, 2026, between 2 and 2:30 p.m. UTC.

"These releases are part of PHP's regular four-week release cycle and will address security vulnerabilities affecting all supported PHP versions," the maintainers said. "The highest severity is CRITICAL."

However, the project also noted that issues rated critical require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups. It did not disclose any additional specifics.

UPDATE: phpAfterShell Details Emerge — Critical PHP Bug Could Enable RCE

The update is expected to include CVE-2026-115560, a remote code execution flaw that succeeds only if the following conditions are met -

An application sets session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration, and its code switches the handler to php with ini_set() before calling session_start().

Session upload progress is enabled, which is PHP's default.

As mitigations, users were urged to set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release and restart the PHP worker for the setting to be applied.

The development comes nearly a month after PHP released fixes for two critical vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively tracked as PHP2Shell that enable unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) via specially crafted HTTP requests.

The shortcomings have since come under limited active exploitation, targeting publicly-accessible Palo Alto Networks management interfaces and Check Point Security Gateways to launch attacks against Active Directory and deliver backdoors.

In a report published on October 30, 2026, Hunt.io said it identified 616 PHP2Shell-related files, spanning shared exploit kits, cloned proof-of-concepts (PoCs), custom heap exploits, scanners, and post-exploitation tooling, across multiple hosts, even as participants in underground forums have sought exploits, discussed prerequisites, and whether circulating PoCs worked.

"Exploit developers are unlikely to create a single universal exploit that works reliably across all affected PHP deployments," CrowdStrike said.

Last month, PHP also released patches to address a critical flaw in Brotli (CVE-2026-111497 aka Node2Shell or Broccoli2Shell), an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the decoder library that could result in arbitrary code execution.

Users are advised to apply the updates as soon as they become available.

Title: Treat Your Honeypot Analysis Like Code: Git, Pull Requests and a Human Gate for AI [Guest Diary], (Wed, Nov 18th)
Context: Conclusion Version control is not new to security teams, where it's commonly seen in areas like detection rules and infrastructure code
Full Text:
[This is a Guest Diary by Kevin Truong, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]

Introduction When conducting analysis of honeypot activity, it's easy for it to start as a pile of terminal output. The process is manual; screenshots of the terminal, plus a text file that gets edited in a common word processing application until it is "done". There is no say whether a certain number came from a certain query, what changed between drafts, or who decided to drop a caveat.

While hosting my own honeypot sensor, I wrote up three attacks:

An SSH brute force that logged in as mysql/mysql [1]

A bot looking for Telegram Desktop sessions and SMS modems [2]

A month of RedTail exploits against PHP plus one oversized multipart POST that matches the shape of PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618) [3].

Instead of a document folder though, I kept every report in a public git repository [4] and changed it only through pull requests. Supporting me in my analysis was an AI coding agent (Claude Code), which also drafted reports as a separate GitHub machine account. I wanted to give my Claude Code sessions a tangible identity in the code submission and review process, where a dedicated GitHub account could propose changes but never approve or merge them.

Even though I drove every part of the analysis process, the code review of each pull request marked a deliberate step in my workflow which acted as both a gate and a spot-check of the content I was producing.

This diary describes that setup, what the git history shows about how well it worked, and what I would change.

Why Do It

The question this post answers are: can version control and a mandatory human review make AI-drafted security analysis trustworthy enough to publish?

It matters for three reasons:

Reproducibility. An indicator list or a timeline is only as good as the query behind it. If the query and its output are stored next to the claim, anyone can check it.

Public safety. Honeypot reports contain things that must not be published: the sensor's own address, its hostname, its cloud account, and sometimes attacker material such as private keys. Once something reaches a public git history, deleting the file does not remove it [4, SECURITY.md].

AI accountability. Language models are fluent and are confident; but fluency and confidence don't mean accuracy. If an AI is part of the workflow, there needs to be a record of what it wrote, what a human changed, and who approved it.

The Setup

The repository has one folder per attack. Each folder holds the summary, every piece of evidence it cites, and a hash list:

Every exhibit in a report's appendix shows the exact jq query that produced it, for example:

Before anything leaves the sensor, output is passed through a filter that replaces the sensor's address with <sensor-ip>, and then hashed. Anyone who clones the repository can confirm the evidence has not changed since it was committed:

The workflow around those files is shown in Figure 1.

The important pieces are:

A separate identity for the AI. Pull requests from the machine account are written by Claude Code sessions. It is a machine account I operate, and the README says so publicly [4].

The AI can write but not merge. A GitHub ruleset on main requires a pull request with one approval, blocks force-pushes and branch deletion and has no bypass actors. The AI account has written access, but GitHub does not let an author approve their own pull request, so it can never get a change into main alone.

A public-safety checklist on every PR. The pull request template asks the author to confirm that they read the full diff, that the secret scan is clean, that every IP and account is a placeholder (attacker indicators excepted), that there are no hostnames or local paths, and that attachments were checked by hand. The AI fills this in and I check it.

A secret scanner before every commit. A pre-commit hook runs gitleaks locally.

Options to Close Gaps

Comparing the ruleset with my own design notes [4, homelab/change-control.md] showed where the live settings fall short:

Fortunately, none of these needs’ new tools. These are repository settings and habits, which is the point. The controls that are deployed are the ones enforced by the server (GitHub), not ones written into a file the AI could edit on its own branch.

Who Benefits

Students and new analysts get a structure that forces each claim to point at evidence, and a history that shows a reviewer how their analysis improved. This works as a solo project, but the benefits grow exponentially with multiple analysts and reviewers.

Honeypot operators and DShield contributors can publish findings with less risk of leaking their sensor's identity, because the scrubbing and checklist happen before a merge, not after.

Teams adopting AI assistants get a pattern they can copy: a separate identity for the AI, server-side merge controls, and a checklist that the AI must fill in honestly. The record shows exactly where the AI's work ended and a human's began.

Readers of the reports can verify them. Every indicator traces to a query, and every query's output has a hash.

Conclusion

Version control is not new to security teams, where it's commonly seen in areas like detection rules and infrastructure code. That said though, treating something like honeypot/log analysis like code gave me reproducible evidence, a reviewable history, and a safe way to use an AI drafter: it proposed, I reviewed, and only I could merge. The history also kept me honest about the parts that did not work. Those gaps are visible because the work was in git, and each has a simple fix in the repository settings.

Context: Start with the right voice First, check GPT-Live’s built-in voices
Full Text:
Even if a voice agent speaks Spanish, it can still sound off for the audience you’re building for. It might use an accent from a different region, choose wording that feels too formal, or read a price in a way a local speaker wouldn’t expect.

While the default options for GPT-Live can go a long way, there are additional considerations when building voice applications for audiences across languages and regions. Let’s look at voice selection and session instructions to get better results, using regional varieties such as Indian English, Spanish from Spain, and Emirati Arabic.

Start with the right voice

First, check GPT-Live’s built-in voices. Some may already have a language or regional influence close to what you need: for example, Bossa and Tempo have a Brazilian Portuguese influence, while Nira is a Hindi voice. Test them with your own conversations before designing something new, as the built-in voices have high naturalness out of the box.

Use lowercase API names when selecting a built-in voice (for example, nira). The voice options guide has the complete current catalog.

If you need a more specific regional sound, you can use prompt-to-voice to generate a synthetic voice from a text description. Describe the region as precisely as you can, along with the pitch, pace, and vocal character you want. When generating a voice, you can use the script_hint field to add representative speech in the target language, and for a bilingual voice, include both languages in the sample text and describe the desired sound in each. Use original adult voices, and don’t impersonate real people. See the responsible-use guidance.

Eligible customers can also create a custom voice from a recording of a consenting speaker. Check the supported models and accents before choosing a recording-based voice. Before uploading, obtain the speaker’s express consent and secure the rights needed to use the recordings and the resulting voice in your application. The consent recording and reference sample must come from the same speaker. For any generated voice, make clear to listeners that they are hearing AI-generated speech.

Voice creation is ineligible for Zero Data Retention. See the data controls guide for the settings that apply to GPT-Live sessions.

Example: Hindi-influenced English with Nira

For an English-speaking agent serving users in India, set session.audio.output.voice to "nira" when creating the session, then add this prompt to the session instructions:

You are in a natural, clean English voice conversation. Speak fluent English in your natural Hindi-influenced Indian English accent. Keep that familiar rhythm throughout.

Example: Spanish from central and northern Spain

Suppose you’re building a shopping assistant for customers in Spain. Rather than asking for a generic Spanish accent, open the voice Playground and try this description in its prompt-to-voice workflow:

An original adult feminine voice, clear and lightly bright, with a medium pitch and gentle warmth. Speak Spanish with a natural standard Peninsular Castilian accent of central/northern Spain, with native Spanish vowels, consonants, stress, and sentence melody. Naturally distinguish s from z and c before e or i, without exaggeration. Use a moderately lively conversational pace, natural pauses, and varied intonation.

Pair it with a Spanish script_hint that gives the voice some ordinary connected speech to work with:

Hola, ¿qué tal? Estoy aquí para ayudarte. Podemos revisar las opciones con calma y elegir la que mejor encaje contigo. ¿Prefieres empezar por los colores o por las tallas? Esta chaqueta azul combina bien con unos zapatos cómodos. Acércate a la ventana para ver el color con luz natural.

This targets a particular variety of Spanish; the distinction described in the prompt isn’t universal across Spain or the Spanish-speaking world. With this prompt, you can generate a few candidates, keep the saved voice you prefer, and test it on a fresh sentence that wasn’t in the creation script until you’re satisfied.

Example: Emirati Arabic from Dubai

Arabic is another case where naming the language alone leaves a lot unspecified. For a conversational Dubai voice, an Arabic voice-design description might be:

صوت رجالي خيالي أصلي لرجل بالغ، بلهجة أهل دبي الإماراتية الحضرية المعاصرة. نطق الحروف وحركة الكلام وإيقاعه محليّان ومتناسقان، وتبقى الكلمات واضحة داخل الكلام اليومي المتصل. طبقة متوسطة تميل للانخفاض، ورنين دافي وصافي. يتكلم على مهله، والجملة تمشي كفكرة وحدة بنبر متنوع حسب المعنى.

The description asks for an original adult masculine voice with a contemporary urban Dubai accent, warm resonance, a slightly lower pitch, and connected, relaxed speech. Use a conversational Arabic script_hint as well:

هيه، شفت رسالتك. أنا هني صوب الحديقة، لا، أقصد صوب المواقف عند الباب الثاني. زين؟ المكان أهدى من اللي كنا فيه أمس. خذ راحتك، أنا توني واصل وما عندي شي مستعيل عليه. تبانا نتمشى شوي ولا نقعد؟ عادي، اللي يريحك.

In general, keep the voice design focused on sound. Managing details like whether the agent should answer an Egyptian caller in Emirati Arabic, switch into English, or confirm an order belongs in the session instructions, which we’ll cover later on.

Test the voice on what your application will actually say

But having a solid voice is only the starting point. Once you have a voice, you can build a small listening set with fresh sentences, realistic conversations, and the words or values your application handles most often to stress-test your voice.

A few edge cases are particularly useful to test:

Pronunciation in context: Include names, place names, product names, and specialized vocabulary. For Japanese, for example, give the agent a reading such as 承る（うけたまわる） and test it in a full support sentence. Or if your agent is pronouncing Lakshmi with a “my” ending instead of the intended “mee,” you can include guidance in the session instructions: लक्ष्मी — अंत में ‘क्ष्मी’, ‘क्ष्माई’ नहीं. For tonal languages, listen to important words in several sentence contexts.

Regional number conventions: The Indian system of numeration uses lakh and crore. One lakh is 1,00,000 (100,000), and one crore is 1,00,00,000 (10,000,000). For an English-speaking agent serving India, test whether ₹1,25,000 is spoken as “one lakh twenty-five thousand rupees” when that’s the intended convention.

Identifiers and corrections: Have a caller spell a fictional booking code, pause, and correct one character. Check that the agent waits for the correction and reads back the final code accurately. Test email addresses and other alphanumeric inputs your product accepts.

Mixed-language speech: Try an Arabic sentence containing an English product name and a price, then switch languages for the next turn. Check the spoken amount, currency, and product name separately from the accent.

For dates, amounts, and identifiers, validate what your application actually sends to the backend as well as what the caller hears. In many regions, 04/05 could mean two different dates, so it may be worth asking for clarification and reading the month back by name.

Prompt the agent for the conversation

Once you’ve chosen a voice, select it when creating the GPT-Live session. For a saved generated voice, set session.audio.output.voice.id to the returned voice ID. Put the agent’s role, language policy, delivery, and conversation behavior in instructions, and reinforce the original voice description there.

For a single-language application, write the instructions and examples in the language you want the agent to speak. Here’s a starting point for the Spanish shopping assistant:

Eres un asistente de compras. Habla en español de España, con acento castellano del centro y norte de la península, un ritmo conversacional y una entonación natural. Usa un tono cercano y respetuoso, sin sonar como un anuncio. Responde en español salvo que el cliente pida cambiar de idioma. Haz una pregunta cada vez. Si un nombre o una talla no están claros, pide que los repita. No confirmes precios, disponibilidad ni cambios en un pedido hasta que el sistema los haya verificado.

For a multilingual application, decide what should trigger a language switch and whether the underlying regional speaking style should remain fixed. Those are separate choices. For an Emirati Arabic and English assistant, first extend the earlier voice description with English delivery guidance, such as “In English, speak naturally with a light Emirati influence while keeping the same warmth and lower pitch.” Include representative English speech alongside the Arabic in script_hint, such as “I can check the available sizes for you,” before generating the bilingual voice. Then use a session policy like this:

Answer in the language of the caller's latest clear utterance. Switch between Arabic and English when the caller clearly switches. A short “OK,” number, name, or English product name inside an Arabic sentence does not by itself change the conversation language. When speaking Arabic, use conversational urban Emirati Arabic from Dubai, even when the caller speaks another Arabic variety. Prefer natural local wording where appropriate: شو for “what,” الحين for “now,” وين for “where,” and مب for negation. Keep the dialect coherent without exaggeration. In English, keep the same speaker identity. Use these as phrasing examples, not fixed answers: - Clarification: «تقصد العلبة الصغيرة ولا الكبيرة؟ وكم وحدة تبا؟» - Unclear name: «الاسم مب واضح عندي، ممكن تعيده أو تتهجّاه لي؟» Say amounts in the current conversation language and preserve their exact value and currency. Only confirm a lookup, price, or completed action when the backend supports that statement.

This example deliberately keeps the assistant’s Arabic dialect fixed while allowing English language switches. If your product should accommodate a caller’s requested dialect instead, write and test that policy explicitly. While voice descriptions and session prompts can steer an accent, they don’t guarantee that every reply will retain it, so test switches in both directions, including after a session reconnects.

Give examples of the register you want

Language and accent also leave the level of formality open. In Hindi, a courteous support agent might use आप and respectful verb forms. You can make that preference concrete in the session prompt:

ग्राहक से "आप" कहकर बात करें। सम्मानजनक भाषा और क्रिया रूपों का उपयोग करें। "हाँ, बताओ" की जगह "जी, बताइए" कहें। "तुम कैसे हो?" की जगह "आप कैसे हैं?" कहें।

The examples distinguish a casual “yes, tell me” from a more courteous equivalent. That gives the model a clearer target than simply asking it to sound professional. Use phrases a local support representative would actually say, and test them in context rather than translating an English script word for word.

For more on pronunciation cues, personality, greetings, and interruption behavior, see the GPT-Live prompting guide. The voice agent evaluation guide covers how to turn your listening cases into a repeatable evaluation as you change voices, prompts, or models.

Title: Step-up authentication: how to right-size authentication to risk
Context: If you request step-up through InitiateAuth on a user pool that isn’t on the Essentials or Plus plan, the API returns a FeatureUnavailableInTierException
Full Text:
Not every action a user takes in an application carries the same risk. Viewing an account balance in a banking application isn’t the same as wiring several thousand dollars to a new payee. In practice, though, many applications ask users to prove their identity once at sign-in and then treat every action the same from that point on, whether that sign-in used a password alone or included multi-factor authentication (MFA). That creates a tension: if the sign-in is strict enough for the most sensitive operation, everyday tasks carry unnecessary friction. If it’s easy enough for everyday tasks, the most sensitive operations might not be protected well enough. Even a strong sign-in from hours earlier says little about who is at the keyboard when a high-risk request arrives.

Amazon Cognito now resolves that trade-off by supporting step-up authentication, which records the authentication assurance level and the methods used, and including both in the JSON web tokens (JWTs) it issues. You ask for a target assurance level when a user signs in. Amazon Cognito returns the level the user reached in an acr claim (authentication context class reference) and the methods they completed in an amr claim (authentication methods reference). These claims are part of the OpenID Connect Core specification, so your application can reason about authentication strength in a standard way and match it to the potential risk of what the user is trying to do. In this post, I explain how the claims support step-up authentication and walk through four patterns that put them to use: transaction-level step-up in a banking app, varying risk postures across a portfolio of applications, step-up enforced on API and SDK sign-in, and authentication assurance carried across a federated third-party OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider.

You can request authentication levels through Amazon Cognito managed login using the standard OIDC acr_values and max_age parameters, and through the SDK and API using the USER_AUTH flow with TARGET_ACR_VALUES and MAX_AGE. Requesting step-up authentication requires the Essentials or Plus feature plan. ; For the complete list of features, behaviors, and limitations, see the Authentication levels with ACR and AMR claims.

What ACR and AMR tell your application

Amazon Cognito defines four assurance levels, and the factor combinations that satisfy each one are fixed. You can use the default names as is or rename the level URIs to fit your organization’s own naming scheme. Renaming changes only the label. If you need to relate Amazon Cognito levels to a framework such as NIST SP 800-63 or eIDAS, make that mapping in your application. The following are the default Amazon Cognito defined levels.

Level 1 (urn:cognito:loa:1) is password only.

Level 2 (urn:cognito:loa:2) is a single one-time password (OTP) over SMS or email.

Level 3 (urn:cognito:loa:3) is a passkey on its own, or a password combined with an SMS or email OTP.

Level 4 (urn:cognito:loa:4) is the highest: a password with a time-based one-time password (TOTP) code from an authenticator app.

Amazon Cognito assigns the highest level the user’s completed factors fully satisfy, so a user who signs in with a password and a TOTP code lands at level 4, even though they also met the assurance requirements for every level below it.

Four claims in the token facilitate a step-up decision. The acr claim is the level the sign-in reached and is what your application compares against what the operation requires. The amr claim lists the methods behind that level, so you can confirm a specific factor was used. The auth_time claim records when the user last authenticated interactively and is what max_age is measured against. The iat claim only records when the token was issued, so a refreshed token carries a new iat but keeps its old auth_time. Finally, send a nonce in the request and verify it on the returned ID token, so the result is tied to the request you made.

The following is an example access token for a user completing a level 4 authentication. Notice the four claims I’ve discussed: acr, amr, auth_time, and iat.

{ "sub": "387173a0-60c1-700a-4a02-e84b49bcc7a9", "iss": "https://cognito-idp.<region>.amazonaws.com/<region>_123abc", "aud": "123abcn2ci4a99a4ieno123abc", "exp": 1445470140, "iat": 499163700, "auth_time": -446666160, "token_use": "access", "acr": "urn:cognito:loa:4", "amr": ["pwd", "otp", "mfa"], "email": "marty@example.com", "cognito:username": "387173a0-60c1-700a-4a02-e84b49bcc7a9" }

Two important behaviors are worth understanding before you build on this. First, a token refresh preserves the acr and amr values, so a user who reached level 4 keeps level 4 across refreshes and isn’t asked to prove it again on every rotation. Second, a refresh doesn’t reset the auth_time claim. That field records when the user interactively authenticated, not from a non-interactive token refresh. This is what lets you reason about freshness of authentication separately from assurance strength.

At a high level, every step-up interaction in this post follows the same loop: the application checks the token it already holds, redirects for a stronger level only when the operation requires more than the user has, and re-validates the acr claim on the freshly issued token before it proceeds. The following diagram provides a general step-up authentication flow.

Figure 1: General step-up authentication flow to access a sensitive operation

How you request a level, and what stays your responsibility

The request side is deliberately straightforward. On managed login you add acr_values and optionally max_age to the or endpoint. In the SDK and API, you pass TARGET_ACR_VALUES and MAX_AGE in the USER_AUTH flow of the API. Both acr_values and TARGET_ACR_VALUES accept an ordered list of target levels. The same parameters work whether you’re setting the level for an initial sign-in or raising the level of a user who is already signed in; the patterns later in this post show both. Amazon Cognito acts only on what you send. It doesn’t infer the level you meant, so if you omit the parameter or request the wrong level, the user might not be stepped up the way you intended.

That points to the part your application and API owns: what assurance authentication level is needed. Amazon Cognito issues a token that honestly reports the level the user reached based on what your application requested. For example, deciding that a given operation requires an assurance level 3, checking the token’s acr against that requirement, and refusing the operation when it falls short is enforcement your application and API performs. Amazon Cognito produces the evidence; your code acts on it. In practice, that means checking the token you already hold before you redirect, so you don’t send a user to re-authenticate who already meets the bar, and validating the acr and auth_time claims on the tokens Amazon Cognito returns before you grant access. Amazon Cognito computes these claims itself, so you can’t customize, add to, or suppress them with a pre-token-generation Lambda trigger.

There is one more detail that saves debugging time later. If you rename your acr level URIs after tokens have already been issued, an older token might carry an acr value that no longer matches any configured level. Amazon Cognito treats that as an unrecognized level rather than an error. It still honors the token’s amr values and prompts only for factors not already present, without crediting any particular level. The amr list, in other words, remains meaningful even when a renamed level string goes stale. See Configuring ACR level names to learn how to configure this.

With the claims and the division of responsibility in place, the following four patterns show how they work in practice. Each one applies the same loop from Figure 1 to a different situation: a single application, a portfolio of applications, API-driven sign-in, and federation.

Pattern 1: Transaction-level step-up in a banking app

Consider a retail banking application. Signing in and viewing balances is routine, and the bank is comfortable requiring a moderate assurance level for it. Moving money is considered a privileged action, and a large transfer deserves stronger proof that the person at the keyboard is really the account holder.

The bank sets its baseline at level 2, so a user signs in with a one-time code over SMS or email and can see balances, statements, and pending transactions. When that same user initiates a transfer above $1,000, the application’s own policy says the operation requires level 4. Before it shows the transfer initiation screen, the application inspects the acr claim in the token it already holds. The user authenticated at level 2, level 2 is below the required level 4, so the application redirects the user to managed login with acr_values=urn:cognito:loa:4.

GET https://auth.example-bank.com/oauth2/authorize ?response_type=code &client_id=abc123def456 &redirect_uri=https://app.example-bank.com/callback &scope=openid &acr_values=urn:cognito:loa:4

Amazon Cognito now requires the user to complete a factor combination that satisfies level 4, for example entering their password and then a TOTP code from their authenticator app. When authentication finishes, Amazon Cognito issues fresh tokens with acr set to urn:cognito:loa:4, amr set to ["pwd", "otp", "mfa"], and a fresh updated auth_time claim. The application validates that the new token meets its requirement and only then lets the transfer proceed. A transfer under the threshold never triggers any of this, so the everyday experience stays light and the friction lands exactly where the risk is.

The application logic reads naturally, here’s a pseudo JavaScript snippet:

// Use your own URIs here, if different than defaults. const ACR_RANK = { "urn:cognito:loa:1": 1, "urn:cognito:loa:2": 2, "urn:cognito:loa:3": 3, "urn:cognito:loa:4": 4, }; const REQUIRED_LEVEL = "urn:cognito:loa:4"; const HIGH_VALUE_THRESHOLD = 1000; function canAuthorizeTransfer(accessTokenClaims, amount) { if (amount < HIGH_VALUE_THRESHOLD) { return true; // baseline session is sufficient } // High-value transfer: require level 4. // An unrecognized acr ranks 0, so it never passes. const achieved = ACR_RANK[accessTokenClaims.acr] ?? 0; return achieved >= ACR_RANK[REQUIRED_LEVEL]; }

You can extend the same idea to freshness. A bank might accept a level 4 session for a high-value transfer only if the user authenticated within the last 5 minutes, which you express by adding max_age=300 to the request. Amazon Cognito compares that window against the auth_time claim in the access token and reauthenticates the user if the window has passed, even if the token was refreshed seconds ago.

Pattern 2: A portfolio of applications with different risk postures

Assurance levels are just as useful across a set of applications as they are within one. Suppose an organization runs five applications from a single Amazon Cognito user pool using managed login, and each one carries a different risk posture.

An internal cafeteria menu is low risk, so it’s fine with level 1, password only. An employee directory and an expense viewer hold personal data but nothing that moves money, so they require level 2: a one-time code over SMS or email on top of the password. A source code portal warrants a passkey or a password plus a one-time code, which is level 3. The production financial console is the crown jewel, so it demands level 4: a password with a TOTP code.

Each application requests its own floor by setting acr_values to the level that matches its risk, and each validates the acr claim on the returned token before granting access. Because the applications share a user pool, managed login keeps a single sign-on (SSO) session across them. A user who has already reached level 4 for the financial console is redirected to managed login when they open another application, finds the existing session, and receives tokens for that application without another prompt, provided the application doesn’t send a max_age that the session has outlived. Each application then compares levels by rank, so a level 4 token satisfies a level 2 floor. Someone who signed in at level 1 for the cafeteria menu, on the other hand, is stepped up the first time they open the expense viewer, because level 1 doesn’t meet the level 2 floor that the application enforces. The user pool stays single and central; the assurance requirement travels with each application’s own policy.

Renaming the level URIs helps here. If the organization already classifies systems against an internal assurance standard, it can set AcrConfiguration on the user pool so that, say, level 3 reports as urn:example-corp:assurance:standard and level 4 as urn:example-corp:assurance:high. The factor combinations behind each level stay fixed; only the names change, so every application validates against strings its developers already recognize.

Pattern 3: Step-up on API and SDK sign-in

Managed login covers browser-based flows, including federation, but plenty of clients authenticate directly against the Amazon Cognito API, and the same assurance model applies there, such as using the USER_AUTH flow with the InitiateAuth API. This matters for a mobile app, a desktop client, or a service that drives sign-in programmatically and needs to raise assurance before a sensitive call.

Take a mobile trading app that signs its users in with the SDK. A user opens the app with a password and reaches level 1, which is enough to browse watchlists and market data. When they place a trade, the app’s policy requires level 4. Because the app authenticates through the API rather than a browser redirect, it starts a new USER_AUTH flow and passes the access token it already holds along with TARGET_ACR_VALUES, requesting the level it needs. Amazon Cognito drives the user through a factor combination that satisfies level 4, then returns tokens whose acr claim the app validates before it submits the order. The InitiateAuth request would look similar to the following API call.

{ "AuthFlow": "USER_AUTH", "ClientId": "abc123def456", "AuthParameters": { "USERNAME": "user@example.com", "ACCESS_TOKEN": "eyJraWQiOi...", "TARGET_ACR_VALUES": "urn:cognito:loa:4", "MAX_AGE": "300" } }

Passing the access token the app already holds lets Amazon Cognito step the user up from the factors in that token; without it, Amazon Cognito authenticates the user from scratch. The MAX_AGE parameter behaves the same way it does on managed login. It ties the requirement to auth_time, so a trade placed after the window elapses forces a fresh authentication even if the app refreshed its tokens in the meantime. One behavior specific to the API path is worth knowing when you test on a lower Cognito feature plan. If you request step-up through InitiateAuth on a user pool that isn’t on the Essentials or Plus plan, the API returns a FeatureUnavailableInTierException. Managed login handles the same situation differently: the authorize endpoint silently ignores acr_values and proceeds with normal authentication rather than raising an error.

Pattern 4: Carrying assurance across a federated OIDC identity provider

The three patterns so far assume Amazon Cognito is where the user authenticates and the authoritative source for the identity. Many organizations federate sign-in to a third-party OIDC provider, so the person proving who they are is doing it against an external identity provider (IdP), while Amazon Cognito brokers the session. The assurance model follows them there.

When your application requests a level, it sends acr_values and optionally max_age to the Amazon Cognito authorize endpoint exactly as before. If that user is configured to federate through an OIDC IdP, Amazon Cognito sends the authorization request to that IdP on the user’s behalf. It translates the level you requested into the acr value the IdP expects, using the mapping you configured, and passes max_age along with it. A standards-compliant OIDC IdP honors acr_values the same way Amazon Cognito does: it drives the user through an authentication that satisfies the requested level, and it returns its own acr value describing what the user reached. max_age carries forward in the same way, so a freshness requirement is enforced at the provider that actually authenticates the user rather than being lost at the broker. Keep in mind that this is only supported with OIDC identity providers.

The request is unchanged from the application’s point of view. It still directs to Amazon Cognito:

GET https://auth.example.com/oauth2/authorize ?response_type=code &client_id=abc123def456 &redirect_uri=https://app.example.com/callback &scope=openid &identity_provider=PartnerOIDC &acr_values=urn:cognito:loa:3 &max_age=300

The interaction gains a third participant, the downstream IdP, but the assurance requirement is persisted through the entire federated authentication flow as shown in figure 2.

Figure 2: Federation with an OIDC third-party IdP, persisting the acr_values and max_age request parameters

The value that comes back from a partner IdP won’t use Amazon Cognito’s level URIs, so this lets you map the provider’s acr values onto its own levels with the AcrMapping field on the OIDC IdP configuration. A partner IdP that reports, say, https://partner.example/assurance/strong can be mapped to Amazon Cognito level 3 (urn:cognito:loa:3), so that by the time the token reaches your application the acr claim speaks the same vocabulary regardless of whether the user authenticated locally or through a federated provider. Your resource server keeps a single enforcement rule and authorization logic and doesn’t need to have special handling depending on where the user ultimately authenticated. See Step-up authentication for federated users to learn how to map external OIDC IdP acr levels to Cognito.

This is the same pattern that RFC 9470, the OAuth 2.0 Step Up Authentication Challenge Protocol, describes: the assurance level is requested at the edge of your application, travels through Amazon Cognito to whatever provider authenticates the user, and returns normalized to a vocabulary your code already understands. A user federating from a corporate IdP and a user signing in against the same user pool directly both arrive at your resource server carrying an acr claim that means the same thing.

Conclusion

In this post, I showed you how the acr and amr claims in Amazon Cognito let you match authentication strength to the risk of what a user is doing, instead of settling for one bar at the front door. Your application requests a target level with acr_values and max_age (or TARGET_ACR_VALUES and MAX_AGE in the USER_AUTH flow), Amazon Cognito reports the level reached and the methods used, and your application enforces what each operation requires. The four patterns, from a banking transfer to a federated third-party IdP, follow that same loop, and one enforcement rule at your resource server covers every sign-in path.

The larger shift is that assurance is now something Amazon Cognito expresses in a standard way and your application reasons about directly, without building your own step-up tracking. To get started, move your user pool to the Essentials or Plus feature plan, decide the level each operation requires, and add acr_values to your existing authorize requests. For the complete parameter reference and federated behavior, see the Amazon Cognito Developer Guide.
