Title: Artex Is Criminals’ New Favorite ‘Point-and-Shoot’ AI Hacking Tool
Context: Over the past year, security researchers have warned that AI agents could vastly speed up cybercriminals’ ability to launch cyberattacks, breach companies, and ultimately steal...
Full Text:
Over the past year, security researchers have warned that AI agents could vastly speed up cybercriminals’ ability to launch cyberattacks, breach companies, and ultimately steal money, data, or sensitive information from those compromised systems. For at least one subset of hackers, it appears that era has now arrived.

Since around the end of August, multiple companies, government agencies, and banks around the world have been targeted by cybercriminals adopting a new wave of AI-powered penetration testing tools. These setups​​—many of which mimic legitimate defensive penetration testing techniques—use LLMs to autonomously scan potential hacking targets and attempt to force their way into poorly secured networks, then carry out attack plans written by human operators.

Dozens of these AI penetration frameworks or “harnesses,” which detail how an AI model should carry out cybersecurity testing or attacks, are increasingly being linked to real-world attacks. The tools do not introduce new ways to attack websites or servers and are not sophisticated, according to alerts from around half a dozen security companies. Instead, they allow cybercriminals to launch attacks at speeds that would be impossible for humans to do.

Hackers also don’t need to be skilled to use the tools, researchers say, and attacks that would have taken days are completed in just hours. “Agentic frameworks have progressed from experimental use to sustained, multi-objective offensive operations that run with minimal human intervention,” CJ Moses, AWS’s chief information security officer, wrote in a company blog post recently.

The most prominent of these tools is Artex. Written in the programming language Go, the open-source framework was first published on GitHub in July by a pseudonymous developer using the handle Autumn-27, and it’s been spreading across some hacker communities ever since. Artex has been used across all parts of attacks, from conducting initial analysis of networks and gaining access to moving within systems and preparing data to be exported.

“It’s really an all-in-one product,” says Jacob Larsen, an offensive security researcher and founder of security firm Cypen. “Previous iterations of AI agent pen-testing tools would either only do reconnaissance—like the scanning and analysis [of targets]—and some would only do testing. This is really a point-and-shoot weapon.”

As with other AI hacking frameworks, Artex isn’t an AI product itself. Instead, it is essentially a guide that points external frontier and open-source AI models—that can be connected to it via APIs—to a series of existing penetration testing tools and processes. People using Artex or other similar setups can give simple, natural-language prompts to begin their operations. “Launch a penetration attack on [Redacted victim] to gain access to the site’s admin panel, database, or server,” one set of hackers prompted Artex, according to researchers at the security firm Check Point.

Title: Most SecOps Leaders Are Changing the L1 Role as Agent Use Grows
Context: Half (49%) of respondents said they’re hiring for new skills like AI detection engineering and automation, while two-fifths (42%) are retraining L1 analysts to supervise agents
Full Text:
The vast majority (87%) of security leaders are redesigning their security operations centers (SOCs) because of AI agents, but roles are being adapted rather than eliminated, according to Strike48.

The security startup polled 534 security and IT leaders at organizations with 200 or more employees and a security operations function in the UK, Canada and US to produce its latest report: The State of Agentic Security H2 2026.

It revealed that agents have already gone mainstream and 74% of respondents said they have deployed the technology in their SOC, up from 36% in May. Half (49%) are using it in multiple use cases.

However, L1/Tier-1 analysts are being redeployed rather than replaced. Half (49%) of respondents said they’re hiring for new skills like AI detection engineering and automation, while two-fifths (42%) are retraining L1 analysts to supervise agents.

A slightly smaller share (38%) are moving L1s into investigation roles while 30% are even growing their team with more entry-level analysts.

Read more: AI SOCs Will Still Need SOC Analysts, Security Vendors Say

The findings will allay common concerns in the industry that AI will take the roles of entry-level SecOps employees, eliminating a vital career on ramp.

A Swimlane report from September revealed that a quarter (24%) of SOC analysts feel the technology has limited their ability to build skills. One in 10 said they expect fewer opportunities for junior analysts to gain experience.

Building Trust for Autonomy

The report also highlighted that, despite widespread adoption of agents in the SOC, a lack of trust is constraining organizations' ability to make the most of deployments.

Only 30% of teams claim to allow their agents to act with high or full autonomy, while half (47%) keep humans executing actions or preapproving them, and a quarter (23%) let agents act within defined boundaries.

Trust seems to rise as use cases expand and governance is put in place. Respondents’ top five requirements for trusted autonomy are:

Proven accuracy in their environment over time (57%)

A full audit trail of every action and the data behind it (53%)

Technical enforcement that the agent cannot exceed limits, not just instructions telling it not to (46%)

A precisely defined scope for each agent (44%)

A reliable rollback or undo for any action (40%)

“Most teams start the same way: one agent, one long prompt telling it to act like a Level 1 analyst, and a pile of tools bolted on. Then it meets a real alert queue, and you find out a single prompt can’t carry an entire triage process. In my view, this is why distrust of agent outputs is highest for teams with just one use case,” Tim Leehealy, co-founder and president, Strike48, told Infosecurity.

“I’d argue the models are mature enough. What’s immature is how most teams use them. The SOC teams that get to agent autonomy break the work into narrow jobs and fixed, deterministic workflow steps.”

Title: AI-powered cyber threats are changing the rules of enterprise recovery
Context: These questions are becoming increasingly important as organizations confront both traditional threats and emerging AI-powered cyberattacks
Full Text: Cybersecurity has long been a contest between attackers finding new ways in and defenders trying to keep them out. Artificial intelligence is making that contest more complicated, giving cybercriminals new ways to develop and adapt their attacks while putting additional pressure on conventional cyber defences. For enterprise IT leaders, the challenge extends beyond preventing a breach. What happens when an attacker gets through? Can compromised data be identified, clean copies recovered, and essential systems brought back online without prolonged disruption? These questions are becoming increasingly important as organizations confront both traditional threats and emerging AI-powered cyberattacks. A successful defense strategy must, therefore, account for what happens after an incident, not just the measures designed to prevent one. Making recovery part of the defence This is where cyber-resilient enterprise storage has an important role to play. Rather than relying solely on traditional backup processes, organizations need ways to protect critical data, detect potential compromise, establish which copies can safely be recovered, and restore those copies as quickly as possible. Infinidat addresses this challenge through its InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA enterprise storage platforms, which incorporate the company’s InfiniSafe cyber resilience and recovery software suite. InfiniSafe combines immutable snapshots, which cannot be altered or deleted during their protected retention period, with logical air-gapping to isolate the management plane from the data plane. Fenced forensic environments provide a separate space for validating data before recovery. The technology also supports automated cyber protection, allowing security monitoring data center wide cyber security software applications or a Security Operations Center (SOC) to automatically talk to InfiniBoxes and trigger immutable snapshots when suspicious activity is detected. This helps reduce the window in which critical data might be exposed. For organizations concerned about recovering compromised information, optional InfiniSafe Cyber Detection uses AI-based analysis to help identify cyber affected data and locate the last known good copy of the data for recovery. Speed is another consideration. Infinidat guarantees recovery of immutable snapshots in one minute or less for InfiniBox and InfiniBox SSA, subject to the guarantee’s terms and conditions. Ultimately, cyber resilience isn’t about assuming every cyberattack can be stopped. It’s about ensuring that when defences are breached, organizations have the tools and processes to recover trusted data and limit the operational consequences. For enterprise IT teams, that makes recovery readiness an essential part of the cybersecurity conversation. Sponsored by Infinidat

He pleaded guilty in April to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and aggravated identity theft, and he’s the fifth and final defendant sentenced in this case.

Employees who typed their credentials into those pages handed over account access, personal information and company data. The conspirators built a phishing kit that captured those logins and piped them straight to a Telegram channel Buchanan ran with another member. When police searched his home in Scotland in April 2023, they found files tied to numerous victim companies.

Spanish police arrested the British national who was suspected of being a key member of the cybercrime group Scattered Spider (also known as UNC3944, 0ktapus). The man was arrested in Palma de Mallorca while attempting to fly to Italy. During the arrest, police confiscated a laptop and a mobile phone. The arrest resulted from a joint operation conducted by the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Spanish Police.

Spanish police tracked the suspect to Mallorca after he entered Spain via Barcelona in late May 2024.

Buchanan has been in U.S. custody since April 2025. Between 2021 and 2023, he and his group targeted companies and individuals across several sectors. They sent large SMS phishing campaigns that mimicked trusted services and tricked employees into sharing credentials and personal data. Using this access, they broke into corporate systems and stole sensitive information, including intellectual property and user data.

“The SMS phishing messages contained links to phishing websites designed to look like legitimate websites of a victim company or a contracted IT or BPO supplier. The websites then lured the recipient into providing confidential information, including personal identifying information (PII), account usernames, and passwords.” reads the press release published by DoJ.

“As part of the scheme, the conspirators created a phishing kit that captured login credentials entered the fraudulent phishing websites by a victim company’s employees. The stolen credentials were then transmitted to an online Telegram channel administered by Buchanan and another co-conspirator.”

Buchanan admitted he kept files linked to many victim companies at his home in Scotland. He and his accomplices used stolen data from corporate breaches to target individuals and access their cryptocurrency accounts and wallets, stealing millions. To do this, they broke into online accounts and carried out SIM swap attacks, taking control of victims’ phone numbers and intercepting two-factor authentication codes sent via SMS or calls. This let them bypass security protections and fully access accounts. Investigators also found sensitive data on his devices, including names, addresses, login credentials, and even cryptocurrency seed phrases tied to victims’ wallets, showing how the group combined corporate intrusions and personal targeting to maximize profits.

“Buchanan further admitted that he and several co-conspirators used the information stolen from company intrusions to identify and gain access to virtual currency accounts and wallets belonging to individual victims to steal millions of dollars’ worth of virtual currency.” continues press release.

Noah Michael Urban, also known as “Sosa” and “Elijah,” received a 10-year prison sentence and must pay $13 million in restitution after pleading guilty to fraud charges. Ahmed Hossam Eldin Elbadawy and Evans Onyeaka Osiebo each got 45 months, and Joel Martin Evans got two years.

The cybercrime group Scattered Spider is suspected of hacking into hundreds of organizations over the past two years, including Twilio, LastPass, DoorDash, and Mailchimp.

Scattered Spider members are part of a broader cybercriminal community called “The Com,” where hackers brag about high-profile cyber thefts, typically initiated through social engineering tactics like phone, email, or SMS scams to gain access to corporate networks.

“Those thefts had severe, life-altering consequences for many victims and underscore both the seriousness and far-reaching impact of this conspiracy,” prosecutors argued in a sentencing memorandum.

A restitution hearing is set for 11 December.

The investigation pulled in the FBI, the US Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of North Carolina, the Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, Police Scotland, Spain’s Cuerpo Nacional de Policía, and FBI field offices in four cities. SIM swapping defeats SMS-based two-factor authentication specifically, so an authenticator app or a hardware key closes that door even when a text message doesn’t look suspicious. The case is a reminder that your phone number is a password too, and one you can’t change as easily.

The Justice Department sums up the method plainly: “SIM swapping” is a technique in which a criminal fraudulently induces a mobile carrier to reassign a cell phone number from the legitimate subscriber’s SIM card to a SIM card controlled by another without the legitimate subscriber’s authorization or knowledge.

Title: New EggStreme Malware Variant Goes Silent to Evade Security Tools in Government Attacks
Context: " The end result is that the changes allow it to bypass static signatures and heuristic detections built around the EggStreme malware framework when it was first exposed in...
Full Text:
The suspected Chinese advanced persistent threat (APT) group behind the sophisticated EggStreme malware has rebuilt its toolkit as it continues to target government organizations in the Philippines.

"When attackers are exposed, the cheap response is to rotate," Bitdefender said in a technical report shared with The Hacker News. "A file hash changes with every recompile, a domain costs a few dollars, and a new IP address costs less."

"The EggStreme operators did more than rotate – the agent we now see uses a different network protocol, has an enhanced command set, and comes in a passive variant that never beacons out. The infrastructure appears to be moving away from the one certificate authority that tied its older servers together."

The end result is that the changes allow it to bypass static signatures and heuristic detections built around the EggStreme malware framework when it was first exposed in September 2025.

Delivered via an as-yet-unknown initial access vector, EggStreme's defining characteristic is the use of DLL sideloading to execute payloads. It features multiple components as follows -

EggStremeFuel (aka RawCookie), which conducts system profiling and deploys EggStremeLoader

EggStremeLoader, which sets up persistence and decrypts and executes EggStremeReflectiveLoader

EggStremeReflectiveLoader, which executes EggStremeAgent

EggStremeAgent (aka Gorem RAT), the core component and a full-featured backdoor that enables system reconnaissance, lateral movement, data theft via an injected keylogger called EggStremeKeylogger, and reverse shell and file upload/download capabilities via a secondary backdoor called EggStremeWizard

It's worth noting that some components of the framework, such as EggStremeFuel and EggStremeLoader, have been put to use by another cluster tracked by Palo Alto Networks as CL-STA-1048 between March and September 2025.

The latest findings from Bitdefender show a significant retooling of EggStreme's capabilities, including removing the keylogger from every agent build observed since then. Within two weeks after public disclosure, the threat actors are also said to have made other changes -

The method EggStremeFuel uses to protect its configuration

EggStremeLoader's cryptography and payload format, moving from RC4 to RC5 and to a custom cipher by the end of October 2025

Added commands in EggStremeAgent that facilitate Active Directory reconnaissance, Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) querying, TCP traffic forwarding, and execution of PowerShell, Portable Executable (PE), .NET assembly payloads

Moving from a single certificate authority to campaign-specific certificate authorities

In addition, where lateral movement previously relied on Impacket-like tooling and on EggStremeAgent itself, newer incidents make use of an unmanaged system that sits outside of the organization's endpoint management but is still reachable by other workstations to stage the payloads and launch them via DLL sideloading using a Visual Basic Script (VBScript) file remotely run over Server Message Block (SMB).

Some of the newer builds have been found to run in passive mode by opening a listening port and waiting for the operator to connect in as opposed to contacting an external command-and-control (C2) server.

There is also some evidence that the attackers have also targeted Taiwan, but it has been treated with low to medium confidence.

"The speed of the loader changes says as much about the operators' maturity as about the cost of exposure," Bitdefender concluded. "The build-time design appears to be what makes rebuilds this fast. What they did not change is how they operate: sideloaded DLLs under system library names, staging through file shares, running from memory, and requiring mutual TLS."

Mustang Panda Targets Philippine Government Using ASEAN Summit Lures

As of late October 2026, Philippine government officials have also been targeted by Mustang Panda, a prolific China-aligned cyber espionage group, using ASEAN Summit lures to deliver PlugX using established tactics like DLL sideloading.

Mustang Panda attack chain

"The package impersonated a Laos–Philippines bilateral meeting agenda from the Lao Ministry of Foreign Affairs," Dream Research Labs said in a report published last week.

"It named five officials and referenced plausible diplomatic priorities, requesting that the reader provide confirmation before the summit. Behind it was a delivery chain that installed PlugX remote-access malware while displaying the decoy agenda."

Earth Alux Uses Stealthy Tradecraft to Strike Southeast Asia

The disclosure comes as a China-nexus threat actor tracked as Earth Alux (aka Ink Dragon, Jewelbug, REF7707, and UAT-11587) has been attributed to a fresh set of attacks targeting Southeast Asian government entities since at least July 2025. Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 has assigned the activity the designation TGR-STA-0049 (formerly CL-STA-0049).

"The defining signature of the threat actor behind the activity is the targeting of government entities, combined with the use of advanced custom payloads that are designed for high-stealth intelligence collection operations, with an emphasis on evading security detection tools," Unit 42 researcher Tom Fakterman said.

Attacks mounted by the group have historically deployed an advanced backdoor known as FINALDRAFT (aka Squidoor) since 2023. However, it has since expanded its malware arsenal to include two previously undocumented remote access trojans (RATs) called PerfectPioneer RAT (in July 2025) and KUKURAT (in March 2026).

Initial access to target networks is achieved via exploitation of vulnerable, unpatched Microsoft Exchange servers to deploy web shells like ASPXSpy and Godzilla, which are then used to deploy the RAT payloads. Alternatively, Earth Alux has leveraged phishing emails using decoy PDFs and lookalike domains to compromise victim hosts.

PerfectPioneer RAT is a Go-based malware that's launched via three different methods -

DLL sideloading to launch a malicious DLL that reads, decrypts and executes XOR-encrypted shellcode containing the RAT

Decoy installers for Palo Alto Networks GlobalProtect that installs the legitimate program but also writes the malware to disk and executes it in the background

Disguising executable files as PDF documents in phishing emails that, once launched, opens a decoy PDF document while the malware is launched in the background

The malware supports a number of features that enable the operator to gain remote control of the infected host. It facilitates file operations, shell execution, process management, keylogging, SOCKS5 proxy, screenshot capture, Window enumeration and manipulation, and CPU and memory utilization monitoring.

PerfectPioneer RAT execution chain

It also ensures a connection to the C2 server remains active at all times and systematically cleans up temporary files and runs garbage collection if memory usage exceeds 100 MB to minimize forensic traces.

Furthermore, select variants of the malware come with an "isDangerousCommand" feature to avoid running administrative commands that would be highly destructive or noisy, thereby allowing it to be detected by security programs installed on the host. These include rm, curl | bash, wget | bash, and powershell -e, among others.

KUKURAT, in contrast, functions as a modular implant that's executed in networks already compromised by PerfectPioneer RAT. Written in C++, the backdoor implements its functionality as a separate DLL module that's loaded dynamically at runtime directly from the C2 server.

This allows the malware to be highly evasive and adapt its capabilities on the fly in response to shifting operational objectives. It supports the following features -

Send system information and receive a configuration from the C2 server

Take screenshots

Log keystrokes

Enumerate and terminate processes

Perform file operations

Execute shell commands via cmd.exe and PowerShell

Conduct lateral movement via PsExec

Carry out SMB credential brute-forcing

Run Beacon Object Files (BOF)

Facilitate local privilege elevation

Ensure the malware remains active by means of a standalone watchdog executable

What's more, KUKURAT initiates bogus, legitimate-looking activity on the endpoint to camouflage and cover up its tracks based on a command issued by the threat actor. This includes -

Generate 10 decoy HTTP requests per operational cycle to randomly selected domains that are extracted from a hard-coded list of 15 popular websites using randomly generated URL paths with an aim to blend C2 communications

Mimic legitimate Google Chrome browser behavior by writing random data to the registry path HKCU\Software\Google\Chrome\BrowserCrashRecovery, reading the data back, and deleting the key

Create temporary files with random names and randomized content inside the system %temp% directory, and delete them

"Both PerfectPioneer RAT and KUKURAT use HTTP/3 as the primary method for communicating with C2 infrastructure," Unit 42 said. "While the adoption of HTTP/3 is rare across the broader malware landscape, its deployment in this campaign reflects an emerging trend among advanced threat actors."

The attacks have also been found to leverage established tools like PsExec, WMI, and Windows Remote Management (WinRM) to move laterally across compromised enterprise networks; collect credentials using Mimikatz, ProcDump, and SharpDPAPI; compromise Domain Controllers to deploy KUKURAT on local endpoints; and exfiltrate sensitive data such as files and emails.

"Through the deployment of KUKURAT and the PerfectPioneer RAT, the attackers behind this activity are actively evolving to stay ahead of traditional network defenses by implementing protocol-level evasion via HTTP/3 and QUIC over UDP," Unit 42 concluded.

"What makes this group particularly evasive is the extensive effort invested in maintaining operational security and remaining hidden on compromised endpoints. The group demonstrates a mature understanding of modern defensive ecosystems. They have even gone so far as to embed hard-coded administrative safety switches within their binaries to prevent their own operators from running loud or destructive commands that might trigger security alerts."

Title: Suspected Chinese APT Rebuilds EggStreme Malware After Exposure
Context: A suspected Chinese advanced persistent threat (APT) group rebuilt parts of the EggStreme malware framework after it was exposed by Bitdefender
Full Text:
A suspected Chinese advanced persistent threat (APT) group rebuilt parts of the EggStreme malware framework after it was exposed by Bitdefender. The company said the timing suggested its report was a likely trigger.

Bitdefender detailed the changes in an update to its cyberespionage research, first published in September 2025. It made no new attribution claim. It assessed with high confidence that the operation targeted multiple Philippine government organizations and with low to medium confidence that it targeted Taiwan, calling the latter a lead, not an established fact.

In the original research in September 2025, Bitdefender found a Chinese APT group had compromised a Philippines-based military firm using the EggStreme fileless malware framework.

What the Operators Changed

EggStremeFuel, one of the framework's components, changed how it protected its configuration in a build compiled 12 days after the original report, Bitdefender said.

Two weeks after that, the operators compiled a loader with a new cipher and payload format. That cipher was replaced again by late October 2025, swaps Bitdefender said offered little real protection but still defeated detections built for the old cipher.

The EggStremeAgent backdoor dropped its previous protocol for raw TCP connections still secured with mutual TLS, in which both sides present certificates.

Newer builds added Windows domain mapping and in-memory PowerShell, and none of those analyzed carried the keylogger. Two of them ran in passive mode, waiting for the operators to connect rather than calling out. Bitdefender first saw these builds after the report, though some were compiled earlier.

Bitdefender said the framework's design, which let operators swap capabilities with a new build, appeared to explain the speed.

Read more on Chinese cyberespionage: Suspected Chinese Malware Supplier Tied to Three Hacking Campaigns

What Defenders Can Still Track

Older EggStreme servers traced back to one certificate authority, created in 2019 and linked to 32 domains. No new domains appeared under it after the report. Newer activity suggested a shift to campaign-specific ones, which Bitdefender said was unconfirmed, though some links between old and new infrastructure remained.

Despite the rebuild, four behaviors stayed constant: DLL sideloading (getting a legitimate program to load malicious code), movement through file shares, in-memory execution and mutual TLS. Bitdefender said the operators "spent at the tools level and kept their methods."

Bitdefender's recommendations included restricting built-in Windows tools an environment did not need, detecting DLL sideloading by library name and location, finding unmanaged machines that could still reach workstations and watching for new inbound listeners on workstations.

The company argued that exposure could cost operators more than one campaign, since tooling is often shared. It said that raised a question about handing such operations to autonomous AI tools, where the chance of discovery was high, though its data did not test it.

Title: Who protects the antivirus? How we secure Malwarebytes itself
Context: The evidence is accumulating: In July 2025, Google reported that its AI agent Big Sleep discovered a critical SQLite flaw (CVE-2025-6965) that attackers already knew about
Full Text:
An antivirus is also software, and it can have weaknesses of its own.

That makes antivirus development particularly demanding. The product must safely handle files that may be hostile, run reliably across very different Windows environments, and resist attackers who try to abuse its privileges or shut it down completely.

Imagine a piece of malware that can disable your antivirus and leave you unprotected. That’s exactly what we as engineers work to prevent.

The attack surface of a privileged process

You might wonder why vulnerabilities matter for a desktop application that runs locally.

Our software runs with high privileges, so it has access to the entire system. That access is what lets it protect the system from exploits, data theft, and ransomware. It also makes our software an attractive target. An attacker who can disable our protection, or abuse it to gain those privileges, has a much easier path to taking over the system.

Two layers, one critical boundary

At a basic level, Malwarebytes has two layers: a user interface running as the signed-in user, and a background service running as SYSTEM. They communicate through COM (Component Object Model), a built-in Windows mechanism that lets one program call functions in another program, even one running in a separate process.

The UI can’t do much on its own. When you add an exclusion, restore a file from quarantine, or pause real-time protection, the UI only asks, and the SYSTEM service does the work. Those are exactly the operations malware would like to perform: excluding its own folder from scanning or turning protection off.

And malware doesn’t need our UI to act. Any process running as the same user can write its own COM client and call the same methods. So on every call, the service must answer two questions: who is really calling, and is this caller allowed to do this specific operation?

This is just one small example of an attack surface we keep in mind and protect. An antivirus has many more, and every fix to any of them has to preserve protection, performance, and system stability.

AI is making vulnerabilities cheaper to find

Finding a vulnerability usually involves four stages, and AI now speeds up every one of them:

Identifying possible weaknesses

Preparing test code and an environment

Running the tests

Analyzing the results before trying again

AI is a multiplier not just in development or business processes, but in finding vulnerabilities as well.

AI can explain unfamiliar code, generate diagnostic programs, and interpret compiler errors, logs, and debugger output. That lets people attempt investigations that used to be beyond their skills or would have taken far longer, even though a model alone still can’t reliably compromise an antivirus.

An experienced Windows engineer already understands privileges, process boundaries, and common security mistakes, and they know which assumptions to question. AI turns those questions into tests without the engineer having to write every variation by hand. It can build a diagnostic client and repeat the same test under different user accounts, integrity levels, and configurations, while the engineer decides whether the results show a real security failure.

The next step is already here: agents that combine a model with code navigation, build tools, a debugger, and a test environment. They propose a hypothesis, generate a test, observe the result, and refine the investigation in a loop. The hard part is still verification: telling a suspicious pattern apart from a real weakness. But a few years ago, none of this was possible.

The evidence is accumulating:

In July 2025, Google reported that its AI agent Big Sleep discovered a critical SQLite flaw (CVE-2025-6965) that attackers already knew about. Google says this stopped attackers from exploiting it.

Mozilla confirmed 22 security-sensitive bugs found through its collaboration with Anthropic and fixed by Firefox 148. Mozilla rated 14 bugs from the work high severity.

HackerOne reported a record 46,947 vulnerability submissions in March 2026, 76% more than a year earlier, with the share of valid, exploitable findings holding steady at about 25%.

In November 2026, OpenAI reported that an autonomous AI pipeline running an unreleased model built working root exploits for 948 unique Linux kernel local privilege escalation (LPE) vulnerabilities in a single scan.

Vulnerabilities will be found in greater numbers and at greater speed, and teams need to be ready.

Finding is only half the problem

Discovering is easier, but fixing vulnerabilities still takes substantial engineering effort, and the industry is already feeling the gap. HackerOne’s 2026 report found that the backlog of valid, unresolved findings grew 131% in two years, even though critical issues are being resolved faster than before.

If discovery speeds up and remediation doesn’t, the backlog grows, and open vulnerabilities present an opportunity for an attacker.

For a security company, the goal is to get ahead of the pace of discovery, and that takes dedicated resources and focus.

How we keep pace: prevent, detect, fix, learn

The inter-process boundary from the example above is just one of many areas attackers may target, and new ones appear as the product grows. At Malwarebytes we approach security as a continuous engineering process.

Prevent

Security by design. Before writing code, we build a threat model for each new feature: how could it be attacked, what privileges can it reach, and where does it accept untrusted input? Each component gets only the privileges its job requires, so a flaw in one part can’t easily lead to a full system compromise.

Zero trust between components. No component trusts another by default. Even our own processes must authenticate and be authorized on every privileged request, so a compromised or spoofed caller can’t ride on someone else’s trust. This is the per-call check the SYSTEM service runs in the two-layer example above.

Minimize the attack surface. Every interface we expose is something an attacker could probe, so we expose as few as possible. Features that aren’t needed are turned off, and privileged operations are reachable only through well-defined, authenticated entry points.

Secure development practices. Our engineers follow secure coding standards that define how to handle memory, untrusted input, and privileged operations, and which unsafe functions and patterns are not allowed. These rules are enforced in code review and by automated checks, not left to individual judgment. The compiler is part of our defense too: strict warning levels catch risky code at build time, and built-in protections such as stack protection, control-flow integrity, and address randomization make any remaining bugs much harder to exploit.

Detect

Static and dynamic analysis. Memory-safety bugs such as buffer overflows and use-after-free errors are among the most common causes of arbitrary code execution. Static analysis catches dangerous patterns before code runs; dynamic analysis catches memory and runtime errors as they happen in our test builds.

An AI vulnerability scanner. We built an internal scanner using modern AI models for source code analysis. It reasons about context and follows untrusted data through the code.

AI security review on every pull request. A dedicated AI agent reviews every pull request purely for security: unsafe memory handling, missing validation, privilege-boundary problems, and more. Engineers still do the regular review, but every change, however small, gets security attention.

Fuzzing and hostile testing. Malware authors craft files to attack scanners, so our file parsers, unpackers, and inter-process communication (IPC) interfaces are tested with malformed data, huge data streams, and fuzzed input on every release build.

Company-wide pipelines continuously scan our repositories for exposed secrets, vulnerable dependencies, and insecure configurations.

Fix

Structured triage. Every finding, whatever its source, is validated and reproduced. We then establish what an attacker would need to do to exploit it, give it a CVSS score, and assign an owner with a deadline based on that severity.

Safe fixes. Let’s imagine an authorization vulnerability between layers is found. The obvious response is to add an additional check. In practice, that check is often tricky to get right. An antivirus is made up of many components that authenticate each other; some start at boot, and some run in the kernel. If one piece breaks, the whole product can fail.

In a large codebase with years of history, even a small patch can cause a blue screen of death (BSOD), slow the system down, or break features for millions of users at once. A security fix has to preserve protection, performance, and stability.

AI-assisted remediation. AI helps our engineers investigate suspicious code, test hypotheses about exploitability, and explore possible fixes. Engineers review every change to confirm it fixes the root problem without introducing regressions.

Safe delivery. Fixes reach users through cryptographically signed updates, with critical security fixes released first.

Learn

A vulnerability isn’t closed when the patch is merged. For each fix, we add a regression test and put the triggering input into our fuzzing corpus. We search for the same bug pattern elsewhere in the code, analyze why the flaw was introduced, and update our scanner rules, fuzzing targets, and coding guidelines. We also track time to remediation, so we can make sure that fixes are shipped on time according to their severity.

What this costs us

Running Prevent, Detect, Fix, and Learn as a continuous loop isn’t free, and we accept the costs on purpose.

The tradeoff on people is time.

Security work takes roughly 10–20% of every sprint. We guard that time, so it isn’t pulled into new feature development.

The tradeoff on AI review is noise.

AI pipelines review pull requests, scan source code, and propose fixes, but an engineer still checks every finding and proposal. Each month, as the models and our process improve, the agent raises fewer false alarms.

The tradeoff on testing is volume.

Every fixed vulnerability gets its own tests, so the same flaw can’t quietly return. That’s more tests to write, run, and maintain, but a regression in a security fix is a flaw we’ve already paid for once.

The tradeoff on runtime checks is execution time.

Verifying who is calling across the boundary, locking down our files, folders, and processes, and hardening installs and updates all add a little work to every operation. We accept that overhead so every task runs securely.

What this means for you

You won’t see most of this work, but it protects you every day:

Protection that holds up under attack. Malwarebytes is designed so that malware can’t switch it off, tamper with it, or turn its privileges against you. We protect every point where attackers might try, from how components talk to each other to our own files and processes.

Fixes don’t trade one problem for another. Every security fix has to keep protection, performance, and stability intact.

Fixes reach you safely. They arrive as cryptographically signed updates, with critical security fixes first.

Fixed stays fixed. Each fix gets a regression test, and we look for the same bug elsewhere in the code.

Security comes first

AI has lowered the cost of finding vulnerabilities, for defenders and attackers alike, and that shift isn’t slowing down. For a product that runs with the highest privileges on a machine and protects millions of users, the only durable answer is to keep up with, and get ahead of, the discovery of flaws. That’s why at Malwarebytes we treat security as one continuous loop—prevent, detect, fix, and learn—where every finding makes the next release stronger.

When your application protects other applications, its own security deserves the same attention as the threats it detects.

“One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.”

Title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938): Who’s Exposed and How to Fix It
Context: The flaw isn't in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, Canada's Cyber Centre said it wasn't aware of attacks, and Calif is holding back its exploit code
Full Text:
Java4Shell, tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a heap overflow in Java's hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder. Researchers at Calif say it can let attackers without an account run code on Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak and other Java applications. Oracle and the OpenJDK project shipped fixes on Nov. 17, 2026, and CISA urged organizations to patch immediately. No exploitation in the wild has been reported.

Patch it, but read the conditions before you rank it next to Log4Shell. The vulnerable code runs only on x86-64 servers whose processors support AVX-512 VBMI, so a server's exposure depends on its CPU as much as its Java version. The same container image can be vulnerable on one host and safe on the next, and that is the detail most patch plans will miss.

Which Java versions and servers are affected?

A server is exposed only when three conditions hold at once.

1. A vulnerable Java build. Java 17.0.6 and later on the 17 line, plus Java 21, 25 and 27 before the November fixes. Standard Java 8 and 11 don't contain the flawed code, but the Java SE 8 Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf does, as do recent GraalVM builds.

2. The right CPU. The vulnerable path runs only on x86-64 chips with AVX-512 VBMI: Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids and Granite Rapids, and AMD Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 servers, including AWS Graviton, don't run it. On Linux, this command should print all four flags if the chip qualifies:

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'

3. A reachable decoder. An attacker has to get malformed Base64 into Java's standard decoder. Many servers decode Base64 before checking who you are, in HTTP Basic login headers, SAML artifacts and CSRF tokens, which is what makes the attack possible without a login.

Calif reports pre-authentication code execution under default settings on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, and with a login on Apache Kafka, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. It says the list is incomplete.

Products that bundle their own Java runtime, from CI servers to appliances, need an update from their vendor, not just a new system JDK.

How Java4Shell works

When a method runs often enough, Java's JIT compiler swaps the standard Base64 decoding loop for a hand-tuned assembly routine, an "intrinsic," that uses AVX-512 VBMI instructions. That routine miscalculates the output size when the input ends with an unexpected = padding character. Wiz gives the example of 64 A characters followed by a single =.

The result is a write of 62 or 63 bytes past the end of the output array on the Java heap. Java does reject the malformed string, but only after the write has happened. That ordering is the whole bug: input validation in your application can't help, because the damage is done inside the decoder.

The overflowed bytes are fixed by the decoder, which is why early readings predicted a crash, not code execution. Calif's researchers got around that by arranging heap memory so the overflow enlarges a neighboring array. They then used that array to write chosen bytes and a second array to read memory back, a step they call JavaBleed, and worked from there to code execution.

There is no universal exploit. Each application needs its own memory layout and timing, and some attempts are sensitive to network delay. A failed attempt usually crashes the JVM, and an attacker can often try again.

One uncomfortable footnote: a pull request to OpenJDK on Sept. 9 described an overflow in the same decoder and included a triggering input. It was closed unmerged in early November after eight weeks of inactivity.

Is Java4Shell being exploited, and why do the scores disagree?

As of Nov. 18, 2026, no exploitation has been reported. The flaw isn't in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, Canada's Cyber Centre said it wasn't aware of attacks, and Calif is holding back its exploit code.

Independent labs have confirmed the dangerous part, though. Upwind reproduced the memory corruption on an Intel Ice Lake server on AWS until Java crashed. Blackpoint Cyber crashed a test Spring Boot app with about 28,300 malformed login requests in roughly 20 seconds, without logging in, and used the JavaBleed technique to read a secret from memory in all 30 local runs. Neither reproduced remote code execution.

9.8 (preliminary)

No login required

Amazon

8.8

JVM crash for unauthenticated users; code execution for low-privileged users in some environments

Oracle / OpenJDK

8.1 (CVSS 3.1)

No login required, but hard to exploit

The practical read: a pre-auth crash of any affected Java service is easy today. Reliable code execution takes per-target work, but the researchers have shown it can be done, and the triggering input has been public since September. Treat it as urgent.

How to fix and mitigate Java4Shell

Find every affected runtime. Inventory Java 17 and later, including runtimes bundled inside products. Then check the CPU on each host with the command above. Mixed fleets and autoscaling groups can change exposure from one instance to the next.

Patch. Install the fixed build for your distribution from the table above, then restart Java services and rebuild and redeploy container images so the running process actually uses it. Red Hat users need the workaround until Red Hat ships fixes.

If you can't patch yet, turn off the vulnerable path. Start the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, which removes only the faster Base64 code. -XX:UseAVX=2 disables AVX-512 entirely, but use it only on x86-64, because Java on ARM64 won't start with it. Upwind warns that -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock on its own stops Java from starting. Remove the flag once the fixed build is in.

Reduce exposure at the edge. CISA recommends validating Base64 input at application boundaries, enforcing input-size limits and limiting unauthenticated access. A reverse proxy that buffers complete requests, as nginx does by default, blocks some attacks but not all.

Hunt for attempts. Look for Base64 tokens of 32 characters or more that end in = and whose length isn't a multiple of four, especially in Authorization headers; bursts of IllegalArgumentException from java.util.Base64$Decoder; and unexplained hs_err_pid crash logs or restart storms. None of these proves a compromise, and their absence doesn't prove you're safe.

Frequently asked questions

What is Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)?

Java4Shell is a heap buffer overflow in the AVX-512 Base64 decoder of OpenJDK's HotSpot JVM on x86-64. Malformed Base64 ending in an extra = makes the decoder write 62 or 63 bytes past its output buffer. Calif, which disclosed it on Nov. 17, 2026, demonstrated unauthenticated code execution against six widely used Java applications.

Which Java versions are affected?

Java 17.0.6 and later on the 17 line, and Java 21, 25 and 27 before the November 2026 fixes. Fixed Oracle builds are 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1. The server must also have an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI, such as Intel Xeon Ice Lake or later, or AMD Zen 4 or later.

Are Java 8 and Java 11 affected?

Standard Java 8 and 11 builds don't contain the vulnerable code. The exception is the Java SE 8 Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf, which is affected; Oracle's latest Performance Pack build is 8u513.

Is CVE-2026-114938 being exploited?

No exploitation in the wild had been reported as of Nov. 18, 2026, and the flaw wasn't in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Independent labs have reproduced crashes and memory reads but not remote code execution.

Is Java4Shell as bad as Log4Shell?

It's narrower. Log4Shell could be triggered by almost any logged string on any hardware with a simple, reliable exploit. Java4Shell needs specific CPUs, a reachable Base64 decoder and target-specific exploitation work. A pre-auth crash is easy, though, so treat it as urgent.

How can I mitigate Java4Shell without patching?

Start the JVM with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable the vulnerable decoder path, or -XX:UseAVX=2 on x86-64 only. Add input-size limits and Base64 validation at the edge, and remove the JVM flag once you've installed a fixed build.

Title: Java4Shell Vulnerability Allows Remote Attacks on Major Java Apps
Context: Java4Shell: A Hardware-Bound Exploit Despite the criticality and widespread impact of Java4Shell, several security firms noted that the vulnerability is difficult to exploit
Full Text:
Weeks after PHP2Shell, another critical vulnerability has been leaked before its planned disclosure and authorities are now urging organizations to apply patches.

The new vulnerability, known as ‘Java4Shell’ and tracked as CVE-2026-114938, is a memory corruption vulnerability in Open Java Development Kit (OpenJDK), an open-source implementation of the Java Platform, Standard Edition (Java SE) co-maintained by Oracle and a global community of developers and companies, such as Red Hat, Amazon and Microsoft. OpenJDK runs most Java applications.

The vulnerability was found by California-based security firm Calif, which published details on November 17 after some information was leaked before coordinated disclosure.

The flaw affects OpenJDK 17, 21, 25 and 27 and is rated with a high-severity score of 8.1 by Oracle (using CVSS v3.1) and a critical severity score of 9.2 by Calif (using CVSS v4.0).

The exploitation of Java4Shell can allow unauthenticated attackers corrupt memory in Java servers with a single malformed message.

According to a write-up from Calif, the blast radius of a potential exploit could be broad, with many Java-based applications built on OpenJDK also vulnerable.

Services vulnerable to a remote code execution (RCE) attack which has exploited Java4Shell include Keycloak, Atlassian’s products like Jira and Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate as well as many distributions based on OpenJDK:

Amazon Corretto

Eclipse Temurin

Microsoft Build of OpenJDK

Azul Zulu

BellSoft Liberica

SAP SapMachine

Red Hat OpenJDK

Oracle OpenJDK

Oracle Java SE

Oracle GraalVM for JDK

Other services can also be vulnerable to a Java4Shell exploit, but only if the attacker is able to authenticate. These include Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker.

Maintainers of OpenJDK have published a fix, but each Java vendor will ship its fixed build on its own schedule.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) published an emergency advisory on November 17 urging organizations to apply patches as soon as they are available.

Java4Shell: A Hardware-Bound Exploit

Despite the criticality and widespread impact of Java4Shell, several security firms noted that the vulnerability is difficult to exploit.

In two separate reports, VulnCheck and Endor Labs highlighted that exploitation of the vulnerability is hardware-specific, depending on the Java version, the underlying server processor and the application running on it.

Both research teams noted that the flaw affects CPUs supporting AVX-512 VBMI instructions, while ARM-based servers, including AWS Graviton, are not affected.

VulnCheck said its researchers had successfully reproduced the vulnerability on Ice Lake hardware, adding that processors without AVX-512 VBMI and BW support use an alternative decoding path that does not contain the defect.

Endor Labs noted that the affected processors include recent Intel and AMD server chips, which account for much of current cloud capacity.

As of November 18, no attacks exploiting the vulnerability had been reported in the wild.

CISA Mitigation Recommendations

CISA recommended the following mitigation measures:

Identify affected Java installations: review software inventories for Java Development Kits (JDKs) and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications, container images and appliances, as they may not appear as separate inventory entries

Apply security patches: install relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they become available, prioritizing internet-facing systems

Implement safeguards: where immediate patching is not possible, implement temporary safeguards, such as validating and restricting Base64 input at application boundaries, enforcing input-size limits and limiting unauthenticated access

Review vendor guidance: consult Oracle’s security advisory for additional patching instructions and recommendations

Monitor for suspicious activity: watch for indicators of potential exploitation, including rogue Java runtimes, unexpected Java Virtual Machine (JVM) crashes and suspicious Java processes

Title: New Attack Bypasses TPM Lockout to Crack Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs in Days, Not Years
Context: The chipmaker says attacks requiring physical access fall outside its product security threat model, but that "RPMC is intended to stop this type of interposer attack
Full Text:
On AMD-based PCs and some Intel PCs, the TPM lockout for Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs can be reset by someone who opens the PC's case, researchers at Technische Universität Berlin say.

That leaves short PINs open to guessing. In lab tests, the researchers found a four-digit Hello PIN on an AMD laptop and a 6-digit BitLocker PIN on an Intel laptop this way.

Both PINs were set by the researchers and found within 236 tries. From the speeds they measured, they calculate a worst-case of 40 hours for a four-digit Hello PIN, compared to 69 days with the lockout working as documented. For a default six-digit BitLocker PIN, the worst-case time drops from 19 years to 20 days.

AMD confirmed yesterday that its processor firmware has a flaw that allows the attack on some PCs with its chips. It plans fixes for most of those chips between November and February 2027. For now, the researchers advise adding at least two digits to Hello and BitLocker PINs.

The TPM in these PCs is a firmware TPM, built into the processor. Unlike a separate TPM chip, it has no secure storage of its own, according to the research paper the researchers posted late last week. So it keeps its saved state, including the count of wrong guesses, encrypted on the mainboard's flash chip.

If someone copies that saved state and later writes the old copy back, the count goes back too, unless the PC detects it. Newer PCs try to catch this with counters inside the flash chip, called RPMC, that can only go up.

On AMD PCs that use these counters, the processor's firmware never verifies that a counter actually increased. A small board placed between the processor and the flash chip can block the update and report success, causing the PC to accept the old state.

RPMC chips from flash maker Winbond have a different weakness, the researchers found. A brief drop in the chip's power supply, called a voltage glitch, can cause the chip to reveal the secret key that signs its counter values. With that key, which took about a second to extract with their best settings, the board can forge any counter value.

On the Intel laptop they tested, one glitch was enough: the laptop's firmware feeds the chip the same value at every boot, so the leaked key kept working after each restart.

For the Hello test, the researchers attacked a locked HP OmniBook 3 with an AMD Ryzen AI 5 330 processor and a BitLocker-encrypted drive. Their setup typed PINs from 1000 upward and reached the correct one, 1235, after 236 tries in 57 minutes.

Windows still forced a restart after every 5 incorrect PIN attempts on that laptop, but no lockout delay was applied. Microsoft's lockout defaults lock the TPM after 32 wrong tries and forget one failure every 10 minutes.

The BitLocker test ran on a Framework Laptop 13 with an Intel Core Ultra 5 125H processor and Winbond flash. BitLocker's startup prompt adds no limit of its own, so each reset gave a fresh 32 tries. The setup found the PIN, 123457, after 236 tries in 6 minutes and 55 seconds.

In both tests, the researchers took the flash chip off the mainboard and wired in their own board. A script read the screen, typed PINs, and restarted the laptop through a KVM switch. They also changed firmware settings to slow each laptop's link to the flash chip, because their board could not keep up at full speed.

The researchers make two further claims that their tests did not cover. Either method could be used against either PIN. A recovered Hello PIN can also unlock keys tied to the device and enable Hello-based single sign-on at work, and, in some configurations, pass a multi-factor check.

The researchers have published their attack firmware, board designs, and scripts. They say reproducing the RPMC attacks is not plug-and-play and needs one of their boards. Neither the paper nor the vendor notices published so far describe attacks outside the lab.

Which PCs the Attack Works On and What Vendors Say

Whether the attack works depends on the processor and the flash chip:

AMD-based PCs with RPMC flash: open to the board that blocks counter updates. The chipmaker has confirmed the firmware flaw behind this and plans to fix it.

AMD-based PCs without RPMC flash: on two AMD desktops in the researchers' tests, writing an old copy back with an ordinary flash programmer reset the count, requiring no board. They conclude that AMD processors likely have no other protection against this, though two desktops may not be representative of all AMD systems.

PCs that rely on Winbond RPMC flash: the researchers say these are open to the leaked-key method whatever the processor, and that only a new chip design can fix it.

Intel PCs without RPMC-like flash: three Intel systems detected the same write-back in those tests.

The researchers expect the AMD firmware flaw to affect AMD PCs that use the Microsoft Pluton security core as their TPM, but did not show this.

On an AMD PC, the owner can boot Linux, for example from a live USB stick, and run the command grep . /sys/bus/pci/drivers/ccp/*/rpmc_* from the researchers' exposure check. The output indicates whether RPMC flash is present and enabled, which tells the owner which of the two methods applies. Missing files do not mean the PC lacks RPMC.

For Intel PCs, the researchers know of no such check. Owners would have to open the PC and look for a Winbond chip marked 25R or 74M.

AMD tracks the flaw as CVE-2026-43613 and assigns it a CVSS score of 5.1 in a security bulletin published yesterday.

The chipmaker says attacks requiring physical access fall outside its product security threat model, but that "RPMC is intended to stop this type of interposer attack." The researchers first told it about the flaw in February.

The chipmaker's fix targets run from November to February 2027 across Ryzen, Ryzen AI, Ryzen Threadripper, Athlon and EPYC chips, and one unnamed product has no date yet. These are planned dates for its own firmware, not updates already out for PCs.

The bulletin does not cover AMD PCs without RPMC flash. It also does not say whether the update will prevent an attacker from installing older, unfixed firmware on the PC, which the researchers say a fix must prevent.

Intel, whose processor was in the BitLocker test laptop, said in a security announcement earlier this week that the research "did not demonstrate a vulnerability in an Intel component". That matches the tests, in which the attack on the Intel laptop needed the Winbond chip's flaw.

According to the researchers, Intel's security team called the reused value a weakness rather than a vulnerability.

The researchers told Microsoft in April. According to them, the company rated the Windows Hello report as "moderate severity" and below its bar for an immediate fix, issued no CVE or bounty, and committed to raising its recommended minimum Hello PIN length to six digits.

At the company's request, the researchers filed the BitLocker finding as a separate report for a different team. The company declined to give them any further written statement for the paper.

Separately, a Windows 11 test build released late last week makes six digits the minimum for personal-account Hello PINs, with an option to use four. The release notes give no reason, and features in that test channel may never reach regular releases.

According to the researchers, Winbond was first told about its chips' weakness to voltage glitches in January 2025 and received a second report in April showing that a glitch also leaks the key. The flash maker is studying the issue, possibly including a new chip design, but has not committed to a fix or a date.

What Owners and Admins Can Do

Two extra digits make a large difference in the researchers' figures:

Worst-case time to find a numeric PIN

PIN length

With the documented lockout

Hello attack (AMD laptop)

BitLocker attack (Intel laptop)

4 digits

69 days

6 digits

20 days

8 digits

1,903 years

* BitLocker accepts a four-digit PIN only if an admin lowers the six-digit minimum. The times are worst cases calculated from speeds measured on one laptop each.

In May, Microsoft advised moving BitLocker from TPM-only to TPM+PIN to block the YellowKey bypass, as part of its YellowKey mitigation. The same TPM lockout guards that PIN.

Steps for each setup:

Windows Hello for Business: raise the Minimum PIN length policy, under Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > PIN Complexity. If it is not set, Windows requires six digits, a worst case of 168 days in the table above, and admins can set it as low as four. The PIN policy settings page lists it on the PIN settings tab.

BitLocker: raise the Configure minimum PIN length for startup policy, which allows 4 to 20 digits and requires six by default. Turning on "Allow enhanced PINs for startup" lets letters and symbols, which the BitLocker PIN guidance recommends for older hardware.

AMD-based PCs: install the firmware update with the chipmaker's fix when one is available for your PC. Until then, the chipmaker advises keeping PCs under physical control and watching for signs of tampering.

PCs that rely on Winbond RPMC flash: the flash maker has not committed to a fix, according to the researchers. Intel advises its customers to ask their PC maker about updates.

Title: AI Pentesting Checklist for Web Apps: 15 Questions to Ask Before Choosing a Vendor
Context: TL;DR Attackers move first
Full Text:
TL;DR

Attackers move first. On average, exploitation now starts before a patch exists (Mandiant M-Trends 2026). In 1H 2026, 23% of vulnerabilities VulnCheck added to its exploited list were hit on or before disclosure day.

AI pentesting vendors aren't interchangeable. Most look convincing in a demo. The gaps show up in your logged-in flows, your coverage, and your production safety.

Make them prove it on your own web apps. Score each vendor on context, reach, validated findings, guardrails, and retests.

Choosing an AI pentesting vendor? Get 15 questions, red flags, and a scorecard to test what vendors deliver, not just what they demo. Download the free checklist →

AI is speeding attackers up

For the first time, Google's Threat Intelligence Group identified a threat actor using a zero-day exploit it believes was developed with AI: a 2FA bypass rooted in a logic flaw that conventional fuzzing and static analysis can easily miss (GTIG).

Agentic pentesting can close that gap, and 87% of US security leaders surveyed are planning, piloting, or using it. Choosing the agent is the hard part.

Every Demo Looks Good. Your App Is the Real Test.

Picture three agents that all demo well. The first finds real flaws but stops at your login page. The second navigates your app but can't answer a basic question: coverage of what? The third exploits real issues but has no hard limits for production.

Each looks impressive on the vendor's target. The difference shows up on yours. A structured bake-off surfaces it before you sign.

Ask What the Agent Knows Before It Attacks

Every tester has to learn your site before the first payload. That recon is real attack work. The cost is redoing it from scratch on every engagement, when most of the map hasn't changed. In CyCognito's model, recon and analysis take 20 to 30 of a manual pentest's 63 to 95 hours.

Agents differ here. Some start from a blank URL and rebuild the map on every run. Others start from an existing model of your site and keep it current between runs. Ask which one you're buying, what carries over between runs, and whether the agent keeps discovering beyond its starting map. A starting map should be a head start, not a boundary.

Without context, an AI agent behaves like a smart scanner. With context, it can reason about your application. That changes what it finds, not just how fast. When a security researcher hunted for flaws in Apache Airflow, their AI assistant called the search a dead end. Testing how the deployment’s parts trust each other, instead of reading the code, turned up an unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2026-68982).

Ask for Proof, Not Suspicion

A suspicious pattern is not an exploitable vulnerability. Ask whether the agent exploits what it suspects, reproduces its findings, and hands over evidence your team can verify. A list of suspected issues is not a validated pentest.

Here is what proof looks like. During an authorized assessment of a major insurer's production website, an AI pentesting agent found that the one-time passcode request could send login codes to any email address. It proved the flaw by logging in with a code sent to its own inbox, and guardrails then stopped the test. The insurer said it had pentested the site about six months earlier (Reflectiz case study on The Hacker News).

Three Questions That Expose a Weak AI Pentesting Vendor

A demo can look convincing without proving that the agent reaches your logged-in workflows, validates what it finds, or confirms your fixes. Here are three of the 15 checks to run before you choose.

The other 12, covering starting context, coverage proof, attack chaining, access across roles, data handling, and guardrails, are in the full checklist.

Run a Bake-Off, Not a Demo

Demos run on the vendor's target. Bake-offs run on yours.

Same target, same week. Same app, test accounts, and scope for every vendor.

Log three timestamps. Access granted, discovery complete, first test.

Score every check. The checklist's scoring sheet weights what matters and gates on safety.

Context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
Full Text:
CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2024-10441 Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Vulnerability

CVE-2026-40217 BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel Vulnerability

CVE-2026-90436 Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-90817 Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.
