Title: Attackers hijack Microsoft’s agent-framework package to steal Azure and CI credentials
Context: The attacker did not stop after the first release
Full Text:
Attackers briefly hijacked Microsoft’s official Agent Framework package on PyPI and used it to distribute credential-stealing malware capable of harvesting cloud tokens, developer secrets and CI/CD credentials from developer workstations and automated build systems, according to multiple security researchers.

Two malicious versions of the package, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, appeared on PyPI on November 17 and stayed live for less than an hour.

“The package is a credential stealer: it harvests environment secrets, cloud and package-manager credentials, and Azure managed identity tokens, then exfiltrates them to an attacker-controlled webhook,” OX Security, one of several security firms that flagged the releases, said in a blog post.

The payload ran automatically every time Python started, even if no code imported the package, OX said. The malicious versions also installed the genuine framework code, so applications kept working, and the compromise was easy to miss. The package has 192,534 monthly downloads, according to the firm.

Other security firms, including Aikido Security, Endor Labs, and SafeDep, published similar analyses of the attack.

Microsoft has not said publicly how the attacker got access to publish the package. The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

How the stealer worked

The stealer collected environment variables with names containing words such as TOKEN, SECRET, PASSWORD, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, and OPENAI, OX said. It also read up to 60 credential files. These included Azure CLI settings, Git and Docker credentials, npm and pip configuration, Hugging Face tokens, Azure DevOps build agent credentials and application .env files. It pulled secrets from up to 300 other running processes as well.

The stealer also asked for new tokens. Inside Azure DevOps pipelines, it requested an identity token that can be exchanged for Azure access, OX said in the blog post. It also requested managed identity tokens for Azure services, including Resource Manager, Microsoft Graph, Key Vault, Storage, Cognitive Services, AI Foundry, and Azure DevOps.

Endor Labs said the attack was aimed mainly at automated build systems. “Developer laptops are in scope, but the payload is written for CI runners and Azure workloads,” the firm wrote in its analysis.

The code was disguised as diagnostics. It sat in a module named _telemetry.py and sent data with a user agent labeled “af-runtime-diagnostics,” OX said. The stolen data went to a webhook.site address as compressed, encoded JSON.

The attacker did not stop after the first release. While OX was researching the malware, version 1.26.1 was reverted to the clean 1.26.0. The attacker then uploaded 1.26.2, which used a different file path for the same payload, the firm said.

The first version went up at 20:35 UTC and the second at 21:08 UTC, according to Aikido Security. Both were gone by about 21:20 UTC.

“This attack isn’t just a one-off exfiltration attempt, but a planned, live and coordinated effort to reach as many victims as they can, while still being able to bypass blocks and restrictions,” OX said.

OX said the attackers appear to have found a way to hijack the process that builds the package’s wheel files. Endor Labs, in its analysis, said both malicious versions were uploaded as wheel files only, without the source code package that came with the clean release. Microsoft has not confirmed how the breach happened.

The short window may not limit exposure. Any unpinned install during that time pulled in a malicious version, Endor Labs said. Container images, CI caches, and lockfiles built in the window could still contain it.

AI pipelines in focus

OX said the attack shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it. The stealer’s target list includes OpenAI and Hugging Face tokens and Azure AI Foundry access.

It is also not the first time this year that attackers have compromised an official Microsoft Python package. In May, Endor Labs detected three trojanized versions of durabletask, Microsoft’s Python SDK for Azure Durable Functions. No researcher has linked the two attacks.

What security teams should do

Removing the package does not undo the damage. “Removing the package stops future runs, but it doesn’t undo anything that was already sent,” Aikido said.

OX advised teams to check all environments, CI images, and lockfiles for either version and remove it. Teams should look for agent_framework_meta.pth and agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py on hosts and build agents, the firm said. Version 1.26.2 used different files, af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py, according to Aikido.

If the package ran anywhere, every secret reachable from that host should be treated as compromised, OX said. The firm recommended rotating Azure service principal secrets, personal access tokens, and GitHub, npm, PyPI, NuGet, Docker, Hugging Face, and OpenAI tokens. OX also advised teams to review Azure sign-in and activity logs for use of managed identities and federated credentials from affected build agents. Ox recommended pinning the agent-framework to a verified Microsoft release with hash checking and blocking outbound traffic to webhook.site from build infrastructure.

Title: Java4Shell Flaw (CVE-2026-114938) Enables Pre-Auth RCE in Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak and More
Context: 6 and later, and the vulnerable code runs only on x86-64 Intel and AMD chips that support the AVX-512 VBMI feature
Full Text:
A Java flaw called Java4Shell can let attackers without an account run their own code on Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak, and three other widely used applications, says Calif, the security research firm that disclosed it this week.

The flaw is present in Java 17.0.6 and later, and the vulnerable code runs only on x86-64 Intel and AMD chips that support the AVX-512 VBMI feature.

Tracked as CVE-2026-114938, the fix was released today by Oracle and the OpenJDK project, whose open-source code underpins Java builds from many vendors. Amazon has fixed its Corretto Java builds, but Red Hat is still preparing fixes for its own.

The researchers are holding back their attack code for the six applications, and other labs have so far reproduced crashes and a memory leak but not the code execution. Canada's Cyber Center said this week that it was not aware of any attacks exploiting the flaw.

Servers often decode Base64-encoded data, such as HTTP Basic login headers, SAML artifacts, and CSRF tokens, before checking whether a user is logged in. That is how an attacker without an account can exploit the flaw.

The flaw is in a faster version of Java's Base64 decoder that runs on chips with AVX-512 VBMI. Java switches to it after compiling the decoder for speed, which it does for code that runs often.

A malformed string that ends with an extra = makes this decoder write 62 or 63 bytes past the end of its output. Java rejects the string, but only after the write.

The bytes written past the end are fixed, so an attacker controls only where they land. For that reason, early readings of the source code had pointed to a crash rather than code execution, as The Hacker News noted in an earlier report yesterday.

The attacks worked without a login under the default settings of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, and with a login on Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, Calif says in its technical write-up. The researchers' lists are incomplete, and they rate the flaw as 9.2 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0.

They get past the fixed bytes by arranging the server's memory so that the overflow expands a neighboring array. They then use that array to write bytes of their choosing and a second array to read back from memory, a step they call JavaBleed. From there, the researchers say, the attack reaches the parts of Java that run code.

There is no single exploit that works everywhere. Each target requires its own memory layout and timing, and some attacks are sensitive to network delays.

A proxy that waits for complete requests, as nginx does by default, blocks some attacks but not all. A failed attempt can crash Java, and an attacker can often try again.

Security company Upwind reproduced the memory corruption on an AWS server with an Intel Ice Lake chip, where it damaged the next object in memory and eventually crashed Java, according to its lab results.

Blackpoint Cyber's Adversary Pursuit Group crashed a test Spring Boot application by sending about 28,300 malformed login requests over roughly 20 seconds, without ever logging in.

The group also used the JavaBleed step in a local test to read a secret stored next to the overflow, which worked in all 30 runs. It did not reproduce remote code execution, its test results show.

Oracle scores the flaw 8.1 out of 10 under CVSS 3.1, rating it hard to exploit but requiring no login. The description in its CVE record says, "Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE."

Red Hat also rates it as requiring no login, with a preliminary score of 9.8 out of 10. Amazon scores it 8.8 out of 10 and describes the risk in its Amazon Linux entry as "a JVM crash for unauthenticated users or, in certain application environments, code execution by an authenticated low-privileged user."

Canada's Cyber Centre also describes the flaw as exploitable remotely without authentication in its government alert.

The flaw was not in the KEV catalog of exploited vulnerabilities, kept by the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), when The Hacker News checked it today.

Who Is Exposed

The vulnerable code is in Java 17.0.6 and later on the Java 17 line, and in Java 21, 25, and 27. Standard Java 8 and Java 11 do not contain it, but the Java SE 8 Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf is affected. GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21.0.3, GraalVM for JDK 21.0.13.0.3, and GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20.0.3 are also affected.

It runs only on x86-64 chips that support AVX-512 VBMI. These include Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, and Granite Rapids chips, as well as AMD Zen 4 or newer chips. ARM64 chips do not run it.

Because the vulnerable code runs only on these chips, the same container image can run it on one server and not on another. On Linux, this command shows whether a server's chip has the four features the vulnerable code needs, and all four must appear in its output:

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'

The attacker also needs malformed Base64 to reach Java's standard decoder, through paths such as the login headers and tokens described earlier.

Calif also says a Java program that opens a TLS connection to a malicious server can be compromised, even if the program runs no service of its own. The exploit for this came from another researcher, samczsun, and the researchers have not published how it reaches the decoder.

Fixes and Workarounds

The OpenJDK project's vulnerability advisory lists the flaw as fixed in this week's releases, and Oracle's security advisory lists the affected versions of its builds.

For Oracle Java, the fixed builds are the new .1 releases in the table, all released this week. The release notes for 17.0.21.1 say it includes the update's security fixes, and the notes for 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1 and 27.0.1.1 say the same.

For the Java 8 Performance Pack, the latest build is 8u513, available in both standard and Performance Pack versions. For GraalVM, the November security releases are GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21.1, GraalVM for JDK 21.0.13.1, and GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20.1.

The Corretto changelog for 17.0.21.1.2 lists the flaw as fixed, as do the changelogs for the new 21, 25, and 27 builds. Amazon Linux also marks its Corretto 17, 21, 25 and 27 packages as fixed.

Azul's November update fixes the flaw in Zulu 17, 21, 25 and 27, according to its Zulu release notes.

Red Hat has not yet released fixes for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9 and 10, or for its OpenJDK 17, 21 and 25 builds, according to its security bulletin. Containers based on its images need to be rebuilt once updated images are out.

SAP released SapMachine 17.0.21.1, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, and 27.0.1.1 this week, but their release pages do not specify what they fix. Eclipse Temurin, the Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, and BellSoft Liberica had not listed fixed builds when The Hacker News checked today.

Products that bundle their own Java runtime need an update from the product's maker. After updating, restart Java services, and rebuild and redeploy container images so the running process uses the new build.

If you cannot update yet, start the JVM with one of these flags, and remove it once the fixed build is installed:

-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics turns off only the faster Base64 code, which removes the vulnerable path and leaves other AVX-512 speedups in place.

-XX:UseAVX=2 turns off AVX-512 entirely. Use it only on x86-64 servers, because Java on ARM64 does not recognize it and will fail to start.

In Upwind's lab, both flags stopped the overflow on every affected version it tested. The company warns that another flag, -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock, stops Java from starting when it is used on its own.

To spot attempts, it suggests checking for the signs below, while warning that none of them proves a compromise and that their absence does not prove a server is safe:

Base64 tokens of 32 characters or more that end in = and whose length is not a multiple of 4, especially in Authorization headers

Bursts of IllegalArgumentException errors from java.util.Base64$Decoder

Unexplained hs_err_pid crash logs or bursts of restarts

A malformed input that triggers the overflow was posted publicly on September 9, in a proposed fix submitted to OpenJDK's code repository as a pull request. The proposal described an overflow in the same AVX-512 Base64 decoder code.

Its author closed it without merging it in early November, after an automated notice that it had been inactive for more than eight weeks.

Context: Oracle notes it can only be exploited by supplying data to the affected APIs, such as through a web service

In this article

Java4Shell can cause memory corruption and, in some applications, remote code execution

Exploitation depends on the Java runtime, processor and application

Most home users are unlikely to be affected, but organizations should patch promptly

A critical-sounding Java flaw is making headlines. Most consumers are unlikely to be affected, but companies running Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and similar tools have work to do.

On November 17, Oracle and the OpenJDK project shipped fixes for CVE-2026-114938, a memory-corruption bug in Java’s Base64 decoder. Security firm Calif discovered the flaw and named it Java4Shell. CISA urged organizations to patch immediately.

After a run of high-profile computer problems and security scares, it’s understandable that another vulnerability with a catchy name would set alarm bells ringing. But it’s important to separate the potential damage from the likelihood of being affected. This is a serious issue for organizations running vulnerable applications, not a reason for every home user to assume their computer is at risk.

It doesn’t help that organizations give out different CVSS scores for the same vulnerability.

Oracle rates it 8.1 under CVSS 3.1 and describes it as “difficult to exploit.”

Calif rates it 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS 4.0.

Meanwhile, there are currently no reports of abuse in the wild. Calif demonstrated remote code execution without logging in on default installations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate. It also demonstrated post-login code execution on Kafka, Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker.

Technical details

Base64 is a common way of representing binary data as text. It’s used in login protocols, file uploads and network messages. To decode it faster, OpenJDK uses special x86-64 CPU instructions.

The bug is in hand-written assembly code for that fast path. A short, malformed input can write 62 bytes past the end of a memory buffer.

For remote code execution, several conditions have to line up:

The right processor. The flaw only affects x86-64 CPUs that support the AVX-512 VBMI instruction set. Examples include Intel Xeon from Ice Lake onward and AMD Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 chips aren’t affected.

A recent OpenJDK-based Java. The flaw affects OpenJDK from 17.0.6 onward, and the distributions built on it.

An exposed Java service. The attacker has to feed crafted data to a Java application that decodes it. Oracle notes it can only be exploited by supplying data to the affected APIs, such as through a web service. It can’t be exploited through untrusted Java Web Start applications or applets.

A target-specific exploit. Calif says there is no universal exploit. Each chain needs a decoder route, a feedback path, a heap layout, and an application-specific action. The attack also works best with low, stable network latency, and Calif rented a VM in the same region as its target.

An ordinary home PC rarely runs a Java server that accepts Base64 input from the internet. Organizations running affected Java applications on vulnerable processors should patch promptly, since attackers may find narrow, application-specific paths to remote code execution.

Title: Norwegian Gas Giant Equinor Says It’s Under Cyberattack. Production Keeps Running
Context: It warned that cyberattacks could disrupt critical services such as water and electricity
Full Text:
Norwegian Gas Giant Equinor confirms cyberattack on IT systems, with no impact on production or confirmed data theft.

Equinor, Europe’s largest gas supplier, said on 17 November it had detected an ongoing cyberattack against some IT systems. The Norwegian company said the attack had not affected operations and production, and it had taken steps to neutralise it.

“Equinor has detected an ongoing cyber-attack against certain IT systems. Relevant resources have been mobilised to neutralise the attack and regain full integrity.” reads the statement published by the company. “As this is not a virus attack, there is no risk of the attack spreading. At present, there is no indication that the attack has consequences for employees, partners or suppliers. Production remains unaffected.”

The energy giant said there was also no indication data had been stolen. A company spokesperson declined to give further details.

The disruption reached everyday work, not the wells. Norwegian news agency NTB reported, citing the company, that IT applications and internal systems were affected, and a person at Equinor told Reuters the internal email system was down.

Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) said it was aware of the attack and was ready to provide support if needed. Last month, the agency raised its cyber threat level to four on a five-level scale. It warned that cyberattacks could disrupt critical services such as water and electricity. NSM also reported that successful cyberattacks against Norwegian companies had tripled in the previous six months.

“The incident currently being ⁠experienced ​by Equinor confirms that this risk ​is indeed high,” the NSM spokesperson said on Tuesday.

This isn’t Norway’s first brush with this kind of pressure this year. In August, a pro-Russian group claimed a cyberattack that disrupted multiple Norwegian government digital services for several days. Separate claims from that period don’t establish who’s behind this week’s attack on Equinor, and nobody has named a group yet.

Treat the gap between claim and evidence as the story for now. A company confirming an attack and ruling out operational impact is a fact; who did it and why is not, until someone shows proof.

Title: 65 Characters to RCE: Inside the Java4Shell Vulnerability
Context: “It took our own Quang Luong an hour to discover the vulnerability, and two more hours to develop the first working exploit
Full Text:
Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical OpenJDK Base64 bug enabling pre-auth RCE in Jenkins, Jira, Keycloak and more. Patches are out. Update now.

Calif researchers disclosed Java4Shell, a memory-corruption bug, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (CVSS score of 9.2), in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder. OpenJDK is the world’s most common Java runtime. OpenJDK (Open Java Development Kit) is the open-source implementation of the Java platform. It provides the tools and components needed to develop and run Java applications, including the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), libraries and development tools. It is widely used in enterprise systems, servers and cloud environments.

Base64 shows up everywhere: authentication, file uploads, network messages. To decode it fast, OpenJDK uses special x86-64 instructions that process many bytes at once, and the bug lives in that hand-written machine code. A single malformed string triggers it: 64 “A” characters followed by one equals sign, or 128 on older OpenJDK 17.

The flaw sits in how the decoder handles padding at the end of a Base64 string. When the trailing characters are “=”, “==” or similar, the code can compute a negative output length, and that underflow turns into a write of all 64 bytes instead of the few that should go out. For a 65-character trigger, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte buffer and ends up writing 62 bytes past its end.

“At runtime, the decoded buffer length is calculated as (ceil(inp_len / 4) * 3) - padding. When the bug is triggered, with 65 bytes ([64 bytes] + '=') as input, that calculation allocates a 50-byte buffer. During decoding the bug makes output_mask == -1 for evmovdqub, so 64 bytes are written starting at offset 48, an out-of-bounds write past the end of the buffer.” reads the report published by Calif. “On OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 'A' * 128 + '=' instead of 'A' * 64 + '=', because the length threshold to reach the code path is higher.”

Calif demonstrated that attackers could execute code remotely, without authentication, on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate, all using their default settings. Remote code execution was also possible after authentication on Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit and Spinnaker. Applications built with Struts and Spring Boot were also vulnerable. A client-side attack could even target a Java program simply by making it connect to a malicious server over TLS.

The attacker can initially control only where data is written, while most of the data itself is fixed. Calif bypassed this limitation using a technique often seen in browser attacks: corrupting the length of a nearby array so it can store attacker-controlled data. This turns a limited write operation into a much more powerful one. By applying the technique to another array, Calif also achieved the ability to read memory. This allows attackers to expose sensitive data from the Java process before executing code, a technique Calif calls JavaBleed.

Getting two objects to land next to each other in memory took real engineering. Calif used a timing trick over the network, holding back parts of an HTTP request until earlier data was acknowledged, so it could control when the server allocated memory. They even rented a VM in the same region as the target, because a stable, low-latency connection matters more than clever TCP tuning.

“For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration.” continues the report. “In other words, Calif rented another VM in the same region as our target.”

An AI coding assistant found the bug. Researcher Quang Luong pointed OpenAI’s Codex at OpenJDK’s internals and told it to audit the JIT compiler, intrinsics and cryptography, and most early results were useless.

“It took our own Quang Luong an hour to discover the vulnerability, and two more hours to develop the first working exploit.” Calif states. “The total token cost was less than $200.”

Total AI cost: under $200, which buys you a serious headache for a lot of enterprise software.

There’s no universal exploit here. Every target needs its own delivery path, a writer, a reader and an application action, so a patch for one product doesn’t tell you about the next. Calif published a safe proof of concept that overwrites bytes inside a harmless array, and is holding back the weaponized chains until more systems are patched.

Java4Shell affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later, plus Oracle Java SE, Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine and Red Hat OpenJDK. It also needs specific hardware: an x86-64 CPU with AVX-512 VBMI, found in Intel Xeon chips from Ice Lake onward and AMD Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 systems are safe from this one.

Oracle shipped a fix on 17 November as part of its November Critical Patch Update, which covers 655 vulnerabilities total. Update your Java runtime now. If you can’t patch immediately, start OpenJDK with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to disable the accelerated decoder, or -XX:UseAVX=2 on x86-64 hosts to turn off AVX-512, but treat both as a stopgap, not a fix.

Calif frames the bigger problem as one of unused complexity: features built for a few applications ship to everyone, and everyone inherits the risk.

“This is where AI can help to make that work practical at a scale we could not previously afford.

The same centaur hacker that discovered PHP2Shell and Java4Shell can comb a large codebase and flag dead code, bloated features, and needless optimizations. We call this vibe-uncoding: identify the parts a system actually needs, then remove everything else to reduce its attack surface.” the report concludes.

“With AI, everyone is asking, “What can we build?” But maybe the right question for security is, “What can we delete?””

Title: Three AI Models Agree on Just One of 121 Potential Code Flaws
Context: " If an attacker hunts with one model and a defender relies on another, he said, "the defender might never even see the vulnerability the attacker is about to exploit
Full Text:
Three frontier AI models given the same open source code to audit have produced vulnerability findings that barely overlap, according to new frontier AI research. Of 121 distinct potential issues, Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5.1, OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and Z.ai's GLM-5.3 all flagged just one, software security firm Echo found.

Echo published the comparison in its November 18 research. Each model worked through two Maven libraries and one npm package with Echo's own hunting framework and the same validation process. Echo reached GPT-5.6 Sol through Daybreak, the program OpenAI runs for vetted security teams.

Of the 121 issues, 83% (100), came from a single model and 20 from the other two.

Read more on AI vulnerability discovery: AI Cuts Vulnerability Discovery from Nine Months to 90 Hours

Where the AI Models Disagreed

Claude Mythos logged the most validation passes overall, with 25, against nine for GLM-5.3 and eight for GPT-5.6 Sol. But GPT-5.6 Sol accounted for six of the seven passes on one Maven library, and GLM-5.3 found six validated issues on the other that its rivals missed.

Severity ratings split too. GLM-5.3 rated one flaw in an npm package with more than 350 million monthly downloads as Critical, Claude Mythos put it at High and GPT-5.6 Sol treated it as documented behavior rather than a bug. Automated validation rated it Low.

GPT-5.6 Sol finished its hunts in about 24 minutes, against roughly 198 for Claude Mythos and 174 for GLM-5.3. GLM-5.3 was the cheapest overall, with its three hunts costing about $22, against $303 for Claude Mythos and $30 for GPT-5.6 Sol, though Echo said the costs reflected its own access terms.

How Many AI Findings Held Up

The nine runs produced 446 initial findings, cut to 152 after cleanup. Of those, 74 were rated High or Critical, and 55 went through automated proof-of-concept testing after duplicates were set aside. Forty-two passed.

Echo cautioned that the 42 were not necessarily distinct bugs, since an issue found by more than one model could be credited to each. Findings rated Medium or Low were never tested, so a previously known flaw that Claude Mythos rated Medium never reached validation.

Echo security researcher Yuval Saggie said the race to find the best model was "the wrong question." If an attacker hunts with one model and a defender relies on another, he said, "the defender might never even see the vulnerability the attacker is about to exploit."

Each model ran only once, and Echo called the exercise "a controlled comparison rather than a comprehensive benchmark." It said automated validation did not amount to confirmation from the projects' maintainers.

Echo said the projects would stay unnamed, and technical details unpublished, until their maintainers had been notified.

Title: The Silent Consensus
Watchdog Warns UK Government Is Falling Short on Risk Management
Context: The spending watchdog published its report, Risk management in government: improving capability and decision making, on November 18
Full Text:
The number of chief risk officers (CROs) in UK government has more than doubled over the past decade, but most industry professionals working in Whitehall believe they lack influence, according to a new National Audit Office (NAO) report.

The spending watchdog published its report, Risk management in government: improving capability and decision making, on November 18.

It noted that effective risk management is important in helping to manage fast emerging risks, like the recent PHP vulnerabilities, which have the potential to disrupt public services and lead to costly recovery work.

It can also “help public bodies make better decisions, adapt to uncertainty and take well-managed risks to innovate and improve services,” the NAO argued.

However, 58% of risk professionals it polled claimed they are typically brought in too late to shape decisions.

“We found limited evidence of major decisions or organizational direction changing because of input from risk professionals,” the report noted. “In hierarchical organizations, the often low seniority of those leading risk teams can also restrict their access to senior decision-making forums.”

Read more on risk management: 75% CISOs Fear Executives Don’t Understand Cybersecurity Risks Employees Face

In the cyber sphere, a lack of skills and awareness are undermining efforts to embed risk more fully in decision making, the report found.

For example, Audit and Risk Assurance Committees (ARACs) should provide independent advice and challenge the board and accounting officer. But the report noted that “skills gaps among committee members in evolving areas such as cybersecurity” are constraining their effectiveness.

Additionally, leaders don’t always understand the cyber risks outlined in risk registers “or recognize how they relate to their strategic objectives,” the NAO said.

Many government departments are at least defining their risk appetite, but less than half (47%) of those polled said this actually informs decisions. In June 2026, most reported that the majority of their principal risks were outside their stated tolerance.

“Legacy technology and specialist staff shortages may constrain departments’ ability to bring cybersecurity risks within appetite,” the report noted.

In many cases, the result is that known risks aren’t being addressed promptly. The NAO highlighted the case of the British Library, which had already identified risks from growing third-party access to IT systems, but was breached before planned changes were implemented.

Risk Management Critical in Interconnected Environment

Progress is being made, but is uneven across government, with many bodies not making use of performance information, early warning indicators, or assurance mapping to monitor risk management efforts, the report argued.

This is more important than ever given today’s “complex and interconnected” risk environment, it said.

Only a continuous approach to risk monitoring and improvement will do, the NAO argued. This means ensuring risk registers are “robust and ‘living documents’ that reflect significant risks,” it said.

"The past few years have highlighted the scale and complexity of the risks facing government and how quickly they can escalate into crises, with lasting consequences for public services,” said Gareth Davies, head of the NAO.

“Whilst it has made good progress, the government must now put risk management at the heart of how it plans, spends and delivers, making sure that senior leaders are equipped to spot vulnerabilities early and to take well-manged risks to improve public services. This will become ever more important as more decisions and public spending are devolved.”

Title: UK MPs want AI watchdog with power to pull the plug on dangerous models
Context: Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne
Full Text: UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far. In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed. It could halt high-risk training and testing, block deployments, or suspend AI services if the risks can't be contained. LLMs are trained on billions of learned parameters and so developers can't always predict what a model will do in every situation. The recommendations come from Parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, which questioned researchers, former AI employees, and representatives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta. All four companies assured MPs they wouldn't release models they considered unsafe. The trouble is, they don't use the same yardstick for safety, and UK law doesn't generally require them to get an independent opinion before releasing anything. "We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control," said committee chair Liam Byrne MP. Just as with aviation, pharma or nuclear safety, UK government want to rely on manufacturers' assurance alone, and want regulation. "Our hearings exposed gaps in independent scrutiny, incident reporting and powers to stop unsafe systems. Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne. "Protection must begin while systems are being built and tested." The committee's report, Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe, identifies ten holes in Britain's approach to AI safety, including the lack of mandatory incident reporting, limited access for independent testers, and inadequate protections for whistleblowers. The UK already has an AI Security Institute (AISI), which has made a name for itself testing some of the world's most powerful models, but its work depends on voluntary cooperation, and it has no authority to stop a company releasing a model that raises safety concerns. MPs want AISI to continue its testing work while a separate regulator takes responsibility for enforcement. Developers of designated high-risk systems would have to provide evidence supporting their safety claims and give independent researchers access to examine them. Significant changes to a model's capabilities or safeguards would trigger further scrutiny. Former AI employees also told MPs that raising safety concerns can come at a price. Restrictive contracts, commercial pressures, and financial disincentives can all discourage staff from speaking out, the committee heard. MPs want stronger legal protections for whistleblowers and compulsory reporting of AI incidents and near misses. There's a fair bit of money riding on this, too. Using OECD productivity estimates, the committee calculates that AI could leave Britain's economy up to £400 billion larger over the next decade. It also sees an opportunity for the UK to make money from independently testing AI models, building on the expertise already established at AISI. MPs argue that stronger safeguards could encourage businesses, particularly smaller firms, to adopt the technology. "AI firms must be required to substantiate their safety claims, independent experts must be able to scrutinize them, and a regulator must have the power to intervene when risks cannot be controlled," Byrne said. "Ministers, accountable to Parliament, must decide what risks the public should be asked to bear." MPs want the new laws on the books in the next parliamentary session, and say Britain should use its turn at the G20 helm in 2027 to get other countries on board with tougher rules for AI testing, incident reporting, and risky model releases. Whether ministers are prepared to hand a watchdog the power to stop AI development is another matter. The committee's recommendations aren't binding, and the government has yet to commit to the proposed legislation. ®

Title: The resilience gap: Why cybersecurity investment alone is not enough
Context: If two critical services are down, who decides which comes back first
Full Text:
Death, taxes and cyber incidents. It’s not quite the original saying, but for today’s CISO, all three carry a certain inevitability, and most organizations have come to accept that reality.

Protiviti’s 2027 CISO Top Risks and Opportunities study confirms that cybersecurity remains the top investment priority for CISOs. Yet even well-funded security programs can struggle when something goes wrong.

Why? The cause is rarely missing plans or controls; it’s silos. Service owners; security, recovery and crisis teams; and key providers too often plan and operate apart. As a result, organizations are beginning to see that investment and resilience are not the same thing.

Ultimately, the investment didn’t fail; the expectation did. Technology alone can’t deliver an outcome that also depends on people, process, governance and coordination. The lesson is clear: A well-funded cybersecurity program can still be operationally fragile.

The findings in Protiviti’s 2027 CISO Top Risks and Opportunities study illustrate the problem. Cybersecurity remains the leading strategic investment priority, selected by 48% of CISOs. Yet only 41% report high or very high confidence in their organizations’ ability to protect enterprise value, while just 29% express that level of confidence in responding with agility. Another 54% describe their confidence in their organizations’ ability to respond with agility as moderate.

That gap should concern every CISO. It suggests organizations have built security capabilities without fully developing the enterprise operating model needed during disruption.

The real test begins when prevention ends

Security investment matters. But you aren’t buying away cyber risk. You’re buying it down. Even the most mature organizations will eventually face an event they cannot prevent, often involving a third party, technology failure or circumstance outside their control.

What happens next separates resilient organizations from everyone else. Security works to contain the threat while infrastructure and application teams decide what can safely go offline. Business leaders push to restore critical services, sometimes with competing priorities. Legal weighs disclosure obligations with incomplete information. Communications prepares messages for employees, customers and regulators.

Meanwhile, a cloud, software-as-a-service or other technology provider may control part of the environment the company needs to recover.

That’s where resilience usually breaks down: not within any one team, but in the handoffs and decisions between them. In the exercises we run, the hardest questions are often surprisingly basic:

Who has the authority to shut down a revenue-producing system?

If two critical services are down, who decides which comes back first?

If Microsoft 365 or another primary collaboration platform is unavailable, how does the crisis team communicate?

If a critical provider is also down, do its recovery priorities and timelines align with yours?

The useful output of an exercise is not a reassuring score. It is the list of things that didn’t work: unclear authority, gaps in escalation paths, inaccessible backups and dependencies that teams incorrectly assumed had been tested. Consider Quantum Dawn VIII, SIFMA’s sector-wide exercise from November 2025. The polycrisis scenario included an undersea cable cut, and roughly two-thirds of participants said they had either never tested that scenario or weren’t sure they had. That is exactly the kind of blind spot an exercise is designed to expose. Better to uncover it in an exercise than during an actual disruption.

And the event you plan for is seldom the event you get. That’s why resilience cannot depend on following a script. Build a framework that enables collaboration and increases the speed of informed decisions, regardless of what actually happens.

Cyber, AI and third-party risks no longer stay in their lanes

Risks don’t arrive one at a time. A cyberattack can quickly become a privacy issue, a regulatory matter and a business interruption. A third-party outage becomes your outage. And AI can act as a force multiplier, allowing a single issue to move faster and spread across more data, systems and business processes.

The findings support this. Cyber threats remain the highest-rated near-term concern in the Top Risks survey, but privacy, third-party risk, AI, resilience and regulatory uncertainty are now clustered closely behind.

AI doesn’t change the fundamental resilience questions. It raises the stakes. An agent may read customer data, query an ERP system, act through a service account or trigger a workflow without a person clicking the button. So, start with an old question: What can it access? Then ask whose permissions or delegated authority it is using, what actions it can take, where those actions are logged and how quickly you can stop it when something goes wrong.

CISOs appear to recognize that challenge. In our 2027 Top Risks study, 51% identified improving AI governance and accountability as a leading priority, while 45% pointed to workforce readiness. That’s telling. Sustainable adoption requires some basic discipline: maintain an inventory of agents and their owners, map the data and tools each can reach, restrict service accounts and delegated permissions, monitor actions and make sure access can be revoked quickly.

Third parties deserve the same scrutiny. A third-party assessment can tell you a lot about a provider’s controls at a point in time. What it rarely tells you is how that provider will perform on a bad day. Most assessments still rely heavily on documentation, discussion and self-reporting. Those assessments may assure a provider’s security posture, but they do not prove that a critical service will remain available, that the provider’s recovery sequence aligns with yours or that the appropriate people on both sides know how to disconnect, communicate and restore service together.

CISOs should be able to identify the external relationships most critical to business operations, understand the services and data that depend on them, and test what will happen if those relationships are interrupted.

This broader responsibility is increasingly part of the CISO mandate. CSO’s examination of how CISOs can rise to the business resilience challenge describes the role’s evolution from a primarily preventive function toward greater responsibility for response, recovery and business resilience.

Build resilience into the investments already underway

If cyber risk increasingly travels through interconnected systems and infrastructure, resilience has to be part of how those environments are modernized in the first place.

The percentage of CISOs selecting cybersecurity slipped from 53% to 48%, while the percentage selecting infrastructure modernization rose from 21% to 33%. Taken together, those shifts make sense. Security and modernization are increasingly intertwined. A cloud migration, enterprise resource planning (ERP) replacement, identity redesign or data-platform upgrade can retire unsupported systems and standing privileges. It can also create new concentration risk, recovery dependencies and failure points if resilience is not designed in from the start.

CISOs should use these major transformation programs to improve resilience, not complicate it. Questions to ask include:

Are we retiring legacy platforms and connections, or simply putting a new layer on top of them?

Are old accounts, interfaces, backup jobs and vendor dependencies actually being removed?

Can the order-to-cash, payments, customer service or other critical processes be restored faster after the investment?

Are recovery, isolation and alternate-processing requirements in the architecture and acceptance criteria from the start?

Have we tested the new platform’s recovery path, or are we assuming modernization made it more resilient?

Closing the resilience gap

The point isn’t to spend less on cybersecurity. It’s to expect more from the investment. The 2027 Top Risks study shows CISOs balancing cyber threats with AI, third-party risk, resilience and modernization. Those may look like separate priorities on a survey. In practice, they increasingly collide in the same incident.

We aren’t going to prevent every cyber incident. The question is what happens when the next one gets through. Does the organization know what matters most, who makes the hard calls and how to recover? Or does it figure those things out during the crisis?

That gap is the resilience gap. And it is where CISOs should be looking next.

Title: U.S. CISA adds Perforce Puppet Enterprise flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
Context: The critical vulnerability CVE-2026-115731 affects Puppet Server and could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code remotely on a vulnerable server
Full Text:
U.S. CISA adds Perforce Puppet Enterprise vulnerability CVE-2026-115731 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added a Perforce Puppet Enterprise flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-115731 (CVSS score of 9.4), to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

The critical vulnerability CVE-2026-115731 affects Puppet Server and could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code remotely on a vulnerable server. The flaw is caused by improper deserialization of untrusted data in Puppet’s report-processing component.

The vulnerability can be exploited by a client holding a certificate signed by the Puppet Certificate Authority (CA). An attacker can send a specially crafted report through an HTTP PUT request to trigger the flaw and execute code with the privileges of the Puppet Server service account. This could give the attacker control over the server and potentially provide a path to compromise systems managed by the Puppet infrastructure.

The risk is even greater when the CA automatically signs certificate requests without properly verifying them. In this configuration, an attacker with network access may be able to obtain a valid agent certificate without prior authentication and then exploit the vulnerability.

As of the latest available vendor information, there are no reports confirming active exploitation of CVE-2026-115731. Perforce has stated that it is not aware of attacks exploiting the flaw and has found no evidence of customer data being accessed. No specific threat actor or campaign has been linked to this vulnerability.

Perforce released security updates on November 3, 2026. Fixed versions include Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.1, 2025.12.1 and 2023.8.13, and Puppet Core 9.1.3 and 8.22.2. Organizations should upgrade as soon as possible. Until then, they should disable automatic certificate signing unless requests undergo strong verification.

According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities, FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog.

Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure.

CISA orders federal agencies to fix the flaw by December 1st, 2026.

Title: How organizations can secure their AI-generated code
Context: “Spotting those requires reasoning about what an attacker can do, not just what the feature should do
Full Text:
The IT manager didn’t know the company hired a “vibe coder” straight out of school. By the time they met a few months later, the new hire had already built a web application that operated with customer data and private contracts.

The app ran under a domain the new hire controlled, stored data on Supabase’s free plan, and deployed directly from his GitHub repository to Cloudflare’s serverless infrastructure.

“He vibe-codes everything straight into production, on servers all over the world,” the IT manager wrote on Reddit. “We’re EU based.”

When asked whether he had read the AI-generated code or taken any security precautions, the new hire said, “My GitHub repo is private.”

The IT manager took the concern to the CEO, who brushed it aside: “Let it go.”

In many organizations, vibe coders build software without thinking much about security. Their apps may get the job done, but they are ticking bombs.

In SusVibes, a benchmark of 186 real-world feature requests from open-source projects, agents given feature descriptions without security guidance produced working code up to 57% of the time. But only 11.8% of their solutions were secure.

“The failures we saw were not careless errors,” says Danqing Wang of Carnegie Mellon University’s Language Technologies Institute, author of the paper describing SusVibes. “Spotting those requires reasoning about what an attacker can do, not just what the feature should do.”

What has changed, especially this year, is that AI code-generating tools have gotten so good at producing working code that people are just trusting them, says Dr. Katie Paxton-Fear, staff security advocate at Semgrep. “Developers simply aren’t being as critical now as they were when AI was worse at writing code.”

Whether it’s the vibe-coder in marketing or the seasoned engineering team boosting its productivity, AI-generated code is an increasing security concern for CISOs. Much of that is a function of volume, but even as AI has proved highly capable of finding flaws in code bases, it is not yet adept at contributing code without introducing its own.

Treating AI-generated code as ‘untrusted input’

Leading AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and Amazon Q Developer have become developer go-to tools, and CIOs are increasingly enlisting business users to vibe code their own apps.

But as AI-generated code surfaces everywhere, CISOs have only one option: to treat it “as untrusted input that has to earn its way into the codebase,” says Bianca Lankford, VP of engineering at Datadog.

To do so, security leaders are moving security checks closer to where code is written: static analysis, secrets scanning, and dependency checks run on every pull request and, increasingly, in the developer’s editor.

“Companies are also approving specific AI tools, limiting what assistants can access, and training reviewers to spot common AI mistakes like outdated libraries, weak input validation, and overly permissive defaults,” Lankford adds.

At Mimecast, using AI to write code doesn’t remove the developer’s responsibility for it, says Leslie Nielson, CISO at the information security vendor. “A named person owns every AI-assisted change that ships, and that’s recorded in the pull request, not assumed,” he adds. “AI can propose. Only people can approve.”

The volume of code organizations need to review is only growing, and reviewing everything manually can be impossible. That’s why Nielsen recommends security leaders combine automated checks with human judgment.

“We use automation for the known and repetitive, like dependency checks, secrets detection, and standard vulnerability patterns,” he says. “We keep a person accountable for anything involving access, authentication, or sensitive data. Those categories always go to a specialist reviewer, regardless of how clean the scan looks.”

Datadog’s Lankford says the decision to bring in a specialist should depend on what the code could put at risk, not on what entity — human or AI — wrote it. “Anything involving authentication, cryptography, payments, personal data, or infrastructure goes to a specialist, and code owner rules can route those changes automatically,” she says. “Other useful signals include diff size, new dependencies, and changes to permissions or network exposure.”

The goal is to protect the human reviewers’ attention. “A reviewer buried in low-risk changes isn’t reviewing,” Nielsen adds. “They’re approving.”

Another priority should be preserving the knowledge behind the code. “Generative AI may produce software, but it cannot produce understanding,” notes Alex Ștefănescu, security expert and tech activist. “Documentation, a solid test suite, and a written record of every significant architecture decision ever made are going to save developers and organizations countless hours when a security incident hits or when they are debugging complex issues.”

All of this should be created and maintained by people and intended for human use, not externalized to generative algorithms, Ștefănescu adds.

What’s at risk with AI-generated code

The inclusion of third-party libraries or phantom dependencies — dependencies that are not explicitly declared in a manifest file — is a common concern with AI-generated code, as these unreported software packages might not be identified during a scan and can potentially hide vulnerabilities.

One way to address this is to use software composition analysis (SCA) and software supply chain security tools to help identify the libraries in use, as well as the vulnerabilities and potential legal and compliance issues that might bring.

While not unique to AI-generated code, organizations also expose themselves to risks when developers download machine learning (ML) models or datasets from platforms such as Hugging Face.

“In spite of security checks on both ends, it may still happen that the model contains a backdoor that becomes active once the model is integrated,” says Ștefănescu. “This could ultimately lead to data being leaked from the company that used the malicious models.”

When it comes to coding agents and code completion functionality in tools like GitHub Copilot, Ștefănescu worries about hallucinations. “An LLM will always generate the most statistically probable continuation of a given prompt, so there are no real guarantees in place that it will generate a real package from PyPI, for example, after the word ‘import’,” they say. “Some attackers are aware of this and register package names on platforms like npm and PyPI, filling in some functionality that code completion tools suggest in order to make the packages seem legitimate.”

If these packages are imported into real applications, they can do real damage.

Sensitive information inadvertently leaking into codebases because of developers using AI-powered coding tools is another key concern.

To address these risks, CISOs can establish protocols for downloading and integrating ML models or datasets from external platforms such as Hugging Face and ensure those protocols are incorporated in AI code agents’ instruction files where applicable. Such protocols can include implementing automated scanning tools to detect malicious code or backdoors, having a policy that only allows the use of models from verified publishers, or conducting internal testing in isolated environments.

Not all AI-based code comes from teams full of software engineers. “We see a lot of adoption being driven by data analysts, marketing teams, researchers, etc., within organizations,” says Darren Meyer, staff research engineer at Endor Labs.

These teams aren’t traditionally developing their own software but are increasingly writing simple tools that adopt AI libraries and models, so they’re often not aware of the risks involved. “This combination of shadow engineering with lower-than-average application security awareness can be a breeding ground for risk,” he adds.

To make sure these teams are working safely, CISOs must consider forming relationships with these teams early in the process. Cybersecurity leaders might also want to set up training programs tailored to non-traditional development teams to educate data analysts, marketing professionals, and researchers on the potential risks associated with AI-based tools and libraries.

Investing in defense

“Security budgets don’t generally grow at the same pace that software development accelerates, and AI adoption is only widening that gap,” Meyer says. Application security is often underfunded in most organizations, yet allocating sufficient time and resources to it is essential, as AI adoption and AI-assisted coding accelerate the pace of software development.

“A portfolio of high-quality security tools that can help address this gap is no longer optional,” Meyer says. “And while tools are critical to closing the gap, so are AppSec and ProdSec staff that can effectively partner with developers — even non-traditional developers — and understand the technical, compliance, and security implications of AI.”

When it comes to securing enough resources to protect AI systems, some stakeholders might hesitate, viewing it as an optional expense rather than a critical investment. “AI adoption is a divisive topic in many organizations, with some leaders and teams being ‘all-in’ on adoption and some being strongly resistant,” Meyer says. “This tension can present challenges for insightful CISOs and business information security officers (BISOs).”

CISOs that are aware of both the advantages and disadvantages of this might try to set controls to manage risks effectively, but this might create the perception of holding the organization back from innovating if they don’t explain what they do properly. “Organizations need to develop comprehensive strategies that balance the productivity benefits of AI tools with robust security practices,” says Thomas Segura, senior technical writer at GitGuardian.

Cost-effective changes CISOs should implement

But if a security leader has 90 days and no budget to spare, which changes would have the biggest impact?

Datadog’s Lankford says a short, plain-language AI tool policy can make expectations clear. At a minimum, such a policy should spell out which tools employees can use, what code and data they can share, and which changes need specialist review. The aim is to give people answers they can use while they work, with a clear point of contact when they’re unsure.

It’s also important to understand that employees don’t want to circumvent policies. They just want to get their work done without friction and without waiting weeks for approval. Giving them the right tools makes the safer route easier to take.

By contrast, banning tools doesn’t work, because employees will find a way to still use them. A ban can push AI use out of sight, leaving security teams with less visibility into the code being written and the data being shared, Mimecast’s Nielsen says.

CISOs should look across the development process to identify where they can intervene and which risks they can address at each stage. “Understand what layers you can influence and what vulnerabilities you can influence at each layer: in the design phase, in the CLAUDE.md file, as the agent is writing, during a pull request, as part of an AI pentest,” Semgrep’s Paxton-Fead says.

It’s also important to explain to employees who are using AI code-generating tools that security lives in an implicit context: the threat model, the trust boundaries, what the attacker controls. “Agents cannot reliably plan and reason on these, so they optimize for the only signal they have, which is to satisfy the given functionality description,” Carnegie Mellon’s Wang says.

When things go wrong, people in the organization need to feel safe telling security what happened, including which unapproved tools they used and what data they shared. Fear of punishment can delay that conversation, leaving the team trying to contain a problem without the full picture.

“Offer amnesty instead of a crackdown, so people tell you the truth about what they’re using,” Nielsen advises.

Title: Hackers Exploiting Critical Puppet RCE Flaw Affecting Enterprise Management Servers
Context: "If the certificate authority automatically signs requests without strong verification, an unauthenticated network attacker can obtain a valid certificate and exploit the...
Full Text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added a critical security flaw impacting Perforce Puppet, an enterprise infrastructure-as-code (IaC) and configuration management platform, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing reports of active exploitation.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-115731 (CVSS score: 9.4), is a case of deserialization of untrusted data that could result in remote code execution.

"Perforce Puppet Enterprise contains a deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability in Puppet's report-processing code that allows a client with any CA-signed agent certificate to execute arbitrary code on the Puppet Server as the service user by submitting a report containing a crafted rich-data type through a PUT request," CISA said.

"If the certificate authority automatically signs requests without strong verification, an unauthenticated network attacker can obtain a valid certificate and exploit the vulnerability."

The shortcoming impacts the following versions -

Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.0 before 2026.0.1

Puppet Enterprise 2025.0.0 before 2025.12.1

Puppet Enterprise 2023.8.0 before 2023.8.13

Puppet Core 9.0.0 before 9.1.3

Puppet Core 8.x before 8.22.2

It was addressed by Perforce Software on November 3, 2026, in the following versions -

Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.1 (Puppet Core 9.1.3)

Puppet Enterprise 2025.12.1 (Puppet Core 8.22.2)

Puppet Enterprise 2023.8.13 (Puppet Core 8.22.2)

Puppet Core 9.1.3

Puppet Core 8.22.2

It's worth noting that the issue also affects OpenVox, an open-source implementation of Puppet, and has been resolved in the following versions -

OpenVox Agent 9.3.0 and 8.32.0

OpenVox Server 9.2.0 and 8.18.0

Alain Rödel, a security researcher at Neodyme AG, has been credited with discovering and reporting CVE-2026-115731 along with CVE-2026-115732 (CVSS score: 9.0), a critical certificate-name authorization bypass affecting both Puppet and OpenVox. The issues were discovered with artificial intelligence (AI) assistance and precise steering, the German cybersecurity company added.

"The impact highly depends on the Puppet server configuration and the orchestration protocols used, if any are enabled at all," Neodyme said in a report published this month. "Independent of the configuration, an attacker with RCE on a Puppet server can grab the CA signing keys and impersonate other hosts."

"Puppet is a powerful software, often with full access to a fleet of systems in a corporate network. Remote Code Execution on such a central and important system can lead to worst-case scenarios: Deployment of ransomware, mass data exfiltration, and potentially lateral movement to other parts of the network."

As of writing, there are no details on how the vulnerability is being weaponized in the wild. However, a Reddit user named transdimensia noted in a November 4 post that it was being exploited shortly after public disclosure.

"After finding a severely misconfigured CA in my fleet, I traced the actions backwards on a [CVE-2026-]115731 intrusion," the user said.

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are advised to apply the fixes by December 1, 2026, to secure their networks under Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

Title: CISA Urges Immediate Patching of Java4Shell Flaw That Could Allow Remote Code Execution
Context: "This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as 'Java4Shell,' affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java...
Full Text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged organizations to immediately patch a newly disclosed critical security flaw impacting Oracle Java.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (CVSS score: 8.1), refers to a case of out-of-bounds write that can lead to denial-of-service (DoS) or remote code execution under certain conditions.

"This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as 'Java4Shell,' affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK)," CISA said. "Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution."

Patches for the flaw have been released by Oracle and OpenJDK. As of writing, there is no evidence the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild.

As reported previously by The Hacker News, Java4Shell can enable attackers without an account to execute arbitrary code on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, and with a login on Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, under default settings.

Advisories for the flaw have been released by numerous security and software vendors, including Aikido, Amazon Linux, Blackpoint Cyber, Chainguard, Cisco Talos, Cycode, Datadog, Dynatrace, Endor Labs, Field Effect, Hadrian, Horizon3.ai, Miggo, Orca Security, Qualys, Rapid7, Red Hat, SentinelOne, Sophos, Tanium, Tenable, Upwind, VulnCheck, watchTowr, and Wiz.

In an update shared on November 18, 2026, the Keycloak team said an instance can be considered at risk if the following conditions apply -

It runs an unpatched OpenJDK build from 17.0.6 onward, including unpatched OpenJDK 21 and 25 builds

Its x86-64 host or virtual machine exposes the avx512vbmi CPU feature to Java

The running JVM has Base64 intrinsics enabled and has not been limited to AVX2 with -XX:UseAVX=2

"The x86-64 Keycloak container images tagged 26.8.2-1 and 26.8.2-2 bundle an affected OpenJDK 21.0.13 build," the team said. "These image tags alone do not establish whether your deployment is exploitable: check the CPU feature and effective JVM flags."

"A Keycloak ZIP or TAR.GZ distribution started directly on a host can also be affected; the conditions depend on its Java runtime and CPU, not on whether it runs in a container."

Keycloak is also recommending that users run the below command to check the CPU feature on a host or virtual machine -

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | grep -qw avx512vbmi && echo 'AVX-512 VBMI available'

If the output of the command returns nothing, it indicates that the CPU does not expose AVX-512 VBMI and is not known to be affected by the flaw. Keycloak has released temporary mitigations that users can apply until it releases updated Keycloak and Keycloak Operator container images once patched OpenJDK builds are available for them.

"The vulnerability could be reached through a local Spring Boot application using Spring Security," Blackpoint Cyber researchers Sam Decker and Nevan Beal said.

"In this environment, approximately 28,000 unauthenticated HTTP requests carrying a malformed Base64 authentication value caused the JVM to terminate after roughly 20 seconds of sustained requests. Additional testing confirmed corruption of nearby Java objects and changes to live application data without necessarily causing an immediate crash."

CISA is recommending that organizations take the following steps -

Identify affected Java installations.

Review software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances.

Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available.

"If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access," CISA said.

Title: Attackers Compromise Microsoft's Agent Framework PyPI Package to Steal Cloud Credentials
Context: "While directly targeting an official Microsoft package, it seems that attackers found a way to hijack the wheel creation flow to add malicious logic inside
Full Text:
Threat actors have compromised Microsoft's agent-framework package to push a credential stealer, according to reports from Aikido, Chainguard, Endor Labs, OX Security, SafeDep, Socket, StepSecurity, and Google-owned Wiz.

The malicious versions, 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published 33 minutes apart on November 17, 2026, and are designed to run a credential stealer on every Python start. As of writing, both the release versions have been quarantined on the Python Package Index (PyPI) repository. It's unclear how the attacker managed to obtain publishing access.

Agent-framework is the meta-package for Microsoft Agent Framework, an open-source framework for building and orchestrating artificial intelligence (AI) agents using Python.

"Both versions install Python startup hooks that silently collect credentials, environment data, and cloud identity tokens, then exfiltrate them to a webhook[.]site endpoint," Socket said in a report.

Once either of the versions is installed, the package drops a .pth file in the site-packages root directory, which then gets executed automatically on every interpreter start, causing the credential stealer to run whenever Python is started in an environment, even if the package is not explicitly imported.

"Each wheel adds a .pth file to site-packages," Endor Labs said. "Python executes import lines in .pth files on every interpreter start, so the stealer runs on any Python launch in an affected environment, including pip itself, whether or not anything imports Agent Framework."

The names of the .pth files are below -

agent_framework_meta.pth in version 1.26.1

af_runtime_diag.pth in version 1.26.2

The "agent_framework_meta.pth" file contains a single import statement referencing "agent_framework_meta," which then launches the stealer payload. It's capable of capturing the following data -

Environment variables based on substring-based matching

Credential files associated with Azure CLI (~/.azure/*.json), .npmrc, pip.conf, .netrc, .git-credentials, .docker/config.json, Hugging Face, Microsoft Azure DevOps agents, and .env and JSON files

Azure DevOps OIDC tokens

Azure managed-identity tokens

Azure instance metadata and retains up to 8,000 characters of the response

"Besides reading credentials already on disk, the code asks the platform to issue new ones," SafeDep said. "Rotating stored secrets does not cover those."

"In an Azure DevOps pipeline, SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN and SYSTEM_OIDCREQUESTURI are enough to request a federated token for api://AzureADTokenExchange. On Azure compute, it asks the managed identity endpoint for an access token to each of these resources. It uses IDENTITY_ENDPOINT or MSI_ENDPOINT on App Service and Functions, and 169.254.169[.]254 elsewhere. It also pulls instance metadata."

It's worth noting that the Azure instance metadata service (IMDS) is a RESTful web service that runs on a local IP address ("169.254.169[.]254"), and provides information about the virtual machine, its region, tags, and the identity token.

All the collected information is saved into a JSON document, zlib-compressed, Base64-encoded, and sent via an HTTPS POST request to a hard-coded URL ("webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb").

Version 1.26.2, on the other hand, imports a new top-level module, af_runtime_diag.py, collects GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, and expands the search patterns used for harvesting credential-related environment variables.

Given that the package attracts about 190,000 downloads a month, users are advised to perform the following steps -

Isolate affected hosts and runners

Pin the package to the most recent safe version (1.26.0) and restore from a clean environment

Check for exposure to the malicious versions between 8:35 and roughly 9:20 p.m. UTC on November 17, 2026

Search proxy and DNS logs for requests to webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb

Rotate exposed credentials from a clean system

Audit Azure identities and review sign-in and activity logs

Audit GitHub Actions workflows that deploy to Azure

"The malicious agent-framework shows how attackers are targeting the AI developer ecosystem and the CI pipelines behind it," OX Security said. "While directly targeting an official Microsoft package, it seems that attackers found a way to hijack the wheel creation flow to add malicious logic inside."

Agent-framework is the second Microsoft-related PyPI package to be compromised this year. In May 2026, the threat actors behind TeamPCP pushed three malicious versions of durabletask, Microsoft's Python client for the Durable Task workflow execution framework, to distribute the Mini Shai-Hulud worm.
