Title: Holiday shopping in a world of fakes: How AI is changing the game
Context: *Malwarebytes threat intelligence data, collected between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026 Scammers are getting personal Nearly one in four consumers (24%) say they’ve...
Full Text:
It’s the most wonderful time of the year, especially for scammers.

The holiday shopping season is packed with tempting one-day-only deals, gift guides, and retailers promising the perfect present at the perfect price.

And wherever shoppers go, scammers aren’t far behind.

Cybercriminals have always taken advantage of the holiday rush. Now AI makes it easier to create fake storefronts, products, reviews, and promotions that look and sound legitimate. For consumers, knowing what—and who—to trust is getting harder.

Shoppers are worried. According to Malwarebytes research, 77% of consumers are concerned about being scammed by a retailer using a fake AI website, or using AI to misrepresent products or reviews.

That concern is grounded in experience: More than one in four consumers (28%) have experienced an AI-related shopping scam in the past year Some were misled by AI-generated product photos or reviews. Others described ordering products that never arrived, sometimes from legitimate-looking websites that turned out to be fake.

With the holiday shopping season upon us, we’re looking at how AI is changing the shopping experience, where consumers see risks and benefits, and how to shop more safely.

When a great looking product isn’t what it seems

Realistic product images, glowing reviews, and professional-looking websites can make unfamiliar retailers seem trustworthy. AI makes it easier to create all three in one polished package, which is convincing enough to deceive even careful shoppers.

For some, these convincing fakes have made buying online feel unsettling. One survey respondent commented:

“It seems as though when I’m shopping online, I notice the models are AI-generated or even the products themselves and that scares me. I can’t tell what’s real or not anymore. I don’t even know if what I’m looking to buy is real! I don’t know if what is being advertised is the actual product. AI is going too far.”

Survey respondents shared real-life experiences that help explain those fears. One described receiving products that looked nothing like the photos:

“I buy fewer items that I don’t already know from real life because I fell for manipulated images and the delivered items barely resembled the edited pictures in the shop!”

This aligns with what we’re seeing too. As an example, earlier this year we found cat face flower seeds being sold online.

But manipulated images don’t have to look this extreme, or this obvious. As AI improves, telling what’s genuine from what’s fake is getting much more difficult.

Some of our survey respondents described seeing convincing fake storefronts that took their money without delivering anything:

“It was a fake website promoting shoes. I bought them and it turned out to be an AI website. Now I’ll be more wary of these websites and what they look like.”

These experiences are especially common among younger shoppers. 42% of Gen Z say they’ve experienced an AI-related shopping scam, compared with 30% of Millennials, 22% of Gen X, and just 9% of Boomers and older.

The impact goes beyond lost money or a missing package. Respondents described feeling embarrassed, angry and unsettled by how convincing the deception was. For many, that experience left a lasting distrust of online retailers.

How AI brings scams directly to shoppers

Scammers don’t have to wait for shoppers to stumble across a fake website. With the help of AI, they can send convincing, personalized messages that appear to come from familiar brands, bringing scams directly to consumers.

It’s no wonder that global mega-retailer Amazon is the most impersonated brand that we see in our threat intelligence data, followed by Walmart, Temu, Costco, and Steam.

*Malwarebytes threat intelligence data, collected between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026

Scammers are getting personal

Nearly one in four consumers (24%) say they’ve received a scam message that felt highly personalised, sometimes including their name or other personal details. Among Gen Z, that figure rises to almost one in three (32%).

We came across a scam that linked a person’s phone number and name with a fake Facebook Marketplace listing to act as a conversation lure and get them to respond. Answering a message is often the first step in what can become a very costly scam.

Even when shoppers spot the warning signs, a personalised scam can leave them feeling uneasy. One respondent explained:

“I received an email that was clearly directed to me personally, yet it seemed “off” which was an alarm for me. I investigated it before clicking on anything and knew then that it was a scam. It made me feel like nothing is safe out there anymore and you have to be hyper-alert at every moment when online.”

Spotting scams among the shopping noise

Delivery companies are an obvious choice for scammers to impersonate at this time of year. With more purchases being made, it can be hard to keep track of which retailer is using which delivery service, and on which date it will arrive.

*Malwarebytes threat intelligence data, collected between 1 November 2025 and 31 October 2026

Common delivery scam lures we’ve seen include:

A delayed parcel notification, paired with a request to pay a small fee through a link

A failed-delivery claim demanding address confirmation or rescheduling.

Short deadlines or “final notice” language to create a sense of urgency.

Lookalike delivery company domains and off-brand links.

In this example, scammers use a fake missed delivery, the USPS brand, and a sense of urgency (48 hours) in order to get their target to click.

The broader research shows just how challenging this environment has become:

85% agree that sophisticated scams can be hard to distinguish from the real thing

85% believe AI makes it easier for scammers and criminals to target people

Even the most routine messages about purchases and deliveries warrant a closer look, and that’s one more thing for consumers to worry about during an already busy time of year.

Where shoppers accept AI

Despite their concerns, many consumers accept some uses of AI in retail. In the survey, 43% say it’s okay for businesses to use AI-generated websites to sell products, while 36% accept AI-generated salespeople. Including neutral responses, those figures rise to 72% and 64%, respectively.

There’s also growing acceptance of AI on the retailer side. 43% say it’s okay for businesses to use AI-generated websites to sell products, while 36% are okay with AI-generated salespeople. Including those who feel neutral about these practices, the figures rise to 72% and 64%, respectively. That shows how willing consumers are to let AI into the shopping process, despite their concerns.

That acceptance extends to product images: 60% say using AI to enhance them is no different from existing advertising practices. Product photos have long been staged, edited and polished to make merchandise look its best; AI can do the same.

Shoppers’ responses show that concern about AI and acceptance of its use can coexist. In the holiday rush, distinguishing a useful shopping aid from a convincing deception can be difficult.

Shoppers are taking precautions, but the burden is growing

Some shoppers are responding in practical ways, starting with where they choose to buy:

36% have limited purchases from unfamiliar online retailers.

26% have limited purchases from social media accounts

As one respondent explained:

“I am more wary of purchasing something from an ad I see on social media. I tend to search for the item online myself and find a legit website to order from.”

Others are checking information more carefully:

One respondent described checking reviews on another website after watching a convincing product video on social media, only to uncover signs of a scam. Another now deliberately seeks out negative or neutral reviews and real customer photos. Others describe comparing information across multiple sources rather than taking any online content at face value.

One respondent summed up the need for extra caution:

“I tell my children not everything that glitters is gold. Always be careful and check everything yourself. With AI today you can make everything look beautiful but beautiful doesn’t mean true, correct or authentic. Fact checking is the order of the day.”

Beyond checking information for themselves, consumers also value having another person to turn to when they need help. Nearly seven in ten (69%) say they’d spend extra time or pay more for human customer service, while 43% say they’ve tried to talk to a real person rather than an AI customer service system.

AI may make shopping more convenient for some, but that doesn’t mean consumers want to rely on it for every interaction.

How to spot AI-powered shopping scams this holiday season

AI can make fake stores, product photos, and reviews look extremely convincing. Here are four ways to protect yourself:

Slow down. Scammers use urgency to rush you. During the holidays, limited-time deals and delivery alerts can be especially persuasive. Don’t let a countdown or unexpected message stop you from checking first.

Guard your information. Be wary of unexpected requests from sellers or delivery services for passwords, payment details, or other personal information. A message can use your name or mention a recent purchase and still be fake. You can check which data

Verify the source. Check independent reviews and compare product photos and details across websites. Go to the retailer’s official site directly instead of following links in messages. Remember that logos, email addresses, and caller IDs can all be faked.

Use anti-scam/scam detection tools. Malwarebytes offers free tools to help you spot and stop potential scams. If you’re worried about the legitimacy of a DM, text, email, link, or number, upload it to Scam Guard. We’ll give you a verdict on whether it’s safe, along with guidance on what to do next. You can also use Browser Guard as you shop to block scammy and fraudulent websites, and stop card skimmers in their tracks.

About the research

The research in this article is based on a March 2026 survey about AI, identity, and digital trust, conducted among 1,500 respondents in the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. The research was prepared by an independent research consultant and distributed via Forsta.

Title: New GitDoor and GraphDoor Backdoors Turn GitHub and SharePoint Into Covert C2 Channels
Context: The malware then fetches three plugin modules from the server and launches them in parallel to carry out screenshot capture, process listing, and keylogging
Full Text:
Government sectors in Asia and Africa have been targeted by an active cyber intrusion campaign that delivers to previously undocumented backdoors that leverage legitimate services like Microsoft SharePoint and GitHub for command‑and‑control (C2).

The activity has been codenamed Operation ShadowCloud by Kaspersky. The Russian cybersecurity company said it identified the campaign in early 2026.

"The threat actor behind it is abusing the legitimate MeshAgent utility to drop two brand-new backdoors," Kaspersky researchers Saurabh Sharma and Noushin Shabab said in a two-part analysis. "These implants hide their command‑and‑control (C2) traffic behind cloud services Microsoft SharePoint, GitHub, and Ably, allowing the implants to blend in with normal traffic, effectively evading network-based detections."

The modular backdoors, dubbed GraphDoor and GitDoor for their choice of the cloud platform used for C2, enable the download of additional plugins on demand and the execution of shellcode directly in memory to extend their functionality. Traffic between infected systems and the C2 servers is proxied by deploying a modified Erfrp client and Ably messaging service-based plugins.

The starting point of the attack has been traced back to a MeshCentral Agent, a legitimate remote access tool that's used for remote desktop control, command‑line access, and file management. The attack is said to have targeted an unspecified Taiwanese organization.

The exact method by which the utility is installed on the host remains unknown. However, signs point to the "reuse of a prior infection already present on the network," Kaspersky added.

The MeshCentral Agent is configured to contact a hard-coded C2 server ("wss://27.102.66[.]162:443/agent.ashx") and then fetch three payloads staged on the endpoint -

A legitimate binary used for DLL sideloading (start.exe, pythonw.exe, and zoomit.exe)

A rogue loader DLL used to unpack and execute the next-stage malware (jli.dll, SbieDll.dll, python39.dll, WINMM.dll, and libcef.dll)

An encrypted file containing the core payload

At least two different DLL loaders have been identified to date, each employing its own method to decode and launch the encrypted backdoor payload by injecting it into the current process's memory.

"Loader (Type 1) employs a hybrid scheme: first running the data through an RC4 stream cipher and then applying an XOR mask, while Loader (Type 2) simplifies the process by using a straight XOR operation alone," Kaspersky noted.

The end goal is to deploy backdoors like GitDoor and GraphDoor, which employ a number of encryption and obfuscation techniques like control flow flattening and nested helper functions to complicate analysis efforts and make it harder to trace genuine execution flow.

GitDoor, as the name implies, uses GitHub for C2. It relies on two distinct repositories for receiving command payloads ("/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Havo") and uploading the results of the execution ("/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW/Trix"). While the Havo repository is public, the Trix repository is private.

The creation date of these repositories suggests that preparations for the campaign have been underway since at least the end of 2024. GitDoor supports 26 commands that allow the backdoor to -

Perform file management

Log keystrokes

Launch a proxy, including using Ably

Load shellcode to Base64-encoded Common Object File Format (COFF) binaries and terminate the backdoor

The custom shellcode feature is used to download and run different modules that facilitate the following functions -

Conduct process injection using methods like Asynchronous Procedure Call (APC) injection

Enumerate and manage Windows services

List files and directories, wipe file contents, and recursively delete a directory

Conduct network-related activity by displaying active TCP connections and modify firewall rules

Manage processes, including dumping the memory of the process with a specified process ID into a file and terminating specific processes

Execute commands using "cmd.exe"

Enumerate, create, and run scheduled tasks

Enumeration Windows Registry keys and values recursively and set a value in the Registry

Extract user information, along with local groups and its members

Add of a new Windows user account or add a user to a global or a local group

Record keystrokes to a file ("%APPDATA%\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Cache\logs.dat")

Dump cookies from Google Chrome and Microsoft Edge directly from the process memory using CookieKatz

Use Mimikatz to dump credentials from Windows LSASS

Capture screenshots of the entire screen or a specific window identified by its process ID

Extract WhatsApp's database decryption key

Initiate NTLM authentication to an attacker-controlled destination

Calculate system idle time and display the last time a user was active on the host using mouse movement and keyboard input

GraphDoor, on the other hand, opens a named pipe, creates a directory named "Intel_Log" inside the system's Application Data folder, and gathers system information to send back to the attacker.

To establish communications with the C2 server, it authenticates with a malicious application using "login.microsoftonline.com" on port 443 and uses the access token to communicate with the Microsoft Graph API and ultimately stage the data on the SharePoint drive.

The malware then fetches three plugin modules from the server and launches them in parallel to carry out screenshot capture, process listing, and keylogging. It also proceeds to reestablish contact with the SharePoint website to retrieve the commands to be executed on the machine.

The complete list of plugins supported by GraphDoor is as follows -

kl.ts, to log keystrokes at "%APPDATA%\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Cache\logs.dat"

pr.ts, to list running processes

scr.ts, to take screenshots of the window that matches a supplied process ID and save them as JPEG images

moveDir.ts, to move the legitimate executable, the malicious loader DLL, and the encrypted backdoor file to specific target path

channel.ts, to launch the proxy

abchannel.ts, to use the Ably messaging service to proxy traffic

ab2channel.ts, a covert SOCKS5 proxy that tunnels TCP traffic through Ably's Pusher‑compatible WebSocket service

In addition, GraphDoor's custom shellcode capability expands on GitDoor to support two additional commands that allow it to run commands using "cmd.exe," as well as MZ executables.

The identity of the threat actor behind the campaign is unknown, but Kaspersky said it shares some degree of overlap with a China-nexus activity that Sophos tracks under the moniker Bronze Sandcastle. Tactical similarities have been observed with prior campaigns undertaken by FamousSparrow and CopperTurtle (aka BlackTech).

"On several victim systems, these groups shared the same staging directories as the GitDoor backdoor, with their implants deployed within a one-day window of GitDoor deployment," the company concluded. "While this does not prove a direct link, it suggests that a Chinese-speaking group may be developing and/or utilizing the GitDoor and GraphDoor backdoors."

"By using cloud-based storage and messaging services, the actors blend in with normal traffic (as cloud API calls to Microsoft Graph, GitHub, and Ably are indistinguishable from legitimate enterprise usage, evading many network-based detections), and enable dynamic payload delivery, where on-demand plug-ins and shellcode are retrieved from cloud repositories, allowing for rapid updates and functional extensions without modifying host files."

Modules: Email and Collaboration Security; Threat Intelligence; Identity Security Posture Management
Title: Hackers exploit Microsoft 365 outage to launch credential phishing campaign
Context: Cybercriminals are exploiting genuine cloud service disruptions to make phishing attacks more convincing
Full Text:
Cybercriminals are exploiting genuine cloud service disruptions to make phishing attacks more convincing. Just a day after a prolonged outage disrupted several Microsoft services, including Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams and Copilot, Microsoft Threat Intelligence identified a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign targeting organisations across multiple industry sectors.

The attackers impersonated service notifications and sent emails disguised as legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health notifications. Claiming emails held during the outage would be permanently deleted within 24 hours unless recipients restored them, the threat actors created a false sense of urgency, tricking recipients into clicking malicious links and potentially exposing their login credentials.

“We assess that the activity was likely credential phishing; however, the available evidence does not confirm credential capture, malware delivery, or post-compromise activity. Multiple threat actors may continue to look for ways to exploit notable global events in any social engineering pretext,” Jeremiah Jasmin, security researcher at Microsoft, said in a blog post.

Outages in cloud services bring about uncertainty and panic, an area where attackers always thrive, said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners. “In cases where employees cannot access their emails and other applications, they will easily fall victim to any email promising to restore their service or help recover their account. This is especially dangerous for industries like finance, health care, government and educational institutions because employees in such organizations work with sensitive data and rely heavily on cloud services,” said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners.

Carefully constructed phishing trap

The attackers used several techniques to make the emails appear relevant to recipients while evading basic email security filters. These included using specific sender domains, randomised outage-related subject lines, recipient-specific tracking links and a common non-Microsoft destination domain. The combination made the messages harder to identify through conventional pattern matching.

The campaign began with emails sent from domains including moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com, and newbooker[.]com. Their subject lines followed the pattern “Outage” followed by a randomised string of characters. Microsoft also found a fake email conversation embedded in the message body, positioned to remain hidden from recipients. This appeared to be an attempt to evade email filtering mechanisms.

The messages impersonated Microsoft 365 service health notifications. They used recipient-specific display name prefixes and referenced Microsoft services, including Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint and Copilot.

To create a sense of urgency, the emails claimed that messages held during the November 12 Exchange Online disruption would be deleted within 24 hours. Recipients were prompted to click a prominent “RESTORE MESSAGES” button. The links contained recipient-specific tracking URLs that recorded or routed clicks before redirecting users to reallifeaccounting[.]com, including the path /themelist0.html.

One of the emails analysed by Microsoft had a subject line following the pattern “Outage – ” and a display name comprising a three-character organisation-style prefix followed by “Outage Notification.” Its body referred to a purported Exchange Online incident on November 12, claimed that four messages had been held during the outage and warned that they would be deleted within 24 hours unless restored.

A successful credential theft attempt could expose more than an employee’s email account. Dhar explained that, depending on the permissions of the user, threat actors can gain access to sensitive emails, customer information, balance sheets, SharePoint, OneDrive Storage, and Microsoft Teams communication. Moreover, attackers can pretend to be representatives of the company and send believable emails to colleagues, clients, and contractors for the purposes of money fraud or theft of credentials.

From containment to preparedness

Microsoft said it had not observed any evidence of account compromise linked to the campaign. Messages detected and protected by Microsoft Defender for Office 365 were being blocked or quarantined. However, the company has advised organisations to remain vigilant and take several precautionary steps.

CISOs should search email telemetry for the identified sender domains, display-name and subject-line patterns, lure phrases, tracking hosts, and destination domains. Matching messages should be quarantined, and copies already delivered to inboxes should be removed in accordance with the organisation’s incident response procedures.

Security teams should also identify users who clicked on campaign links and review click telemetry, proxy logs, and browser or endpoint evidence to establish whether they reached the malicious destination and potentially entered their credentials. If credentials were exposed, organisations should immediately reset the affected passwords, revoke active sessions and refresh tokens, and verify multifactor authentication registrations.

They should also check affected accounts for suspicious sign-ins, unauthorised OAuth consent, new inbox or forwarding rules, delegate permissions and unusual access to Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive or Teams. Microsoft has also advised security teams to block or closely monitor reallifeaccounting[.]com and the observed /themelist0.html path while the activity is investigated. Employees should be reminded that legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health communications do not direct users to non-Microsoft domains to recover held emails.

Dhar added that organizations should make cybersecurity an integral part of their business continuity planning. Any technology disruption should trigger heightened security monitoring and clear internal communication to ensure employees know how to verify service-related updates. He also recommended conducting phishing simulations during such disruptions to test how employees respond to suspicious communications. CIOs and CISOs should regularly conduct tabletop exercises to assess their preparedness for attacks that exploit technology outages.

The article originally appeared on ComputerWorld.

Title: Apple Tightens macOS App Permissions to Limit Data Access Amid AI Agent Security Risks
Context: "Additional entitlement details will be available soon
Full Text:
Apple on Monday introduced new controls that allow Mac users to give more granular access to data they give to apps, including those that use artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

The changes, currently previewed in macOS 27.3 beta 2, relate to increased transparency and more options for two of its APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access.

"Before granting an app such extraordinary access, users should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk," Apple said in a statement. "These changes are designed to help them do that and to empower them to make informed decisions about their own data and privacy."

To that end, Device Control and Data Access is being split into two settings: System & App Protection Override and Accessibility.

Other changes include -

A single method for granting permissions by selecting the requesting app from a list

Encouraging users to grant access to just the specific apps (for System & App Protection Override) or folders (for Full Disk Access) that are required for their workflows

Increased visibility into the range of data that apps will receive access to or have control over when users grant full permissions

An option for users to configure apps to ask every time they require access

A transparency indicator when one app is controlling another app using System & App Protection Override

Apple stressed that app permissions previously granted by users will remain intact, adding that developers should be prepared to make changes to their onboarding workflows to ensure their apps can handle scenarios where access is granted to only a limited set of folders or apps via these APIs.

In addition, apps that use Full Disk Access for disk backup or the new Accessibility settings for assistive technologies can request entitlements to offer the same experience for new installations that they offered before macOS 27.3.

"Currently, known apps aren't affected and will keep the same experience without an entitlement," the tech giant added. "Additional entitlement details will be available soon."

The development comes a little over a month after Apple began taking steps to tighten controls around a macOS setting called Full Disk Access (FDA) due to security risks posed by artificial intelligence (AI) agents.

Title: A phishing page interested in MX records, (Tue, Nov 17th)
Context: Of course, MX records are publicly available, and there is nothing preventing an attacker from looking them up independently
Full Text:
I’ve mentioned before in some of my diaries that it can be instructive to look at what appear to be “generic” phishing messages in detail from time to time, since some of them might prove not to be as generic as they initially appear. I came across a good example of this while going over phishing messages delivered to our handler inbox over the past few weeks, when a message that, at first glance, appeared to be a fairly ordinary attempt at stealing e-mail credentials turned out to lead to a page interested in collecting a little more information than just the victim's password.

As you can see, the original message was not especially noteworthy on its own, being a spin on the usual “your password will expire today” approach…

The link pointed to an HTML page hosted on Google Cloud Storage, with the recipient's e-mail address included in the URL fragment:

hxxps[:]//storage[.]googleapis[.]com/alx2/03/1a/we.html#[recipient_e-mail_address]

After opening the link, the recipient would be presented with a generic login form, personalized using the domain part of their e-mail address. The page also attempted to use a screenshot of the legitimate website of the recipient's organization as its background, which it retrieved using the thum.io service. This didn't work quite as intended for isc.sans.edu, since the screenshot service returned an error message instead of the requested image. However, when I modified the URL to contain an e-mail address from another domain, the resulting page looked considerably more convincing.

Looking at the source code revealed a couple of layers of URL-encoding and additional JavaScript obfuscation. Once these were removed, the page turned out to contain a fairly typical credential-harvesting kit, which supported multiple languages and attempted to collect not just the submitted password, but also the visitor's public IP address, geographic location, browser information and language. This information, along with a timestamp, was supposed to be sent to the attacker using the Telegram Bot API.

Such extensive collection of information is not particularly unusual. In fact, another phishing page that I examined recently collected a similarly extensive set of information and also sent it to the attacker using Telegram. In the present case, however, one additional field included in the information sent to the attacker caught my attention – it was labeled "MX Record".

A closer look at the corresponding code revealed that the JavaScript actually performed a DNS-over-HTTPS query for MX records associated with the victim's e-mail domain, using Google's public DNS service. The relevant parts of the code (slightly simplified and reformatted for readability) looked as follows:

... const response = await fetch( "https://dns.google/resolve?name=" + domain + "&type=MX" ); const data = await response.json(); return data.Answer.map(answer => answer.data).join("\n"); ...

The retrieved records were then included in the message containing the stolen credentials:

... message += "MX Record : " + await getMXRecord(domain) + "\n"; ...

The use of MX records in phishing is certainly not new. For example, Infoblox documented a phishing-as-a-service operation called Morphing Meerkat in March 2025, which used DNS-over-HTTPS queries for MX records to identify victims' e-mail service providers and dynamically select appropriate phishing templates[1].

In the present case, however, the MX records weren't used to customize the phishing page. Instead, the lookup was performed as part of the credential collection process, and its results were included in the information sent to the attacker.

Of course, MX records are publicly available, and there is nothing preventing an attacker from looking them up independently. Nevertheless, including them with each set of stolen credentials would help the attacker automatically identify the e-mail infrastructure used by the targeted organization, which could be useful for further attacks or for prioritizing the collected credentials.

Whether the threat actor behind this particular phishing actually used the collected MX records in this (or any) way is impossible to say. Still, having the phishing page perform a little additional reconnaissance on the victim's organization, and including the results with the stolen credentials, seems like a noteworthy detail in an otherwise fairly ordinary phishing kit…

[1] https://www.infoblox.com/blog/threat-intelligence/a-phishing-tale-of-doh-and-dns-mx-abuse/

Title: Google spots the first hacker AI system that finds and exploits flaws autonomously
Context: Google said it had identified a hacker-operated AI framework designed to discover software vulnerabilities and execute exploits without human intervention, marking the first...
Full Text:
Google said it had identified a hacker-operated AI framework designed to discover software vulnerabilities and execute exploits without human intervention, marking the first time its researchers had observed such a system being used by threat actors.

The findings, published in a report by Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant, suggest that attackers are moving beyond using generative AI to assist individual tasks and are beginning to automate larger portions of cyberattacks.

The system could give attackers a way to exploit publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, known as n-days, before companies finish applying security updates. Google’s researchers discovered it on an exposed staging server and identified it as a multi-agent framework called exploit_agent.

The framework connects to multiple large language models (LLMs) and is configured to examine changes in application code following security patches, identify vulnerabilities, and generate exploits without requiring an operator to direct each step. It can also execute the exploits automatically.

Google found data exfiltrated from targeted victims on the server, along with scripts designed to support further activity after an initial compromise. Evidence suggested that the operator was particularly interested in French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries and the education sector. The report did not establish whether the framework’s autonomous operations were responsible for the theft.

Google also cited a separate campaign involving vulnerabilities in PaperCut print management servers. According to research by GreyNoise referenced in Google’s report, a threat actor likely used AI tools to develop and test exploits before launching a campaign against hundreds of organizations four days after the vulnerabilities were disclosed.

In separate cases, Google observed other AI frameworks being used by attackers. CAIRN was deployed in intrusion activity targeting organizations that included the US aerospace sector, while a customized platform based on PentAGI was used to conduct reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against organizations across Asia.

Pressure on enterprise response times

Despite the growing use of AI in cyberattacks, the underlying techniques remain largely unchanged, according to Jonathan Ong, senior analyst at Omdia.

“This is more of an acceleration of existing attack techniques,” Ong said. “These are pentesting/red-teaming frameworks with established techniques, albeit significantly sped up with an LLM model.”

Keith Prabhu, CEO of Confidis, said there is still limited evidence that AI makes individual attacks more successful. The greater risk, he said, is that attackers could launch more attempts in less time, potentially increasing the number of successful compromises even if each attempt is no more effective.

Ong said the frameworks typically generate considerable detectable activity, meaning enterprises with properly configured and monitored endpoint detection and response (EDR), extended detection and response (XDR), or managed detection and response (MDR) capabilities should still be able to identify much of the malicious activity.

Google also warned that although the frameworks generate activity that makes detection easier, they remain capable of achieving their objectives.

Rather than overhauling their defenses, security leaders should continue prioritizing established security practices, particularly cloud and identity hardening. Ong pointed to multifactor authentication, strong passwords, and measures to block repeated login attempts as effective safeguards.

“The one thing that has changed is that the containment and response timeline needs to be faster, to match the speed at which attackers using these frameworks are moving,” Ong said.

Prabhu said the problem is compounded by fragmented security visibility and response processes that still depend on manual decisions. He recommended that CISOs prioritize continuous asset discovery and risk-based vulnerability remediation. He also called for better detection capabilities that connect suspicious activity across enterprise environments.

Amit Kumar Jena, development manager for AI at Kanerika, said organizations must give particular attention to vulnerabilities in systems exposed to the internet, where attackers could exploit flaws soon after they become public.

“Internet-facing systems should be treated as their own class, with a fast-track patch path and virtual patching while fixes are tested,” Jena said.

For incident containment, Prabhu suggested automating actions that are well understood and can be reversed, while retaining human approval for decisions that could have significant operational consequences.

Jena also recommended defining in advance which containment actions could be automated, citing endpoint isolation and session revocation as examples.

“The aim is not to remove human oversight, but to eliminate avoidable delays and regularly test that response works at the pace of an attack,” Prabhu said.

Lower barriers for cybercriminals

Open-source agentic frameworks could lower the technical barriers for less-experienced cybercriminals by helping them coordinate existing tools and adapt their attacks based on results, Prabhu said. However, these capabilities do not eliminate the need for technical expertise or guarantee successful compromises.

Prabhu said smaller organizations and service providers with limited security resources could be particularly exposed.

The risk is not necessarily concentrated in any particular industry, he added. Organizations with poorly maintained legacy systems or weak identity controls could face greater exposure regardless of their sector.

Title: ICO Issues GTA 6 Scam Warning as Release Date Nears
Context: The UK’s data protection regulator has warned gamers to be on the lookout for phishing and other cyber-attacks designed to exploit excitement around the imminent release of...
Full Text:
The UK’s data protection regulator has warned gamers to be on the lookout for phishing and other cyber-attacks designed to exploit excitement around the imminent release of Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6).

The much-anticipated title is set to launch worldwide on November 19, but the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) urged caution when opening messages with GTA 6 themes.

These could be crafted to steal passwords that are used to log into victims’ gaming accounts and other online accounts that share the same credentials.

The ICO said that email inboxes, financial information and other personal details could be at risk.

Read more on ICO advice: ICO Publishes Five-Step Plan to Counter Emerging AI-Powered Attacks.

“Phishing emails and other cyber vulnerabilities can be used to access people's personal information. And if you’re using the same password across multiple accounts, one mistake could give criminals the keys to much more than your gaming profile,” said ICO group director – regulatory assurance and cyber, Ian Hulme.

“Our message is simple: enjoy the game, but protect your data. Use unique passwords, switch on two-step verification for your accounts and think carefully before clicking links or sharing personal information.”

Five Steps to Protect Personal Information

The ICO’s advice for GTA 6 fans is useful best practice for any computer user. It urges individuals to:

Use different passwords across multiple accounts to reduce the blast radius of an attack if a scammer gets hold of one

Choose passwords carefully, avoiding those based on personal information such as a pet’s name or date of birth. Consider using a password manager to create and store strong, long and unique passwords

Be wary of suspicious links in unsolicited messages or emails – especially those promising free downloads, exclusive content or early access

Think before sharing personal information online, including full name, date of birth, address and account details

Check you’re using a legitimate website and understand who is collecting your data before entering personal information

Grand Theft Auto and its developer Rockstar Games have been popular targets for attack over recent years.

In 2022, Rockstar Games was hacked by an alleged member of the infamous Lapsus$ collective, with the perpetrator posting around 50 minutes of in-development footage online.

The teen responsible was also linked to a series of extortion attacks on Nvidia, Uber, BT and EE.

In June this year, it was revealed that scammers had registered a number of fake sites falsely claiming to offer early access to GTA 6 in return for crypto payments.

Title: Fully Autonomous Agentic Attacks Are Three Months Away, Google Warns
Context: ” Attacks Are Easy to Spot GTIG said the “low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits and massive scaling potential” is going to make such frameworks an enduringly...
Full Text:
Google expects sophisticated, fully autonomous agentic attacks to emerge in the next three to six months after observing a “paradigm shift” in the use of pen-testing frameworks like ARTEX in the past quarter.

The tech giant’s Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) shared the news in its latest quarterly GTIG AI Threat Tracker published on November 16.

Compiled from Mandiant incident response telemetry, global threat actor tracking and live platform defenses, the report warned that ARTEX and open source, multi-agent frameworks such as CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI and PentAGI, are increasingly popular among threat actors.

Groups are also experimenting with custom-built harnesses, it added.

Read more on ARTEX: Microsoft: Chinese State Actor Used AI to Compromise ConnectWise Tenants.

Frameworks like ARTEX effectively manage a collection of sub-agents to plan, execute and adapt across multiple kill chain stages including reconnaissance and scanning, initial access, persistence and privilege escalation, internal reconnaissance and lateral movement, and completion of objectives.

“While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a new defensive challenge,” the report explained.

“These frameworks share several core capabilities: discovering and exploiting low-complexity vulnerabilities, using LLMs to generate single-use payloads on-demand, and using real-time execution feedback to dynamically adjust tactics.”

Attacks Are Easy to Spot

GTIG said the “low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits and massive scaling potential” is going to make such frameworks an enduringly popular choice for both cybercrime and nation state groups.

“Concurrently, as capabilities evolve, we suspect these operations will continue to move further along the autonomous scale, approaching fully agentic intrusions,” it added.

Threat actors are currently trading stealth for velocity, meaning that attacks generate plenty of forensic signals, “recognizable identifiers” and “code-level traces,” which can help defenders to detect and mitigate, the report noted. However, stealth will certainly increase going forward, it warned.

Sally Vincent, senior threat research engineer at Exabeam, argued that better behavioral monitoring by SOC teams could help to spot and block such threats by flagging unfamiliar tool use or unusual data access.

“It can also identify changes in activity volume. These changes can help expose an attack even when the attacker uses legitimate tools and valid credentials,” she added.

Google said its security operations (SecOps) team has deployed specialized behavioral and volumetric rulepacks to detect use of ARTEX. Mandiant has also released a hardening guide and defensive framework designed to help organizations counter the “speed and scale advantage” of AI-powered attackers.

Just last week, the FBI warned of the growing use of ARTEX in attacks, with South Korean financial institutions among the many victims.

Title: Hijacked Optimizely Scripts Served Card Skimmer and iOS Exploit Kits to CNN, BBC and Zoom Visitors
Context: In an incident notice posted at 01:02 UTC, Optimizely said the attacker had "exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation" and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some...
Full Text:
An attacker exploited a flaw in Optimizely Web Experimentation to plant malicious code in some of the scripts that customers' websites load from the service, Optimizely said early today.

Visitors to sites run by at least 178 organizations, including CNN, the BBC and Zoom, received the code yesterday, according to Report URI, a firm that monitors the scripts websites run.

The code was built to replace crypto wallet addresses with the attacker's own addresses and to capture card details, but the firm cannot see how many card numbers were exposed to the attacker. The vendor says it has fixed the flaw and removed the code.

On iPhones and iPads, the code was also set up to load a second stage that the firm identifies as an iOS exploit kit, but it reports no iPhones actually being taken over.

In an incident notice posted at 01:02 UTC, Optimizely said the attacker had "exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation" and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.

The vendor has also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and added protections to stop unauthorized code from being delivered. The notice does not say how the flaw worked, how many projects were changed, when the fix went in, whether the attacker still has any access, or what customers should do.

Smartsheet's script was cleaned once and then re-infected with a hidden version of the code, which indicates the attacker still had access at that point, according to the firm.

Writing before the notice appeared, the firm said it did not know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: "That's for Optimizely to explain."

Sites that use the service to run experiments on their pages load a script from the vendor, called a snippet. The snippet updates itself whenever the customer changes a setting, according to the vendor's snippet documentation. Each time it loads, it runs a field of custom code called Project JavaScript.

The attacker wrote a loader into the Project JavaScript of customer projects and left the rest of each snippet untouched, Report URI said in its technical analysis. The snippets were still served from cdn.optimizely.com with the vendor's own certificate, so every page that loaded one also ran the loader.

Some sites serve the snippet from their own domain, and those were affected too, because the content comes from the same project.

The loader came in three versions. Most snippets loaded 1688360[.]cc/track.js directly, one version hid that address in base64 so a text search for the domain would miss it, and another carried a full copy of the payload that runs if the domain is blocked.

Cynet, whose endpoint detection flagged browser connections to the attacker's server, traced the loader to a file served from cdn.optimizely.com in an endpoint investigation. Its researchers also captured the code on CNN and Zoom pages. A site that delivered the code has not necessarily had its own systems compromised, the researchers say.

The firm checked 1,611 Optimizely snippets, mostly identified through its own crawl data, and found code in 188 of them, belonging to 178 organizations. It says the real number is likely higher because it could only check the snippets it found in time. Its post lists all 178, with their domains.

Besides CNN, the BBC and Zoom, the infected snippets belonged to Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock, among others. The vendor's own main site and login page also carried the code. Some researchers call the campaign OPTIMJACK.

The first injection was seen at 04:21 UTC yesterday, in the BBC's snippet. A mass cleanup began at about 20:40 UTC, and by 21:52 UTC only TalkTalk's snippet still carried the code.

That first injection loaded webshell[.]lol, which the firm calls the same actor's injector. The injector had also been planted through Kissmetrics, StorifyMe and Minute Media scripts since late last week, and it first appeared on Turkish sites on September 17.

The payload, a file called track.js, replaces valid crypto wallet addresses with the attacker's in page text, forms, links, the clipboard and outgoing requests.

It swaps only an address that passes its chain's checksum and sits near a payment word such as wallet, deposit or send, according to a payload analysis by StepSecurity. Copying is not safe either: an address a visitor copies from one of these pages may already be the attacker's by the time it is pasted into a wallet.

A card skimmer, added at 13:43 UTC, captures the card number, expiry date, and CVV when they are submitted via the site's form fields and sends them to the attacker's server. It cannot read cards entered in a cross-origin payment iframe, such as Stripe's hosted fields or Adyen's.

The code sends the visitor's cookies and a screenshot of the page to the attacker only after it swaps an address near wallet or payment wording. It cannot read cookies marked HttpOnly.

The firm identifies the iOS exploit kits as Coruna and DarkSword, as documented by Google researchers. The Coruna exploit kit targets iOS 13.0 to 17.2.1, and the DarkSword exploit kit targets iOS 18.4 to 18.7.

On iPhones and iPads, the code loads a script called boot.js from two .icu domains. That script reads the iOS version and opens an exploit chain in a hidden iframe: Coruna for iOS 13 to 17, DarkSword for iOS 18, and, for iOS 26, a separate chain that so far only collects details about the device.

Between 17:13 and 17:57 UTC, the attacker also added a Coruna iframe to every visit from iOS 18.6 or earlier. Those pages reload every 60 seconds to retry the exploit, a sign a visitor could notice. The kit's own comments mark iOS 18.7.3 and later, and iOS 26.3 and later, as patched, according to the firm.

Cynet's researchers retrieved the second stage using an emulated iPhone browser and describe what they saw as conditional delivery, "not a successful compromise of a physical iPhone or iPad."

The firm says crypto has already been stolen. As of 19:25 UTC yesterday, the attacker's wallets had received about $7,040, all within roughly nine hours.

StepSecurity put the total across the same addresses at about $6,600. Two of the addresses were already in use before the injections began, and its analysts wrote that "the chain does not show which transfers came from victims."

What Site Owners and Visitors Should Check

Report URI recommends these checks for sites that use Optimizely Web Experimentation:

Open the Project JavaScript in every project and the custom code in every experiment, and look for 1688360, atob( or any script you did not write. The atob( check finds the base64 version of the loader.

Review which users, API tokens and integrations can write to your account, and rotate their credentials.

If your own forms take card details, treat cards entered on Monday as possibly exposed.

Treat session tokens or other secrets kept in cookies without the HttpOnly flag as exposed, and rotate them.

Deploy a Content Security Policy with a strict script-src and connect-src. Allowing cdn.optimizely.com does not help, because the code came from that host, and strict-dynamic or unsafe-eval let the payload run on some sites.

Consider telling your customers that your site served them the code.

The firm kept a copy of every infected snippet, with hashes and timestamps, and could share them with affected organizations and CERTs (computer emergency response teams) on request.

For anyone who visited an affected site on Monday, the firm advises:

Update iPhones and iPads to iOS 18.7.3 or later, or iOS 26.3 or later.

Compare any crypto payment made that day with the address you meant to pay. If the two differ, the address may have been swapped.

If you paid by card on one of the sites, watch your card statements.

A snippet that is clean now may still have served the code on Monday. StepSecurity also advises:

Block the indicators below, and search logs back to 08:00 UTC on Monday.

Fetch every snippet you serve, search it for 1688360, .icu and track.js, and record its Last-Modified header.

Ask Optimizely which of your project IDs were changed, and when and how.

Keep third-party tags off checkout pages, and take card details through the payment provider's own fields in a cross-origin iframe.

Replace any card entered on an affected site on Monday, and check wallet addresses on a hardware wallet's screen rather than against copied text.

Consider having iPhones and iPads on iOS 18.6 or earlier that visited affected sites checked for signs of compromise.

Cynet treats cdn.optimizely.com as a legitimate delivery host rather than an indicator, and it advises against broad blocks of that host or of the affected news sites.

The payload changed multiple times during the day, so a single file hash will not capture every version. These indicators come from the researchers' published lists:

Domain: 1688360[.]cc, the payload host, with the paths /track.js, /card.php and /hit.php

IP: 136.113.106[.]136, the address 1688360[.]cc pointed to

Domain: 5vobauua3ojpklx[.]icu, iOS stage

Domain: eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu, iOS stage

Domain: webshell[.]lol, the injector loaded by the first injection, seen at 04:21 UTC on Monday

SHA-256: f7b84b9a94f749f8ced3f0112d0a66894e8bbc3b4aa5592021d1b8976a9bad40, final version of track.js

SHA-256: 617df364120adc47fb4f55dcc0c69a9b6c9e108a92c60bc2b64a266254ab02f3, earliest captured version of track.js

Title: pnpm Introduces New Lockfile Format to Reduce Git Merge Conflicts
Context: Incompatible tools could omit packages, misidentify resolved versions, or fail to process the dependency graph, potentially affecting vulnerability detection and other supply...
Full Text:
pnpm has introduced an experimental lockfile format designed to reduce Git merge conflicts by changing how dependency relationships are recorded. The new format, available starting with pnpm 12.19.0, previews changes planned for pnpm 13 and is available as an opt-in setting.

The change addresses a common frustration in JavaScript development, particularly in projects with multiple contributors or large dependency trees. Updates to dependencies can produce substantial changes in pnpm-lock.yaml, creating merge conflicts when developers work on separate branches.

The new format aims to reduce those conflicts by keeping related dependency information together and limiting the number of lines affected when peer dependencies change.

A New Structure for Dependency Relationships #

The existing v9 lockfile format uses separate packages and snapshots sections to store package metadata and resolved dependency relationships. The experimental v13 format consolidates that information into a single packages section. The top-level importers section is also renamed to projects.

Package references now use bare version numbers rather than identifiers containing peer dependency or patch suffixes. Peer dependency bindings are represented through with mappings, while optional peers use a new notation. Registry package integrity hashes also move directly onto package entries.

These changes reduce the number of entries that need to be modified when dependencies change, particularly when updating peer dependencies.

The format also introduces JSON-like syntax with tabs and trailing commas, although the file remains valid YAML. As pnpm clarified on X, the reduction in Git conflicts comes from the structural changes, not the syntax.

Experimental Support Ahead of pnpm 13 #

The new format was introduced in pnpm 12.19.0 on November 10, 2026. Subsequent releases have continued refining its behavior.

Version 12.20.0 added support for recording dependency specifiers of local directory packages and addressed issues involving peer dependency cycles. Version 12.21.0 fixed additional problems involving lockfile generation, injected workspace packages, and frozen installations.

Developers can enable the format by adding the following setting to pnpm-workspace.yaml:

lockfile: format: v13

The default remains v9. Once enabled, pnpm writes the new format when resolving dependencies or when developers run pnpm install --lockfile-only.

According to the pnpm documentation, versions supporting the setting can read both formats, regardless of which format is configured for writing.

However, older pnpm versions that predate the setting cannot read v13 lockfiles. The project also cautions that the experimental format may change before pnpm 13 is released, potentially requiring developers to regenerate their lockfiles after upgrading.

Compatibility Implications for the JavaScript Ecosystem #

The changes also affect tools that rely on lockfiles to reconstruct dependency graphs, including security scanners, software composition analysis platforms, and software bill of materials (SBOM) generators.

Although v13 remains valid YAML, tools that expect separate packages and snapshots sections, parse peer dependency information from package identifiers, or read integrity hashes from resolution objects may need updates.

Successfully parsing a lockfile does not guarantee that a tool can accurately reconstruct its dependencies. Incompatible tools could omit packages, misidentify resolved versions, or fail to process the dependency graph, potentially affecting vulnerability detection and other supply chain analysis.

The new format does not introduce additional security protections. Its primary purpose is to reduce merge conflicts, but its eventual adoption as the default in pnpm 13 will require compatible tooling across the JavaScript ecosystem.

Title: ConnectWise Warns ScreenConnect Attacks Continue as SCKit Targets Unpatched Systems
Context: As highlighted by Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber last week, unknown threat actors are suspected to be exploiting an authentication flaw in RMM+ versions 1
Full Text:
ConnectWise on Monday said it completed its investigation into unauthorized access targeting partner ScreenConnect environments, and recommended customers to ensure that the technician client is running version 26.6.5 or later.

The company said additional activity targeting on-premises environments continues to be reported where the identified third-party extensions remain enabled, and ScreenConnect has not been updated to the latest version.

"On-premises partners must immediately disable the identified extensions and update ScreenConnect to the latest supported version," the company said.

It's worth noting that version 26.6.5 addresses a critical-severity flaw in ScreenConnect client tracked as CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9) that could allow files to be transferred and executed through an active remote session without authorization or Host confirmation in certain circumstances.

As highlighted by Huntress and Blackpoint Cyber last week, unknown threat actors are suspected to be exploiting an authentication flaw in RMM+ versions 1.0.31 and 1.0.32 to execute unauthorized commands while bypassing ScreenConnect's regular authentication controls.

The attacks have been found to deploy a multi-component toolkit dubbed SCKit that's capable of spreading from infected customer devices to MSP technicians' computers and compromising additional managed networks by means of a C# module called RelayTrap ("RelayTrap.cs").

Specifically, the malware employs a worm-like technique that exploits CVE-2026-84869 to execute malicious code on a technician's workstation when they connect to an infected device to investigate a problem. There is no evidence this worm-like behavior has succeeded in the latest campaign.

Huntress has since said it detected another spike in SCKit-related activity on November 13, 2026, impacting 205 hosts across 41 organizations.

"Across the incidents, we saw the new ScreenConnect client being hosted at 185.241.211[.]197, which is associated with 1337 Services GmbH, a bulletproof hosting provider known for previously hosting malicious traffic," the company said.

"In one of the incidents, we saw a rogue ScreenConnect client establish persistence via a service called Windows Update Agent, posing as a legitimate system component. The service executable (UpdateConnect.ClientService.exe) was placed in C:\ProgramData\Windows Update Agent (de362a425905bcc4)\ and configured to run under the LocalSystem account."

In response to the incident, ConnectWise has taken the step of disabling five third-party extensions, including Labtech Plus, RMM Plus, RMM+, RMM Plus Password Link, and RMM+ Password Link, across 400 partner environments. That said, the presence of these extensions alone does not imply those environments were impacted.

The company is also urging partners not to re-enable or reinstall the extensions until further guidance. "Disabling extensions and updating software do not remove unauthorized access or persistence already established on affected devices," it added.

Title: Japan's Fugaku supercomputer has decidedly un-super security
Context: It sounds like whatever the attackers did to that dashboard allowed them to move across the RIKEN network, because they were able to reach several servers that store data...
Full Text: The RIKEN Center for Computational Science, the home of the Fugaku supercomputer, has revealed unauthorized attempts to access the machine after a data leak. According to a statement issued by RIKEN yesterday, between November 10 and 13 an unknown entity attacked a web dashboard that displays operational status data for Fugaku. It sounds like whatever the attackers did to that dashboard allowed them to move across the RIKEN network, because they were able to reach several servers that store data belonging to authorized users, and install malware. The servers stored users’ names and email addresses, plus credentials used to access supercomputers and services not operated by RIKEN. The attacker has tried to use those credentials. RIKEN is working with the organizations that host those other supercomputers to investigate whether the attackers succeeded. The research outfit doesn’t know how the attack happened and can’t say with certainty what information attackers were able to access and/or steal, beyond saying that 4,222 registered users of Fugaku are at risk, along with 375 registered users of its smaller Rikyu supercomputer. RIKEN does know that on November 13, someone attempted to log onto Fugaku. RIKEN quickly took the machine offline. Fugaku comprises 158,976 nodes, each packing a 48-core processor and 32GiB of available RAM, for a total of 7,630,848 cores and over five petabytes of memory. Those specs saw Fugaku lead the Top 500 lists of Earth’s mightiest supercomputers for two years between 2020 and 2022. It ranks ninth on the update of the list released on Tuesday. RIKEN’s other super, Rikyu, operates 288,000 cores. If attackers managed to run a workload on either machine, they could do a lot of damage. The intrusion has already had serious consequences because Fugaku is currently offline. As the machine is used for scientific research, and RIKEN schedules use of the machine, the outage will disrupt researchers who were waiting for their turn to use the supercomputer. At the time of writing, RIKEN has found no evidence that users’ research data has leaked but isn’t yet sure what info did make it out of the building and whether it contains any data describing third parties. The research org has promised to conduct a detailed investigation into the incident, which is the latest in a long string of significant cyberattacks that have struck Japanese clouds, telcos, retailers and government agencies, leading Tokyo to release emergency funds in the hope that extra money can quickly shore up the nation’s cyber-defenses. ®
