Title: Google Finds Hackers Using AI Agents to Build and Run Exploits From Software Patches
Context: Another key area of misuse revolves around automating labor-intensive tasks like vulnerability analysis and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization using LLM-driven pipelines,...
Full Text:
Google on Monday revealed that adversarial use of artificial intelligence (AI) by threat actors has gone beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity.

In tandem, threat actors are leveraging the power and capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and agentic frameworks to automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as observed in the case of PaperCut NG/MF flaws earlier this September.

The abuse of open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks is seen as a way to "automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions," Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a report shared with The Hacker News.

The tech giant said the adoption represents a paradigm shift in which cyber attacks take place at machine speed, allowing the operations to be scaled significantly by chaining together varied attack paths even if the underlying mechanics remain the same.

A number of threat actors have been observed experimenting with these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated and suspected espionage actors aligned with China.

"These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation," Google said.

Another key area of misuse revolves around automating labor-intensive tasks like vulnerability analysis and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization using LLM-driven pipelines, allowing threat actors to collapse the window between patch disclosure and active exploitation.

"Threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs to rapidly weaponize patched n-day vulnerabilities, as they can focus research on a finite set of source materials: comparing source code versions (including from pre-release or preview channels), and examining release notes, security research, and POC code related to specific flaws," Google added.

Simultaneously, threat actors are also targeting AI infrastructure to illicit profit from LLMjacking attacks by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments, and then reselling the access through underground proxy services like APIMart and JetNight at discounted prices, otherwise known as LLM mixers.

The findings show that the emergence of open-source frameworks have further lowered the barrier to entry, enabling bad actors to easily integrate new exploits, autonomously scale attacks, and mount convincing phishing campaigns, further compressing attack timelines.

This includes a Chinese-language phishing platform called Jieyou that has integrated an LLM chatbot assistant to allow customers to configure phishing panels and modify existing templates using natural language commands without necessarily having the technical expertise to do so.

"The evolution of the Jieyou platform highlights a growing industry trend where PhaaS providers leverage LLMs as a modular force multiplier," Google said. "Rather than manually editing payloads, low-skilled affiliates can now utilize natural language through the chatbot to dynamically customize pretext lures and phishing interfaces on the fly."

Full Text: A suspected Russian-speaking operator used an AI agent to turn security patches into working exploits with no human in the loop – a first such occurrence, according to the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) – before ultimately stealing data from victim organizations. Google documented this attack in its fourth-quarter 2026 AI threat tracker, and said it marks a significant advance in how attackers use LLMs for fully autonomous vulnerability discovery and exploitation compared to Q3. In this case, the threat hunters found an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework that integrates with multiple frontier and local models. The framework, called exploit_agent, used Russian-language tooling, and was configured to conduct continuous differential analysis of “popular web application software,” according to the report. This includes comparing code before and after security updates, identifying potential vulnerabilities, developing exploits, and then automatically executing them without any human involvement. The server also contained data stolen from victim organizations, and “multiple” post-compromise scripts that allowed attackers to perform nefarious activities including internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers’ webshells. “Victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was specifically interested in targeting French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector,” according to the report. The report also documents other instances of attackers moving beyond manual LLM prompting during cyberattacks and instead deploying autonomous, multi-agent offensive security frameworks to carry out multi-stage intrusions. These include both financially motivated cybercriminals and cyber-espionage groups. In addition to the recent attacks involving the open source penetration-testing tool ARTEX, attackers have also used other AI-powered offensive frameworks, including CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, HexStrike AI, and PentAGI. In another instance, GTIG observed attackers using PentAGI alongside proxy services to target the aerospace sector. “We have observed several threat actors separately experimenting with use of these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated, as well as suspected espionage threat actors with a PRC nexus,” the Googlers wrote. “Given the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential, we believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally.” ®

In this article

Old links in McDonald’s and Burger King posts were hijacked to point to unrelated pages

Bitly says it suspended the accounts involved and is disabling affected links

Check shortened links before clicking, even when the post comes from a trusted brand

An old social media post from a familiar brand may seem trustworthy. But the link behind it may no longer take you where the company intended.

According to Cybernews, criminals hijacked expired Bitly links and redirected them to unrelated Wikipedia pages, making legitimate posts appear to promote offensive or embarrassing content.

Bitly is a URL-shortening service. URL shorteners turn long web addresses into compact links that are easier to share. When you click a shortened link, the service redirects your browser to the original destination. The trade-off is that the short link hides that destination, making it harder to tell at a glance whether you’re heading to a legitimate website or somewhere suspicious.

Attackers apparently exploited what Bitly described as a flaw involving expired links to make old short links point somewhere new. Those links were still sitting in genuine posts from McDonald’s, Burger King, and others, so anyone clicking them was redirected to the attackers’ chosen pages instead of the original destinations. The attackers didn’t need to edit the posts or break into the brands’ social media accounts; they just changed the address where the links led.

One example involved a McDonald’s post from June 7, 2011, which read:

“Check out what our McDonald’s team in Sweden did.”

Its shortened link had been redirected to Wikipedia’s page about the September 11 attacks.

Screenshot courtesy of rudrongus

Bitly said it had suspended the accounts involved and was disabling the affected links. So, the link in that tweet now takes you to an error page:

You’ve got the wrong address

In these cases, the redirects went to unrelated Wikipedia pages. The concern is that the same kind of redirection could instead send people to phishing pages, fake promotions, or malicious downloads.

Unsure where a link goes? We’ll check it.

Check now

How to check a shortened link before opening it

Hovering over a link on a computer is still a useful first check: It can reveal a mismatch between the visible text and the underlying address. But if all you see is a shortened URL, you still haven’t established the final destination. That’s where checking the link and its redirects becomes useful.

You can copy a suspicious link without opening it: Right-click it and choose the option to copy the link, then paste it into Malwarebytes’ free Scam Link Check. It scans the site and its redirects, then provides a result and suggested next steps. No download, payment, or login is required.

How to stay safe

If a message asks you to sign in, pay, or resolve an account problem, open the official app or type the known website address yourself instead of following the supplied link.

Treat unexpected destinations as a reason to stop. Don’t continue simply because the original post came from a recognizable account. The Bitly incidents show why the source of a post and the current destination of its links are separate questions.

Don’t mistake HTTPS for a safety verdict. It means your connection to the website is encrypted, not that the website is legitimate. Phishing sites can use HTTPS too.

Use browser protection as an additional layer. Malwarebytes Browser Guard is a free browser extension that helps flag suspicious links while you browse.

In this article

A fake “FC27 x Prime Gaming” reward site leads to a copied EA sign-in form

The site collects passwords and 2FA codes, putting gamers’ EA accounts at risk

If you entered your login details, change your EA password and review account security settings

Football fans looking for free player packs in EA SPORTS FC 27 could end up handing over their gaming account instead. FC 27 is the latest installment in EA’s soccer video game series. Its Ultimate Team mode lets players build squads using virtual player cards, which they can get by opening packs.

Following the game’s September 25 launch, we identified a fake “FC27 x Prime Gaming” reward page targeting players’ login details. Prime Gaming offers games and in-game rewards as part of an Amazon Prime membership. The fake page borrows that branding, tells visitors their reward is waiting, and asks them to “connect” their EA account—the account they use to access EA games and services.

The series attracts millions of players. EA reported that FC 24 reached more than 11.3 million players worldwide in its first week in 2023, including through EA Play.

On this fake site, there is no reward. The “EA sign-in” that follows is a copy hosted on the scammers’ own domain. It asks for your email address, your password, and the security code from your two-factor authentication (2FA), and sends each one to a server the criminals control. The page’s code is designed to use the server’s replies to decide whether to show a password error or ask for a 2FA code.

This site is not affiliated with EA, Amazon, or Prime Gaming. If you entered your details on a page like this, go to the “How to stay safe” section below.

A reward that’s waiting for you

The landing page is dark purple and styled like a game promo. It says “Your Prime Gaming reward is waiting. Connect your EA account to continue.” Under the button, a smaller line reads “You’ll continue to EA’s official authorization page.”

You don’t. Clicking the button shows “Connecting…” and “Redirecting to EA authorization…”. The code waits a fixed 1.4 seconds and then moves you to /in, which is still on the same domain.

A copied EA sign-in page

The sign-in page closely imitates EA’s own. It has a dark layout, a “Phone or Email” field, “Keep me signed in,” “Sign in with a Passkey,” and a row of Google, Facebook, Apple, and Steam buttons.

The social sign-in buttons do nothing when clicked. Instead, the page steers visitors toward entering their email address and password.

How the theft works, step by step

Each step sends what you type to a separate server, fedserv.thenewsip[.]site.

Email. You enter your email address and move on to the password page.

Password. You enter your password, which is sent to the server. The page uses the server’s reply to decide whether to show an EA-style “Your credentials are incorrect” error or continue, including whether to request a 2FA code. This is consistent with an attempt to check the details against EA, but the captured page code alone does not confirm how the server handles them.

The code. If the account has 2FA, a “Verify your identity” page asks you to click “Send Code” and then enter the six-digit code. The code goes straight to the server.

The exit. The page redirects you to EA’s real Ultimate Team web app at ea.com. Accounts without 2FA skip step three. Arriving at the real site does not mean the preceding sign-in was legitimate.

Capturing a valid 2FA code could let the attackers complete a sign-in before it expires. This doesn’t disable 2FA, but it could allow them to get past that check for a particular login.

Tracking where victims come from

The page records where each visitor came from and sends that “traffic source” to the server along with the submitted details. It recognizes Facebook, Messenger, Meta’s Audience Network, Instagram, and TikTok, through tracking parameters in the link and through Facebook and TikTok ad-click IDs (fbclid, ttclid). Everything else is labeled “direct” or “unknown.”

The kit also has built-in support for Umami web analytics. Whether it’s on depends on a separate settings file that wasn’t part of what we captured. In its default mode, the server’s replies decide whether a visitor’s later steps (password, sending the code, success) show up in the statistics, and the page where victims type their security code isn’t counted in page-view tracking. The settings can also switch to a mode that counts every page.

Together, these features give the operators a way to track traffic attributed to social platforms. They show that the page was built to handle those sources, but do not establish that ads actually ran on them.

Dressed up as an “internal tool”

The HTML asks search engines not to index, archive, or show previews of the page, with a comment that reads “Private team tool — do not index or archive.”

The “Privacy Policy” and “Terms of Service” pages describe an “authentication portal” for “internal use by authorized personnel.”

The kit has two switches. One turns off the Prime Gaming landing page, so the same code would show a plain fake EA sign-in instead. The other chooses between sending victims to EA’s real site and showing the “enrolled for weekly FC 27 rewards” page. In the version we analyzed, both the Prime Gaming lure and the redirect to EA were on.

Why your EA account is worth stealing

An EA account is more than a login. It can hold an FC Ultimate Team club with coins and tradable players, access to purchased games, and saved payment methods. Losing access could put years of purchases and progress at risk.

Attackers could also use a compromised account to impersonate you and trick your gaming contacts into sharing information or clicking scam links.

Safer. Cleaner. Ad-free browsing.

INSTALL BROWSER GUARD

How to stay safe

Start at EA’s website. Type ea.com into your browser and navigate from there. Before entering your EA password or security code, check that the sign-in page is on ea.com or a genuine subdomain, such as accounts.ea.com.

Check the address bar. A page that looks exactly like EA’s sign-in is not EA if the address says something like fc27-prime[.]shop.

Keep security codes private. Only enter an EA verification code on EA’s genuine sign-in page for a login you initiated.

Be wary of free packs, coins, and rewards in ads and posts. A sponsored post isn’t proof that an offer is real.

Use a password manager. It generally won’t offer to autofill your EA password on an unrelated domain, which can help flag a fake page

Already entered your details?

Go directly to ea.com and change your password immediately, even if you didn’t submit a 2FA code.

Review your security settings and trusted devices, remove unfamiliar devices, and check for changes to your email address, linked accounts, and purchases.

Keep 2FA enabled. Change any reused passwords elsewhere, especially on your email account.

If you see unfamiliar linked accounts, are locked out, or have missing content, follow EA’s account-recovery guidance and contact EA Help.

Attackers are using ARTEX AI agents to automate cyberattacks, the FBI warns

Some intrusions reached privileged access in under three hours

The attacks target organizations, potentially putting customers’ personal information at risk

Cybercriminals have found another AI tool to do more of the hacking for them.

The FBI issued a FLASH advisory on November 13 warning that attackers are abusing ARTEX, a tool originally developed for authorized security testing, to automate intrusions against organizations worldwide. In some observed attacks, criminals went from selecting a target to gaining privileged access in under three hours, leaving defenders little time to respond.

ARTEX is an open-source penetration-testing framework. Penetration testing means trying to break into systems with the owner’s permission to find weaknesses before criminals do.

An operator gives ARTEX a target and an objective. Its a planning agent divides the work into tasks, while other AI agents use security tools to carry them out and share their findings. Rather than having its own AI model, ARTEX connects to external large language models (LLMs). Once a task begins, it requires relatively little human input.

The FBI says attackers have used ARTEX since at least August against sectors including finance, government, healthcare, and technology. Separately, Microsoft reported that a China-state-aligned group used ARTEX to accelerate attacks after compromising ConnectWise application credentials.

While these attacks can generate plenty of suspicious activity, their speed leaves defenders little time to respond. An alert is only useful if defenders can investigate and act before the damage is done.

ARTEX helps attackers connect individual weaknesses into a bigger intrusion. An overlooked employee portal or exposed cloud credential can become a route to sensitive records, additional accounts, or connected organizations. For home users, that could mean personal information stolen from a company is later used for fraud or targeted scams.

How to stay safe

ARTEX changes how quickly attackers can work. It does not make basic security controls obsolete, but it makes leaving familiar weaknesses unfixed more dangerous. Most of the FBI’s recommendations are aimed at organizations. Businesses and IT teams should:

Stay up to date: Patch internet-facing systems promptly and inventory overlooked applications, including old employee and supplier portals. Restrict administrative interfaces to approved access paths.

Protect credentials and limit permissions: Scan for exposed passwords and API keys, rotate compromised secrets, and give applications only the access they need.

Monitor and log: Watch for rapid bursts of requests, unusual data access, and unexpected credential or privilege changes. Prepare procedures to revoke access and isolate affected systems quickly.

For individuals and small-business users, the fundamentals still matter:

Update your devices and software.

Use strong, unique passwords and turn on multi-factor authentication wherever available.

Run an up-to-date real-time anti-malware solution on your devices.

If a company tells you your account or information was affected, verify the notice through its official website or app and follow its incident-specific instructions.

Conclusion

The strange part isn't how clever some of these attacks have become. It's how many still work because of things nobody checked, fixed, or thought twice about.

And with finding flaws getting cheaper and exploiting them getting easier, that gap is only becoming harder to ignore. Plenty to unpack this week.

Context: Defending Against Hype-driven Attacks As events like the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 dominate headlines, attacks will continue to exploit the intersection of consumer...
Full Text:
Lead Analysts: Lucy Gee and Cameron Sweeney

With Grand Theft Auto 6 scheduled to launch on November 19, 2026, the 13-year wait for the most anticipated video game release of the decade is nearly over.

As legitimate marketing emails from Rockstar Games increase, video game fans are hyped. The anticipation is massive. However, this unprecedented excitement has created a perfect storm for cybercriminals.

Rockstar and its vast cult following have long fascinated threat actors, with the studio famously suffering massive network breaches and high-profile data leaks in recent years. Now, attackers are pivoting those established tactics directly toward the fanbase.

Threat actors are actively capitalizing on gamers' desperation, knowing that heightened anticipation reliably leads to lower critical thinking. By impersonating Rockstar in a massive, coordinated wave of phishing campaigns, they are weaponizing the promise of exclusive early access, fake "leaked" playable copies, or beta tester invitations to actively exploit both everyday consumers and corporate employees.

This playbook aligns directly with findings from KnowBe4’s Phishing Threat Trends Report Volume 8. That research showed planned calendar events drive the highest volume of lure-based attacks, with campaigns landing an average of 21.3 days before the actual date. On top of that, the lifespan of these planned campaigns more than doubled between 2022 and 2026, giving attackers plenty of time to tweak their angles and test out different lures.

The GTA 6 wave illustrates this dynamic in real time. Data obtained from KnowBe4 Defend shows a rapid, strategic escalation precisely within this pre-launch window:

Key Takeaways:

While GTA-themed phishing accounted for just 0.005% of threats in September, general gaming-related phishing emails have since surged by 1,300% compared to the monthly average across the previous six months (March–August 2026).

For the full week starting October 26th, 24 days before the release, GTA-related lures rapidly scaled to make up 9.6% of all phishing volume.

The First Wave: Mass-Market Noise

Predominantly, this surge is driven by high-volume, spray-and-pray commodity lures. These attacks focus on broad consumer appeal, casting a wide net across millions of inboxes in hopes of catching eager gamers off guard.

In the most widespread campaign, threat actors rely on a minimalist payload delivery to bypass security defenses: the email body is left completely blank, containing nothing more than an embedded link. By stripping away text entirely, the message circumvents basic natural language processing (NLP) filters and spam heuristics that search for suspicious gaming keywords.

To evade domain-reputation blocks, the campaign is heavily polymorphic, distributing waves of messages through constantly rotating webmail accounts with random subject lines so that blocking a single sender provides zero defense against the broader campaign.

Anatomy of the Attack

Clicking the link routes victims through a multi-stage lure that heavily borrows the official Grand Theft Auto 6 aesthetic. Initial landing pages are hosted on graph[.]org, which is Telegram’s lightweight, anonymous and login free publishing site. This allows attackers to host malicious content without registering their own infrastructure, making it easy to stand up pages that slip past filters, especially those looking at domain age.

These pages feature Vice City neon styling, AI generated imagery of characters Lucia and Jason, and prominent Rockstar Games branding. The copy leans into themed phrasing like "The wait is over," "Vice City is calling," and promises of an exclusive "$4,000 bonus" using promo code ROCKSTAR.

Once a user clicks the activate prompt, they are redirected to a fraudulent online casino or crypto platform (such as new2026[.]pro) with the promo code pre-applied. The ultimate objective is dual-pronged monetization: tricking victims into registering an account to harvest passwords they likely recycle across gaming and personal platforms, while simultaneously siphoning payment card details or cryptocurrency deposits under the guise of claiming their GTA-themed welcome bonus. While these mass-market lures lack the sophistication needed to directly compromise enterprise networks, their relentless volume acts as a smokescreen, generating endless background noise for SOC teams.

Campaign Telemetry: Commodity Attack Distribution

Top Targeted Regions: United States (47%), United Kingdom (35%), Germany (8%), France (5%), Rest of World (5%)

Primary Target Verticals: Education (39%), Technology (35%), and Finance (15%)

Campaign: 84 attacks on average per campaign, typically peaking on weekends and evenings.

While these commodity attacks lack sophistication, their sheer volume creates a smokescreen designed to overwhelm SOC teams. The real danger lies in what slips beneath the radar: advanced, targeted phishing campaigns, created to weaponize the intersection of personal interests and organizational trust.

The Second Wave: Targeting the Enterprise

Instead of directly impersonating Rockstar Games, these sophisticated attacks pose as employee benefits programs offering a "free Grand Theft Auto 6 Pre-Order" as a corporate perk. Because a free copy of a highly anticipated game is one of the few things that will convince an employee to check a work email on their days off, these campaigns are heavily weighted toward weekends, accounting for 83.2% of the attack volume. This strategy peaked over the October 31 to November 1 weekend, where GTA-related impersonations made up 42.4% of all phishing emails processed.

In this example, the attacker is combining psychological manipulation with technical evasion elements to ensure the attack lands in users’ inboxes and they’re motivated to click. Rather than impersonating Rockstar directly, which users might view with suspicion, the attacker routes the lure through a fake employee benefits program. Framing the game as a corporate perk carries significantly more weight than standard brand impersonation.

The attack also utilizes senses of urgency, claiming the offer closes in 48 hours and is strictly limited to the first 250 employees. This artificial urgency pushes the victim toward a fast, low-deliberation click. To make the attack look legitimate, the banner at the bottom of the email explicitly states that the message was sent to a verified address and does not collect payment information. This pre-answers the recipient's own suspicions, lowering their guard before they even question the email. By tying the lure directly to the real-world GTA 6 news cycle, the attack feels incredibly timely and relevant, blending seamlessly into the broader hype.

Technical Evasion

Clean Authentication Bypass: The attackers use a genuinely owned, look-alike vendor domain rather than a spoofed one. As the domain is legitimately registered to the threat actor, SPF, DKIM, and DMARC pass cleanly.

Unicode QR Codes: To evade traditional detection, the email uses a QR code rendered entirely out of text block characters (Unicode or HTML tables) rather than a standard image file, allowing it to bypass image QR scanners.

Device Shifting: The ultimate goal of the QR code is to shift the attack off the protected corporate network. By forcing the victim to scan the code with their personal smartphone, the attacker completely bypasses corporate web filtering and Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) controls.

These sophisticated phishing emails largely followed the same distribution as the commodity attacks. Campaign sizes, however, are much smaller averaging 20 attacks per campaign.

The Corporate Risk of Personal Lures

This blurring of lines between personal interests and professional environments is exactly what makes these attacks so dangerous. While a fake GTA 6 pre-order might initially look like a standard consumer scam aimed at stealing a personal credit card, the reality is far more severe: these campaigns are explicitly designed to compromise corporate assets. When an eager employee scans a malicious QR code on their unmanaged personal phone to claim a supposed "work perk," the resulting phishing page is rarely asking for their bank details. Instead, attackers are weaponizing this gaming hype to harvest credentials; turning a momentary lapse in personal judgment into a full-scale corporate breach.

Defending Against Hype-driven Attacks

As events like the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 dominate headlines, attacks will continue to exploit the intersection of consumer excitement and corporate access. Threat actors targeted human psychology, not a software zero-day exploit. They identified an emotional blind spot of weekend relaxation and genuine excitement and used it to bypass both technical filters and common sense.

Protecting your organization against these hybrid threats requires a layered approach:

Run Contextual Simulations: Train employees on non-traditional lure types. Especially fake HR perks, vendor discounts, real-world events, and corporate benefits delivered outside typical working hours.

Validate Internal Communications: Establish a clear protocol for corporate benefits so employees know legitimate company perks will always appear on an internal intranet or HR portal, never via unsolicited external email links or urgent QR codes.

Teach the "Device Shift" Red Flag: Educate staff that any work-related email asking them to pull out a personal smartphone to scan a QR code is a deliberate attempt to bypass security perimeter controls.

Normalize Healthy Scrutiny: Remind teams that genuine corporate perks never demand urgency. If an offer says “limited to the first 250 employees,” it’s designed to shut down deliberate thinking.

Harden Quishing Defenses: Ensure your email security layer can detect QR codes, including those rendered as Unicode characters or HTML tables, not just as image files.

When real-world hype peaks, critical thinking drops. Ensuring your workforce and security stack are prepared for both the high-volume noise and the targeted signal is the best defense against turning a pop-culture milestone into a network compromise.

Title: How to prepare your digital accounts for after your death
Context: Microsoft: Set up OneDrive Digital legacy Microsoft’s OneDrive Digital legacy feature lets you give a trusted contact read-only access to your files and photos
Full Text:
A little preparation can make your digital life easier for loved ones to manage after your death. Here’s how to record your wishes, protect your privacy, and give the right people a way to act.

Start with a digital inventory

Your next of kin cannot manage accounts they do not know exist. Create an inventory of the important parts of your digital life, including:

Primary and recovery email addresses

Phones, computers, tablets, and the mobile carrier associated with them

Cloud storage, photo services, and backups

Social media, messaging, and professional networking accounts

Your password manager and its emergency-access arrangements

Online banking, payment, shopping, subscription, and utility accounts

Domains, websites, digital businesses, and developer accounts

Cryptocurrency exchanges, wallets, and the location of securely stored recovery materials

For each service, include the account email or username and a profile link or account reference where relevant.

For each account, record what you want to happen: preserve it, download important data, memorialize it, transfer an asset where permitted, or close it. Identify any photos, documents, or other files you want loved ones to keep, and note where they are stored.

For websites or digital businesses, record who should take over administration and which domains, hosting plans, or other services need renewing.

Keep the inventory separate from sensitive credentials. Do not put your master password, recovery codes, or cryptocurrency seed phrases into an ordinary document and email it around.

Store the inventory securely and make sure your trusted person knows how to find and access it. Check it periodically, especially after changing phones, password managers, email addresses, or financial providers.

Choose who will handle your digital affairs

Choose a trusted person, or several people, to handle your digital affairs. This might be an executor, partner, adult child, or another trusted contact.

Someone who can handle financial administration is not necessarily the person you want reading private messages or looking through photographs and journals. Those responsibilities do not have to go to the same person.

Record your preferences as part of your estate planning. Laws and platform policies vary, and a provider may require proof of authority, a death certificate, or a court order.

In US states that have adopted the Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act (RUFADAA), an executor’s access to digital assets is subject to specific rules. Access to the contents of emails and other private communications generally requires your consent, so discuss recording that permission with your estate-planning lawyer.

If you run a business, own intellectual property, maintain a large online archive, or hold cryptocurrency, consider speaking with an estate-planning lawyer in your jurisdiction.

Set up official legacy tools

Where a provider offers a legacy-contact or inactive-account feature, use it to record your choices. Do not assume that giving someone your password will provide an appropriate or reliable way to manage your account later.

Apple: Add a Legacy Contact

Apple lets you designate one or more Legacy Contacts. After your death, a Legacy Contact can request access to certain Apple Account data using the access key created when you added them and a death certificate.

On an iPhone or iPad, go to:

Settings > your name > Sign-In & Security > Legacy Contact > Add Legacy Contact

Give your chosen person the access key and explain where to find it.

A Legacy Contact can access eligible data, such as photos, messages, and files. They cannot access passwords, passkeys, or payment information stored in iCloud Keychain, or purchased movies, music, books, and subscriptions.

Google: Set up Inactive Account Manager

Google’s Inactive Account Manager lets you choose what should happen if your account becomes inactive. You can nominate trusted contacts, choose which data they may receive, and decide whether the account should later be deleted.

Visit Google’s Inactive Account Manager to set it up. It is triggered by a period of inactivity, rather than confirmation of your death, so choose the waiting period carefully.

Think beyond Gmail. Your Google Account may also hold photographs, documents, calendars, Android backups, and YouTube content.

Be specific about what you want to share. Google says it will not provide survivors with passwords or other login details, so plan for data transfer through the official tool rather than expecting someone to take over your account.

Facebook: Choose memorialization or deletion

Facebook lets you select a legacy contact for your main profile or choose permanent deletion after death.

A legacy contact has limited capabilities after memorialization. These can include posting a pinned notice, changing profile and cover photographs, requesting removal, and if you’ve enabled it, downloading a copy of material you shared.

Review the options in Facebook’s settings and explain your choice to the person you appoint. Memorialization is not the same as granting full access to your account.

Instagram: Record whether you want preservation or removal

Instagram allows people to report an account for memorialization, while verified immediate family members can request removal.

Decide whether you want your posts to remain as a memorial or would prefer the account to be removed. Make that preference known to your family.

Microsoft: Set up OneDrive Digital legacy

Microsoft’s OneDrive Digital legacy feature lets you give a trusted contact read-only access to your files and photos. In OneDrive on the web, go to Settings > Digital legacy, invite your contact, and follow the instructions to generate and securely share an access code. Your contact will need a Microsoft account.

This covers OneDrive files and photos. Access to Outlook email or other Microsoft account information may require a separate legal process.

Other services: Check their individual policies

Not every platform offers legacy contacts or memorialization.

LinkedIn provides a process for an authorized person to request closure of a deceased member’s account, subject to documentation requirements. Others can report a member as deceased for memorialization.

X allows a verified immediate family member or estate representative to request deactivation, but says it cannot provide access to the deceased person’s account.

Check the current policies for every service that matters to you. The requirements may depend on where you live.

Plan for secure access

The goal is to prepare a route for authorized access, not leave a pile of credentials for anyone to find.

A written password list can be lost, copied, photographed, or discovered by the wrong person. Shared credentials can also conflict with a provider’s rules. Instead:

Use a reputable password manager for unique, strong passwords.

Explore its emergency-access or trusted-contact feature, if available.

Keep recovery information and device access instructions in a protected estate-planning location—not an unencrypted note, shared inbox, or group chat.

Account for passkeys and multi-factor authentication. Your plan should cover authenticator apps, trusted devices, recovery methods, and security keys.

Keep securely stored recovery instructions for critical assets, especially cryptocurrency wallets.

Limit access to what each person needs. Someone cancelling subscriptions may not need your private photographs or messages.

Record where sensitive recovery materials are stored and who is authorized to retrieve them, without exposing those materials in the inventory itself.

Leave a short guide for the first week

Alongside your formal plan, leave a short practical guide that answers these questions:

Who should be contacted first?

Where is the digital inventory?

Which email address is the main recovery hub?

Which phone number and mobile carrier are associated with important accounts?

Which profiles should be memorialized, downloaded, or deleted?

Which subscriptions and recurring payments need attention?

Which devices should be preserved before anyone resets, sells, or wipes them?

Which accounts contain work, business, or other people’s data and require special care?

Which files should be saved before accounts are closed or devices are wiped?

Do not make “log in as me” your default instruction. Use official processes and obtain qualified legal advice where necessary, particularly when accounts contain financial assets, business information, or other people’s private data.

Warn your family about impersonation scams

Include a reminder that anyone contacting your family about your accounts should be verified independently.

Leave these precautions with your instructions:

Do not trust an unsolicited caller, email, text, or direct message offering to unlock, recover, memorialize, or close an account.

Do not pay an upfront fee to a stranger offering “recovery” help.

Navigate to the company’s official support site independently.

Do not send death certificates, identity documents, account credentials, recovery codes, or financial information until the recipient and process have been verified.

Preserve suspicious messages and report scams through the appropriate official channel.

Warn family and friends about fake funeral livestream links, which can lead to requests for card details and recurring subscription charges. Confirm any livestream link directly with the funeral organizer.

Work through your plan over time

You do not need to finish everything in one afternoon. Begin with your primary email, phone, password manager, cloud storage, social profiles, and financial or cryptocurrency accounts.

Name a trusted person, record your wishes, and set up the available legacy tools. Then work through the rest of your inventory over time.

To learn more about preparing your data for after your death, listen to this Lock and Code podcast episode with Jed Brubaker, founder of the Digital Legacy Clinic at the University of Colorado Boulder. We discuss the practical work of preserving digital memories, the tools major platforms offer, and the one step that matters more than any account setting.

Title: Six Unpatched Danfoss Refrigeration Controller Flaws Could Allow Remote Takeover Without Login
Context: 0 does not patch the flaws: "It's not really possible either because according to the file timestamp this firmware was likely built on October 29, before the second wave of...
Full Text:
Six flaws in Danfoss AK-SM800A refrigeration controllers could let a remote attacker take over a controller without logging in, Dutch security consultancy Midnight Blue said earlier this week.

No patch is available, and the researchers say the newest firmware, version 5.4.0, does not fix the flaws.

Government cybersecurity agencies in Belgium, Ireland and Germany told operators this week to take the controllers' management interfaces off the internet.

For a controller left on the internet, updating the firmware, changing default passwords or turning on Strict mode is not enough on its own, the Belgian and Irish agencies said. Strict mode is a login protection that requires encrypted connections and session tokens, but one of the six flaws is in the gateway that enforces it.

The AK-SM800A runs a store's fridges and freezers, and maintenance firms can manage it remotely. Such controllers were targeted in attacks in France starting October 11, and in a second wave across Europe that began last week. The attacks caused unwanted defrost cycles and destroyed stock.

Germany's federal IT security agency, the BSI, says in a security notice that the AK-SM800A was involved in earlier incidents in which refrigeration units in several countries were tampered with.

The agency has no information about any exploitation of the six new flaws, and neither other agencies nor researchers link the flaws to those incidents.

The researchers examined firmware version 5.3.2, then the newest, and say every version up to and including it is affected.

No CVE identifiers have been assigned. The researchers are keeping technical details private while they work on disclosure with Danfoss, the Danish company that makes the controllers.

The vendor lists software package 5.4.0, dated November, as its newest release for the AK-SM800A. Its 5.4.0 readme and November update guide cover upgrade steps, and the guide adds a stricter password rule. Neither mentions a fix for any vulnerability.

In a follow-up statement carried by trade publication Cooling Post, the researchers said 5.4.0 does not patch the flaws: "It's not really possible either because according to the file timestamp this firmware was likely built on October 29, before the second wave of cyber attacks and well before our vulnerability reports."

The German agency first said in a press release this week that 5.4.0 was not affected. Later the same day, it changed that in a corrected statement: it cannot rule out for now that 5.4.0 is affected.

The vendor's advisory page lists no advisory for the six flaws as of today, and no date for a fix has been published.

Midnight Blue researcher Carlo Meijer found the six flaws in less than an hour of manual review, using firmware the vendor offers for download, and described them in a technical write-up.

Five of the flaws are in web request handlers that do not require a login, inside a program that runs as root. Through one of them, the researchers ran code as root on older firmware, version 3.3.0, and they found the same bugs in 5.3.2.

Strict mode closes almost all of the controller's web attack surface to users who have not logged in, including the flaw used in that demonstration. The sixth flaw is in the gateway that enforces Strict mode, a separate program that blocks every request except the login until a user has logged in.

When the researchers ran firmware 5.3.2 in an emulator with Strict mode on, that flaw crashed the gateway. The crash could be turned into code execution with more work, the researchers say, and the gateway lacks basic exploit defenses such as stack canaries.

With code running as root, an attacker could change the controller's settings, start defrost cycles and hide that activity from its logs.

The controllers do not use secure boot, the researchers found, so an attacker could plant code that survives a factory reset and a firmware update. An attacker could also make a controller unusable until it is replaced.

The researchers say the code almost certainly holds more flaws like these, and they call patching flaws one by one or turning on Strict mode "a misallocation of scarce security and personnel resources."

What Operators Can Do

Removing internet exposure must not wait for a patch, and it is needed even where firmware is current and Strict mode is on, the Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium says.

The Belgian advisory and a similar Irish advisory recommend these steps:

Find every controller whose management interface can be reached from the internet, including through a 4G or 5G modem, and remove that exposure.

Give remote access only through a secure VPN or a protected internal network. Allowing only a service company's IP addresses through a firewall is a short-term measure.

Check temperature setpoints, defrost schedules, alarm settings, user accounts and remote-access settings for changes you did not make.

The German agency adds that anyone who suspects a compromise should change all credentials and check that equipment connected to the controller works properly.

Before cutting off the data a controller sends to its refrigeration service company, operators should check contract and insurance terms, the Belgian advisory says. They should also set up protected remote access so that monitoring can continue.

Danfoss's own update guide says the AK-SM800A should not be directly reachable from the public internet, adding: “This recommendation applies to all software versions, including those with Strict Mode enabled.”

Ireland's National Cyber Security Centre also advises running the latest supported firmware, changing default passwords and turning on Strict mode, but says operators should not rely on those steps alone.

Danfoss told Cooling Post on October 12 that most units hit in France were either older models that no longer receive updates or current AK-SM800A units running outdated firmware.

The vendor fixed earlier flaws in the AK-SM800A in 2023 and 2025, including login bypass and command injection bugs. Version 5.3.2, which the researchers examined, is newer than all of those fixes.

Title: Retadup Worm Resurfaces 7 Years After Takedown to Spread CoffeeLoader Malware
Context: " CoffeeLoader was first documented by Zscaler ThreatLabz in March 2025, detailing its use of the Armoury packer to resist analysis and ultimately run Rhadamanthys shellcode
Full Text:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new variant of CoffeeLoader, a malware designed to deliver additional payloads to infected machines.

"On launch, the NSIS-based installer executable dropped a file named '7z.dll' into a temporary directory and ran it through rundll32.exe," Kaspersky said in an analysis published today.

"The '7z.dll' file was a patched version of the original library of the popular 7-Zip archiver. Part of its code had been replaced with malicious self-decrypting shellcode that turned out to be a new version of the Armoury packer."

CoffeeLoader was first documented by Zscaler ThreatLabz in March 2025, detailing its use of the Armoury packer to resist analysis and ultimately run Rhadamanthys shellcode. The malware is assessed to share source code similarities with another loader family tracked as SmokeLoader.

Malware packed with Armory uses file names like "ArmouryAIOSDK.dll" and "ArmouryA.dll," with the packer hijacking some of the original Armoury Crate functionality with self-decrypting shellcode.

Notably, the shellcode extracts code that executes a decryption routine on a system's GPU by making use of the OpenCL library. The end goal is to install CoffeeLoader, establish persistence, and execute it by injecting it into a newly created "dllhost.exe" process.

The latest version of the packer continues to use the GPU, but replaces OpenCL with the OpenGL library. In addition, the new version of the packer delivers intermediate shellcode instead of a DLL. This shellcode serves as a downloader responsible for fetching the main CoffeeLoader malware.

"To establish persistence, the Trojan copies '7z.dll' to subfolders of %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%," Kaspersky said. "The Run registry key is used for autorun. The subfolder, library, and registry value are named with eight hexadecimal digits generated from system volume information."

"To protect itself, the downloader creates a registry key that prevents the user from disabling autorun through Task Manager."

Once persistence is successful, the malware launches one of the legitimate processes (e.g., "dllhost.exe," "WerFault.exe," "svchost.exe," "OpenWith.exe," or "AtBroker.exe") and then injects itself into it, after which the malware shellcode is downloaded from a hard-coded command-and-control (C2) server.

The shellcode then decrypts and runs the CoffeeLoader payload. It supports the same three commands to run the next-stage malware from the C2 server -

Injecting it into a process

Saving it to disk as an executable and then running it

Saving it as a DLL and then running it via "rundll32.exe"

As for how CoffeeLoader is distributed, it takes place via Retadup, a Windows computer worm that was disrupted by French law enforcement authorities in August 2019. The malware, which spreads via infected USB drives, has been used to drop additional payloads like cryptocurrency miners, the Stop ransomware, and the Arkei password stealer.

"Two years ago, someone began re-registering the domain names that Retadup had used as C2 servers and using them to issue commands to download third-party malware," Kaspersky said. "At first, this was the SmokeLoader downloader packed using the 32-bit version of Armoury, but in early 2025, the same servers started serving CoffeeLoader."

It remains unclear whether the worm's author or some other threat actor was instrumental in bringing the C2 servers back online. Kaspersky said it blocked around 15,000 systems from being infected with the resurrected version of the worm, most of them located in Peru, Angola, Russia, and Bolivia.

Title: Alibaba touts 62% lower task costs with Qwen4-Max, adds cyber safeguards
Context: “For cybersecurity, we filter data according to the specific purpose of each task, retaining data for defensive tasks such as vulnerability verification, detection, and...
Full Text:
Alibaba has released Qwen4-Max, a 2.4-trillion-parameter flagship model, claiming it reduces the average cost of completing professional tasks by 62% compared with its predecessor while introducing additional safeguards against offensive cybersecurity capabilities and other high-risk uses.

“According to Work360 — a proprietary benchmark evaluating performance on challenging industry tasks across 721 specialized fields — Qwen4-Max outperforms its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, overall while using 35% fewer tokens at High effort reasoning mode and reducing the average cost per task by around 60%,” Alibaba said in a blog post.

The Qwen team’s announcement puts the average task cost at $1.67 for Qwen4-Max, compared with $4.43 for Qwen3.8-Max, representing a 62% reduction.

The model keeps the 2.4-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts backbone of its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, but activates about 71 billion parameters per token instead of about 95 billion, the company said. It supports a 1-million-token context window.

The company attributed the savings to lower token use and new list prices of $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens, down from $2 and $6. Anthropic lists Claude Opus 5.5 at $20 per million output tokens.

Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said enterprises should treat the figure as a vendor benchmark rather than an assured reduction in their own AI spending. The relevant measure, he said, is the cost of an accepted result, including retries, reasoning tokens, and employee time spent checking outputs.

“Alibaba has published the mileage it got on its own road, and a buyer’s bill depends on the road the buyer drives,” Gogia said.

Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of Security Brigade, said enterprises should measure successful task completion rather than token prices alone.

“An enterprise should benchmark what it costs to complete 1,000 real business tasks successfully, not what it costs to generate a million tokens,” Kadakia said.

Alibaba also cited improvements across coding and agentic evaluations, including Code Arena and Agents’ Last Exam. In an automotive manufacturing demonstration, the company said Qwen4-Max reduced manual workpiece programming time from approximately 475 minutes to 24 minutes.

Security claims need independent testing

Alongside the cost figures, Alibaba set out changes to what the model learns about hacking at the training-data stage.

“For cybersecurity, we filter data according to the specific purpose of each task, retaining data for defensive tasks such as vulnerability verification, detection, and remediation, while removing data for offensive tasks aimed at enhancing attack capabilities,” the Alibaba blog post said.

The company said code security checks added during training lifted the share of functions passing both functionality and security tests on Last Secure Code Bench from 22% to 31.8%. Its internal security experts found the model’s defensive capabilities had “improved substantially,” the post added.

Kadakia questioned whether offensive and defensive cybersecurity knowledge can be reliably separated through training-data filtering.

“One of the fundamental challenges with cybersecurity AI is that offensive and defensive knowledge are largely the same knowledge,” he said, noting that understanding SQL injection is necessary both to exploit and prevent it.

Gogia said the distinction requires independent validation, recommending that CISOs seek assessments from government evaluators or established external red teams rather than rely solely on Alibaba’s internal testing.

The announcement follows an October investigation by Canadian AI company Cohere, which reported that an earlier Alibaba model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, attempted to send a test file to an Alibaba Cloud storage destination in Beijing during a security test. Cohere said its sandbox blocked the request.

A subsequent investigation by Check Point replayed the behaviour 64 times and found 52 different destination hosts. It suggested unpredictable model behaviour was a more likely explanation than a deliberately configured backdoor.

The incident involved an experimental model, not Qwen4-Max.

Besides, Government evaluators have begun testing Chinese models independently. In July, the US Center for AI Standards and Innovation found that the safeguards on Z.ai’s GLM-5.2 allowed assistance with agentic cyber exploit development. Gogia said CISOs should treat Alibaba’s filter “as a promise until a government evaluator or an established outside red team has tested it.”

Data governance and open-weight risks

For enterprises outside China, Gogia said the geographic scope of Alibaba’s global service, prompt-retention policies, and jurisdiction governing stored data should be considered before deploying the model for sensitive workloads. He pointed to prompt retention of up to 30 days and longer retention of flagged content, including under zero-retention arrangements.

Kadakia said enterprises should examine where prompts, retrieved documents, tool outputs, and logs are processed, who can access them, and what permissions agents have across internal systems.

“The biggest risk with enterprise AI is no longer simply what information employees type into a chatbot. It is what an autonomous agent can access, what decisions it can make, and what actions it can execute across connected enterprise systems,” he said.

Alibaba also plans to release smaller Qwen4 models with open weights. Kadakia said developers modifying those models through fine-tuning should not assume the original security safeguards will remain intact.

“Safety training is not a permanent property of a model,” he said, recommending fresh adversarial testing and controls over tool access for customised versions. Gogia similarly recommended reassessing each modified model rather than automatically inheriting the original model’s security assurances.

The article originally appeared on InfoWorld.

Title: How to prepare your data for your death (Lock and Code S07E23)
Context: Protect yourself from online attacks that threaten your identity, your files, your system, and your financial well-being with our exclusive offer for Malwarebytes Premium for...
Full Text:
Your family will one day want your photos. They may not be able to get them.

For a considerable portion of our shared history, whenever people have died, they have left behind physical remains. There are the photo albums, and jewelry, and clothes, even cars. And as surviving loved ones were forced to puzzle out who keeps what, much of the work—at the very least—was tangible.

Death today is different. It’s digital. Photo “albums” are increasingly stored on smartphones and handwritten letters have become a series of texts (never mind the loss of cursive), while social media posts, streaming playlists, and shared online documents have developed a sometimes-equal feeling of sentimentality.

But digital remains can be thorny to preserve. For starters, they’re often managed by companies, not by people. Further, there’s a whole lot more digital remains than most people can organize.

In fact, according to Jed Brubaker, founder of the Digital Legacy Clinic at the University of Colorado Boulder, the average American internet user has 190 online accounts to their name. And preserving what’s in those accounts, Brubaker said, is deeply important not only to loved ones, but to the preservation and continuation of the human species.

“What’s at stake is nothing short of our personal, family, and cultural heritages. All of the things that we use, whether it’s us as individuals to reflect on who we are and our parents, whether it’s that aunt we all have who’s the family genealogist, or whether it’s cultural historians, they have relied on materials that are now increasingly digital. And when everything’s wrapped up into these digital vaults, we are at real risk of that being lost.”

This enormous task, which has very personal demands, is actually within reach.

Earlier this year, Lock and Code looked at what happens to a person’s data after they die, including what rights they have to, say, not be used for training by an AI chatbot. But knowing what happens after your death is hardly useful information if you don’t know how to prepare before.

Today, on the Lock and Code podcast with host David Ruiz, we speak with Brubaker about what can be done beforehand: the actual work of preserving digital remains, what the biggest platforms have built for death, and the one step that matters more than any account setting.

“The most important thing I would encourage them to do is actually not a technical thing. It’s an interpersonal thing, and it’s to tell your loved ones what you want. And you know what? If you don’t know what you want, or if you don’t care, tell them that too.”

Title: Google Project Zero to Cut Disclosure Deadline to 30 Days by 2028
Context: It also argued that severity should not set disclosure timing: "A vulnerability's severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its...
Full Text:
Google's Project Zero has scrapped its "90 + 30" disclosure policy and will publish vulnerability details 90 days after reporting them, whether or not a fix exists, before cutting the disclosure deadline to 60 days and then 30 days.

Project Zero outlined the changes in a November 13 post and tied the changes to AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

Project Zero said, "We are finding several vulnerabilities a week in targets where we once found a few vulnerabilities a year."

Project Zero Replaces 90 Plus 30 Policy

Under the new policy, dubbed Full X, Project Zero will disclose vulnerabilities X days after reporting them to vendors. The policy begins as Full 90, moves to Full 60 on February 2, 2027 and reaches Full 30 on January 3, 2028.

The 30-day 'soak time', the grace period and the variant policy have been removed. Three exceptions remain: vulnerabilities actively exploited in the wild, bugs whose details have already been made public and cases where vendors ask Project Zero to publish the details.

Project Zero said 'soak time' was no longer meaningful because attackers can almost immediately work out bug details from a patch.

Vendors consulted by Project Zero warned that an immediate change could expose unfixed bugs, push them to fix Project Zero's reports ahead of more severe ones or lead some to stop trying.

Defenders Pressed to Close the Patch Gap

Ivan Milenkovic, VP of risk technology at Qualys, told Infosecurity that Project Zero had "removed the snooze button on responding to issues." Pointing to Project Zero's finding rate, he said: "This describes an arrival rate that most patch programmes were never built for."

For organizations, he said, patching monthly now means you're slower than disclosure. He called the vendors' objection to an immediate change to the disclosure policy "a fair response, but the alternative was letting attackers set the deadline."

Read more on vulnerability disclosure: N-able Rushes Out N-central Fixes After 33 Zero-Days Go Public

Project Zero said its new policy was intended to encourage vendors to reduce the patch gap, the period between a fix becoming available and users installing it.

It also argued that severity should not set disclosure timing: "A vulnerability's severity does not affect the likelihood that it will be discovered by attackers, only its impact on users."

The group said it would still track whether bugs were fixed, but that fix status would no longer decide when technical details were published.

The FBI has warned of a growing number of malicious cyber intrusion campaigns leveraging the open-source, AI-powered penetration testing tool ARTEX.

In a FBI Flash notice, published on November 13, the Bureau said a variety of malicious cyber actors have used ARTEX to conduct campaigns targeting organizations globally since at least August 2026.

Targets range across multiple sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications and legal industries.

Recent incidents have included financially motivated attacks against South Korean financial institutions which resulted in the exfiltration of personal information from approximately 67,000 individuals and a supply chain compromise affecting ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers that enabled access to more than 2250 downstream tenants.

The FBI noted that ARTEX significantly reduces the time required to chain attack techniques and some intrusions have progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours.

Read more about ARTEX: India Warns of New AI-Driven Cyber-Attacks Targeting Financial and Crypto Businesses

ARTEX Origins and LLM Integration

ARTEX is an open-source, AI model-driven, autonomous penetration testing framework released on GitHub by a user known as ‘Autumn-27’ in July 2026.

Written in Go with an embedded Next.js web console, ARTEX offers an offensive command-and-control (C2) platform that communicates with several AI agents and can be plugged in to large language models (LLMs).

The FBI highlighted that ARTEX does not include its own AI model, rather it integrates with external LLM providers, including frontier models (Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT) and open-source or Chinese-origin models (DeepSeek, GLM, Grok, Kimi).

“Analysis of attacker-controlled ARTEX instances shows Chinese models are most prevalent, with DeepSeek Flash family models dominating usage due to their balance of capabilities, relatively low cost and lack of observable guardrails when framed for penetration testing,” the FBI notice read.

The original GitHub repository for ARTEX was taken down by its creator in October 2026 due to widespread threat actor abuse. The author claimed they were not involved in the ARTEX-linked attacks and that the tool was only meant for authorized penetration testing.

Nevertheless, the framework continues to proliferate globally via community forks, including localized variations such as ScopeWeaver and a commercial version dubbed ARTEX PRO.

Key Risks: Automation, Overlooked Systems and Supply Chain Attacks

The FBI assessed that ARTEX poses several risks as threat actors adopt it.

It automates the time-consuming enumeration and exploitation phases of intrusions, allowing even small groups to run multiple campaigns at once.

It also lowers the technical barrier to entry, enabling actors with minimal expertise to carry out sophisticated attacks.

ARTEX is particularly effective at finding and exploiting overlooked systems that receive less security attention than flagship applications, such as partner and supplier portals, mobile backends, employee and sales-support tools, legacy services and third-party integrations.

It has also demonstrated supply chain capabilities, including modifying iOS application distribution infrastructure through exposed cloud credentials. By mapping trust relationships between organizations, it can compromise weaker vendors or CI/CD pipelines and pivot into high-value enterprise networks.

Although ARTEX generates noisy traffic that may trigger alerts, its speed leaves defenders little time to coordinate a response before attackers achieve their objectives.

The FBI provided a list of recommended security controls and operational measures organizations can take to prevent and mitigate ARTEX.

The Bureau is also seeking any helpful information on ARTEX and malicious campaigns using the tool, including infrastructure artifacts, authentication and access logs, application and API activity, LLM and AI infrastructure indicators, cloud and container activity and exploitation and persistence artifacts.

Title: Information Commissioner’s Office Receives 300+ Reports of Medical Snooping
Context: In May, 11 staff were sacked and 14 given written warnings after unlawfully accessing the records of victims of the 2023 Nottingham knife attacks
Full Text:
The UK’s data protection watchdog has written to health service leaders after receiving hundreds of reports of staff illegally accessing patient records.

The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) said it has asked over 200 NHS bosses across the UK to provide personal assurances that measures are in place to prevent and detect unauthorized insider access.

The letter itself details four areas that healthcare organizations must focus on: effective access controls, effective auditing and monitoring for unauthorized access, regular training for staff and consistent action when things go wrong.

“You should investigate suspected unauthorized access promptly and consistently. You should consider the impact on the person affected, including your obligations to notify the individual,” it said. “You should also consider your obligations to notify the ICO. Where you establish wrongdoing, you should take appropriate disciplinary, professional, regulatory or other action.”

The ICO said it has already received over 300 reports of unauthorized access by NHS staff, including workers looking at records with no legitimate need, and viewing or sharing the records of people they know.

Read more on NHS data leaks: ICO Cautions Healthcare Worker After Princess of Wales Incident

The letter comes on the back of several high-profile incidents impacting the health service.

In May, 11 staff were sacked and 14 given written warnings after unlawfully accessing the records of victims of the 2023 Nottingham knife attacks. A month later a Cambridgeshire hospital launched an investigation after around 40 staff accessed the records of a seriously injured child without good reason.

In June the ICO issued a former healthcare worker a formal caution after they tried to access and sell the medical records of the Princess of Wales at a private hospital.

What the ICO Wants to Know

ICO chief executive, Paul Arnold, sent out practical advice and recommendations to healthcare organizations back in June.

In his new letter, he said that NHS chief executives need the right processes, culture and behaviors in place to safeguard patient data.

“Accessing someone's health records without a legitimate reason isn't harmless curiosity. It can cause enormous distress to patients and jeopardise the vital trust people place in our health service,” Arnold added.

“This message goes beyond the health sector: any organization entrusted with people's most sensitive information has a duty to protect it and we will take action if they fall short. I strongly encourage leaders in every sector to ask themselves whether their safeguards would stand up to the same scrutiny.”

The ICO is now asking NHS CEOs to confirm that their organization is:

Actively and continuously managing access to patient records

Spotting suspicious access using effective monitoring and audit systems

Confident that every member of staff knows what is expected of them what the consequences are of illegally accessing medical records

Investigating suspected unauthorized access promptly and taking appropriate action if wrongdoing is established

“Senior leaders should confirm that they have reviewed their organization’s approach in these areas within the past six months,” the ICO said. “Those who have not are expected to complete a review within the next three months. The responses will help shape the regulator’s next steps to respond to this issue and help protect patient’s privacy.”

Title: SANSAR Linux Cryptomining Malware Uses Modified NVIDIA Library to Hide GPU Activity
Context: " In the attack chain documented by the company, initial access is said to have been achieved via an exposed Ray job agent, allowing the threat actor to execute commands
Full Text:
A financially motivated threat activity cluster tracked as REF3364 has been attributed to a Linux-focused cryptocurrency mining operation that tampers with the readings used to detect high GPU workloads.

Central to the intrusion is a toolkit called SANSAR, a Rust-based orchestrator that receives commands over the TOR anonymity network to manage CPU and GPU miners. The activity was observed in late October 2026.

"The threat actor also deployed a kernel rootkit to hide selected processes and files, an NVIDIA Management Library (NVML) wrapper to falsify GPU readings, and a separate backdoor named netns," Elastic Security Labs said in a report published last week.

"This backdoor retrieves its C2 [command-and-control] address from an Ethereum smart contract before connecting to the server directly."

In the attack chain documented by the company, initial access is said to have been achieved via an exposed Ray job agent, allowing the threat actor to execute commands. This includes jobs running the NVIDIA System Management Interface (nvidia-smi) to capture and exfiltrate the GPU inventory to an external server.

Subsequently, the attacker submitted a Python reverse shell job that connected to a remote listener, after which an SSH key was added to that account's authorized_keys file to establish persistent access.

"After obtaining root, the actor staged the toolkit under /opt/vadi_, built the acpi_thermal_mgr kernel module through Dynamic Kernel Module Support (DKMS) and added an initramfs loader," security researcher Salim Bitam said.

"An initramfs is a temporary root file system loaded into RAM during early boot, before Linux switches to its normal root filesystem. The module and loader are stored in the boot image on disk, so the rootkit can load again when the host boots with that image."

The installation also delivers a modified NVML wrapper that filters process information and changes GPU telemetry to evade detection. Specifically, the altered wrapper hooks NVML calls used by monitoring tools such as nvidia-smi to report GPU utilization as 0%. In addition, temperature and power readings are substituted with random values between 36 to 46 degree Celsius (96.8 to 114.8 degree Fahrenheit) and 100 to 200 watts.

Also delivered are the following payloads -

sansar, used for TOR C2, launching or stopping the miner, miner configuration updates, connection management, spawning interactive shells, launching an IPv4 TCP SYN traffic task against a specified address and port, and NVML-hook maintenance

kurt (XMRig version 6.25.0), the miner selected by sansar's CPU branch

tilki (SRBMiner-MULTI version 3.6.9), the miner selected by sansar's GPU branch

lyrebird, a legitimate pluggable transport proxy for TOR

acpi_thermal_mgr.ko, a Linux rootkit used for process, directory, and socket-list concealment

netns, an Ethereum-assisted backdoor

Once launched, SANSAR first performs an anti-debugging check by reading the value of TracerPid and exits if it's non-zero. TracerPid indicates the Process ID (PID) of the process currently tracing or debugging the target process.

It then reaches out to an onion service ("efxisnqldelyr5ra25oqfrsut54b34g26e7zrsiuupsoekjof2gho2id[.]onion") for C2 communication via Arti, receiving commands, collecting host and GPU information, and fetching the miner status. The main responsibility of SANSAR is to supervise the mining process and launch the appropriate miner executable based on the miner type (i.e., CPU or GPU) specified in the C2 response message.

The "acpi_thermal_mgr.ko" kernel rootkit, on the other hand, uses Function Tracer (ftrace) to conceal cryptomining activity on Linux systems by hiding processes, files, and socket entries.

It achieves this by intercepting system calls to directory listings, file access, and process termination signals, removing matching records or blocking requests for those hidden processes and files by returning the message "No such file or directory" or "No such process."

The other main component of the operation is the netns backdoor that's registered as a systemd service. It's used to retrieve a controller IPv4 address by sending requests to an embedded contract (0x43eb291f56688c63c93e8a93c4591fc997cf6349) and then sets up a plain TCP connection to that address on port 8080 to open a reverse-shell connection to the specified host and port in the C2 response.

It's not clear who is behind the operation, but Elastic said it found Turkish language comments in the rootkit's source code.

"Organizations expanding GPU infrastructure for AI and LLM workloads should check who can submit jobs and whether GPU monitoring libraries have been modified, as cryptojacking can divert compute capacity from legitimate workloads and increase operating costs," Elastic said.
