Title: Git security vulnerabilities announced
Context: Get an updated version of Git > The post Git security vulnerabilities announced appeared first on The GitHub Blog
Full Text:
Today, the Git project is releasing new versions to address six security vulnerabilities. These include arbitrary code execution when recursively cloning a malicious repository, writes to unintended files, and memory corruption when processing merges or binary patches.

The fixes are included in Git 2.56.1, with backports to Git 2.55.1, 2.54.1, 2.53.1, 2.52.1, 2.51.3, and 2.50.2. We recommend updating to Git 2.56.1 or the patched release for your maintenance series, and updating any applications that bundle Git.

Vulnerabilities in Git

CVE-2026-111760: Code execution during recursive clones

Git checks paths before writing files into a working tree, including rejecting paths that would overwrite its own repository metadata. However, an integer truncation in Git’s index handling can cause an extremely long path to pass validation under one name and then be written using a shorter name.

An attacker can use this discrepancy to replace a submodule’s .git file with a symbolic link pointing to a directory containing malicious configuration or hooks. When Git subsequently uses that directory, it can execute attacker-controlled code during a recursive clone.

The fix rejects extremely long index entry paths before their lengths can be truncated.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-113408: Path traversal through a server’s advertised HEAD

When cloning an empty repository using Git protocol v2, the server can advertise a HEAD symref pointing to an unborn branch (one that has no commits yet). Git did not validate the symref’s target before storing it locally.

A malicious server can supply a name containing path-traversal components. With the files reference backend, a later operation that updates the branch can write outside the intended reference directory.

Git now validates the advertised target before accepting it. The release also validates other reference names and symbolic-reference targets received through protocol v2.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114467: Stack corruption when removing signatures

When stripping GPG signatures from a message, Git assumed there would be at most two signatures. A specially crafted message containing more than two signatures can cause Git to write past the end of a fixed-size stack array.

This can be triggered by merging a tag containing more than two signatures, causing memory corruption and a potential denial of service. Hosting services that perform these merges on behalf of users can also be affected.

The fix removes the fixed-size array and handles messages with any number of signatures.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114469: Out-of-bounds reads when applying binary patches

Git rejects patches larger than approximately 1 GiB because its patch application code cannot safely handle larger inputs. However, this check only considered the size of the patch as supplied.

Binary patches are compressed and encoded, so a relatively small patch can expand beyond that limit. A crafted patch can bypass the input-size check and cause an out-of-bounds read, crashing Git.

Git now also checks the declared uncompressed size before processing a binary patch.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-105437: Heap corruption during large merges

Git’s merge machinery calculates how much memory it needs for a merge result before writing the output. That calculation can overflow when the result is very large, including when many conflicts are combined with a large conflict-marker-size attribute.

The overflow can cause Git to allocate a buffer that is too small, then write outside it, corrupting heap memory. This affects applications and hosting services that use Git to merge untrusted content, as well as local merges.

The fix uses size-appropriate types and checked arithmetic, rejecting merges whose output size cannot be represented safely.

[Advisory]

CVE-2026-114466: Filesystem access through fast-import streams

git fast-import reads a stream of commands to build a repository. Some commands can access files outside the repository, so Git already restricts them when they appear in an untrusted input stream.

Three additional features lacked that protection. The rewrite-submodules-from and rewrite-submodules-to features can read arbitrary files, potentially exposing their contents through error messages. The export-pack-edges option can create files or append data to existing files.

These features are now rejected when supplied through the input stream unless the caller explicitly enables --allow-unsafe-features. Only enable that option when you trust the program generating the stream.

[Advisory]

Additional hardening

Alongside these fixes, the release adds overflow checks to related index entry allocations during checkout and tree processing. These checks complement the path-length limits above, preventing allocation sizes from being truncated or overflowing before Git copies a path into memory.

Protecting GitHub users

We have deployed fixes for these vulnerabilities across github.com, GitHub Enterprise Cloud, and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency.

Updates for GitHub Enterprise Server are available in versions 3.19.15, 3.20.11, 3.21.9, and 3.22.4. We recommend that administrators upgrade as soon as possible.

We are coordinating releases of GitHub Desktop and the GitHub Copilot app that include patched versions of Git.

GitHub Codespaces and GitHub Actions will also receive patched versions of Git.

Update Git

Updating is the most effective way to protect against these vulnerabilities. Install a patched version from your operating system or Git distributor, and update applications that include their own copy of Git. Administrators should also update Git installations used by automation and services that process repositories on behalf of users.

If you cannot update immediately, clone only from trusted servers and avoid recursive clones of untrusted repositories. Avoid merging untrusted content or tags, or processing binary patches or fast-import streams from untrusted sources. These precautions do not replace installing the fixes.

Title: CISA Expands Incident Reporting Form While CIRCIA Mandate Waits
Context: More Granular Questions Add ATT&CK Terms The revised form asks whether an incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat
Full Text:
The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has rolled out a revamped cyber incident reporting form that asks more granular questions about incident types and frames observed activity in MITRE ATT&CK terms.

CISA outlined the changes in an announcement published November 9 and the updated web-based questionnaire is available through its Incident Reporting Portal.

The agency said better data quality will help it connect related threat activity into broader trends that would otherwise look like separate incidents. The update draws on community feedback CISA has received over the years.

More Granular Questions Add ATT&CK Terms

The revised form asks whether an incident involved malware, social engineering, hacking techniques or an insider threat. Questions about observed activity now use MITRE ATT&CK, a framework for describing adversary behavior that CISA said is familiar to the cyber community.

The changes are meant to support rapid but thorough threat analysis, according to CISA.

"In the team sport of cybersecurity, one organization's detection is another's protection," said Chris Butera, CISA's acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity. "As the national coordinator for critical infrastructure cybersecurity and resilience, CISA is able to leverage such incident reporting to identify emerging cyber campaigns, warn potential targets, and strengthen the Nation's collective defense."

For now, only federal civilian agencies are required to report incidents to CISA. The agency encouraged other organizations that experience an incident to report voluntarily, and information they submit can be protected from disclosure under the Protected Critical Infrastructure Information (PCII) Program.

CIRCIA Rule Remains at White House

The update comes as the final rule implementing the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) awaits approval. The rule went to the White House for review on October 1 and remains listed as pending.

Read more on CIRCIA: US Critical Infrastructure Braces for Sweeping New Cyber Reporting Rules

Once the rule takes effect, covered critical infrastructure organizations would have to report qualifying cyber incidents within 72 hours of reasonably believing they occurred and ransom payments within 24 hours of making them, according to CISA.

CISA published its proposed CIRCIA rule in April 2024 but missed an October 2025 statutory deadline to finalize it. Many comments on the proposal asked for a narrower scope, less burden and closer alignment with other federal reporting rules, according to CISA's regulatory agenda.

CISA's announcement did not mention CIRCIA or whether the enhanced reporting form would be used under the pending rule.

Title: Iranian hackers turned up the heat on French supermarket freezers, says France
Context: Iran has been officially accused by France of being responsible for cyber attacks last month that meddled with supermarket freezers, causing some to catch fire
Full Text:
Iran has been officially accused by France of being responsible for cyber attacks last month that meddled with supermarket freezers, causing some to catch fire.

According to French authorities, a hacking unit from Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) sabotaged food refrigeration systems at approximately 700 retail sites, sparking at least 15 fires and causing tens of millions of euros worth of damage.

On the night of 11 October, the hackers seized remote control of refrigeration controllers and changed their defrost settings to high temperatures. As a report published by the French government’s computer emergency response team (CERT-FR) describes, victims of the attack included Casino, Leclerc, Coopérative U, Metro, Carrefour and Intermarché, as well as butchers, a slaughterhouse, and food-processing plants.

According to French media reports, the targeted refrigeration controllers were made by Danish firm Danfoss, and the attackers targeted older versions of its software.

The finger of blame has been pointed by French authorities in the direction of Shahid Kaveh, a hacking unit within the IRGC. Evidence which is said to have led them to that conclusion includes that the same infrastructure was used, during the same period, to scan Schneider Electric equipment at energy and water facilities. and traces of Farsi. Perhaps the most telling clue of all, however, was that the attack was being trumpeted by a propaganda outlet linked to the hacking unit barely a day later.

Shahid Kaveh is said to hide behind a variety of different "hacktivist" guises including CyberAv3ngers, Soldiers of Solomon, and Cyber Isnaad Front.

The official French report names three men: Hamid Reza Lashgarian, head of the IRGC's Electronic and Cyber Center, and Shahid Kaveh commanders Mahdi Lashgarian and Reza Salarvand.

The same hackers are also believed to have targeted small hydroelectric facilities, while a second Iranian unit called Shahid Shoostari (also known as Emennet Pasargad), is held responsible for attacks on Charlie Hebdo and an attempt to hijack display screens during the 2024 Paris Olympics.

In early November there was a second wave of attacks on refrigeration units which hit businesses across Europe, including three French blood service sites. These attacks have not yet been officially attributed to Iran.

Regardless of who is behind the attacks, it is clearly important that any organisation properly defends its refrigeration systems to prevent tampering. As such, it remains good advice to ensure that operational technology (OT) interfaces are not exposed to the internet, that controller software is kept up to date, that default passwords are changed, and that OT networks are segmented and monitored for unexpected changes.

With fridge attacks like this continuing to create disruption and cost millions of euros, we can expect relations between Paris and Tehran to remain frosty for some time.

Title: Chat Feels Safer Than Email. Attackers Are Counting on It.
Context: KnowBe4 Threat Labs turns real-world attack telemetry and more than 15 years of data into live detection models across the Email & Collaboration Security suite, so defenses...
Full Text:
Lead Analysts: Prabhakaran R and Jeewan Singh Jalal

You think twice before clicking a link in an unexpected email. Do you do the same for a message in Microsoft Teams?

A new message arrives in your Teams chat with the familiar notification sound, a participant’s name, and a link. It feels like a colleague, not a stranger. That feeling is the opening attackers look for.

Two things decide whether that message does harm. Can the channel stop it before it reaches your user? And if it gets through, does the user recognize the lure and know what to do? Both matter, and this post covers both.

Modern business depends on external collaboration across sales, finance, and IT. External access and guest participation are standard Teams features, not security oversights, and external access is open to all domains by default. Teams is also no longer where only people talk to people. A message could come from a colleague, an authorized AI agent/chabot, or an attacker, and most people have little to tell them apart.

Attackers exploit this openness by sending external messages that follow the same social engineering patterns as phishing emails and blend into your users' daily routine. They could also aim a message at an agent instead of a person. The question is no longer only whether a phishing message looks real. It is who and what you can trust at work.

KnowBe4 Threat Labs has consistently observed attackers imitating routine messages such as support requests, invoices, and meeting chat posts. Weekly detections grew from five in the week of June 22 to a peak of 301 in the week of September 28 (Figure 1). This post covers what we observed, what the attackers are after, and how the attacks play out.

What makes these messages effective is that a phishing message in chat looks like a routine work message: a link, a support request, a payment follow-up. People may not expect an attack on this channel, so they may take such messages at face value. The words alone rarely settle it. The better question is who is sending, from where and why.

Key Findings

Attackers follow work into Microsoft Teams. Chat and meetings now carry the lures that email has carried for years. Wherever your team works, attackers follow. A small request in chat is usually the first step toward a larger goal, such as device access, stolen money, or leverage for extortion.

Business needs keep the door open. Teams have to stay open to customers, vendors and partners, so blocking outsiders is neither practical nor enough. Attackers blend into that traffic, so judging the words alone is not reliable. Ask who is sending, from where, and why.

Teams have safeguards, but they depend on the user. Teams shows an external label and an Accept/Block prompt at first contact, and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 adds Safe Links and zero-hour auto purge where it is licensed. Attackers succeed when a user clicks through those warnings. Email has sender authentication, link analysis, and gateways. Conversations inside Teams sit outside the reach of third-party email gateways, and Teams chat gives fewer sender checks: display names are easy to choose, links can be disguised, and previews can mislead.

Defense has to cover the conversation and the click. Use both Microsoft's own settings and third-party protection as your technical controls. Train your users on this threat vector, so people know what a lure in Teams looks like and how to report it. Be ready to respond fast when a user acts on a message.

Why Are Attackers Moving Into Microsoft Teams?

Chat and meetings now carry the lures that email carried for years, and the following factors make Teams an attractive place for them.

Outside contact is normal. Your teams have to talk to customers, vendors, and partners, so external messages and guests are expected. A harmful message blends in with the many legitimate ones.

Impersonation is easy. Email has checks that block direct domain spoofing. Chat gives fewer sender-checking signals, and a sender can often choose the name users see.

Awareness is lower. Phishing awareness training has traditionally focused on email, so users may look harder at an unexpected email than at a chat message.

Email security doesn’t automatically cover Teams. Many security vendors now extend protection to collaboration tools. An organization that has not extended its controls to Teams leaves that channel uncovered.

One target list covers two channels. An attacker who already has a list of email addresses can reach the same people in Teams, where external access allows it, with little added effort. That gives them two channels to attack instead of one.

How Does an Attack in Teams Unfold?

Most attacks in a collaboration tool follow the same path, whatever the lure.

1. The attacker poses as a trusted contact. Display names are easy to choose, so the sender can appear as IT support, a vendor, or a colleague. A request from an individual account may show only the name the sender chose and an “External” label.

2. The attacker sends a lure. Default or permissive external-access settings let the message in, such as open external access, personal accounts that can start chats, or trial-only tenants that an admin has chosen to allow. The app, the notification and the chat context all look familiar, and the attacker can build the conversation slowly, so the request feels like a natural next step.

3. The user acts on the request. One step is enough: a click, a session started or a reply, because the request looks like routine work. Attackers may also call the user in Teams to talk them through the steps.

4. The user lands on a fake page or receives a payload. The user leaves Teams for the attacker’s web page, or a payload is delivered. A link can display one address and open another, and senders can edit a message after sending it, so what the user sees later may differ from the original.

5. The user hands over credentials, grants access, or pays. The fake page, tool, or payment request asks for one more action, and the user completes it.

6. The attacker gains access. The attacker now holds credentials, system access or the requested payment.

The attacker can then send the next lure through the compromised account, and the cycle repeats.

What Do Attackers Send in Teams, and What Do They Want?

The message types below are cases we observed. For each one, we describe what the attacker likely wants and where the activity can lead. The messages look different, but they serve a similar set of goals.

The “IT Support” Message

Why it works: Help desk requests feel routine, and people want their problem fixed. The user opens the session themselves, so the attacker gets access with the user’s approval.

What the attacker wants and where it leads: The likely goal is full control of the endpoint. Standard defenses often miss this because remote administration tools are legitimate software. With that access, an attacker can take saved passwords, active session cookies, and sensitive documents. This allows them to reach corporate email, Teams, and wider enterprise systems. It also gives them a foothold for lateral movement across internal networks and for deploying further remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools or ransomware.

2. The Urgent Invoice

Why it works: Payment requests with a deadline push people to act before they check, and a personal greeting makes the request feel real.

What the attacker wants and where it leads: The likely goal is money, stolen credentials, malware deployment, or all three. Depending on what the target does, that can mean payments sent to an attacker-controlled account, malware that steals credentials or sets up remote access, and the compromised account being used to send similar requests to colleagues or vendors.

3. The Ransom Note in Chat

Why it works: The message reaches the user directly, with no email gateway in its path.

What the attacker wants and where it leads: The likely goal is payment or an immediate response. The first message alone rarely shows whether the claim is real: it could follow a genuine compromise, or it could be a bluff meant to exploit fear and force a quick reply. Responding under pressure risks paying a ransom for nothing, overlooking an active breach if the claim is true, or causing internal panic when nothing was compromised.

What Should Defenders Do?

Protect messages and meetings, and be ready to respond fast when a user acts on a message. Start with your people, then your Teams settings.

How can users stop these messages?

1. Treat chat like email. Teach users to question links and requests in Teams, including in meeting chats.

2. Teach the “External” label. Ask users to check it before acting on a message that claims to come from support or leadership. For individual Microsoft accounts it can be one of the few cues available.

3. Preview before accepting. Teach users to read an external message request first and to decline it if it is unexpected, even when curiosity says otherwise.

4. Check the real link. Ask users to hover over a link and read the address before clicking, because the text shown can differ from the destination.

5. Never start a remote session someone sends you. Route support requests through the help desk.

6. Verify payment changes through a second channel. Confirm new payment details by phone with a known contact before paying.

7. Treat a ransom message as an incident. Report it to your security team and do not reply.

8. Stop sharing passwords in chat. Use a password manager or a one-time secret tool.

What if a user already acted?

Plan for the click. Reset the user’s password, revoke their active sessions, check for remote-access tools they installed, and review any payment they made.

How do you narrow the door in Teams?

Attackers can only message your users if your Teams settings allow it. You control those settings, and they are worth a review. Microsoft documents each one in its Teams external access guidance . Your business needs some outside contact, so the goal is not to block everyone. The goal is to allow the contact you need and nothing more. Start by reviewing which external tenants can message your users and who can join your meeting chats.

Settings to review

-AllowFederatedUsers: turns external communication with other organizations on or off.

-AllowedDomains and -BlockedDomains: limit access to trusted partners or block malicious domains.

-AllowTeamsConsumer and -AllowTeamsConsumerInbound: manage chat with unmanaged accounts and block uninvited outreach.

-AllowPublicUsers: controls chat with Skype users.

1. Allow only essential partner domains. Prefer allow-lists to block-lists, because block-lists only stop known threats. Blocking a main domain still leaves its subdomains open. To block all subdomains, run:

Set-CsTenantFederationConfiguration -BlockAllSubdomains $True

2. Block trial-only tenants. Unlicensed trial tenants are easy tools for attackers. Microsoft blocks them by default, but verify that your setting is still “Blocked”:

Set-CsTenantFederationConfiguration -ExternalAccessWithTrialTenants "Blocked"

When the setting is “Blocked,” users from trial-only tenants cannot search for, chat with, call or meet with your team, and they are removed from existing chats. Setting it to “Allowed” turns these safeguards off.

3. Restrict personal accounts. Personal Microsoft accounts are harder to verify: the sender chooses the display name, and no organization vouches for the account. Disable: AllowTeamsConsumerInbound to stop inbound chats from them, and evaluate AllowTeamsConsumer and -AllowPublicUsers against your needs.

4. Block malicious senders. You can block a harmful sender individually without changing global policy:

In the Teams admin center, go to Users > External access.

Turn on “Block specific users from communicating with people in my organization.”

Select “Block a user”, enter the person’s email address or messaging resource identifier (MRI), and select Apply.

The list holds a maximum of 200 users. You can also manage it with Set-CsTeamsExternalAccessConfiguration.

Where Can KnowBe4 Help?

Its behavioral AI protects the conversation and coaches your workforce wherever work happens.

According to KnowBe4 internal data, 97% of users stop before proceeding with a high-risk action when a teachable moment appears.

Title: Russia-Linked Turla Hijacks Exchange Servers to Spy on NATO and EU Emails
Context: "On a compromised Exchange server, the most interesting activity is not always the message that arrives in a user's inbox," wrote Matias Porolli, the ESET researcher who...
Full Text:
Russia-linked threat group Turla has deployed a new toolset called Cereal on compromised government Microsoft Exchange servers, in one case setting it to pick out emails sent to or from NATO and European Union addresses.

ESET has attributed Cereal with high confidence to Turla, also known as Snake and Uroburos, in research published November 10. The group has been active since at least 2004 and is widely assessed to be part of Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB).

The security company identified two national government victims, one in Kazakhstan and one in Romania. It found no external command-and-control (C2) infrastructure: each compromised Exchange server was co-opted to act as the C2 instead.

Cereal Turned Exchange Into a Collection Point

ESET wrote that the toolset was designed to take commands, run them in memory, map the compromised organization and gather selected messages through a new Exchange email collection module.

Cereal kept its payloads encrypted, received commands as separate .NET assemblies and ran the email collection module inside Exchange's own processes. According to ESET, the toolset paired techniques demanding a deep understanding of Exchange internals with unusual .NET execution methods.

"On a compromised Exchange server, the most interesting activity is not always the message that arrives in a user's inbox," wrote Matias Porolli, the ESET researcher who discovered the threat.

ESET's research does not describe how the servers were first compromised, but its white paper and GitHub repository list indicators of compromise.

Government Victims Matched Turla's Regional Focus

Cereal was set to pick out NATO and EU emails at the Romanian victim, found a month after ESET first spotted the toolset in Kazakhstan on November 28, 2025.

ESET wrote that this focus fits long-standing Russian intelligence priorities but may also relate to regional tensions, including Russian drones crashing near or inside Romania since early 2025. For Kazakhstan, it pointed to reported deportations of some Russian exiles since January 2026, suggesting operators may want visibility into Russian dissidents.

Around 70% of the countries Turla has targeted since 2022 have been former Soviet republics or European states once closely aligned with the Soviet Union, based on ESET telemetry.

Read more on Turla: Palo Alto Reveals New Features in Russian APT Turla's Kazuar Backdoor

Cereal was built for long-term, stealthy cyberespionage, ESET concluded. In its assessment, the victims' Exchange servers became collection points, internal execution hubs and cover for Turla's .NET tradecraft, with little left on disk to find.

Title: Introducing JFrog Threat Hub: Turning Vulnerability Intelligence into Blast Radius Analysis
Context: A “medium” on paper can be easy to exploit in the wild, while a “critical” threat may not be relevant to your environment
Full Text:
A new supply chain attack hits the news. A CVE with a dramatic name starts trending. A malicious package turns up in npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face. Within minutes, your Slack channels fill up, your CISO wants an update, and someone asks the question every DevSecOps professional dreads:

“How are we affected?”

Providing a definitive answer should be simple. In practice it often takes hours, and sometimes even days to get the complete picture.

The pain: awareness is easy, blast radius is hard

Security teams are not short on information. Advisories, research blogs, vendor bulletins, social media threads, and mailing lists all announce new threats faster than anyone can read them. The challenging part is leveraging that information to understand how it affects your particular environment.

Until now, that process usually looked something like this:

Separating the signal from the noise. Relevant intelligence is scattered across dozens of sources. Some of it is vetted, some of it is speculation, and some of it is a repost of a repost. Someone has to read it, judge its credibility, and decide whether it deserves attention.

Translating general threats into actionable responses. A blog post describes an attack. It doesn’t hand you a clean list of the affected packages and versions. Someone has to extract the package names, version ranges, and CVE identifiers, and hope nothing was missed.

Figuring out where affected components are hiding. Today, software applications are assembled from many open-source components. Unfortunately, the vulnerability that was just discovered is rarely a direct dependency. It’s usually buried several layers deep in a transitive dependency which is part of a Docker image, or sitting in a build from last quarter. Your artifacts are spread across multiple repositories, projects, teams, and pipelines, making it difficult to identify all the affected components across the entire software supply chain.

Stitching together a holistic view from disparate tools. One tool tracks vulnerabilities, another tracks builds, and a spreadsheet maps services to owners. Correlating these sources manually is a slow and error-prone process, especially in the middle of a high profile security incident where nobody has the time to do it.

Prioritizing remediation with imperfect data. Published severity scores don’t always match real-world exploitability. A “medium” on paper can be easy to exploit in the wild, while a “critical” threat may not be relevant to your environment. Without context analysis, teams either over-react or under-react because they lack the proper information.

All of the above happens while the clock is ticking. The window between disclosure and exploitation keeps shrinking, and every hour spent hunting for an answer is another hour attackers can use to exploit weaknesses in your application. The real cost is often not the vulnerability itself but the time it takes to figure out the most effective strategy for defending against it.

Meet JFrog Threat Hub: taking you from “what happened?” to “what’s affected?” in a single unified interface

JFrog Threat Hub is designed to close the gap. It brings both publicly published security research and JFrog’s own threat intelligence directly into the JFrog Platform, to help determine how it affects your development environment.

What is JFrog Threat Hub?

JFrog Threat Hub is a detailed threat intelligence dashboard accessed from within JFrog Xray. It includes a daily-updated feed of vetted posts about new attacks, CVEs, and malicious packages. Most of the security intelligence is based on reports from the JFrog Security Research team, which monitors public registries such as npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face, runs automated scanners on every new and updated package, and analyzes CVEs for real-world exploitability. Relevant external advisories are also included in the feed.

Each post includes the name of the source, publish date, CVSS score, and descriptive tags, along with a public label that groups the affected packages and versions. A severity mismatch indicator flags cases where JFrog’s research rates a threat differently from its published score, so teams can prioritize by actual, rather than perceived, risk.

One of the most important features is the Check Impact button. With one click, it runs an impact search across your organization and lists every affected artifact, along with its repository, vulnerable component version, scan date, and runtime status. Teams can export these results, set Xray policies, or move straight into triage and remediation all within a single unified platform.

Threat Hub includes updated CVE advisories and impact search across the entire supply chain

Instead of reading about an attack in one place and searching for exposure in another, Threat Hub brings both steps into one seamless workflow. It not only provides early awareness, but also helps map out the true blast radius, taking you directly from reading about a threat to understanding your exact exposure.

Curated intelligence, delivered where you already work

Threat Hub consolidates security posts about new attacks, CVEs, and malicious packages, updates it daily, and then sorts it according to customer preference. In addition, intelligence from the JFrog Security Research Team is integrated as well, including:

Continuous monitoring of open-source repositories such as npm, PyPI, and Hugging Face for the latest security issues

Running automated scanners across new and updated packages

Deeply investigating suspicious findings

Analyzing new and existing CVEs for real-world exploitability

Disclosing newly discovered malware to repository maintainers

For our customers, this means original, vetted research sits alongside the external advisories that matter, without the noise of an open-ended news feed. Each post shows its source, publish date, and tags such as which ecosystems are affected. When a post is tied to a known attack, it applies a label that puts together groups of affected packages and versions, and may link to a fix or advisory.

Just one click to gauge CVE impact

When working from the JFrog Xray interface, the Threat Hub dashboard can be accessed by selecting Xray > Overview. One of the most powerful features of the Threat Hub console is the “Check Impact” button. Click it, and Threat Hub opens an Impact Search specifically for your organization. If you are affected, it shows the matching artifacts and their scan dates, so you can see where the problem lives across your scanned artifacts and decide what to fix first.

For supported CVE and malicious package posts, there’s no manual extraction of package names, no custom queries, and no stitching together results from separate tools. The research and the results are presented side by side.

CVE Severity you can act on

Published scores don’t always tell the whole story, so some posts also show a Severity Mismatch Indicator when JFrog Security Research’s assessment differs from the severity of a publicly available CVE or advisory. JFrog’s research severity reflects real-world exploitability and impact, not just the published score, which gives you the context you need when prioritizing your remediation strategy.

What this changes for your team

Operations and Security teams gain these important advantages:

Faster incident scoping. The question “How are we affected?” can get an answer faster, with less cross-tool detective work.

Less context switching. Reading the research, understanding the impact, and identifying affected artifacts all happen in one centralized interface.

Improved prioritization. Vetted research and severity context from JFrog’s own researchers helps focus on the threats that are more likely to be exploitable.

More precise communications. When leadership asks for a status update, you can present them with the specific affected artifacts and scan dates instead of “we’re still looking.”

See JFrog Threat Hub in action

The next major supply chain attack is a question of when, not if. When it arrives, the teams that respond best won’t be the ones who read the most blog posts. They’ll be the ones who can understand how a specific threat affects their particular environment in the fastest way possible.

Title: Cloud Vulnerabilities Surge Fourfold in Less Than a Year
Context: ” Read more on cloud vulnerabilities: Cloud Attackers Now Prefer Vulnerability Exploits Over Credentials, Google Cloud Finds
Full Text:
The median number of high or critical vulnerabilities in cloud workloads increased fourfold between May and November this year, due to the impact of frontier AI, Datadog has claimed.

The cloud observability and security specialist revealed the findings in its State of Cloud Security 2026 published on November 10. It’s based on analysis of the cloud security posture of thousands of customer organizations around the world.

Datadog claimed that the median number of high/critical severity flaws in cloud workloads surged from four in May, when Anthropic’s Mythos model was released, to 14 in June and 16 in November.

The data was sourced from analysis of vulnerabilities in third-party libraries used by applications monitored through Datadog Code Security’s Software Composition Analysis (SCA) feature, the report noted.

“This data reveals that the increased number of vulnerabilities in the CVE database isn't a theoretical risk,” it added. “It affects an increasing number of real-world applications running in cloud environments, reinforcing the need for cloud security foundations that limit the blast radius of compromised applications.”

Read more on cloud vulnerabilities: Cloud Attackers Now Prefer Vulnerability Exploits Over Credentials, Google Cloud Finds.

The report also highlighted the challenge of long-lived credentials; specifically related to cloud-hosted AI inference services and CI/CD pipelines.

Datadog warned that such credentials are consistently ranked as one of the most common causes of cloud breaches, with automated tools continuously scanning the web for weaknesses.

“Red-team frameworks like Pacu and Datadog’s own Pathrunner along with secret scanners like TruffleHog reliably find over-permissioned credentials and exposed keys at scale,” it said. “That same tooling is available to autonomous attackers, who enumerate for long-lived credentials first because they’re the highest-value, longest-lived prize in the environment.”

The report revealed that nearly half of organizations using Gemini use long-lived Gemini API keys, while the percentage of cloud users with access keys older than three years has reached nearly 30% for AWS IAM and Google Cloud Service Account users.

“Rather than static Bedrock or Gemini API keys, you should access AI inference services through the calling workload’s short-lived identity when supported (IAM role, managed identity, or service account) so the model is reached with the same federated credentials as other cloud resources and not a separate long-lived key,” Datadog explained.

Cloud Dependencies Expose Users to Machine-Speed Attacks

Supply-chain attacks are increasingly run autonomously and at machine speed, with hijacked dependencies one of the most popular routes to compromise, Datadog claimed.

Part of the challenge is the speed with which new dependency versions are adopted by users. If adopted automatically without proper vetting, they can result in the rapid compromise of cloud credentials and services.

Some 60% of organizations Datadog analyzed run versions that were released less than 24 hours earlier, with these versions appearing in more than a fifth (21%) of cloud applications.

The risk is amplified the more dependencies there are, and Datadog found that app workloads running in the cloud have on average 149 software dependencies. The figure across the average organization is 568.

“Organizations should implement dependency cooldowns to lower the risk of malicious dependencies reaching their cloud environments, because the community usually identifies and contains hijacked libraries within a few hours,” the report recommended.

Title: Your Artifact Repositories Need a Firewall
Context: Attackers publish malicious packages, hijack legitimate projects, and turn routine dependency download into opportunities for credential theft or a build compromise
Full Text:
Most organizations spend a lot of time looking for vulnerabilities in the software they build. But what about the malicious packages that enter before development even begins?

Attackers publish malicious packages, hijack legitimate projects, and turn routine dependency download into opportunities for credential theft or a build compromise. Malicious packages can run code during installation, when a developer or build system may already have access to source code, tokens, cloud accounts, or publishing credentials.

CI pipelines and AI agents add to the volume of package requests. They can resolve and install dependencies automatically, often without a human reviewing each request. That makes the point where packages enter the development workflow an important place to evaluate risk.

A repository or package firewall checks dependency requests against threat intelligence and policy before components reach developers, agents, or builds. The protection depends on the quality of that intelligence and where the firewall can evaluate a request.

Recent Attacks Show How Much Can Hide in a Package

In October 2026, a hijacked release of the TensorLake TypeScript SDK used an install hook to search for credentials and accept remote commands.

Sonatype's analysis found code that could modify repositories accessible to the compromised account and could expose collected data through a GitHub fallback. The investigation did not confirm that data was published, repositories were modified, or downstream systems were affected.

Other campaigns used different routes into the same workflows:

Hijacked packages and new malicious packages: Six npm packages delivered the same malware. Three appeared to be hijacked legitimate packages, and three were published with the malicious payload already included. The malware used Ethereum transactions to find infrastructure hosting additional payloads.

Large-scale package flooding: Sonatype identified nearly 850 components in the Flooding Dropper campaign. The packages downloaded and launched additional payloads on Windows, Linux, and macOS.

Credential theft and propagation: The Mini Shai-Hulud wave affected more than 2,200 component versions. Malicious releases of legitimate packages used install hooks to steal credentials and, where publishing access was available, compromise more packages.

Install-time execution: Miasma waves abused binding.gyp and node-gyp to execute during installation, rather than relying only on familiar lifecycle scripts. The Leo Platform compromise report tracked 23 malicious package versions.

These incidents show why package risk is not limited to suspicious names or newly created projects. Malicious code can arrive in a familiar package, run as part of installation, and act with the access available to the developer, build, or agent that requested it.

What a Repository or Package Firewall Does

A repository or package firewall checks dependency requests as they pass from a development environment toward package sources. It evaluates a requested component against security intelligence and, depending on the product's capabilities and configuration, can block or quarantine components that appear malicious or violate policy.

Once a package has been installed, teams may need to investigate the affected machine, identify exposed credentials, check for persistence, and determine whether the package reached other systems. Blocking a known malicious package at the point of entry can help prevent that cleanup from starting in the first place.

A firewall is one layer of software supply chain protection. It does not replace endpoint security, code review, or other controls. It addresses a specific risk: malicious or policy-violating components entering through package requests. And like any control, its coverage depends on which developers, pipelines, agents, and package sources route through it.

What to Look for in a Package Firewall

A repository or package firewall should do more than sit between a repository and a registry. As you evaluate options, consider whether or not it can:

Block malicious components before download, at the point where a package is requested.

Use current, in-depth threat intelligence that can help identify more than known vulnerabilities or suspicious package names.

Protect requests from developers, CI pipelines, and AI agents that can access public package sources.

Fit your repository tools and package sources without requiring a change to established workflows.

Cover the package ecosystems your teams use, and make clear which registries, mirrors, and private sources are included.

Strong firewall protection helps teams stay ahead of threats by identifying and blocking malicious components before they enter the development process. By evaluating package requests at the point of intake, it can reduce the risk of compromised builds and the investigation and rework that follow, while helping teams keep development moving.

How Sonatype's Intelligence Informs Firewall Decisions

A firewall's decision is only as useful as the evidence behind it. Sonatype Firewall combines machine-learning signals with AI-powered analysis, alongside the expertise of Sonatype's security research team, to identify suspicious packages and investigate if they contain malicious code.

By analyzing release behavior, examining package contents, and correlating findings across multiple sources, Sonatype can detect threats earlier, uncover additional affected packages, and turn new discoveries into actionable intelligence that informs Firewall's blocking and quarantine decisions.

That work can involve several kinds of analysis:

Activity and release patterns can help surface packages that behave differently from their project's history or from typical ecosystem activity.

Behavioral analysis can flag unusual signals around a package or release. Researchers can investigate those findings to confirm whether a component is malicious.

Payload analysis examines what the code actually does, including behavior such as credential theft, code injection, or downloading another payload.

Secondary expansion follows the code beyond the original package. Advanced Binary Fingerprinting can help identify embedded or renamed code that may not appear in a package's declared dependencies. In one investigation, Sonatype researchers found code associated with the flatmap-stream incident in 12 additional npm components.

Together, these methods provide context that a package name or manifest alone cannot. That context helps a firewall make a more informed decision about whether to allow, block, or hold a request for review.

Give Every Package Request a Safer Path

Every dependency starts with a request. A developer adds a package, a pipeline pulls it into a build, or an AI agent selects it for generated code. That request is an opportunity to assess a component before it becomes part of your software.

Sonatype Firewall helps teams bring security and development together at the moment open source enters the software supply chain. Backed by Sonatype's research and designed to work with supported repository environments, it helps organizations block malicious components earlier before they reach developers or workflows. That gives teams a chance to stop known threats at the point of entry, reduce avoidable disruption, and keep development moving with greater confidence.

Even if your existing repositories support secure component selection, malicious packages can still make their way into development. The difference comes down to how threats are identified, how quickly new malicious activity is detected, and whether that intelligence can stop a package before it's downloaded. Sonatype Firewall is that difference. Since it's designed to work with a wide range of repository managers, you can add an additional layer of protection to block known risks and avoid downstream work.

Title: CISA Adds Six Known Exploited Vulnerabilities to Catalog
Context: While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog...
Full Text:
CISA has added six new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

CVE-2026-20320 Cisco BroadWorks Improper Restriction of XML External Entity Reference Vulnerability

CVE-2026-111560 Barracuda Networks Multiple Products OS Command Injection Vulnerability

CVE-2026-111793 Openwave Messaging Limited Webtop Media Transcoder Incorrect Resource Transfer Between Spheres Vulnerability

CVE-2026-116606 Barracuda Networks Email Security Gateway (ESG) Authentication Bypass Using an Alternate Path or Channel Vulnerability

CVE-2026-124194 Microsoft Office Outlook Missing User Interaction for Potentially Unsafe Action Vulnerability

CVE-2026-125350 Google Chromium Use-After-Free Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Title: Vanderbilt University Takes Systems Offline After Cyber Incident
Context: Campus WiFi was also confirmed to be available
Full Text:
Vanderbilt University has been hit by a cyber incident, resulting in systems and applications being taken offline.

The Nashville-based institution disclosed that it was responding to an active incident at 10.45am CST on November 9, which it said may impact university devices, systems and cloud-based services.

“We are asking all members of the university community to shut down university devices, disconnect from university WiFi, and remain extremely vigilant. Take immediate action if you notice any unusual or suspicious activity on your devices,” the University wrote in the update on its website.

Such suspicious activity included unexpected pop-ups, warnings or security notifications; unusual changes to files, folders, or permissions in cloud storage platforms; and unexpected requests to enter passwords or approve authentication requests.

A later update by Vanderbilt at 7.15pm CST confirmed that classes will proceed on a normal schedule from November 10, while student services will also be operating normally. Campus WiFi was also confirmed to be available.

However, access to most Vanderbilt systems and applications remains restricted.

“We know this has disrupted important work and caused frustration across the university. Vanderbilt Information Technology is working with government agencies and other partners to manage this situation,” the update added.

The Vanderbilt Hustler, the official student newspaper for Vanderbilt University, reported on November 9 that university IT staff entered classrooms across campus, alerting that school-issued computers were not safe to use.

Read now: Copenhagen University Breach Compromises Data on Half a Million People

Vanderbilt Incident Claimed by BYOD Ransomware

Vanderbilt did not give any details on the nature of the incident, or any alleged perpetrator. However, cyber intelligence firm Venarix reported on X that the BYOD ransomware gang has listed Vanderbilt University on its data leak site.

The group claimed to have locked the university’s databases and accessed a vast volume of data held in its systems.

This includes Vanderbilt’s research data, over one million social security numbers, full names, emails, phone numbers, student and employee records, and a full takeover of the university’s domain controller.

Title: France Blames Iran for Supermarket Fridge Hack, Requests International Arrest Warrants
Context: Laure Beccuau, the Paris Public Prosecutor, said on social media the investigation found links between the October 11 to 12 cyber-attack and the Shahid Kaveh and Shahid...
Full Text:
The recent wave of cyber-attacks targeting refrigeration control systems across 700 supermarkets sites in France was coordinated by Iranian hacking groups, according to French authorities.

Laure Beccuau, the Paris Public Prosecutor, said on social media the investigation found links between the October 11 to 12 cyber-attack and the Shahid Kaveh and Shahid Shoostari groups, two elite offensive cyber units tied to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

In a technical attribution notice published on November 9, the French Computer Emergency and Response Team (CERT-FR) said Shahid Kaveh is linked to a range of purported hacktivist groups, including CyberAveng3rs, Soldiers of Solomon, Mr. Soul and Cyber Isnaad Front.

Investigators from the Anti-Criminality Office (OFAC) and the French domestic intelligence service (DGSI) found IP addresses linked to Iran-based endpoints and observed Farsi words in the traces left by the hackers.

Additionally, the techniques, tactics and procedures (TTPs) employed by the attackers were consistent with previous Shahid Kaveh campaigns.

CERT-FR named three leaders of the IRGC and Shahid Kaveh linked to the cyber-attacks.

The Paris prosecutor's office has now opened a judicial investigation into the cyber-attacks and the damage caused.

France Vows to Take Punitive Measures

According to another statement issued by the French government on November 9, Paris intends to take a series of diplomatic and punitive measures in response to the cyber-attacks.

The government announced that it would summon Iran’s Ambassador to France to formally convey its strongest condemnation of the attacks.

It also stated that it would urge its European partners to introduce additional sanctions targeting Iranian individuals and entities allegedly involved in the cyber-attacks against France, as well as other malicious cyber activities.

The French government stressed that it reserves the right to take further measures, both public and undisclosed, should they be deemed necessary and proportionate to respond to the cyber threats.

Frist Nation-State, Sabotage-Focused Cyber-Attack on French Soil

Historically, France has rarely attributed cyber-attacks to a single country, making this move particularly significant.

“This is an unprecedented campaign in terms of its scale and level of aggressiveness, marking the first cyber-offensive campaign carried out purely for sabotage purposes on French national territory,” the French government explained in its statement.

Commenting on the attribution, Gary Barlet, public sector CTO at Illumio, said he is also “impressed” that France is planning to pursue sanctions at a European level.

“It's not yet clear what form those sanctions will take, so that will be interesting to see. But this needs to happen more often. Too often an attack gets publicly called out, there's outrage, and then nothing happens. It sends a message to attackers that the cost of doing this is close to zero,” Barlet added.

In the CERT-FR technical notice, the French Cyber Crises Coordination Center (C4) said this attack added to a series of other incidents that have been attributed to IRGC-linked groups since at least 2020. These include destabilisation campaigns targeting satirical newspaper Charlie Hebdo in 2023 and a French digital display company in 2024, in the context of the Paris 2024 Olympic and Paralympic Games.

This attribution does not include the cyber-attack on the French Blood Service (EFS) that occurred in early November.

Title: Binance Investigates ShinyHunters Breach Claims
Context: 3bn in virtual currency from Binance after a months-long, multi-stage attack that involved fake job interviews and zero-day malware
Full Text:
Binance is actively investigating claims from a notorious extortion group that it has obtained 335 million customer records.

ShinyHunters posted an ad on PwsForums on November 4 claiming it was selling 335.9 million lines of records including private key wallets, user account passwords, transaction histories, email addresses and phone numbers, internal infrastructure information, KYC data including ID cards and passports, and “crypto assets in Binance’s hot wallet.”

It also demanded $900,000 from the cryptocurrency exchange, claiming it had two remaining choices: “pay or leak.”

However, a message sent to a Binance user by the firm’s customer support account on X said that, based on the sample information and the description of the data “this appears likely to be a scam rather than evidence of a Binance systems breach.”

Read more on ShinyHunters: ShinyHunters Claim Hack of Rival Ransomware Gang Clop

“We have found no evidence that Binance systems, customer KYC data, account credentials, wallet private keys, or internal infrastructure information were compromised in connection with this listing,” the message continued.

“Several aspects of this claim are inconsistent with how Binance stores and protects user data: Binance does not store user passwords in plaintext; Binance does not hold private keys for users’ external wallets; and the listing references jurisdictions where Binance no longer operates.”

Binance said that listings similar to this that have appeared in the past were often the result of infostealer malware installed on victims’ devices rather than a breach of the firm’s systems.

However, it urged users to be on the lookout for follow-on phishing attempts seeking passwords, 2FA codes, seed phrases and private keys.

Laundering Activity Continues

In the meantime, Binance continues to deal with the fallout from a huge theft of cryptocurrency from its platform by North Korean actors at the end of October.

The TraderTraitor group stole around $6.3bn in virtual currency from Binance after a months-long, multi-stage attack that involved fake job interviews and zero-day malware.

The group is now trying to launder the stolen funds by creating meme coins to disguise money flows, according to blockchain investigators.

“Anyone can create a new crypto token, and thousands of new tokens appear every day. Most are meme coins: tokens built around a joke, an animal or a celebrity, and traded on hype rather than any underlying use,” explained Elliptic chief scientist and co-founder, Tom Robinson.

“The launderers' tokens are made to be used once and thrown away. Nobody outside the laundering operation buys them, and their price is whatever the launderers choose to set. That makes them useful as a container, allowing stolen funds to go in on one side of a liquidity pool and come out on the other.”

Title: Security Flaws Across UK Government Sites Exposed ‘God-Tier’ Information
Context: A security researcher has found more than 100 serious vulnerabilities in publicly available UK government code, putting sensitive data at risk as a result of poor cyber hygiene
Full Text:
A security researcher has found more than 100 serious vulnerabilities in publicly available UK government code, putting sensitive data at risk as a result of poor cyber hygiene.

The UK government has defaulted to openly publishing code it produces with public money for around a decade because it’s transparent, and making it easier for code to be reused is cost-efficient. This includes within the Department of Health and Social Care, and the Home Office, as well as local authorities.

But funding squeezes have left departments neglecting maintenance and improvement of their technology estate. While ControlPlane security researcher Chris Nesbitt-Smith found the vulnerabilities using Claude’s Opus and Sonnet AI models, he says that he used consumer-grade models on a laptop and that many of the issues could have been caught by a routine IT health check. “None of this is the level of sophistication that general media is worried about in terms of cyber attacks,” he tells WIRED. “It’s all daft stuff.”

In the most serious case he identified, the Planning Inspectorate, which handles land-use matters across England, had failed to fully remove a login after it accidentally committed them to public repository GitHub. The fact the credentials gave such wide access—and seemingly didn’t expire—compounded with the agency’s accidental publication of them, “made it particularly dangerous for them.”

The complete Microsoft Entra ID would have given “god-tier” read and write access to all SharePoint sites and private employee OneDrive accounts, according to Nesbitt-Smith, including HR records. It also would have given access to sensitive libraries which safeguard evidence under legal hold for statutory planning inquiries and appeals, according to the security researcher who found it. “The option for ransomwaring them, for encrypting all the data, or just stealing all the data, was abundantly there,” Nesbitt-Smith says.

A spokesperson for the Planning Inspectorate told WIRED its cyber monitoring tools immediately detected Nesbitt-Smith’s activity in August and that it had already been handling this as a cyber incident when ControlPlane made contact. The agency identified and fixed this vulnerability within 20 minutes of the report and verified that no data breach occurred. “We have reviewed and strengthened our systems and processes to prevent this type of issue recurring and we are grateful for the researcher’s work and for alerting us to it,” they told WIRED.

The Planning Inspectorate issue “isn’t about open source but internal housekeeping when using public tools,” Amanda Brock, chief executive officer of nonprofit industry group OpenUK. “That data was exposed because of a failure not to follow good process,” she adds. “That’s not an open source security issue.”

In around two-thirds of the 349 public sector codebases across 33 organizations Nesbitt-Smith scanned, he said he found vulnerabilities. Several of these were found in the Department of Education’s code, including in a procurement service used by schools, in a teacher application service containing personal details, qualifications, employment history and identity documents, and England’s main register of government-funded training providers and apprenticeships. He also found a vulnerability in a Scottish Government open data portal which would have allowed any visitor to read administrative account information and to change site configuration. The organizations have since dealt with the issues.

Recently, there have been arguments for public sector departments to stop publishing source code in the open, now that AI has accelerated vulnerability discovery. The NHS reportedly ordered technology teams to transition away from open source code in May amid security concerns about the impact of AI models.

Doing this without immediately fixing the underlying issues would be the “worst case scenario,” according to Nesbitt-Smith, as it prevents researchers like him from finding them, and it’s likely that an adversary has already mirrored these repositories and so will maintain access to them. “Unless you’re going to go and fix all of the problems, if anything, you’re probably drawing more attention to it by closing it,” says Nesbitt-Smith, “because you’re like, ‘Here be dragons over this space. Don’t look here though, please.’”

Title: A New AI Tool From Google DeepMind Proved the Signal Protocol Is Secure
Context: Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning...
Full Text:
Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.

Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.

More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn't have critical vulnerabilities.

Before the AI era, it was incredibly time-consuming for people to describe the characteristics of software they wanted to prove, turn these summaries into formulas, and then develop the proof. Agentic AI can significantly cut down the time of the latter project, enabling analyses like DeepMind's Signal evaluation. But even this analysis was limited in scope—it did not, for example, formally verify the entire Signal mobile app—and DeepMind researchers emphasize that their findings are just one milestone in a larger process.

“We are very excited by this result, but there is a long distance to go before we are able to scale this to all the software of the world, and we want to do that,” Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, tells WIRED.

The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work.

While the speed of the project was notable, the DeepMind researchers point out that they were able to get a head start to a degree because of some past formal verification work that the Signal Foundation has conducted.

Context: Weekend: How two GPT-Live characters share a scene in Wit’s End By Kevin Shen, Senior Software Engineer, and James Wilsterman, Co-founder and CTO at Weekend What we set out to...
Full Text:
Weekend: How two GPT-Live characters share a scene in Wit’s End

By Kevin Shen, Senior Software Engineer, and James Wilsterman, Co-founder and CTO at Weekend

What we set out to build

Our game, Wit’s End, is a voice-first fantasy tabletop game. An AI Game Master, Sir Bart, tells the story and runs the rules, and the players just talk. GPT-Live’s full-duplex audio made it feel like a real table: players interrupt, joke and argue, and Sir Bart reacts while they’re still talking.

The cast was the weak spot. A GPT-Live session speaks in one voice, so the gruff captain at the town gate and the frightened old woman in the tavern both sounded like the narrator. We wanted each scene’s main character to speak for themselves, with their own voice and personality, without losing what makes the game work: players can say anything, and the story still gets to its ending.

Here’s how a scene plays now. The party reaches the gate of Timberfall, and Sir Bart sets it up and stops: “A group of stoic guards stand watch as their captain steps forward, hand on his sword, and looks you over.” Captain Dmitri takes over in a low, gravelly voice. He’s hunting a traitor named Jade, and the party matches the description of her accomplices. One player argues with him, and Dmitri argues back. Another slips him a gold coin. Sir Bart cuts in to say the dice are rolling, narrates how the bribe lands, and hands the moment back to Dmitri, who reacts.

Your browser does not support the video tag.

The solution: Two voices, one director

Who has the floor. Decisions API verdicts on both sessions’ transcripts tell the director who should speak next. It moves the floor between the two voices and starts rolls and scene endings on the Game Master’s backend.

Each scene runs two GPT-Live sessions side by side: one for Sir Bart and one for the scene’s character (Dmitri at the gate, Tabitha in the tavern), each with its own prompt and custom voice. A director (on our game server) decides who holds the floor, and only the floor-holder hears the players. Decisions API transcript triggers on both sessions tell the director what’s happening in the conversation. The Game Master’s backend, a Responses model, is the only part that calls game tools: dice rolls, scene endings and routes.

Two personalities, one story

We split each character into what’s theirs and what’s shared.

Their personality lives in their own prompt.

Each prompt also describes the character’s voice, in the same words we designed the voice from.

Illustrative shared-scene example

The scene is shared. Sir Bart and the character get the same conflict, the same resolution and the same story beats, and each beat names who says it. Dmitri introduces himself and says who he’s hunting; Tabitha tells the party where Jade will meet them. The game won’t end a scene until every beat has been said, by whichever voice owns it.

Prompt structure. Sir Bart’s voice and backend share the scene’s story; the character gets a persona prompt of their own.

From the character’s prompt

You are one actor in a live, spoken scene. A narrator describes the world; you only ever speak as yourself, out loud, in first person. - Never narrate, never describe your own actions or voice, and never speak for the travelers or the narrator. - You never decide whether a risky attempt works. React to it in one short line and stop; the narrator resolves it. - Speak only when a traveler talks to you or you are given the floor.

How the director picks who speaks next

Without generating speech itself, the director uses Decisions API verdicts on incoming transcript fragments to identify who a player is addressing, whether an action needs a dice roll, and when narration or a character’s final line signals a handoff.

Verdicts evolve as a player speaks. The director waits for the settled, end-of-turn verdict to identify the addressee, but sends risky actions to the Game Master as soon as they’re recognized.

Who speaks next

When

Who speaks next

Sir Bart finishes narrating and the cue verdict is 0.6 or higher, or his line ends on a speech verb (“Tabitha calls after you”)

The character

A player talks to the character while Sir Bart has the floor

The character, with the line to answer

A player tries something risky: a bribe, a lie, sneaking past, a fight

Sir Bart, right away, mid-sentence if needed. The director starts the roll on his backend; he narrates the outcome and hands the moment back

A player asks the narrator something or describes what their character does

Sir Bart

The players talk among themselves

Nobody. Whoever holds the floor gets a one-off note to let it pass

The character’s own words end their part (“Go on, then. Keep your heads down.”)

Sir Bart, once they’ve finished. The director starts the scene’s ending on his backend

Whoever was given the floor stays silent for 2.5 s

The same speaker, asked again

Making the handoff

A hand-off does four things:

Mutes the session losing the floor, tells it to stop, and drops any audio it has queued.

Catches the new floor-holder up on what it missed, as quiet context with session.thinking.append. The same lines go to its Decisions context, so its triggers judge with the same history.

Unmutes the new floor-holder and gives it its cue.

Holds the players’ mics until the new speaker’s first sentence has landed, for at most 8 s, so the hand-off can’t be talked over.

Because the character’s session is already running, a hand-off reaches first audio in 0.84 s on average, against 1.54 s for a new session.

Keeping the game moving toward an outcome

The voices improvise. The app decides when something happens.

A bribe while Dmitri holds the floor. The roll verdict arrives mid-sentence, the director gives Sir Bart the floor and starts the roll on his backend, and once Sir Bart has narrated the outcome, a cue verdict hands the floor back to Dmitri.

The director starts rolls and scene endings itself. In one playtest Sir Bart said “You’re going to have to roll the dice for that one” but never handed off to his backend, so no roll ran and he made up the outcome. Now the director starts a response on his backend directly. The voice says a short line while it runs, then narrates the result.

The dice settle each scene. Scene 1 ends on a successful roll. If Dmitri gives way before any roll, the director sends the players’ attempt to the dice instead of ending the scene.

A character can end their part, and the Game Master closes the scene. When Tabitha tells the party Jade will meet them at the Sprite Altar, the director gives Sir Bart the floor, his backend marks the scene complete, and he offers the two roads out.

The lesson

Only one session should hear the players. When both of our systems listened, both answered every test line, often contradicting each other: Dmitri refused a bribe while the Game Master narrated him pocketing it.

Muting a session doesn’t silence it. Tell it to stop and drop its queued audio. When it gets the floor back, lift “stay silent” explicitly: a Game Master still under that rule answered nobody for a whole scene.

Keep every voice warm. A session’s voice is set when it starts, so each voice needs its own session. Starting the character’s session with the scene saves about 0.7 s on every hand-off, the difference between a hand-off and an awkward pause.

Act on each verdict at the right moment. Verdicts arrive while the player is still talking, and the last one lands a median 0.19 s after they stop. Send a risky move to the Game Master as soon as it’s recognized; decide who a line was for when the turn ends and the verdict has settled.

Ask yes/no questions as predicates, set thresholds from real lines, and keep a plain rule as backup. “Should Dmitri speak next?” scored 11 of 12 as a predicate and 8 of 12 as a two-way choice. At a 0.4 threshold, “You’re going to have to roll the dice for that one” passed as a cue and handed Dmitri the floor mid-roll; real cues scored 0.94 and up, so we use 0.6. And “Tabitha calls after you” scored 0.04, so a speech-verb check catches narration that stops where the character’s words go.

Give every outcome to one owner. Only the Game Master’s backend calls tools, and the app, not a voice, starts rolls and scene endings. That lets each character improvise freely without bending the game’s rules.

About the author and company

The team at Weekend makes Wit’s End, a voice-first fantasy tabletop game where an AI Game Master runs the story and players just talk, in the browser and on TV. Play it at witsend.ai.

Weekend, formerly Volley, makes voice-powered games for the TV, so families can turn TV time into together time and play out loud. Its 25+ games, including Jeopardy!, Wheel of Fortune, Song Quiz and Wit’s End, run on Roku, Fire TV, Samsung and LG TVs and have been played in more than 30 million homes. Weekend is backed by Microsoft’s M12, Lightspeed Venture Partners and Y Combinator.
