Title: Post-Quantum Questions to Ask Your Vendors
Context: To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-...
Full Text:
CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As quantum computing advances, widely used public-key cryptography will become vulnerable to compromise from cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs). To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-enabled threats—before CRQCs become available.

Many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services. Cryptography is also embedded in systems and devices that are difficult to update, tied to long asset lifecycles, and require vendor support or replacement—such as industrial control systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Reliance on vendors means that effective PQC transition depends on vendor readiness, and early, structured engagement with these vendors is critical to planning efforts.

Organizations can use the vendor-neutral questions outlined in this guidance to determine whether a vendor understands quantum-related risks, maintains transparency over its cryptographic implementations, and supports a secure, cost-effective and timely transition to PQC.

Visit CISA’s PQC Initiative page for additional resources.

Title: Chinese Nation-State Threat Activity Falls Sharply in Q2 and Q3 2026
Context: The key takeaway is that lower detection levels do not necessarily mean a lower threat, particularly as China-aligned activity remains higher than that of other nation-state...
Full Text:
Despite the sharp fall in China-aligned detections, observed PRC cyber activity remained “substantially higher” than nation-state cyber activity from Russia and Iran during the period, the researchers noted.

“The decline may reflect changes in targeting, infrastructure or detection visibility rather than a reduction in activity. The key takeaway is that lower detection levels do not necessarily mean a lower threat, particularly as China-aligned activity remains higher than that of other nation-state actors,” they wrote.

A number of Chinese nation-state espionage campaigns have gone undetected for long periods in recent years. For example, in 2025, the Chinese-nexus actor Weaver Ant was found to have infiltrated the network of an Asian telecommunications service provider and remained undetected for more than four years.

Such cases highlight that there may be significant ongoing Chinese nation-state activity occurring that has not yet been detected.

US and Turkey Primary Targets for Nation-State Actors

The Trellix report, published on November 4, found that nation-state targeting primarily focused on two countries, the US (38%) and Turkey (37.1%), which collectively represented over three-quarters of all detections from April to September.

The researchers noted that the US represents a valuable target due its status as the world’s largest economy and the concentration of high-value technology, defense and government infrastructure. Meanwhile, Turkey also represents a key strategic target given its location at the intersection of Europe, the Middle East and Central Asia, as well as its NATO membership.

The third most targeted country by nation-state actors was Germany, representing 4.4% of such activity.

Title: GhostMap Bug Leaves Android Phones Stuck in Reboot Loop
Context: Security experts have warned of a new vulnerability in Android smartphones which could plunge devices into a crash loop that can only be fixed by forcing a factory reset
Full Text:
Security experts have warned of a new vulnerability in Android smartphones which could plunge devices into a crash loop that can only be fixed by forcing a factory reset.

Bitdefender said it discovered the issue when an Android package (APK) it collected from the wild crashed the emulators in its labs. It found that the problem wasn’t malware, but a bug in the Android OS itself.

“The operating system mishandles two fields inside a ZIP entry, the compression method and the declared uncompressed length. Reading such an entry causes a SIGBUS (a signal sent by the CPU to stop a process that accesses an invalid memory space) in whichever process touches the file,” it explained in a blog post.

“We call it GhostMap: the malformed entry causes Android to map the file across memory that was never allocated, and the crash occurs when a process reads from that empty space.”

Read more on Android bugs: Google API Keys Quietly Gain Access to Gemini on Android Devices.

Bitdefender said that the crash loop persists after a reboot and continues in safe mode, meaning the only way out is a factory reset which erases all locally stored data.

The bug affects all Android versions from Android 10 and above, but Google has so far failed to address it, claiming the issue is outside the scope of a security fix, the report noted.

It was notified by the security vendor on August 20.

How Threat Actors Could Abuse GhostMap

Bitdefender warned that cybercriminals could theoretically hide the technique in a fake app to disable a victim’s phone, or use the threat of GhostMap as leverage for extortion.

It shared several possible scenarios:

Brick a victim’s phone by first creating a malicious app containing a deliberately malformed resource that Android’s system service needs to read. When it does, the resource triggers a crash in system_server which renders the phone unusable. This could be used for extortion

Make a malicious app impossible to remove. In this scenario an icon contains a malformed resource which triggers a crash when Android tries to display it. The launcher, the app list in Settings, and the app's own info screen all crash when the user tries to access them to uninstall

Disable security tools. Mobile security apps, malware-analysis sandboxes and automated scanning pipelines need to use Android's resource-parsing code to examine suspect apps. By embedding a malformed resource in an APK, hackers could trigger GhostMap to crash anything inspecting it

Delivery through an app update. An app looks trusted on download but, in theory, the malformed file could be introduced later. That would mean it could pass app-store checks and security scans to infect a much larger number of potential victims at once

“This is a flaw in Android itself and, as of publication, no fix is available, so users have limited options on the device to prevent it. The most practical defense is to recognize the file before the bug is triggered,” Bitdefender concluded.

“That's possible because the malformation is visible in the file's structure, without installing or running the app. A scanner can distinguish a crafted file from a normal one by inspecting it, not by executing it.”

The vendor detects this issue as Android.Riskware.Ghostmap.rA.

Title: NATS Air Traffic Control Failure Cost UK Economy £33m
Context: Although not the result of a malicious attack, the incident highlights the ongoing challenge of improving business and IT resilience in critical sectors
Full Text:
A major IT failure at the UK’s National Air Traffic Services (NATS) in September was not caused by a cyber incident, but still cost the economy tens of millions of pounds, a new report has revealed.

The Cyber Monitoring Centre (CMC) claimed in a report published on November 4 that the cost to the UK economy was around £33m ($44m), with 70 domestic organizations affected.

However, it may have reached as high as £42m ($56.6m), according to the CMC’s modelled range, which reflects the cost to UK airlines, airports, ground operations and tour operators of 1152 flight cancellations, alongside significant delays and diversions.

If the impact on overseas airlines is included, the cost may have reached as high as £76m ($102.4m) based on 1800 cancelled flights. The impact on other non-UK organizations was not assessed.

The CMC estimated that 450,000 passengers were affected by cancellations or delays of more than two hours.

Read more on IT outages: CrowdStrike Fault Causes Global IT Outages.

Although not the result of a malicious attack, the incident highlights the ongoing challenge of improving business and IT resilience in critical sectors.

“Like the CrowdStrike software failure in 2024, it nonetheless shows how a failure in a single critical technology can cause widespread disruption to UK organisations,” the report noted.

“Its significance lies less in the scale of loss than in what it shows about the aviation system: a brief outage in a single critical system disrupted airline schedules for several days, and almost all of the cost fell on airlines and other organizations rather than on NATS.”

NATS is already mandated by the existing NIS Regulations 2018 to meet specific security and resilience obligations, and there’s nothing in the new Cyber Security and Resilience Bill that would help to prevent a similar incident in the future, the CMC claimed.

However, the new regime may improve how incidents are reported and overseen, it noted.

Some Lessons Learned

The outage itself was caused by a “previously unknown defect in the legacy software of the National Airspace System (NAS),” when a “routine request for an aircraft identification code and a higher-priority system message collided within about one millisecond,” the CMC said.

Corrupted flight data first appeared at 10am, and at 12:45pm all UK departures were stopped. Following the loss of an automated system link at 1.32pm, NATS declared a major incident and moved to manual fallback procedures, including major traffic restrictions.

Although the flight data system was restored within three-and-a-half hours, flight restrictions weren’t lifted until the evening and the impact on travellers lasted much longer.

CMC recommended the aviation industry to:

Review how well coordination between NATS, airlines and airports worked during the downtime

Examine whether earlier and more frequent assessments of expected outage duration would have helped airlines and airports to limit disruption more effectively than waiting for certainty

Plan for a “multi-hour restriction in air traffic capacity” that includes scenarios which last much longer than the outage itself

CMC technical committee chair, Ciaran Martin said: “Organizations need to understand and plan for the risks that sit in systems they depend on, not just the systems they own.”

The CMC warned that the risk of outages stemming from unidentified software defects “is heightened while NATS continues to rely on legacy systems.”

Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?
Context: In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local...
Full Text:
Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the frequency of outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

Title: Ballots, bots, and backlash.
Context: Attackers also exploited an internal AI tool to expand their access, eventually reaching Binance's wallet signing infrastructure. Barracuda says attackers must first reach the devices’ administrative interfaces.
Full Text:
Election Day brings typical cyber threats, technical glitches, and misinformation. Hackers tamper with European refrigeration systems. OpenAI faces questions over years of security warnings. Nvidia reportedly restricts business with Chinese data center customers. Binance details a six-billion-dollar heist attributed to North Korea. Barracuda patches critical security flaws. Gartner predicts an engineering-heavy future for security operations. Canadians face charges for hacking U.S. universities. Our guest is Heather Ceylan, CISO at Box, discussing Enterprise AI in 2026: what security leaders learned — and what comes next. AI takes the pitch, misses the point.

Today is Wednesday November 4th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Election Day 2026 brings a familiar mix of cybersecurity threats, technical glitches, and misinformation.

Election Day 2026 brought a familiar mix of cybersecurity threats, technical glitches, and misinformation. But the biggest technology story emerging from the midterms may be voters' growing resistance to artificial intelligence.

According to Nextgov, election officials reported unsuccessful attempts to penetrate online services, including efforts to guess login credentials. One state election office experienced five spikes in traffic to its ballot drop-box locator, which subsided after officials implemented a CAPTCHA. As of Tuesday evening, election security analysts had received no reports of foreign influence operations.

Meanwhile, ballot scanner malfunctions in New York's Westchester County quickly became fodder for election conspiracy theories. Officials initially attributed rejected ballots to problems with their thickness. Voters were instructed to deposit affected ballots in secure emergency bags for later counting. Despite no evidence of deliberate interference, misleading claims spread rapidly on X, reaching as many as 100 posts per minute.

Beyond election security, voters delivered a significant political setback to the technology industry's ambitious AI expansion.

Axios reports that roughly two dozen ballot measures restricting data center development appeared headed for approval. In Texas, Democratic gubernatorial winner Gina Hinojosa campaigned on maintaining a construction moratorium until lawmakers address environmental and infrastructure concerns.

With Democrats also winning key races in Ohio, Georgia, and Arizona, analysts estimate nearly two-thirds of planned U.S. data center capacity for 2028 could face delays.

The emerging message from voters: They're increasingly concerned about AI's impact on electricity prices, water supplies, and their communities. Silicon Valley may have enormous ambitions, but it turns out the people living next door to those data centers get a vote, too.

Hackers target refrigeration systems across Europe.

Hackers are targeting refrigeration systems across Europe, remotely changing temperature settings and forcing supermarkets to throw away spoiled food.

Attacks reported in November affected stores in Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland, and Germany, along with food suppliers in the UK. In some cases, attackers switched refrigeration equipment into defrost mode or disabled temperature alarms. Retailers have responded by disconnecting vulnerable equipment from the internet.

The attacks have also raised concerns about medical supplies. In France, hackers reportedly compromised refrigeration equipment supplied to the French Blood Establishment, changing freezer settings from minus 30 degrees Celsius to 110 degrees. An alert technician caught the problem before it disrupted operations, according to French health officials. There's no confirmed loss of blood plasma or harm to patients.

Authorities haven't identified the perpetrators or established whether the incidents are connected. French cybersecurity officials are urging organizations to secure remote access to refrigeration controllers, update firmware, and eliminate default passwords.

The incidents demonstrate how compromising ordinary industrial equipment can have very real physical consequences.

Current and former OpenAI employees say they warned company leadership for years about security weaknesses.

Current and former OpenAI employees say they warned company leadership for years about security weaknesses that could expose sensitive AI research to competitors and foreign governments.

According to Reuters, concerns included broad employee access to internal code repositories, sensitive research documentation, and inadequate security reviews of internal tools. Some employees believed leadership prioritized development speed over security.

Those concerns gained urgency following several incidents, including the arrest of a former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a listening device in an executive conference room, and researchers using a rival AI model to access employee accounts and internal systems.

OpenAI disputes suggestions that it neglected security, pointing to restricted repositories, increased investment, and regular reviews. The company reportedly reassigned a quarter of its production engineers to security improvements in August.

The larger challenge: protecting increasingly valuable AI technology without slowing the research that makes it valuable.

Nvidia sets limits on Chinese data center customers.

Nvidia is reportedly imposing new restrictions on data center customers that provide computing services to Chinese companies.

According to the Financial Times, Nvidia has told operators they must limit Chinese customers to no more than 49 percent of their overall business, with the remaining 51 percent coming from non-Chinese companies.

The policy would require data center operators to track how much business they conduct with Chinese firms, potentially complicating operations for providers serving customers in both China and elsewhere.

The Financial Times says Nvidia's sales representatives and regional teams have communicated the restrictions directly to customers, but the company apparently hasn't issued formal written documentation.

The reported move introduces a new limitation on how Nvidia-powered computing infrastructure can be used, adding another consideration for data center operators navigating business relationships with China.

Binance describes the $6 billion North Korean heist.

North Korea has launched several missiles toward the sea, hours after rejecting FBI accusations that its hackers stole more than six billion dollars from cryptocurrency exchange Binance.

The FBI attributes the theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor group. Pyongyang denies responsibility and says the accusations undermine prospects for renewed diplomacy with Washington.

Meanwhile, Binance has revealed how the attack unfolded. Hackers spent months compromising three engineers' computers, using malicious software disguised as developer tools and a fake job interview featuring a rigged coding assignment.

Attackers also exploited an internal AI tool to expand their access, eventually reaching Binance's wallet signing infrastructure. The company hasn't explained precisely how the AI tool was abused.

Binance says approximately $2.85 billion in stolen assets has been frozen or intercepted, and affected systems have been rebuilt.

Barracuda patches Email Security Gateway vulnerabilities.

Barracuda Networks is urging customers to patch two vulnerabilities in its Email Security Gateway appliances that could allow attackers to execute commands with root privileges.

One critical flaw enables unauthorized changes to global configurations, while the second allows users with administrator permissions to inject operating system commands.

Barracuda says attackers must first reach the devices’ administrative interfaces. Chaining the vulnerabilities could allow them to bypass authorization controls and gain root access.

The company has released patches and recommends updating firmware, applying security fixes, and restricting administrative access to trusted internal networks.

Gartner predicts SOCs will shift toward more engineers.

By 2028, security operations centers could employ 50 percent more engineers than analysts, according to a new Gartner report. The shift reflects AI's growing ability to handle routine security alerts, freeing human analysts to focus on investigating cases, making decisions, and coordinating responses.

Gartner predicts SOCs won't necessarily shrink. Instead, engineers will increasingly build, test, and refine AI workflows, while analysts expand into threat hunting and exposure management.

The transition creates challenges for entry-level analysts, who traditionally learned their craft by processing alerts. Organizations will need new approaches to training and developing expertise.

Gartner also recommends replacing traditional alert-volume metrics with measures of case accuracy and decision quality.

By 2030, the firm expects SOCs to become more proactive, continuously testing their own defenses rather than primarily responding to alerts.

Canadians are indicted for allegedly hacking U.S. universities.

Two Canadian men have been indicted for allegedly hacking U.S. universities to steal data and mine cryptocurrency.

Prosecutors say Ryan James Roach and Mathiew James Stubbings targeted institutions in four states between 2016 and 2019, deploying malware, stealing credentials, and exploiting university supercomputers. They allegedly used servers registered under false identities and compromised systems to conceal their activities.

Roach has been extradited to the United States, while Stubbings awaits extradition. Both face up to ten years in prison and fines of $250,000 if convicted.

Heather Ceylan, CISO at Box,sat down with me to discuss Enterprise AI in 2026: what security leaders learned — and what comes next. Here’s our conversation.

That was Heather Ceylan, CISO at Box, discussing Enterprise AI in 2026: what security leaders learned — and what comes next. If you enjoyed this conversation check out the full interview in the show notes.

AI takes the pitch, misses the point.

WIRED's Will Knight decided to see whether artificial intelligence could outperform him at fantasy soccer. He assembled a team of AI agents, handed them control of his lineup, and waited for the tactical brilliance to begin.

Their opening move? Bench Erling Haaland, one of the world's most prolific goal scorers. Not exactly an auspicious start.

The AI eventually reconsidered, but its subsequent decisions haven't been particularly impressive. After several weeks, Knight's AI-managed team still hasn't outperformed the average fantasy squad.

Meanwhile, researchers studying AI forecasting have found that leading models can sometimes outperform ordinary people at predicting events, although expert human forecasters generally remain formidable competition. Some experiments suggest AI is closing that gap.

Knight suspects AI could eventually become an unbeatable fantasy manager. But he's not particularly enthusiastic about that prospect. After all, fantasy sports are supposed to reward human judgment, even when that judgment is spectacularly wrong.

Delangue noted that agent misbehavior has so far mostly come from big companies that are testing frontier AI in secret. He said that future risks, perhaps involving the biological capabilities of models or their capacity to improve themselves recursively, are likely to emerge from these closed labs, too.

Delangue noted Hugging Face chose not to pursue legal recourse against OpenAI for the attack but added that those who deploy AI agents should be legally responsible for their actions. “Cyber-attacks are illegal, and I think it’s really important we make sure that agentic cyberattacks [are] illegal,” he told the event. “We don’t want to create an environment where there’s no ownership. There’s no responsibility for cyberattack.”

In contrast to some AI researchers who have warned that the technology could pose an existential risk to humanity, Delangue said his P(doom)—the probability of this happening—is “close to zero.” “There are many other topics that could destroy the world,” he said.

Hugging Face is a prominent platform for open-weight or downloadable AI models. Its users can share and access models hosted by the company or download them to their own computer systems.

Nvidia, the world’s dominant AI chipmaker, announced that it would acquire the platform for $12.93 billion this September. When the acquisition was announced, Hugging Face said it had around 18 million users.

Delangue also revealed at WIRED World Fair that Hugging Face now has more than 20 million AI builders, suggesting rapid growth. Delangue also revealed that Hugging Face has sold 50,000 Microducks, a cute, two-legged robot from Hugging Face that can be programmed using AI.

Delangue told the conference that the success of open-source AI will also be crucial in preventing a few companies and individuals from completely dominating the future.

“We could really clearly end up in a world where only a few companies control the majority of AI,” Delangue said. “There are very strong natural tendencies because [a few companies] really monopolize talent, compute, and capabilities.”

Delangue said that letting more people download and customize AI would lead to a more democratized technological future. The Hugging Face CEO said that the Nvidia acquisition would enable the company to compete as AI requires ever more resources.

Title: PolinRider Loader Reappears in Hijacked npm Packages
Context: Hidden Loaders Found in 12 npm Releases On November 4, 2026, Sonatype Research Labs investigated malicious runtime loaders in npm packages and confirmed 12 affected releases...
Full Text:
TL;DR

Sonatype Research Labs identified concealed runtime loaders in 12 npm releases across 10 hijacked packages.

All 12 releases contain loaders designed to decode payload-server IP addresses from Ethereum transactions sent by the same hard-coded wallet previously reported in PolinRider activity, then retrieve, XOR-decode, and execute JavaScript. Six conceal the loader in eval(atob(...)); six use a character-permutation bootstrap and the JavaScript Function constructor.

The manifests show no consumer install or postinstall hooks. The code can run when an affected entrypoint is loaded or, for server-hemera-mongo, when the bundled application starts.

Check direct and transitive dependencies, lockfiles, internal npm mirrors, and build records. If affected code ran, treat the host as compromised and investigate its processes, network activity, and accessible credentials.

Hidden Loaders Found in 12 npm Releases

On November 4, 2026, Sonatype Research Labs investigated malicious runtime loaders in npm packages and confirmed 12 affected releases across 10 hijacked packages. The examined releases contain two loader variants that use the same Ethereum sender wallet and payload-retrieval infrastructure. Sonatype tracks the finding as sonatype-2026-010515.The affected packages support unrelated developer functions, from Redux integration and health APIs to browser activity tracking, utilities, and server examples. Their shared issue is concealed behavior embedded in code that otherwise serves those ordinary purposes.These releases don't rely on a consumer-side installation script to activate that behavior. An application can reach the code when it loads an affected package; the server-hemera-mongo releases run it as the service starts.

Ethereum-based loader concealed by a character-permutation bootstrap

The Shared Loader Uses Ethereum Transactions to Find Remote Code

All 12 releases contain loaders designed to query public Ethereum RPC endpoints, with a Blockscout API fallback, to locate a transaction sent by the hard-coded wallet 0x1eef0849eda15d87f64e51c73c8442cf3c8bcef3. The loader interprets the first four bytes of the transaction's recipient address as a primary IPv4 address and the next four as a secondary address. It retrieves XOR-encoded JavaScript from the primary address over plain HTTP on TCP port 443, using the paths /0x/cls and /0x/ls.

After XOR-decoding the responses, the loader passes the JavaScript retrieved from /0x/cls to eval in the application process and to a detached node -i process through piped standard input. The JavaScript retrieved from /0x/ls is passed only to a detached node -i process. The child processes are unreferenced, allowing them to continue independently of the application process.

The Ethereum wallet acts as a dead-drop resolver: the operator can advertise a new payload-server IP address by sending another transaction without updating the malicious packages. Blocking an individual server therefore does not disable the loader's ability to discover a replacement.

Six Releases Conceal the Ethereum Loader With a Different Bootstrap

Six releases use a character-permutation bootstrap designed to reconstruct and execute an Ethereum-based loader: @adminide-stack/utils@0.0.16-130, cdeops@13.5.31, @adminide-stack/forms-core@5.1.9-alpha.3, @adminide-stack/yantra-help-browser@12.0.194, @cdmbase/wiki-browser@12.0.18-alpha.53, and @pubngo-stack/help-browser@12.0.23-alpha.3. The decoded loader bodies recovered from these six releases are byte-identical. They differ from the loader in the six Base64-wrapped releases but use the same Ethereum wallet, retrieval paths, and XOR keys.

In utils@0.0.16-130, an obfuscated routine follows the package's logger code. It permutes and decodes an embedded blob, obtains the JavaScript Function constructor indirectly, and executes the decoded content.

In cdeops@13.5.31, an obfuscated bootstrap appears in client.js before the module's normal delegation to global.require('cdeops/client'). It decodes embedded content and executes it dynamically, then continues to the expected client delegation. The hidden execution is separate from the documented purpose of that shim.

Shared Wallet and C2 Infrastructure Link the Releases to PolinRider

Sonatype Research Labs independently decoded the loaders in all 12 releases and recovered the same hard-coded Ethereum sender wallet, 0x1eef0849eda15d87f64e51c73c8442cf3c8bcef3. This exact wallet appears in GitGuardian's October 27, 2026 report, "GhostAction Crosses Paths With PolinRider: Inside the October Escalation," where it is identified as the Ethereum resolver used by PolinRider loaders found in compromised GitHub repositories. Those earlier loaders also retrieved stages from /0x/cls and /0x/ls on port 443, matching the retrieval paths and port in the npm samples.

The connection extends to the payload-server infrastructure. Greenflagged'sanalysis of these npm releases decoded transactions from that wallet and reported 95.135.181.151 as the advertised C2 address at its November 3 observation. GitGuardian had already listed the same IP on port 443 as a fallback C2 in a PolinRider persistence script. The exact wallet match, overlapping server infrastructure, and matching stage-retrieval paths support linking these malicious npm releases to previously documented PolinRider activity. This connection does not depend solely on similarities in obfuscation, and it does not definitively establish that PolinRider and GhostAction share an operator.

The Malicious Code Doesn't Wait for an Install Hook

The package manifests show no consumer install or postinstall hooks. Execution occurs when the runtime reaches an injected JavaScript file. For example, require('cdeops/client') selects the affected client.js, while the package's ES module import maps to a separate client.mjs file. In server-hemera-mongo, the injection is in dist/main.js, the application bundle referenced by its start script.

Assess exposure by correlating dependency records with execution evidence. Lockfiles identify resolved dependency versions, while cached artifacts and download logs help trace package acquisition. Build commands, application configuration, process telemetry, and runtime logs help establish whether an injected JavaScript file was executed.

Disabling npm install scripts does not address code that runs during module loading or application startup. The relevant question is whether the affected package code ran in a developer environment, CI worker, build host, or deployed service.

What Teams Should Do Now

Organizations should take these steps to identify affected systems and limit further exposure:

Find affected versions: Check direct and transitive dependencies, package-lock.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, internal npm mirrors, caches, build records, and artifact metadata.

Evaluate repository protections:Determine whether your repository manager or dependency firewall blocked these releases before they reached developers or build systems. Review download and policy logs to identify any deliveries, and ensure all eight versions are blocked from future use.

Remove affected dependencies:Replace affected versions in projects and prevent internal mirrors and caches from serving them. Preserve copies needed for investigation, and use replacement versions that have been independently verified as clean.

Determine whether the code ran: Check which entrypoint the application loaded and whether the runtime could execute the injected code. Correlate this with process and network activity. A lockfile entry does not prove the malicious code ran, and an import error does not prove it didn’t. The import may have failed after the injected code executed.

Investigate affected hosts:If the code ran, treat the host as compromised. Look for detached node -i processes launched by another Node process with piped standard input, and plain HTTP requests to TCP port 443 using /0x/cls or /0x/ls. Payload requests carry a Sec-V header containing A10-npm_inject in the six Base64-wrapped releases, A10-II in utils@0.0.16-130, or A10-E in cdeops@13.5.31. Use these indicators alongside process ancestry, timestamps, and dependency records to identify affected systems.

Assess access and rotate credentials: Identify the credentials and systems available to the affected process. Rotate credentials where exposure is possible, including publishing credentials, source repository access, cloud keys, and CI secrets.

The operator can change the remotely served JavaScript without publishing another npm release. Use available process, network, build, and runtime records to determine what affected systems executed and which credentials and resources those processes could access.

For ongoing details and response guidance, see the Sonatype Security Event and Sonatype Guide research.

Thanks to Sonatype Research Labs' Adam Reynolds for analysis of the affected npm releases and their PolinRider activity. Connect with Adam on LinkedIn.

Title: China-Aligned Group Abuses Sogou Input Method to Deliver Malware
Context: A China-aligned group has hijacked the brand-promotion mechanism of Sogou Input Method to deliver the DarkVigil toolset to users in six countries, turning legitimate application...
Full Text:
A China-aligned group has hijacked the brand-promotion mechanism of Sogou Input Method to deliver the DarkVigil toolset to users in six countries, turning legitimate application traffic into a malware distribution channel.

ESET researcher Anh Ho detailed the activity in research published on November 4, naming the group SlippyNunchucks and tracing its activity to at least September 15, 2023. ESET assessed with high confidence that the group is associated with a nation-state surveillance effort aligned with Chinese government interests.

The campaign began on July 1, 2026, when users of Sogou Input Method, a popular Chinese-language keyboard app owned by Tencent, began receiving DarkVigil implants. The number and geographic spread of victims initially led ESET to suspect an exploit.

Hijacked Sogou Traffic Reached Six Countries

A Sogou component fetched a brand-promotion configuration from a Sogou server over unencrypted HTTP. Domain Name System (DNS) hijacking redirected those requests to attacker-controlled servers, which returned a malicious configuration.

That configuration made the app download the DarkVigil implant and place it where Sogou's own components would run it, giving the malware persistence without a separate mechanism.

ESET does not know where the DNS manipulation occurred. Possibilities include routers set up with malicious DNS settings, routers implanted to hijack DNS and interception at internet service provider (ISP) level.

Victims were in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Sri Lanka and Oman. They included a multinational gambling organization operating from Sri Lanka, the Philippines and Hong Kong, an internet café in Dubai and a university student in Denmark, though ESET gave no victim count.

Read more on China-aligned update hijacking: PlushDaemon Hackers Unleash New Malware in China-Aligned Spy Campaigns

Tencent Fixes Sogou as ESET Flags Remaining Gaps

DarkVigil, also known as FDMTP, is a modular .NET toolset with more than 20 plugins. Darktrace had linked FDMTP to Mustang Panda with moderate confidence, but ESET said its telemetry showed no overlap with that group and tracks SlippyNunchucks separately.

Before the Sogou campaign, the group's only publicly identified distribution method was a supply-chain compromise of QuickFox. ESET linked the gambling-sector targeting to China's gambling restrictions and to China-aligned groups' apparent support for law enforcement action against Chinese individuals tied to regional fraud.

ESET reported the issue to Tencent on September 11, and Tencent acknowledged it on September 21. Sogou Input Method version 16.10, released in late October, moved the affected requests to HTTPS and enabled certificate pinning.

ESET said the downloader component still does not validate downloaded file types or restrict where files are saved.

The fix closes the unencrypted request the attackers abused. Where their DNS hijacking took place remains unknown.

Title: APT29 Watering Holes Target Unpatched iPhones and Android Devices
Context: Sekoia said its analysis supported the idea that APT29 obtained the exploits from a third party
Full Text:
A cyberespionage campaign attributed to Russia's APT29 has served exploit chains for already-patched iPhone and Android flaws to visitors of legitimate websites, with payloads built to steal cookies, device data and Wi-Fi passwords without any user interaction.

Sekoia uncovered the activity in mid-October 2026 and detailed it in research published on November 4. It assessed with moderate to high confidence that the group behind it is APT29, also tracked as Midnight Blizzard and Cozy Bear, or at least one of its subgroups. The group is widely attributed to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR).

The campaign used three delivery routes: scripts injected into legitimate websites, lookalike domains that proxied real sites while adding scripts and a week-long compromise of Plerdy, a Ukrainian website analytics tracker.

Exposed sites included a Ukrainian gas producer, Ukrainian military and military-equipment sites, a US chemical-industry trade association, a Czech far-right movement and a Bulgarian military-related site. The lookalike domains impersonated the America250 initiative and a London hotel.

Read more on Midnight Blizzard: Midnight Blizzard Targets Travelers via Captive Portals

Plerdy Compromise Expanded the Campaign's Reach

Plerdy is loaded by thousands of mostly Ukrainian websites. Sekoia said the compromise, which ran from August 27 to September 3, exposed hundreds of them and their visitors to the exploit kit.

The researchers did not say how many devices were compromised.

The campaign also cast a wider net than an earlier APT29 operation. A 2024 Google report described a campaign on Mongolian government sites that used a hardcoded filter to target specific websites, while this one had no such filter and collected any cookies in the browser.

Visitors were fingerprinted and served exploit chains matched to their devices, and the payloads did not establish persistence.

All Exploits Had Already Been Patched

One chain targeted iOS 16.7 to steal cookies. Another, based on the DarkSword exploit kit, which Sekoia described as suspected to have been developed by a commercial surveillance vendor, targeted iOS 18.5 and collected full device data. A third targeted Chrome 139 to 145 on Android, excluding version 143, for browser cookies and Wi-Fi passwords.

The chains used n-day flaws, meaning vulnerabilities already disclosed and patched: CVE-2025-43529, CVE-2024-27834, CVE-2026-20700, CVE-2025-14174, CVE-2025-43510, CVE-2025-43520, CVE-2026-3910 and CVE-2025-27038.

Sekoia said its analysis supported the idea that APT29 obtained the exploits from a third party.

That also sets the limit of the threat. In Sekoia's words, "a user running an up-to-date operating system is safe from these attacks."

Context: The company specified that only a limited number of Coolworld units were affected and added that "the vulnerability currently being reported in the media concerns a component...
Full Text:
Read more about the wave of cyber-attacks on refrigeration control systems in Europe:

Major French Supermarket Chains Hit by Cyber-Attack, Food Stock Impacted

French Supermarket Cyber-Attack Impacts More Refrigeration Controllers

Cyber-Attack on Refrigeration Systems Hits Supermarkets Across Europe

Cold storage rooms in France's National Blood Service (EFS) were turned to a boiling temperature of 110°C (230°F) in a cyber-attack targeting temperature-controlled storage and refrigeration equipment provider Coolworld.

On November 3, French investigative weekly newspaper Le Canard enchaîné reported a new wave of attacks targeting refrigeration systems in France.

The outlet said unauthorized actors took control of some refrigeration controllers in EFS’s cold storage rooms in the night between November 1 and 2, notably in facilities in the Burgundy and Franche-Comté region, in east-central France.

These cold storage units host blood samples used for health monitoring but also plasma intended for transfusions. While they are typically kept at -30°C (-22°F), the newspaper reported some rooms hit up to 110°C (230°F). This does not mean the equipment or any blood samples reached these temperatures.

The refrigeration control systems of the affected EFS cold rooms are maintained by Coolworld, a Dutch temperature control rental company operating in France, Germany, Ireland, the Netherlands and the UK.

Coolword confirmed on November 4 it was "aware of the cybersecurity incident involving remote monitoring software used in refrigeration systems" and said it "responded promptly by implementing the appropriate measures," without sharing any details on those measures.

The company specified that only a limited number of Coolworld units were affected and added that "the vulnerability currently being reported in the media concerns a component supplied by a third-party provider and not directly controlled by Coolworld."

No Operational Impact on Blood Samples

The French Ministry of Health sought to reassure the public and told Le Canard enchaîné that the incident had caused no operational disruption because it had been detected in time.

According to the EFS, an on-call technician noticed an abnormal rise in temperature in the cold storage rooms overnight, allowing the issue to be identified before it could affect operations.

Speaking to French national news channel BFMTV, EFS president Frédéric Pacoud said that while the EFS “could have lost samples or bags of plasma intended to treat patients,” the early warning meant “there was no compromise to the safety of blood products.”

The EFS also told French media it notified the country's national cybersecurity agency (ANSSI). At this stage, nothing indicates that any EFS IT systems are impacted by the attack.

The EFS was approached for comment but had not responded at the time of publication.

Title: 3AM Ransomware Used Human-AI Hybrid Tactics in UK School Estate Compromise
Context: Bitdefender described the attack as “the first case of this kind that we have documented in Europe
Full Text:
A UK school estate was compromised by the 3AM ransomware group via a unique hybrid human-AI operation, an investigation by Bitdefender has found.

The incident, which took place from September 10 to 19, 2026, resulted in the attackers’ encrypting 37 machines and building domain trust in the compromised estate to reach other schools.

Notably, the investigation revealed that parts of the post-compromise techniques were undertaken by a human operator at the keyboard, while other parts behaved like an AI agent.

Bitdefender described the attack as “the first case of this kind that we have documented in Europe.”

The researchers continued: “What this attack does show is that the hybrid approach works, and we assess that it makes economic sense for attackers, with a person setting the goals and an [AI] model handling the mechanical work. We can expect hybrid attacks like this one to become more common in 2027.”

How 3AM’s Hybrid Attack Unfolded

The research blog, published on November 3, attributed the attack to a 3AM ransomware affiliate. 3AM is a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation, whose Rust-based encryptor was first observed in February 2023.

The researchers were not able to determine how the attacker gained initial access to the school estate. The first recorded activity started on September 10, when the attackers’ accessed credentials stored the estate’s backup infrastructure, before decrypting them with the Windows Data Protection API.

From September 12-13, the threat actor tested connections to other hosts from a machine where SQL Server was the parent process. They sent a sequence of commands to the target’s Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) service, authenticating with stolen administrator credentials. The commands’ outputs were then read by either a person or AI model, who would then choose the next command and repeat the cycle.

A PowerShell command was first used, and re-ran unchanged 41 seconds later, before a single call was changed 49 seconds after that. Next, 47 seconds later, PowerShell was replaced with wmic, the older built-in command-line interface to WMI.

The researchers noted that the fact the complete rewrite arrived as fast as the minor changes before it indicates the commands were written by an AI agent.

The next nine retries followed a similar pattern of the delay before the next command being issued taking between 40 to 101 seconds, whatever the size of the change, while moving on to a new task to minutes.

“That split, longer time between tasks and shorter between retries, is what it looks like if a person is choosing the next step and a model is handling the retries,” the Bitdefender researchers wrote.

In contrast, later commands before the retry sequence were simpler and were sent between two and 16 minutes apart indicative of the pace of someone reading the output and deciding what to do next.

On September 14, the attacker made efforts to gain persistence in the compromised environments. These include running credential dumping tool Mimikatz and creating two backdoor domain-administrator accounts by separate routes.

Next, the attackers copied and 40 financial-related files via the Windows robocopy tool, which were subsequently exfiltrated to their command-and-control (C2) endpoint using HTTP POST.

“The registry-as-transport channel is an unusual choice and a strong indicator to hunt for,” the researchers noted.

On September 19, the attacker joined three separate Active Directory domains with two-way trusts and pushed the backdoor account’s access across the estate within an approximately three-hour window. The researchers said this part of the attack was the clearest example of the hybrid human-AI approach being deployed.

The work involved in joining the estate’s separate domains is highly mechanical, requiring it to be set up correctly on both sides, with one wrong detail stopping everything.

The attackers built the trusts and then ran a series of diagnostic probes and restarted the service that maintains the secure channel between domains. Bitdefender said the hybrid human-AI model suits this work, involving repetitive configuration where the fix comes from a human reading the error.

This work resulted in the attackers reaching 50 machines from the unmanaged host.

Finally, the threat actor made attempts to remove endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools, before decrypting 37 out of the 50 machines accessed.

How to Defend Against Hybrid AI Ransomware Attacks

Bitdefender noted that the attack involved typical approaches observed in other ransomware incidents, including backup credential theft, rogue domain administrators, trusts between domains and use of built-in legitimate tooling.

However, the hands-on work was split between human and AI operators, making use of their respective abilities.

“The approach looks pragmatic: the model takes the mechanical, repetitive work, and nothing in it needed skill or spend that these attackers did not already have,” the researchers commented.

They also noted that the involved of an AI model changes what the traces look like during an incident.

Bitdefender offered the following recommendations for defenders to protect against future attacks that follow a similar playbook:

Keep the administrative accounts of separate domains separate, and never keep privileged credentials for several domains in one place

Treat backup infrastructure as a target, and review your backup strategy for malicious intent

Restrict remote execution and administrative shares

Block interpreters and shells on machines that never use them

Put an endpoint agent on every machine

CVE-2024-27834 Apple Multiple Products Improper Authentication Vulnerability

This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise.

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied.

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria.

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

Title: Police Seize 100+ Servers After Four-Year Investment Fraud Probe
Context: A long-running international operation to disrupt a multimillion-dollar investment fraud operation scored another impressive victory this week after police seized 100 servers...
Full Text:
A long-running international operation to disrupt a multimillion-dollar investment fraud operation scored another impressive victory this week after police seized 100 servers and shuttered several scam websites.

Led by the German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office, the action day on November 3 targeted the company believed to be responsible for hosting the fraudulent investment websites.

Victims were lured to these sites by deceptive ads promising huge gains with no downside. After they recorded their interest, personal data would be shared by the company with criminal groups operating scam call centers, according to Europol.

Scammers impersonating brokers then used a variety of social engineering tactics to persuade the victims to invest their funds in the fictitious schemes. Online accounts set up to perpetrate the scheme apparently displayed illusory gains, persuading them to plough more money into the funds.

When victims asked to withdraw their money, brokers used delaying tactics to block payments before cutting contact and leaving them with no way to recover their funds, Europol claimed.

Investigators estimate losses to exceed €4m ($4.5m), with potential victims in as many as 50 countries.

Read more on investment fraud: Cops Arrest Suspected Multimillion-Dollar Fraud Mastermind.

Alongside the server seizures, the action day on Tuesday resulted in the arrest of seven suspects who will be extradited to Germany. Authorities also searched 17 locations and seized other evidence and assets.

The operation involved cooperation from Albania, Cyprus, Finland, Germany, Israel, Kosovo, and North Macedonia, highlighting the transnational nature of this fraud scheme. Scam call centers have been identified in Albania, Kosovo and North Macedonia, according to Europol.

Four Years in the Making

The case dates back to 2022, when a German couple complained to local authorities that they couldn’t withdraw their funds from an investment scheme they had enrolled in.

An action day on September 6, 2022, led to searches in Belgium and Latvia, and the arrest of two suspects. Evidence was seized which helped police identify seven other members of the network, including the managers of call centers which were used in the scams.

Another action day came on May 13, 2025, when police conducted eight searches simultaneously in Albania, Cyprus and Israel. That resulted in the arrest of one suspect in Cyprus and the seizure of more evidence including electronic devices, documents and cash, Europol said at the time.

Police are not claiming, as they have done in the past, to have dismantled the network.

According to the FBI, investment fraud was the highest-grossing cybercrime type in 2025, amassing nearly $8.7bn for cybercriminals. Other schemes that have come to light in Europe over recent years include an €89m ($100m) ring that was smashed in 2023 and a financial crime organization that made €15m ($17m) until it was disrupted in 2021.

Title: Fake Interview of Software Engineer Led to Binance Mega-Heist
Context: Threat actors targeted multiple software engineers at Binance with sophisticated social engineering and zero-day malware in a months-long campaign that led to a record-breaking...
Full Text:
Threat actors targeted multiple software engineers at Binance with sophisticated social engineering and zero-day malware in a months-long campaign that led to a record-breaking digital heist last week, the crypto exchange has revealed.

Binance revealed the news in a lengthy post on X (formerly Twitter) on November 3.

“It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” it explained.

“The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method.”

Read more on crypto theft: Hackers Exploit BTCPay Server Flaw to Steal Cryptocurrency.

The main point of intrusion appears to have stemmed from an interview the threat group set up with an unnamed “Software Engineer B” in September.

An individual posing as a project director contacted the engineer via a legitimate job-hunting platform, having spotted from their profile that they worked at Binance.

The first-round interview was held with a fictitious HR representative, during which the interviewer shared a social media account with the engineer, including personal photos and videos posted, in order to build trust, Binance said.

“The second interview was conducted in a popular social chat app, near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an ‘assignment’ containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer,” it continued. “The repository contained malicious code that executed during the setup process, initiating a series of unauthorized activities.”

According to Binance, the “zero-day malware” used obfuscation and evasion techniques to ensure it was not detected by the engineer’s endpoint security tools. These included replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and connect with a C2 server.

The Pathway to Wallet-Signing Operations

On October 20, the attacker accessed an internal AI tool via Engineer B’s computer to compromise the machines of two other Binance employees: Wallet DevOps Engineer A and Wallet Software Engineer C.

The former had been scoped out back in June when they unwittingly downloaded a malicious version of Homebrew, a third-party package manager for macOS, after clicking on a malicious search ad.

Although the Binance team “detected the anomaly, replaced the device, and rotated all related credentials” at the time, the engineer’s role and those of his colleagues had already been exposed to the hackers.

After compromising Engineer A’s machine, they found out he had a container deployment permission token on his computer.

“On October 29 between 17:15 and 19:56, the attacker logged onto Software Engineer C’s computer, used the credentials stolen from Wallet DevOps Engineer A, deployed a container, and triggered a malicious script to launch the attack,” the report explained.

Between 20:05 UTC and 20:09 UTC, five Binance hot wallets then sent 233.46 million XRP to an attacker-controlled address, while Binance hot wallets on Solana and Optimism sent around 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker-controlled addresses.

Clean-Up Time

Binance said it has since rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool along with the latter’s access controls, and that it has replaced affected devices.

It also decommissioned engineer credentials and tokens, enhanced security scans across employee devices, improved AI-based behavioral anomaly detection and strengthened wallet service risk controls.

The firm admitted it had already detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korean attacks this year alone. It is currently conducting a review of the incident, setting up a security research fund with industry partners, and has already increased investment in AI-enabled detection, protection and monitoring tools.

Experts from Fortra questioned the controls that were originally in place to protect employee, and especially developer, machines.

“In a world where quiet quitting exists, it should come as no surprise that employees are interviewing on company time. Organizations need to counter this with adequate controls in place. Particularly, controls around what can be downloaded and executed on a corporate laptop, as well as the permissions granted to the user,” argued Tyler Reguly, associate director, security R&D at Fortra.

“At the end of the day, developer laptops are among the hardest devices in an organization to lock down safely without being detrimental. Organizations need to find the balance point."

Title: Democracy without a safety net.
Context: Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre warns that AI-powered malware is highly likely to feature in financially motivated cyberattacks against critical infrastructure, including hospitals, airports, and power stations, by 2028. Ivanti has patched two additional Connect Secure vulnerabilities exploited in zero-day...
Full Text:
CISA scales back its Election Day role. Google takes down a massive Android TV botnet. The UK warns of AI-powered attacks on critical infrastructure. German lawmakers face potential spyware threats. An AI-enabled infostealer ranks its victims. Ivanti patches more exploited zero-days. NATO launches cyber war games in Estonia. A Harvard breach exposes data linked to 850,000 email addresses. Our guest is Alex Weinert, Chief Product Officer at Semperis, on protecting the identity fabric in the AI era. Democracy is calling. And texting.

Today is Tuesday November 3rd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

CISA steps back from the midterms.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is taking a dramatically reduced role in today’s midterm elections, abandoning the coordinated national election security operation it has maintained since 2018, the New York Times reports.

Under the Trump administration, CISA has lost roughly a third of its workforce, scaled back intelligence sharing, and discontinued election-specific cybersecurity assessments. There will be no national election security war room or scheduled press briefings, leaving state and local officials with less federal support for responding to cyber threats, technical disruptions, and disinformation.

CISA insists it's fully prepared, pointing to regional teams available to assist election officials and hundreds of security-related engagements.

Former officials disagree, warning that the retreat leaves dangerous gaps in nationwide threat awareness and coordination.

States have significantly strengthened their election defenses since 2016, including expanded use of paper ballots. But experts say the federal government's ability to identify and communicate threats that cross state lines has substantially weakened.

Google dismantles a set-top-box botnet.

Google says it has dismantled a massive botnet built from more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes shipped with malware already installed.

The botnet, dubbed XCPE, allegedly originated with Chinese manufacturer Videostrong Technology, which Google says secretly turned customers' devices into residential proxies, renting their internet connections to third parties for activities including advertising fraud and other cybercrime.

Google severed ties with Videostrong and took legal action against the infrastructure controlling the botnet. Researchers say the disruption could also cut off access to more than 10 million additional compromised devices.

The malware wasn't limited to streaming boxes. Researchers also found it on Android-based healthcare equipment, karaoke machines, and digital signage.

Google says it has addressed the weakness that allowed the malware to activate during initial device setup. The case highlights a troubling supply-chain threat: devices compromised before customers even plug them in.

The UK’s NCSC warns of likely attacks on critical infrastructure.

Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre warns that AI-powered malware is highly likely to feature in financially motivated cyberattacks against critical infrastructure, including hospitals, airports, and power stations, by 2028.

In its annual State of the Cyber Nation report, the NCSC also predicts Russia and China will routinely incorporate AI into their cyber operations.

Agency chief Richard Horne says the danger isn't necessarily new attack techniques, but AI's ability to discover and exploit existing vulnerabilities at unprecedented speed and scale.

He criticized organizations for running outdated systems, postponing security upgrades, and failing to monitor their networks.

The British government is responding with new investments in cyber defenses, AI security research, and vulnerability detection.

Horne warned that organizations face a choice: invest in resilience now, or risk serious disruptions to essential services later.

Warnings from Apple prompt German authorities to highlight potential spyware.

German authorities are warning lawmakers and prominent public figures about possible spyware attacks following a new round of threat notifications from Apple.

Germany’s federal cybersecurity agency, the BSI, confirmed that members of parliament and other notable individuals received alerts indicating they may have been targeted by sophisticated surveillance software.

Apple sent similar warnings to users in 99 countries. The company doesn't identify suspected attackers or confirm whether targeted devices were successfully compromised.

The spyware involved in these campaigns can potentially steal messages, location data, and other sensitive information, sometimes exploiting vulnerabilities that require no interaction from victims.

German officials say they're taking the warnings seriously and advise recipients to assume their devices may be compromised.

It's unclear who's responsible for the latest campaign, or whether any German officials were successfully hacked.

A new infostealer uses AI to identify the most valuable victims.

Researchers at Cisco Talos have uncovered a new infostealer that uses artificial intelligence to analyze stolen data and identify the most valuable victims.

Dubbed Volta-Autodoxer, the malware collects passwords, authentication tokens, cookies, payment information, and cryptocurrency credentials. It also targets active sessions on platforms including Discord, Telegram, Steam, and Roblox.

But Volta goes beyond simply stealing data. It conducts additional searches through victims' accounts, gathering information about their locations, habits, and purchases to build detailed personal profiles.

The malware then submits that information to commercial AI models, asking them to act as intelligence analysts and produce structured assessments that help attackers prioritize targets.

Volta defaults to Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6, with fallback options including Moonshot AI's Kimi and Google's Gemini.

Researchers haven't confirmed the malware has been deployed in the wild, but its design demonstrates how AI could make traditional credential theft more targeted and efficient.

Ivanti patches additional Connect Secure zero-days.

Ivanti has patched two additional Connect Secure vulnerabilities exploited in zero-day attacks since early October. Attackers chained a privilege escalation flaw and a file upload vulnerability with an authentication bypass bug patched last month, enabling unauthenticated root-level code execution. Researchers at Volexity say the attackers avoided deploying malware, instead repeatedly exploiting devices to execute commands and tampering with logs to hide their activity. CISA has ordered federal agencies to patch the authentication bypass vulnerability by Friday. More than 5,000 Connect Secure instances remain exposed to the internet.

NATO’s Crossed Swords cyber exercise kicks off in Estonia.

NATO's Cooperative Cyber Defence Centre of Excellence has launched Crossed Swords 2026 in Tallinn, Estonia, bringing together more than 250 participants from over 40 countries.

The exercise focuses on coordinating offensive and defensive cyber operations with conventional military and special operations missions, where timing can be critical down to the minute.

This year's exercise introduces a dedicated AI agent track, allowing participants to build, deploy, and work alongside autonomous systems while maintaining human oversight. The training environment also incorporates OpenAI's Daybreak cyber defense technology.

Military cyber operators, threat hunters, forensic specialists, and command staff are participating, alongside civilian partners helping integrate critical infrastructure protection into operational planning.

Crossed Swords has grown significantly since its beginnings in 2014, reflecting the increasing importance of coordinating cyber capabilities with traditional military operations.

A data breach at Harvard exposes more than 850,000 email addresses.

A data breach at Harvard University exposed personal information associated with more than 850,000 email addresses, according to breach notification service Have I Been Pwned.

Attackers compromised Harvard's Alumni Affairs and Development systems in November 2025, stealing names, email addresses, phone numbers, physical addresses, dates of birth, donation details, and other biographical information.

Harvard says the affected systems did not contain Social Security numbers, passwords, or payment card information.

The ShinyHunters extortion gang claimed responsibility and published a 1.1-gigabyte archive of stolen data in February after Harvard reportedly refused to pay a ransom. Harvard has not publicly attributed the attack.

The incident was part of a broader series of university breaches, with Princeton and the University of Pennsylvania also reporting compromises involving donor information in November 2025.

Democracy is calling. And texting.

As Americans head to the polls for today's midterm elections, WIRED reporter Dhruv Mehrotra has a cautionary tale about the machinery behind political fundraising.

Since 2022, he's received more than 1,700 fundraising texts intended for a relative named John, whose modest donations to Democrats somehow got associated with Mehrotra's phone number.

Mehrotra replied STOP 49 times. The messages kept coming.

Investigating the deluge, he traced nearly half this year's messages to tracking codes apparently associated with Sterling Data Company, which uses AI and personal information to identify potential donors.

Sterling's CEO acknowledged that campaigns can rent the same contact records and that database mistakes happen, but didn't confirm responsibility.

His advice was to stop responding entirely.

So, on Election Day, a reminder that while Americans get one vote apiece, political fundraising texts apparently come with no such limits.

Title: Binance Says Hackers Used Well-Known Tricks to Carry Out a $6.34 Billion Heist
Context: The hackers were then able to move through the company’s network, exploit an internal AI tool, and gain access to a wallet signing service that allowed them to make transactions...
Full Text:
For almost a decade, North Korean cybercriminals have targeted the cryptocurrency industry—large and small. While these hacks have been frequent, the country’s hackers allegedly made off with their biggest heist to date last week when $6.34 billion was siphoned from the wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.

In a new security update issued on Tuesday, Binance detailed its initial findings into how the company was compromised and hackers were able to steal billions in just 20 minutes. The hack, according to Binance, was the result of an engineer falling for a fake job interview and downloading malicious software. The hackers were then able to move through the company’s network, exploit an internal AI tool, and gain access to a wallet signing service that allowed them to make transactions outside of normal withdrawal procedures.

“This should not have happened, and we apologize for the concern, disruption and uncertainty it caused our users, partners and the wider industry,” Binance wrote in its security update, where it also says it has set aside funds to cover the losses and has “rebuilt or replaced” internal systems impacted in the attack. “It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident,” the company says.

Although more than $6 billion was stolen from Binance accounts, almost half of this—where it was possible to do so—was frozen by parts of the cryptocurrency industry, meaning the hackers could not access the funds. However, that still leaves billions controlled by North Korea’s hackers, who have been trying to launder the stolen money into a form where it can be accessed and cashed out. That process could take months.

Binance’s analysis says the hack was the accumulation of months of work by hackers, with the ultimate attack taking place on October 29. Shortly after funds started to be moved from Binance’s hot wallets, across more than 10 different blockchains, multiple cryptocurrency tracing firms attributed the attacks to the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea’s (DPRK) hackers, in particular the sophisticated TraderTraitor group that previously stole more than $1.5 billion in a separate hack last year. The FBI quickly linked TraderTraitor to the Binance hack on October 31.

“Binance’s account aligns with what we know about the TraderTraitor playbook,” says Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos. “The attackers didn’t simply steal a wallet key. They compromised engineers, used that access to understand and move through the environment, and ultimately subverted the systems used to authorize transactions.”

Binance stops short of directly blaming the TraderTraitor hackers itself; however, the company points to the FBI’s attribution to North Korea and acknowledges a prior targeting by DPRK’s cybercriminals. “Throughout 2026, Binance's security team detected and prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases,” the company’s update says.
