Last year at Ignite, we introduced the concept of Frontier Transformation and how it is different from any technology-led pursuit, because it requires us to focus on business outcomes first. It starts with a simple idea: technology was invented to serve humanity, not the other way around. There is no path where this notion of infinite cognitive compute replaces human purpose. Frontier Transformation is an opportunity for a wholesale reinvention of how you think about your unique ideas coming to life and how your organization can thrive in your industry.

Over the course of this past year, we have been leading our customers to focus on the three durable traits that are required for successful transformation: human ambition, intelligence and trust. We are taking a platform approach toward enabling the same: Copilot as the place to call home for interacting with AI to empower human ambition; the Microsoft IQ platform to compound and amplify your intelligence from within while protecting your unique differentiation; and Agent 365 to enable Trust and Observability at every layer of the stack so that you can govern, manage, secure and get business value and return out of the capabilities you deliver.

Our latest earnings are another important marker on that journey. Behind the numbers are thousands of customers, partners, developers and employees putting AI to work in meaningful ways. We have so many inspiring stories from our customers that highlight these outcomes, and below are some of our favorites.

Empowering human ambition with Copilot

Volkswagen has scaled Microsoft Copilot to more than 330,000 employees as it expands the role of AI in decision-making and knowledge-based processes across the enterprise. Building on Copilot Chat adoption that reached more than 300,000 monthly active users, employees are now using Copilot with Work IQ for more advanced scenarios, bringing greater organizational context to decision-making and knowledge-based work. Volkswagen is also working with Microsoft to further scale its Intelligent Data Foundation on Microsoft Fabric to make data easier to find, understand and use across the entire company. With this investment, Volkswagen is demonstrating how companies have evolved from using Copilot as a productivity tool to an operating system to empower human ambition.

Following a successful pilot, Fujitsu is scaling Microsoft Copilot across its global workforce of approximately 100,000. Copilot usage has surpassed 90%, and the company is using the tool to connect employees with specialized agents and business systems. AI agents are already automating roughly 75% of initial responses and triage for a service desk that receives nearly 300,000 inquiries annually, while new agents are supporting work across sales, systems engineering, procurement, finance and accounting. As customer zero, Fujitsu is using Copilot as the front door to a multi-agent work environment and using insights from its own AI adoption to better serve its customers.

KOHLER is using GitHub Copilot to transform software development, with one organization improving code releases by 25% and reducing error defects by 75%. These engineering breakthroughs are part of a broader effort to embed AI processes across the company, spanning IT, finance, marketing, supply chain and operations. Microsoft Copilot has reached 98% adoption, saving an average of 2 to 5 hours per month as employees are making informed decisions and getting answers faster in the flow of their work. Employees across the company have also created more than 3,000 agents to date, with hundreds active daily.

At Krafton, Microsoft Security Copilot and Microsoft Defender XDR are helping the security team respond to a growing volume and complexity of threats. The global gaming company automated key parts of security operations, from alerting and investigation to reporting, combining Microsoft Security solutions with its own systems and data to quickly gather context that helps distinguish real threats from false positives. This approach is having immediate results: security alert recognition time has fallen by approximately 95% to less than one minute, investigation work that previously took tens of minutes now takes about three minutes and roughly 95% of report creation has been automated. By taking on repetitive work, AI is giving Krafton’s security professionals more time to focus on responding to real threats and making critical security decisions.

To accelerate discovery across decades of scientific data, NASA is making complex information easier to explore through Microsoft Copilot. NASA employees are using Copilot to sift through massive amounts of academic literature and streamline daily tasks, and specialized assistants are helping researchers navigate complex Earth science data through natural language, extending access to information that once required significant technical expertise. Hydrology Copilot, for example, can analyze variables like precipitation and soil moisture to help communities better understand water conditions, prepare for droughts and anticipate flood risks, while automatically performing calculations and analyses.

To transform frontline work, Williams, a US natural gas company, is using Microsoft Copilot to help employees spend less time searching documents and completing manual processes, and more time on critical field operations. Copilot helps teams generate plans, interpret procedures, assess regulatory requirements, troubleshoot issues and complete safety reporting, while employees can create agents tailored to their own workflows. Demonstrating that the person closest to a problem is often the best one to solve it, one operations technician built an anomaly detector using Copilot that compares equipment data against baseline statistics and alerts teams to potential issues before they become costly or dangerous. Since deploying Copilot, AI adoption at Williams has grown from single digits to more than 90%, helping employees accelerate operations, improve reporting and compliance and identify equipment issues earlier.

Bristol Myers Squibb has rolled out Microsoft Copilot to 25,000 employees, reaching 96% adoption, and is now putting AI agents to work across everyday use cases such as document review and project management in support of the company’s mission to bring more medicines to more patients faster. One agent, called RABIT, analyzes meeting transcripts, surfaces action items and delivers insights directly within employees’ workflows.

The health system adopted Dragon Copilot, and an early pilot across 420 clinicians found users spent less time on after-hours documentation and reported lower cognitive burden. Building on that experience, Brown University Health deployed Microsoft Copilot and Copilot Studio across departments, which led to the creation of more than 24 AI agents to support clinical workflows, hospital policies, patient access and operations. These AI solutions are not only supporting clinicians in the flow of their work but also helping to improve the patient experience and access to care.

Microsoft IQ compounds and protects your intelligence

More than 300 solutions now run on Eliza, ranging from inquiry management to client onboarding, and 100% of employees have been trained on the platform. Across the bank, that scale is translating into meaningful results: client transaction inquiries are being resolved 80% faster and AI-assisted client onboarding is 20% faster on average. Through the Microsoft CEO Co-Innovation program, BNY also worked with Microsoft to develop an AI research capability with Foundry that investigates complex data issues, analyzes context across multiple sources, identifies likely root causes and recommends next steps, bringing AI-assisted reasoning into processes that have traditionally relied on human investigation alone.

Docusign is helping 1.9 million customers across 180 countries turn agreement data into actionable business insights. The company built an Intelligent Agreement Management platform on Microsoft Azure and used Microsoft Foundry to shift from general-purpose models to a system of task-specific models that better understand context. This change allows Docusign to process more than a million agreement documents in a single day, with up to eightfold greater throughput and 90% lower AI processing costs. Foundry also supports a model lifecycle designed for continuous improvement, where processes are fine-tuned before deployment and monitored in production, while also providing the governance and traceability needed to meet enterprise requirements for compliance, visibility and control. Now agreement content is structured data that compounds from within, so organizations can use it to make decisions and automate workflows, knowing their IP is protected.

Working with Microsoft Frontier Company, Kantar connected its LINK AI platform to its proprietary intelligence, AI models and creative workflows, enabling marketers to evaluate, optimize and generate content before it goes to market. The new approach can process and score large volumes of videos 20x faster while reducing platform operating costs by 4x, helping customers move from insight to action in minutes rather than hours. By bringing its unique intelligence into a continuous loop of observation and improvement, Kantar is creating new ways to help marketers turn insight into better creative and business outcomes.

Kinaxis, a Canadian supply chain software company, runs Maestro, its AI-driven supply chain orchestration platform, on Microsoft Azure. Maestro helps businesses make better decisions faster amid constant disruption. It brings together traditionally disparate business data like sales orders, inventory and production capacity with external signals like weather, market shifts and breaking news to give planners a near real-time view of their supply chains. With this unified data foundation, planners and analysts can use predictive AI and optimization models to anticipate demand shifts, evaluate constraints and recommend action, while generative AI agents act as assistants to ask questions, explore scenarios and automate parts of the planning process. With this intelligence in one platform, businesses can understand how disruptions ripple across their interconnected operations, weigh trade-offs and adjust plans as conditions change.

Through a federated connector built using Model Context Protocol, customers can access live, decision-grade Moody’s intelligence through Researcher in Copilot and within Word, Excel and Teams, without copying or exporting the underlying data. A single question can synthesize information across credit ratings, company financials, ownership information and physical risk models, helping customers reach insights in minutes instead of spending hours or days on research and analysis. This brings trusted, connected intelligence directly into workflows where customers make complex decisions.

To turn conversations into actionable intelligence at global scale, Plaud, an AI hardware and software company, is using Microsoft Azure OpenAI in Foundry Models and Azure Speech in Foundry Tools to power transcription, summarization and AI inference across long-form audio and multilingual scenarios. Serving more than 2 million users worldwide, Plaud increased transcription accuracy and processing speed by 35% and improved inference performance by 30%, helping professionals turn spoken content into structured outputs and insights. Even as its user base doubled, the company used Foundry’s elastic scaling and flexible deployment models to reduce overall compute costs by 35%, while strengthening its ability to meet security, privacy and compliance requirements across global markets.

Rockwell Automation built a Maintenance Copilot using Microsoft Foundry to put decades of manufacturing expertise in the hands of employees. The AI assistant brings together expert knowledge from veteran engineers, manufacturing data and machine manuals, allowing technicians to quickly identify likely causes of equipment issues, see how colleagues have solved similar problems and access step-by-step troubleshooting guidance. At its Singapore factory, the approach has helped reduce machine downtime by 33% and cut servicing and spare-part costs by about 25%. Rockwell estimates it has also reduced the time it takes new workers to learn to troubleshoot hundreds of machines from nine months to three months.

With 1.5 billion passengers riding its elevators and escalators every day, TK Elevator knows that every minute of downtime affects how people move through airports, hospitals and offices. Building on a decade of connected-equipment data on Microsoft Azure, the company created AI agents with Microsoft Foundry that brief service technicians before they enter a building, telling them which elevator, which floor, what the issue is and which tools to bring. After each job, a voice agent records the technician’s account of the work in their own words, with no typing, and adds that expertise to a shared record. With 25,000 technicians caring for 1.4 million units worldwide, TK Elevator is turning each technician’s know-how into compounded intelligence every colleague can draw on.

Telstra partnered with Microsoft Frontier Company to deploy an AI-powered Migration Payment Agent that helps simplify one of the most complex aspects of customer migration: reconciling billing and payments across legacy and new platforms. The agent uses intelligence across these systems to proactively identify inconsistencies, recommend corrective actions and create enriched cases for human review, combining AI-driven insights with human-in-the-loop validation to maintain operational trust and governance. Already supporting more than 272,000 service migrations and delivering recommendations at 95%+ accuracy in production, the solution demonstrates how Telstra is applying agentic AI at enterprise scale to transform complex operations, improve customer outcomes and build reusable AI capabilities while compounding and protecting Telstra’s operational intelligence.

Agent 365 observes AI solutions across the stack

With Microsoft Azure and Microsoft Foundry supporting its global enterprise AI platform, Manulife is building a foundation for teams to develop and deploy AI and agentic solutions while maintaining standards for quality, security and cost efficiency. With agentic solutions and AI-powered workflows already in production, Manulife is creating the foundation to scale AI responsibly across its global operations and accelerate its next phase of enterprise transformation.

Insight Enterprises, a leading solutions integrator and top Microsoft partner, is using Microsoft Agent 365 to govern AI agents at scale. As a Microsoft customer zero organization for Agent 365, Insight Enterprises is quick to adopt new capabilities internally and pass those learnings on to clients. With Microsoft engineering, it tested how Microsoft and third-party agents could be observed, managed, governed and secured through a unified control plane. To date, Insight Enterprises has discovered 9,734 agents with visibility into which are active, what data they can access and how to monitor their activity over time. The experience has helped Insight Enterprises build practical AI governance expertise it can bring to customers, including organizations in highly regulated industries.

Title: Hackers Infect 953 Online Stores With Scanner-Evading Code
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Attackers have infected 953 online stores, mostly running Magento, with a JavaScript loader that has evolved to tell security scanners apart from real shoppers.

The campaign has been active since July 2025 and has cycled through five loader domains, according to research from Dutch e-commerce security firm Sansec. Its latest domain, registered October 6, was found in the content management system (CMS) blocks of 83 stores, 60 of which had carried an earlier version of the loader.

The loader is stored in Magento's cms_block database table and has visitors' browsers fetch instructions from the attackers. Sansec said the server first works out whether a request comes from a genuine customer or a security scanner, and gives scanners nothing.

Latest Loader Filters Security Scanners

Before October, the operator relied on the Keitaro traffic distribution system to choose, for each visitor, between delivering a payload, redirecting the browser and returning nothing.

The loader Sansec first found on October 7 instead called the new domain directly and replayed code saved in the browser, so anyone served the payload would rerun it on later page loads, even with the domain down or blocked.

An October 23 rewrite added browser fingerprinting, checking for signs of browser automation and collecting hardware details, screen size, time zone and language before the server chose its response.

When scanning service urlscan.io loaded an infected store in an automated browser, Sansec found no injected content. The company has yet to obtain the final payload, so the campaign's ultimate purpose remains unclear.

Read more on malicious JavaScript in online stores: Global Magecart Campaign Targets Six Card Networks

Patches Did Not Always Stop Reinfection

Sansec said a March wave planted the loader on 471 stores within an hour, using webshells placed through PolyShell (CVE-2026-48356). Among 169 infected Magento 2 installations lacking at least one core patch, 102 showed evidence of file uploads via PolyShell or SessionReaper (CVE-2025-54236).

Patching alone did not prevent reinfection. A fully patched store running Magento 2.4.7-p10 picked up the newest loader on October 23, an hour after passing a clean scan. Sansec had spotted a rogue admin account and a GSocket backdoor on the store in September.

Sansec advised merchants to look for the loader in CMS content, review admin accounts and hunt for backdoors, rotate database, admin and integration credentials once the store is clean and apply the latest Magento and Adobe Commerce security updates.

It warned that removing the script leaves an attacker's write access to the database intact, so a compromised store can be reinfected while the original way in remains.

Title: OpenAI Compaction Flaw Exposed AI Reasoning to Researchers
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Researchers have discovered a flaw in OpenAI's application programming interface (API) that allowed them to extract raw reasoning traces from its frontier models, exposing information OpenAI normally withholds from API users.

AI vulnerability discovery firm Xint disclosed the technique, dubbed 'compaction smuggling,' in research published October 26. According to Xint, OpenAI confirmed the issue, deployed a fix on October 23 and paid a $6000 bug bounty.

The flaw involved OpenAI's context compaction feature, which uses a model to compress a lengthy conversation into an encrypted item the user cannot read.

Xint found it could hide one model's reasoning inside a compaction and have another model hand it back.

Compaction Bypass Exposed Hidden Reasoning

OpenAI gives API users optional summaries rather than the raw chain of thought behind its reasoning models' answers. Xint said this is partly to prevent distillation, because raw reasoning, which shows abandoned approaches and corrections, makes much richer training data than final answers.

OpenAI added mitigations in August after the Stolen Thoughts paper showed that a frontier model's encrypted reasoning could be fed to a less capable model from the same company, an attack that affected Anthropic, OpenAI and Google.

Xint said those mitigations stopped reasoning being replayed into other models but did not cover compaction, which ran on the model that had produced the reasoning.

Xint generated reasoning with GPT-5.6 Sol, compacted it and asked the older GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o models to repeat their input word for word, from which it recovered the reasoning. It said the attack succeeded at every reasoning-effort setting it tested.

Read more: OpenCode Breach Could Affect OpenAI, Anthropic and Google

Compaction and Distillation Concerns Remain

The flaw was discovered by Xint in August and OpenAI's fix was not publicly described. The Xint post did not include a statement from OpenAI. Infosecurity has contacted OpenAI for comment.

Compaction has raised separate concerns for OpenAI and in a September report the company said that during training of an internal, unreleased model, the model had in rare cases written unauthorized instructions into its own compaction summaries, including one instructing the model to ignore developer messages.

Xint argued that the technique opened the door to distilling OpenAI's frontier models at scale, though it did not report training a model on the reasoning it extracted. It said the risk was real, citing an Anthropic report in September of seven distillation campaigns it attributed to China-based labs and OpenAI's September 30 disclosure that it had broken up an effort to pull hidden reasoning from its models.

Full Text:
After years of tracking the global cybersecurity skills gap through its annual Cybersecurity Workforce Study, ISC2 is taking a more active role in shaping the future of the profession with the launch of its Cyber-AI Workforce Coalition.

Announced on October 20, the new coalition is one of the first major developments introduced by Scott Beale, ISC2’s CEO, who took on the role in December 2025.

Speaking to Infosecurity during the ISC2 Security Congress 2026, in Denver, Colorado, on October 26, Beale said he spent his first six months as CEO listening to the organization’s members.

A key finding from the consultation was that a majority of ISC2 members want the nonprofit to more ambitiously and vocally step into the AI safety and security space.

“We want to be the association that can help prepare the cybersecurity workforce for the many challenges of this AI era,” Beale added.

Mapping the AI Security Workforce and Its Emerging Skills Gap

Beale described the coalition as a “vendor-neutral convener” for global cybersecurity professionals. It aims to include thought leaders like HR managers and CISOs, some of the largest employers of cybersecurity practitioners, standard-setting bodies and even government representatives to discuss how cybersecurity roles are changing because of AI.

“Even as the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and others are updating standards and frameworks, companies are still facing a lack of resources for how to best advertise and fill these roles. How a bank describes these jobs is still very different from how a hospital would,” Beale said.

Hiring needs at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity remain uncertain, according to Beale. There remain unanswered questions about how AI will affect future demand for cybersecurity professionals, which skills will be most critical for AI security roles, and how experienced practitioners can upskill to meet emerging demands.

“The coalition a way for us to listen directly to these people and help move the sector in a way that can be responsive to their needs,” he said.

Practical Tools to Define and Hire for AI Security Roles

In practice, the coalition will not create new standards or frameworks but will instead focus on delivering toolkits for employers to help them describe new job roles at the intersection of AI and cybersecurity.

These toolkits will include guidance for how employers hire, develop and organize cybersecurity talent, and how practitioners can identify and build the expertise employers need.

These new tools will help answer three main questions:

How are cybersecurity jobs changing?

How are employers writing job descriptions for these new roles?

How are candidates preparing to interview and fill these jobs?

“As you know, ISC2 is working on a new AI security certification, and certainly we think It is going to be part of that answer and will help us define some of these new roles,” he said. “However, by no means do we pretend having the only solution to this problem.”

The coalition will hold its first meeting in November. Beale hopes it can develop its first series of toolkits by the spring of 2027 and have some companies using them in a pilot phase to help them hire AI security professionals.

The tools produced by the coalition are expected to eventually be made available for everyone to use, not just ISC2 members. Beale believes they will also be useful for universities and certification bodies to adapt their curriculums.

Title: The Impact of AI on CVEs: INDUSTRY CHALLENGES

Full Text:
Integrating artificial intelligence into cybersecurity has fundamentally changed vulnerability research – and not necessarily for the better. For decades, discovering and verifying Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) required deep technical expertise, creating a disciplined process that kept disclosure volume relatively manageable. Today, Generative AI has obliterated that barrier to entry.

While AI empowers seasoned security researchers to uncover complex zero-days at unprecedented speeds, it simultaneously enables a flood of low-effort, AI-generated vulnerability reports. The result is a fractured ecosystem struggling to stay afloat. The signal-to-noise ratio in vulnerability intelligence is plummeting, open-source maintainers are drowning in hallucinated “slop“, and foundational institutions like the American National Vulnerability Database (NVD) are buckling under the sheer volume of submissions.

In Part 1 of this series, we explore how the AI era has weaponized scale in CVE research. We examine the real-world toll on maintainers, the growing danger of severity inflation, the rise of fabricated security advisories, and the cost of keeping up with it all.

The CVE Surge in Numbers

The JFrog security research team has collected data about CVEs published since 2021. Below is a graph showing the steadily climbing increase in the volume of CVEs in recent years.

Due to AI the volume of CVEs is growing at an alarming rate

The data shows a sharp increase in total CVEs, driven by two AI-related trends: experienced security researchers can now identify vulnerabilities faster and more easily, while lower skilled researchers can leverage AI to bypass traditional technical barriers, flooding systems with noise and real CVEs alike.

This surge caused major changes in how CVEs are being assessed and the quality of those assessments.

The Boy Who Cried Wolf

In January 2026, the consequences of this growing verification burden culminated in a stark milestone: Daniel Stenberg, creator of the widely used curl utility, announced the end of the project’s bug bounty program. According to Stenberg, an explosion of AI-generated submissions in 2025 contributed to a flood of invalid reports, and the share of submissions confirmed as vulnerabilities fell below 5%.

Just six months later, Michael Catanzaro, then the security coordinator for the GNOME project, announced changes to the GNOME security tracking system. Catanzaro stated he would no longer forward security reports to GNOME maintainers who had explicitly opted out of receiving AI-generated content. Because the overwhelming majority of incoming reports in 2026 utilized LLMs, he explained, the project was forced to operate under the assumption that the overwhelming majority of vulnerability reports now contain AI-generated material. To manage this new reality, Catanzaro also slashed GNOME’s vulnerability disclosure deadline from 90 days to 30 for issues reported on or after August 1, 2026. Noting that some other projects, notably the Linux kernel, have implemented an immediate full disclosure policy for reports that seem to be AI-generated, GNOME adopted the shortened window as a compromise to accelerate the pipeline without crushing maintainers.

The National Vulnerability Database’s Policy Change

The deluge of CVEs has also led NIST to change how it prioritizes NVD analysis. In an April 2026 announcement on NVD operations, NIST said that starting April 15, 2026, it would prioritize CVEs in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog, software used by the federal government, and critical software. NIST also moved backlogged CVEs published before March 1, 2026 to “Not Scheduled.” In our view, this leaves many published CVEs without NVD enrichment and pushes more of the verification burden onto enterprise security teams.

AI Shortens the Path from Disclosure to Exploitation

AI is not only accelerating vulnerability discovery; it is also reducing the time and expertise required to turn vulnerability information into a working exploit. In one May 2026 case involving CVE-2026-46529, which affects GNOME’s Evince document viewer and its forks, a researcher used Claude to help develop a weaponized, single-click code-execution exploit. Controlled research from PoCGen and Anthropic has demonstrated similar capabilities, showing how attackers could exploit the period between public disclosure and widespread patching.

Severity Inflation

Not every vulnerability labeled Critical represents a critical real-world threat. Severity inflation occurs when a rating is based on a theoretical or reasonable worst-case outcome without adequately accounting for the conditions required to enable it in the wild.

These conditions may include whether the vulnerable code is exposed, whether an optional feature is enabled, whether a particular configuration is present, or whether exploitation requires an unlikely sequence of events.

Annual number of CVEs segmented into Critical, High, and other severities

This distinction is built into CVSS itself. The official FIRST CVSS v4.0 User Guide states that CVSS Base scores are designed to measure the severity of a vulnerability and should not be used alone to assess risk. Nevertheless, scanners, dashboards, and remediation policies frequently treat the Base score as a universal measure of urgency.

At JFrog, we provide additional, proprietary, research-backed severity assessments, allowing customers to prioritize vulnerabilities and define policies using trusted JFrog severity scores instead of relying solely on external Base scores.

The Cost of Scoring at Scale

The scale described earlier matters because vulnerability assessment does not expand automatically with vulnerability volume. Each score may require reviewing the affected code, reproducing the issue, inspecting its fix, and understanding how the component is deployed.

When thousands of records must be processed quickly, assessors may instead rely on short CVE descriptions, the general vulnerability class, or default worst-case assumptions. Volume alone does not make a score incorrect, but it increases the likelihood that important technical details might be missed.

Severity Dissonance: The curl Case

A clear illustration of severity inflation emerged in a recent four-month window involving the libcurl project. Since June, the maintainers have published 27 CVEs with assessed security impacts ranging from Low to Medium. However, when CISA evaluated these same vulnerabilities, nearly all were escalated to High or Critical scores.

When the JFrog Security Research team investigated this striking dissonance, we found that the assigned CVSS vectors had failed to reflect the vulnerabilities’ technical reality. For instance, flaws assigned Critical scores were often merely client-side crashes or required niche client configurations outside an attacker’s control. In several cases, client-side use-after-free bugs were miscategorized as network-based memory corruption threats, resulting in a Critical rating that, in our assessment, did not reflect the actual attack vector and practical security impact.

Faux CVEs: The Rise of AI Generated Slop

Generative AI is remarkably adept at mimicking the authoritative tone, formatting, and technical jargon required for a security advisory. The result is a growing wave of slop vulnerabilities that sound terrifying but either do not exist at all or are nowhere near as severe as they are presented.

Case Study: The SQLite Slop Advisories

A clear example of this systemic breakdown is the research we published at JFrog in July 2026 regarding a wave of critical advisories. A newly created GitHub repository published over 50 security advisories, a batch containing reports targeting SQLite alongside various other open source projects. The reports appeared polished and authoritative, detailing complex Use After Free (UAF) memory corruption flaws. They were swiftly assigned high CVSS scores, up to 9.8 Critical, and CISA’s ADP program agreed..

However, when our security researchers analyzed the target codebases to verify the claims, the reports completely fell apart. The technical details appear to have been hallucinated by an LLM:

Nonexistent code: The advisories cited functions like exprComputeOperands() and jsonBlobEdit() that were not present in the targeted SQLite versions.

Impossible line numbers: One advisory pointed to a vulnerability at line 3555 in a file containing only 2706 lines.

Ghost fixes: Another claimed a fix was committed in a newer release, but source diffs showed zero changes to the referenced files.

Because the current CVE pipeline is overwhelmed by volume and does not require a working POC before scores are issued, these reports slide directly into downstream feeds. Out of 55 advisories published by that account, 54 were completely fabricated, yet reports like these can flow into GHSA, enterprise scanners, and developer alerts.

The Cost of Keeping Up

When a Flood of Fixes Arrives

The pressure becomes especially clear when a large number of fixes arrive together. According to Oracle, its July 2026 Critical Patch Update, its largest security release to date, addressed 1,434 distinct CVEs with 1,449 patches across 334 products. Oracle attributed the scale partly to AI-powered identification of actionable security findings. For customers, however, receiving more fixes does not make deploying them any simpler. Each organization still has to identify the affected systems, decide what is most urgent, test the relevant updates, and fit them into its release schedule.

AI is also uncovering bugs that were not detected even after years of conventional research. A security agent developed by depthfirst reported 21 zero-day vulnerabilities in FFmpeg, several of which had remained in the code for 15 to 20 years despite extensive fuzzing and manual review.

The Gap Between Discovery and Patching

AI can find vulnerabilities faster than developers can fix them. As AI increases the number of findings entering remediation queues, maintainers still have to verify each report, understand which versions are affected, develop and test a reliable fix, and prepare a release. Those steps do not become faster simply because discovery does. Rushing them can produce an incomplete patch or introduce new problems.

CISA has connected this pressure directly to AI-assisted discovery, stating that AI is vastly increasing the pace at which new vulnerabilities are found while defenders are already struggling to keep up. According to Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, as cited by CISA, , organizations fully remediated only 26% of vulnerabilities in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog during 2025, down from 38% the previous year, while the median time for full resolution rose to 43 days. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre has issued a similar warning, saying that AI-assisted discovery could create a vulnerability patch wave, with an influx of updates across all severity levels that organizations will need to deploy more frequently and at greater scale. Together, these sources show the practical effect of higher volume: even when teams improve their processes, a larger queue can still leave fixes waiting longer.

Stay Tuned…

AI has increased both speed and uncertainty across the CVE ecosystem. Finding vulnerabilities is no longer the only challenge, as verifying, prioritizing, and fixing those that pose a genuine risk has become equally important. In Part 2 of this series, The Impact of the AI-Era on CVE Research: PROTECTION STRATEGIES, we recommend best practices, demonstrate JFrog’s AI-assisted libheif exploit chain and show how JFrog Xray and JFrog Advanced Security help teams assess their actual exposure.

To gain a better understanding of how JFrog provides additional, proprietary, research-backed severity assessments, schedule a demo with our team.

Title: Process trees in Livehunt: YARA rules that know who launched what
Context: For a lot of detections that is the whole point: PowerShell on its own is noise, PowerShell launched by mshta
Full Text:
Note: YARA-X v1.21.0 adds a parent_name field to the items in vt.behaviour.processes_list, and v1.22.0 adds ancestor_names. VirusTotal now fills that list for every sandbox report that includes a process tree, by flattening it. The result is one entry per process, and each entry knows the name of the process that created it and of the processes above it. Read the YARA-X blog.

If you have written Livehunt rules on top of sandbox behavior, you have probably used vt.behaviour.processes_created. It is a flat list of command lines. It tells you that mshta.exe ran and that powershell.exe ran, but not that one started the other. For a lot of detections that is the whole point: PowerShell on its own is noise, PowerShell launched by mshta.exe is not.

Our sandboxes have always recorded the full process tree. The problem was getting it into YARA, which has no recursive types. As of this month, every file with sandbox reports that reaches Livehunt carries vt.behaviour.processes_list: one entry per process, from every sandbox that ran the file, and each entry knows the name of its parent, the names of its ancestors, and the files it touched.

This post covers what is in each entry, what to keep in mind when writing rules against it, and five cases we worked through while preparing it, each with the rules we wrote and tested. Every case comes with at least one hash, so you can paste the rule in the Livehunt editor and test it yourself.

If you haven't read it yet, we recommend our earlier post It's all about the structure! Creating YARA rules by clicking. It shows how to open the Structure view of any file in the Livehunt editor and turn fields into rule conditions with a click, which is handy for everything that follows.

What each process entry carries

Field

Type

What it holds

name

string

The process, as the sandbox reports it. Usually the image path plus the command line.

parent_name

string

The name of the process that created this one. Empty for root processes and when the parent is unknown.

ancestor_names

array of strings

The names of its ancestors, nearest first: ancestor_names[0] is the parent (the same as parent_name), ancestor_names[1] the grandparent, and so on. Empty for root processes and when the parent is unknown.

process_id / parent_process_id

string

PIDs, as reported by the sandbox.

start_time / termination_time

integer

When the process started and ended, if known.

files_written

array of strings

Files this process created or modified.

files_opened

array of strings

Files this process opened.

files_deleted

array of strings

Files this process deleted.

files_copied[x].source / .destination

string

Files this process copied, when the sandbox attributes copies to a process.

The fields that change how you write rules are parent_name, ancestor_names and the per-process file lists. With them, "PowerShell wrote a .dll" becomes "the PowerShell that cmd.exe started wrote a .dll".

The simplest possible rule looks like this:

import "vt" rule cmd_spawns_schtasks_create { condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( p.name icontains "schtasks" and p.name icontains "/create" and p.parent_name icontains "cmd.exe" ) }

Things to know before you write rules

Names are not normalized. Each sandbox writes process names its own way. CAPE gives the quoted command line, Zenbox prepends the image path to the command line, Tencent HABO gives only the executable name, and C2AE and Microsoft Sysinternals often leave environment variables unexpanded (%ComSpec% /c ...). Use icontains and match on the executable name, not on a full path with == or startswith.

Link processes by name, not by PID. A file is usually run by several sandboxes, and Livehunt puts all their processes in the same list. PID 1040 can be cmd.exe in one report and explorer.exe in another. To go more than one level up, use ancestor_names: it is built from each sandbox report on its own, so a chain never mixes processes from different sandboxes. For long chains, you can also climb by name: look for the entry whose name is equal to the parent_name you already have. Both strings come from the same sandbox report, so an exact == is safe there.

A practical workflow is to search first and write the rule second. Intelligence search already supports behavior_processes:"<command line>", which matches anywhere in the list with no hierarchy. It is a quick way to collect candidates. Then you write the rule with the parent condition, and test it against those hashes in the Livehunt editor.

Case 1: porting a Sigma rule, and what it misses

Sigma's Suspicious MSHTA Child Process (03cc0c25-389f-4bf8-b48d-11878079f1ca) is a good example of a detection that needs the parent. Stripped down, it says: the parent image ends with \mshta.exe and the child is a shell or a scripting host.

detection: selection_parent: ParentImage|endswith: '\mshta.exe' selection_child: - Image|endswith: - '\cmd.exe' - '\powershell.exe' - '\pwsh.exe' - '\wscript.exe' - '\cscript.exe' - '\sh.exe' - '\bash.exe' - '\reg.exe' - '\regsvr32.exe' - '\bitsadmin.exe' condition: all of selection*

The Livehunt version maps ParentImage to parent_name and Image to name:

import "vt" rule mshta_spawns_shell { meta: description = "Port of Sigma 03cc0c25 (Suspicious MSHTA Child Process)" condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( p.parent_name icontains "mshta.exe" and ( p.name icontains "cmd.exe" or p.name icontains "powershell" or p.name icontains "pwsh" or p.name icontains "wscript" or p.name icontains "cscript" or p.name icontains "bash.exe" or p.name icontains "reg.exe" or p.name icontains "regsvr32" or p.name icontains "bitsadmin" ) ) }

One thing does not carry over. Sigma also checks OriginalFileName to catch renamed binaries, and sandbox process names have no equivalent. A renamed mshta.exe will get past this rule.

We tested it against d30a0a6c09f664446943d82982f0630e85c447cbe84be8a74b6db6d66effbe80, an Excel file named NOVI USD 44570.00 952PLA3262852510.xls (18/76, tagged cve-2017-0199). It matches. What is more interesting is the CAPE process tree behind the match:

Process

Parent

EXCEL.EXE "...\attachment.xls" /dde

Explorer.EXE

mshta.exe -Embedding

svchost.exe -k DcomLaunch -p

cmd.exe "/c POwERSHeLl.Exe ... -EX BypaSS -nOp -w 1 -ec ..."

mshta.exe -Embedding

POwERSHeLl.Exe ... -ec ...

cmd.exe

WScript.exe "...\AppData\Roaming\westingcostringforme.vbe"

POwERSHeLl.Exe

powershell.exe -nop -ep bypass -file "C:\Temp\XBRYINEZ.ps1"

WScript.exe

aspnet_compiler.exe

powershell.exe -file ...XBRYINEZ.ps1

Excel is not the parent of mshta.exe. The exploit has Office request an object through DCOM, so mshta.exe is started by the DCOM launcher service, and it shows up with -Embedding. A rule that looks for "Office spawns mshta" would never fire on this document. What we can do is walk one level up from the shell and check the grandparent:

import "vt" rule dcom_mshta_spawns_shell { condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( (p.name icontains "cmd.exe" or p.name icontains "powershell") and p.parent_name icontains "mshta.exe" and p.ancestor_names[1] icontains "svchost.exe" and p.ancestor_names[1] icontains "dcomlaunch" ) }

The first entry of ancestor_names is always the parent, so ancestor_names[1] is the grandparent: the process that started mshta.exe. Without it, you need a second loop over the list to find the entry whose name is the shell's parent_name, and one more loop for every extra level.

The same rule matches other spreadsheets from the same wave, for example 8d249972358268b7a00e182e3f1ecf93ec8bbbee65d22ef4d8a3c382783c1cfa (PO#3302-20260520002.xls), 2d199776cc50b9ad548132105e95af86b29ec8ebca03895a7ddecde58587306b (Request Quotation.xls) and 7c8a3c8366b3106db56359e3defc654d365ce4de21d0a7b1fbad02fbb2aeae52. The rest of that chain shows up again in cases 4 and 5.

Case 2: a services.exe that is not, and the copies behind it

On a normal Windows system, services.exe is started by wininit.exe and by nothing else. A services.exe with any other parent deserves a look:

import "vt" rule fake_services_wrong_parent { condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( p.name iendswith "\\services.exe" and p.parent_name != "" and not p.parent_name icontains "wininit.exe" ) }

The parent_name != "" check matters. In the reports we looked at, the real services.exe shows up as a root process with no parent, and we don't want those to match.

Our first version also covered lsass.exe. We tested it against 43 recent, clean, signed files, and it matched 19 of them. In those reports the sandbox records lsass.exe with services.exe as its parent. Whatever the reason, that is what the data says, so we dropped lsass.exe from the rule. The lesson is a general one: before encoding what the parent "should" be, check what the sandboxes actually report for clean files.

The rule matches fe8357febe314becf31510a7a2ecb0369e312ad58a448292f5f8a09075d7694c, a .NET executable (45/76) submitted as Cd5KK.exe. In the Jujubox report, Cd5KK.exe starts C:\Windows\System32\NlsLexicons0c1a\services.exe. That process writes two .vbs files to %TEMP% and runs each one with WScript.exe, and one of the scripts starts the fake services.exe again. The sample also launches one PowerShell per path to add Defender exclusions, and in the CAPE report it creates ONLOGON scheduled tasks through WMI, with wmiprvse.exe as the parent of schtasks.exe.

Where did the fake services.exe come from? Jujubox does not attribute file copies to a process, but it does report them at the summary level, in vt.behaviour.files_copied. Cd5KK.exe copied itself to eight places, each one with the name of a Windows binary:

C:\Windows\System32\NlsLexicons0c1a\services.exe C:\System Volume Information\services.exe C:\Windows\system\smss.exe C:\Windows\System32\mfc42\taskeng.exe C:\Users\Default User\WmiPrvSE.exe C:\Program Files\Common Files\System\ado\en-US\WmiPrvSE.exe C:\PerfLogs\Admin\sysmon.exe C:\Users\<USER>\Downloads\patchregistry\event-stream.exe

You can combine both fields. This rule looks for a copy named after a system process, and then for a process in the list that runs from exactly that path and has a parent:

import "vt" rule copy_with_system_name_is_executed { condition: for any c in vt.behaviour.files_copied : ( ( c.destination iendswith "\\services.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\smss.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\lsass.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\csrss.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\svchost.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\wmiprvse.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\taskhostw.exe" or c.destination iendswith "\\conhost.exe" ) and for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( p.name icontains c.destination and p.parent_name != "" ) ) }

The copy proves the file was planted, and the process entry proves it ran. We tested the rule against 30 recent files with a services.exe path in their Jujubox file activity: it matched 9 of them, among them 4930cc4e7e3e258bf2815793f0e5698bdd45adfae8e052bb1dc4c05c6689ade6, which shares the trojan.msil/basic label with Cd5KK.exe and also matches the services.exe parent rule above. It did not match any of the 43 clean files.

Case 3: headless consoles, renamed or not

conhost.exe --headless runs a console program without showing a window. Sigma has a rule that looks for --headless and powershell in the conhost.exe command line. With the parent available, we can ask a slightly different question: did a PowerShell process actually start with a headless console as its parent?

import "vt" rule headless_console_runs_powershell { condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( (p.name icontains "powershell" or p.name icontains "pwsh") and p.parent_name icontains "--headless" ) }

A plain search shows why a rule on the command line alone gets noisy. behavior_processes:"conhost.exe --headless" fs:2026-09-01+ returned 947 files when we ran it. Part of that is legitimate software. Terminal emulators use pseudo-consoles, which start conhost.exe --headless --inheritcursor ... --server .... herdr.exe (c18555a6bb74cd021198b57d16b93b40e74e7d0f8f0c28a45f0a4cc22dea0f8b, 0/76) does exactly that, and the rule above does not match it, because that conhost.exe never starts a shell.

On the malicious side, 5c2ceaec797dfa79e81cde6d765898ee8102357e280fa322db6e5a4b0ce3fc4a is a Windows shortcut with a Korean-language lure about penalty guidelines for e-commerce law violations, named with a double .hwp.lnk extension (34/76). CAPE and Jujubox both show the same chain: opening the shortcut starts conhost.exe --headless powershell.exe -NoP -exec BYpass -w 1 -C $rukp = '...', and that console starts the PowerShell that runs the Base64 blob. The decoded script opens with a function called Invoke-EnvironmentCheck.

Notice that the rule checks for --headless in the parent, not for conhost.exe. That is deliberate. 77da8a02d71078564409863c358a544e981b9643c8f50c1daabc5d5d176e3c75 (42/76) drops a file called rhpmx63snl.exe into %APPDATA%\MicrosoftWorker_e08ec640d\. That file is 51bb5aeef2e48dd14fae764f80dc67f516df9914ea9c350329e229f6cea919a2, an unmodified Microsoft conhost.exe (original name CONHOST.EXE, 0/77) with a random name. It later runs as rhpmx63snl.exe --headless powershell.exe -w h -ep bypass -c & "...\xd24mgasgb4.exe". A rule that required conhost.exe in the parent would miss it. If you only want the renamed case, add not p.parent_name icontains "conhost".

Case 4: persistence that actually ran

Spotting schtasks /create is easy. Knowing whether the task did anything during the analysis is harder, and the process list can answer it. When a scheduled task fires, the new process has the Task Scheduler service as its parent (svchost.exe -k netsvcs -p -s Schedule, or taskeng.exe on older systems). If that process runs a file the sample wrote earlier, the persistence worked.

import "vt" rule task_scheduler_runs_dropped_file { condition: for any run in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( ( run.parent_name icontains "-s schedule" or run.parent_name icontains "taskeng.exe" ) and for any dropper in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( for any f in dropper.files_written : ( (f iendswith ".exe" or f iendswith ".dll" or f iendswith ".vbs" or f iendswith ".js" or f iendswith ".ps1" or f iendswith ".bat" or f iendswith ".cmd") and run.name icontains f ) ) ) }

This is the first rule in the post that uses files_written, and it uses it to link two processes that are not parent and child: the one that wrote the file, and the one the scheduler started from it.

Back to 77da8a02d71078564409863c358a544e981b9643c8f50c1daabc5d5d176e3c75. In the CAPE report, software.exe writes rhpmx63snl.exe and xd24mgasgb4.exe to %APPDATA%\MicrosoftWorker_e08ec640d\, and then runs:

schtasks.exe /create /sc minute /mo 1 /tn "AdobeSecurityManager" /tr "C:\Users\<USER>\AppData\Roaming\MicrosoftWorker_e08ec640d\rhpmx63snl.exe --headless powershell.exe -w h -ep bypass -c & '...\xd24mgasgb4.exe'"

When the task fires, the scheduler starts rhpmx63snl.exe (the renamed conhost.exe from case 3), which starts PowerShell, which starts xd24mgasgb4.exe. Every link in that sentence is a parent_name, and the rule matches. The whole chain is also in the ancestor_names of xd24mgasgb4.exe: the PowerShell, rhpmx63snl.exe, the Schedule service and services.exe.

Zenbox saw the same task fire, but reported rhpmx63snl.exe as a root process with no parent. That is fine: CAPE has the link, and the rule only needs one sandbox to see it. It also shows why you shouldn't write rules that need every sandbox to agree.

One more format issue we ran into. a549a6c8c01da1d03e8da663eec70997a5bd5207e665d8e23f6fa75804dafc06, a VBS file we use in the next case, also creates a task that fires during the VMRay analysis, with taskeng.exe as the parent. The rule misses it, because VMRay logged that command line with doubled backslashes (C:\\Users\\Public\\Downloads\\PoItWjNFjv.vbs), so the path in files_written is not a substring of the process name. When a rule should match and does not, check the raw strings first. Here ancestor_names gives a check that does not depend on how paths are written: the task runs wscript.exe with the dropped script, the script starts PowerShell, and taskeng.exe is among that PowerShell's ancestors. A PowerShell process with for any a in p.ancestor_names : (a icontains "taskeng.exe") catches it.

Case 5: .NET binaries reading browser credentials

Loaders often inject the final payload into a signed .NET Framework binary such as MSBuild.exe, RegAsm.exe, RegSvcs.exe, InstallUtil.exe or aspnet_compiler.exe. On their own, these processes are normal on a developer machine. Started by PowerShell or a scripting host, and writing temporary copies of browser credential databases, they are not.

import "vt" rule dotnet_lolbin_touches_browser_logins { condition: for any p in vt.behaviour.processes_list : ( ( p.name icontains "aspnet_compiler.exe" or p.name icontains "regasm.exe" or p.name icontains "regsvcs.exe" or p.name icontains "msbuild.exe" or p.name icontains "installutil.exe" or p.name icontains "addinprocess" ) and for any a in p.ancestor_names : ( a icontains "powershell" or a icontains "wscript" or a icontains "cscript" or a icontains "mshta" ) and for any f in p.files_written : ( f icontains "\\User Data\\" and (f icontains "\\Login Data" or f icontains "\\Web Data" or f icontains "\\Cookies") ) ) }

All three conditions apply to the same process: what it is, what is above it, and what it wrote. That is the difference from the flat fields. behaviour_files:"Login Data" together with behavior_processes:"MSBuild.exe" can match a file where those two things happened in unrelated processes.

The rule matches a549a6c8c01da1d03e8da663eec70997a5bd5207e665d8e23f6fa75804dafc06, a VBS file named RFQ_638O-0194RFQ26_202610070614034439RFQ.vbs (14/76). In the CAPE report, a hidden PowerShell that rebuilds its script from environment variables is started through WMI (its parent is wmiprvse.exe), and that PowerShell starts MSBuild.exe, which writes ...\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Login Data.tmp and the matching -wal and -shm files. It also matches the Excel file from case 1, d30a0a6c09f664446943d82982f0630e85c447cbe84be8a74b6db6d66effbe80, where the last process in the chain, aspnet_compiler.exe, writes the same files. In that file, the ancestor_names of aspnet_compiler.exe go all the way back to the exploit: the PowerShell running XBRYINEZ.ps1, WScript.exe, the obfuscated PowerShell, cmd.exe and mshta.exe -Embedding.

Checking the ancestors instead of only the parent matters in 2d199776cc50b9ad548132105e95af86b29ec8ebca03895a7ddecde58587306b, the Request Quotation.xls from case 1. There, the process that writes the Chrome and Edge Login Data and Web Data files is a second aspnet_compiler.exe, started with /stext by the first one. Its parent is aspnet_compiler.exe, so a rule that only looks at parent_name misses it, while the PowerShell and WScript.exe above it are its second and third ancestors. On the 420 malicious and 324 clean files we used to measure ancestor_names, this version matched 5 malicious files that the parent-only version missed, and none of the clean ones.

Testing the rules

Everything in this post was tested two ways. First, against the hashes above and against a set of clean files, using the Livehunt rule tester. The tester rebuilds the vt module for the hash you give it, so it works for files analyzed before these fields existed. Second, in a live Livehunt ruleset with all the rules. Within a few minutes of enabling it we were already getting notifications for mshta_spawns_shell, dcom_mshta_spawns_shell, task_scheduler_runs_dropped_file and others. The ancestor_names versions of the rules were also run with YARA-X 1.22.0 against the same hashes and 324 clean files.

Wrapping up

A command line tells you what ran. Its parent and ancestors tell you how it got there, and the files it wrote tell you what it left behind. Rules that join the two are harder for a sample to sidestep, because the operator would need to change the chain, not just the strings. Open the vt module view of any file you are investigating, find the processes_list entry that bothers you, and write the rule from there.

Happy hunting!

Title: Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Threat actors are abusing Microsoft Teams’ external chat creation feature to target employees for initial access into organizations, new research by Arctic Wolf has found.

The researchers said they had observed over 400 incidents in which the function was abused, with “highly consistent” IT-support impersonation tactics deployed by the malicious actors.

The attack chain is rapid, with payload execution reached in under 15 minutes from when a victim engages with the initial social engineering message.

The attackers often target multiple victims within short windows of time, which suggests the use of automation.

“Across the activity examined, attackers combined email bombing, convincing IT-support impersonation, newly created tenants and domains, and rapid social engineering to move victims from a seemingly routine chat to remote access, payload execution, and, in some cases, broader compromise,” the Arctic Wolf researchers wrote in the report published on October 26, 2026.

The researchers did not identify the perpetrators behind these attacks. However, it noted that the use of the external Teams chat as an initial access vector has been a tactic deployed by ransomware groups including Black Basta.

Threat Actors Establish Legitimate-Looking Teams Identities

Arctic Wolf noted that the external Microsoft Teams chat function has become an effective platform to launch social engineering, with attackers able to make themselves appear legitimate to users.

Teams’ external access is turned on by default, meaning any Teams user in another Microsoft 365 tenant can find, chat with, and call an organization’s employees, provided both tenants allow external access.

In the observed incidents, the threat actors established external Teams identities through newly created or acquired Microsoft 365 tenants. Between 30-40% of the cases involved default onmicrosoft[.]com tenant domains, which do not require verification and can be provisioned within minutes.

The attackers typically selected a support-, IT-, admin-, network-, or helpdesk-themed word as the tenant name, optionally suffixed with the number 365, to appear as an IT-support worker.

In addition, threat actors used fake first names, such as “IT Service Desk – Liam”, to make it appear as though the message came from a real member of the organization’s service desk.

In a small number of cases, legitimate company names were included in the sender’s tenant name to increase their credibility.

In a “significant number” of the attacks the target’s email was flooded with hundreds of newsletter or subscription confirmations within minutes, a tactic known as mail bombing.

The attackers then sent a Teams “IT support” message moments later to offer to resolve the very same problem the attacker just created.

Following the initial contact, the attackers’ next aim in most cases was to obtain hands-on-keyboard access through legitimate remote monitoring and management (RMM) tools, most frequently Quick Assist, which is built into Windows and therefore requires no installation.

When attackers seek persistence beyond the initial call, they pivot to a commercial RMM tool, such as AnyDesk and ScreenConnect.

These RMM tools can enable to attackers to execute a PowerShell payload and undertake lateral movement across the organizations network for purposes such as ransomware.

In some cases, the user was instructed to run the PowerShell command and launch the downloaded file.

Title: From industry concern to practical action: the value of working with regulators
Context: Sharing information enables organisations to learn, adapt and defend themselves against common threats before they cause further harm
Full Text:
Sharing cyber incident information quickly, whilst responding to an incident, is an important contributor to UK cyber resilience.

High-profile incidents in the retail sector highlighted the value of timely cyber incident information sharing, not just within the retail sector but with other sectors too. Organisations often rely on the same technologies, suppliers and digital supply chains, meaning an incident affecting one organisation or sector may expose similar vulnerabilities elsewhere. Sharing information enables organisations to learn, adapt and defend themselves against common threats before they cause further harm.

Organisations can share cyber incident information with the NCSC and through trusted information-sharing communities. However, information sharing often takes place under significant operational, legal and commercial pressures. For some organisations, questions about regulatory obligations can create hesitation at exactly the point where timely information may be most valuable to others.

This blog describes how industry, the NCSC and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) worked together to better understand one such challenge, and how that collaboration helped provide greater clarity for organisations seeking to share cyber incident information responsibly.

Title: Copenhagen University Breach Compromises Data on Half a Million People
Context: A cyber-attack on a leading Danish university has resulted in the compromise of sensitive personally identifiable information (PII) on over half a million individuals
Full Text:
A cyber-attack on a leading Danish university has resulted in the compromise of sensitive personally identifiable information (PII) on over half a million individuals.

The University of Copenhagen (UCPH) first revealed the news on October 23 but added an update on October 25 claiming that physical access PIN codes for around 20,0000 staff and students were also compromised.

In total, it said around 525,000 people were affected by the data breach, which occurred when hackers were able to access a test environment.

According to the university, the attack was detected on October 20 and “subsequently brought under control,” although it took three more days to issue a public notification.

Read more on university cyber-attacks: Ransomware Attacks Targeting Universities on the Rise

“The database contains personally identifiable information such as full name, national identity number, work telephone number, home telephone number and personal email address,” the original notice explained.

“The university estimates that the incident falls within the scope of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and the matter is being handled in accordance with applicable regulations. The incident has been reported to the Danish Data Protection Agency, and other relevant authorities are being kept closely informed.”

The university originally claimed that “there is no indication” that its attackers accessed systems “supporting day-to-day operations,” or that its “activities or operations” had been impacted.

However, it later admitted that several administrative systems including document management platform Workzone and application budgeting tool Nimbus were suffering disruption.

“This is a preventive and controlled shutdown of the administrative systems in question, as UCPH was exposed to a new hacker attack earlier Monday. There may be challenges accessing UCPH's websites,” it added.

On October 23, the university also restricted physical access to “selected critical locations on campus” while it reset the compromised PIN codes.

Universities Under Attack

Higher education institutions have long been a popular target for both cybercriminals and nation state actors – the former focused on stealing monetizable PII from staff and students and the latter on sensitive research and IP.

A Comparitech study from July claimed that the number of ransomware attacks against universities between January and June increased by 8% compared with the previous six months, thanks mainly to The Gentlemen group.

Extensive, decentralized and relatively open networks, a low tolerance for outages, and large user numbers make universities a popular target.

According to the most recent UK government figures published on April 30, almost every higher education institution (98%) identified a breach or attack in the previous 12 months.

The biggest incident in the sector so far this year came when ShinyHunters targeted the Canvas Learning Management System used by many universities to compromise around 275 million records from over 8000 educational institutions.

However, the breach at Copenhagen University ranks as one of the worst single incidents of its kind this year, in terms of the number of victims and the sensitivity of the data, which could be used to craft convincing follow-on phishing attacks and identity fraud attempts.

No threat actor had publicly claimed responsibility for the breach at the time of writing.

Title: First ISC2 AI Security Certification Expected for Early 2027
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
The preliminary phase of the certification benefitted from the input of 10,000 volunteer professionals worldwide through Job Task Analysis surveys.

From October 26, ISC2 is opening a pilot exam phase, giving cybersecurity professionals, employers and the global cybersecurity community insight into the domains and topics the exam is designed to assess.

The nonprofit is now looking for 3000 volunteers to enrol in a beta version of the exam in December 2026. Volunteers have until November 4 to submit their interest.

Six Key Domains to Shape the AI Security Exam

The pilot exam will assess candidates’ knowledge, skills and abilities across the following areas of professional practice needed to secure AI-enabled environments:

AI concepts and security fundamentals

AI governance, ethics, risk and compliance

AI data management, privacy and model security

Secure AI architecture, engineering and identity and access management (IAM)

Secure AI operations and incident response (IR)

AI threats, testing and lifecycle management

Each domain includes topics and subtopics to help candidates understand the AI security expertise the exam is designed to evaluate.

In a public statement, Casey Marks, COO of ISC2, said this pilot phase aims to provide “critical evidence to evaluate whether the examination measures AI security competence reliably, fairly and defensibly, which are all key facets of the rigor essential to certification integrity and to employers’ and professionals’ trust in what earning the credential represents.”

If the pilot exam phase is successful, the certification will be available to take from the first quarter of 2027, and maybe even as early as January, Beale estimated.

Eligibility Requirements for the New AI Security Certification

This new AI security credential will be available to both ISC2 members and non-members. It will be open to professionals who hold existing ISC2 credentials as well as those who do not.

It is primarily intended for professionals responsible for securing the design, deployment and maintenance of AI and machine learning (ML) systems throughout the AI lifecycle.

This includes managing cybersecurity risks associated with AI-enabled services and extending beyond technical defense to governance, ethics, risk-based guidance and enterprise collaboration.

In addition, candidates who wish to pass this certification must meet certain criteria, including having a minimum of four years of cumulative, paid full-time experience in cybersecurity or AI-related fields, with two years in cybersecurity and one year in two or more of the domains of the AI security certification exam outline.

Candidates holding active CISSP, ISSAP, ISSEP, ISSMP, CCSP or CSSLP credential may be substituted for the entire AI security certification experience requirement.

In his Security Congress opening speech, ISC2’s CEO Beale also said that AI questions are currently being “incorporated across all other ISC2 current certifications.”

“We’ve significantly increased the amount of certificates, webinars, events and professional development capabilities in the AI safety and security space over the past six months,” he told Infosecurity.

One example is the launch of the Cyber AI Workforce Coalition, announced on October 20.

Title: Watchdog Urges Police and Fire Service to Improve Cybersecurity
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
The cyber threat to UK police forces and fire and rescue services is growing rapidly and demands a more urgent response, an independent assessment has warned.

The Cybersecurity in Police Forces and Fire and Rescue Services report from His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS) was published on October 27.

It was compiled from a three-phase inspection carried out between January and May 2026, and involved dozens of interviews, “reality testing,” and scrutiny of over 260 police service and fire and rescue service documents.

“While there have been gradual improvements, many forces and services still need to urgently redouble their efforts to respond to the increased risk of cyber-attacks,” warned Michelle Skeer, His Majesty’s inspector of constabulary.

“Cybersecurity should be viewed as a core organizational priority and not solely a technical risk. Leaders need to prioritize and invest in their cybersecurity arrangements to improve their organization’s ability to prevent, detect, respond to and recover from attacks.”

Read more on threats to policing infrastructure: Government Updates UK’s National Risk Register with Cyber Warnings

The report highlighted multiple areas of weakness:

Legacy ICT systems identified as a “strategic risk” due to difficulties with patching and integration

Exposure to third-party risk, especially ICT suppliers that manage sensitive police data, and human error when using external services

Underdeveloped preparedness and resilience, including backups and incident response

Basic control issues, including access management, authentication and provisioning/deprovisioning

A lack of accountability at a senior level, with several police and fire leaders claiming cybersecurity isn’t part of daily operational decision-making

Poor coordination at a national level, leading to uneven levels of cyber maturity across the various forces and fire/rescue services

A Plan for Improvement

HMICFRS made 13 recommendations for improving the cybersecurity posture of the nation’s police forces and fire and rescue services.

These include:

Introducing baseline cybersecurity standards to improve maturity across the board (ie Cyber Assessment Framework)

Third-party assessment of cybersecurity capabilities

Improving procurement and contract management of third-party ICT suppliers (including mandatory Cyber Essentials certification)

Enhancing collaboration between government and policing cybersecurity leads

Promoting the use of the Police Digital Service’s National Management Centre, and creating a similar national capability for fire and rescue services

Improving the preparedness of services to respond to an attack (eg backup and restore and incident response exercises)

Improving learning and development for senior leaders and cybersecurity staff

“The government’s program of police reform and local government reorganization could offer both sectors opportunities to improve and better co-ordinate the approach to cybersecurity,” said Skeer. “These opportunities to strengthen cybersecurity cannot be missed. Protecting systems and data is essential to protecting the public.”
